title: Norman Conquest: William the Conqueror seizes English throne
summary: In 1066, William the Conqueror, a French bastard landing with an armed force, established himself as king of England against the consent of the natives—an origin story Paine used to demolish the divine right of kings.

citation.quote: Paine disposed of the idea of the divine right of kings by a pungent history of the British monarchy, going back to the Norman conquest of 1066, when William the Conqueror came over from France to set himself on the British throne.

title: Columbus builds Fort Navidad on Hispaniola, first European military base
summary: Columbus constructed a fort from the timbers of the stranded Santa Maria on Hispaniola, leaving 39 crew members with instructions to find and store gold.

citation.chapter: Chapter 1 – Columbus, the Indians, and Human Progress
citation.quote: On Hispaniola, out of timbers from the Santa Maria, which had run aground, Columbus built a fort, the first European military base in the Western Hemisphere. He called it Navidad (Christmas) and left thirty-nine crewmembers there, with instructions to find and store the gold.

title: Columbus sights land in the Caribbean
summary: After 33 days at sea from the Canary Islands, a sailor named Rodrigo sighted an island in the Bahamas, marking the first European contact with the Americas on this voyage.

citation.chapter: Chapter 1 – Columbus, the Indians, and Human Progress
citation.quote: It was early October 1492, and thirty-three days since he and his crew had left the Canary Islands, off the Atlantic coast of Africa... Then, on October 12, a sailor called Rodrigo saw the early morning moon shining on white sands, and cried out. It was an island in the Bahamas, the Caribbean sea.

title: Columbus's men conduct a mass slave raid on the Arawaks
summary: The Spanish rounded up 1,500 Arawak men, women, and children, selected 500 to ship to Spain. Two hundred died en route; the survivors were sold by the archdeacon.

citation.chapter: Chapter 1 – Columbus, the Indians, and Human Progress
citation.quote: In the year 1495, they went on a great slave raid, rounded up fifteen hundred Arawak men, women, and children, put them in pens guarded by Spaniards and dogs, then picked the five hundred best specimens to load onto ships. Of those five hundred, two hundred died en route.

title: First Black slaves brought to Hispaniola; governor complains of fugitives
summary: When the very first Black slaves were brought to Hispaniola in 1503, the Spanish governor complained to the Spanish court that fugitive Negro slaves were teaching disobedience to the Indians.

citation.quote: When the very first black slaves were brought into Hispaniola in 1503, the Spanish governor of Hispaniola complained to the Spanish court that fugitive Negro slaves were teaching disobedience to the Indians.

title: Las Casas arrives on Hispaniola and documents Indigenous death toll
summary: Bartolomé de las Casas arrived on Hispaniola to find 60,000 survivors, estimating that over 3 million people had perished between 1494 and 1508 from war, slavery, and mining.

citation.chapter: Chapter 1 – Columbus, the Indians, and Human Progress
citation.quote: When he arrived on Hispaniola in 1508, Las Casas says, 'there were 60,000 people living on this island, including the Indians; so that from 1494 to 1508, over three million people had perished from war, slavery, and the mines.'

title: Arawak population on Hispaniola reduced to 50,000
summary: After being worked as slave labor on encomienda estates at a ferocious pace, only about 50,000 Indigenous people remained on Hispaniola.

citation.chapter: Chapter 1 – Columbus, the Indians, and Human Progress
citation.quote: They were worked at a ferocious pace, and died by the thousands. By the year 1515, there were perhaps fifty thousand Indians left.

title: Slave revolts in Hispaniola, Puerto Rico, Santa Marta, and Panama
summary: During the 1520s and 1530s, slave revolts broke out in Hispaniola, Puerto Rico, Santa Marta, and what is now Panama, leading the Spanish to establish a special police force to chase fugitive slaves.
location: Hispaniola; Puerto Rico; Santa Marta; Panama

citation.quote: In the 1520s and 1530s, there were slave revolts in Hispaniola, Puerto Rico, Santa Marta, and what is now Panama. Shortly after those rebellions, the Spanish established a special police for chasing fugitive slaves.

title: Only 500 Arawak Indians remain on Hispaniola
summary: A century after Columbus's arrival, the original Arawak population had been reduced to just half of one thousand survivors on Hispaniola.

citation.chapter: Chapter 1 – Columbus, the Indians, and Human Progress
citation.quote: By 1550, there were five hundred.

title: Venetian secretary Ramusio writes of the kingdoms of Timbuktu and Mali
summary: In 1563, Ramusio, secretary to the rulers of Venice, wrote to Italian merchants praising the kingdoms of Timbuktu and Mali as stable, organized states worthy of trade.

citation.quote: In 1563, Ramusio, secretary to the rulers in Venice, wrote to the Italian merchants: "Let them go and do business with the King of Timbuktu and Mali and there is no doubt that they will be well-received there with their ships and their goods and treated well, and granted the favours that they ask. . . ."

title: Richard Grenville sacks and burns an Indian village in Virginia
summary: Before any permanent English settlement, Grenville landed with seven ships in Virginia. When one Indian stole a silver cup, he sacked and burned the entire village.

citation.chapter: Chapter 1 – Columbus, the Indians, and Human Progress
citation.quote: In 1585, before there was any permanent English settlement in Virginia, Richard Grenville landed there with seven ships. The Indians he met were hospitable, but when one of them stole a small silver cup, Grenville sacked and burned the whole Indian village.

title: Dutch report describes the West African kingdom of Benin
summary: A Dutch report from around 1602 described the kingdom of Benin as a great and orderly town, with streets broader than Amsterdam's and houses as well-ordered as those in Holland.

citation.quote: A Dutch report, around 1602, on the West African kingdom of Benin, said: "The Towne seemeth to be very great, when you enter it. You go into a great broad street, not paved, which seemeth to be seven or eight times broader than the Warmoes Street in Amsterdam. . . ."

title: Powhatan delivers plea for peace to English settlers
summary: In the first year of English settlement, Chief Powhatan addressed John Smith with a speech offering peace, trade, and warning of the consequences of war.

citation.chapter: Chapter 1 – Columbus, the Indians, and Human Progress
citation.quote: In that first year of the white man in Virginia, 1607, Powhatan had addressed a plea to John Smith that turned out prophetic.

title: Jamestown colonists face catastrophic starvation in the "starving time"
summary: During the winter of 1609–1610, desperate Jamestown survivors resorted to eating corpses and other extreme measures; five hundred colonists were reduced to sixty.

citation.quote: Among them were survivors from the winter of 1609–1610, the "starving time," when, crazed for want of food, they roamed the woods for nuts and berries, dug up graves to eat the corpses, and died in batches until five hundred colonists were reduced to sixty.

title: Church letter endorses legality of African slave trade
summary: On March 12, 1610, Brother Luis Brandaon wrote to Father Sandoval confirming that the Board of Conscience in Lisbon had reviewed and found no fault with the capture, transport, and enslavement of African blacks.

citation.quote: A letter dated March 12, 1610, from Brother Luis Brandaon to Father Sandoval gives the answer:

title: English colonists massacre Powhatan Indians and destroy their village
summary: After Powhatan refused to return escaped English colonists, soldiers attacked an Indian settlement, killed 15-16 people, burned houses and crops, threw children overboard, and stabbed the tribe's queen.

citation.chapter: Chapter 1 – Columbus, the Indians, and Human Progress
citation.quote: When the English were going through their 'starving time' in the winter of 1610, some of them ran off to join the Indians... When the summer came, the governor of the colony sent a messenger to ask Powhatan to return the runaways... Some soldiers were therefore sent out 'to take Revendge.' They fell upon an Indian settlement, killed fifteen or sixteen Indians, burned the houses, cut down the corn growing around the village, took the queen of the tribe and her children into boats, then ended up throwing the children overboard 'and shoteinge owtt their Braynes in the water.' The queen was later taken off and stabbed to death.

title: Virginia sends first tobacco cargo to England
summary: Virginia planters, having figured out how to grow tobacco, sent the first cargo to England in 1617, finding it highly profitable and intensifying their demand for labor.

citation.quote: They had just figured out how to grow tobacco, and in 1617 they sent off the first cargo to England.

title: First twenty enslaved Africans arrive at Jamestown, Virginia
summary: A Dutch-flagged ship arrived at the English settlement of Jamestown in the colony of Virginia, trading twenty enslaved Africans — the beginning of African slavery in North America.

citation.quote: A black American writer, J. Saunders Redding, describes the arrival of a ship in North America in the year 1619:

title: House of Burgesses established and first black slaves imported to Virginia
summary: The Virginia House of Burgesses was created as the first representative assembly in America. The same year marked the first known importation of black slaves to the colony.

citation.chapter: Chapter 3 – Persons of Mean and Vile Condition
citation.quote: In the year 1619, the Virginia House of Burgesses, born that year as the first representative assembly in America (it was also the year of the first importation of black slaves), provided for the recording and enforcing of contracts between servants and masters.

title: Ninety women shipped to Jamestown as wives for colonial settlers
summary: In the same year the first Black slaves arrived in Virginia, ninety women were transported to Jamestown and sold as wives to settlers, their price equal to the cost of their passage.

citation.quote: In 1619, the year that the first black slaves came to Virginia, ninety women arrived at Jamestown on one ship: "Agreeable persons, young and incorrupt . . . sold with their own consent to settlers as wives, the price to be the cost of their own transportation."

title: Virginia Native Americans massacre 347 English colonists
summary: Twelve years after the 1610 massacre, alarmed by growing English settlements, Native Americans launched a massacre of 347 English men, women, and children, triggering total war.

citation.chapter: Chapter 1 – Columbus, the Indians, and Human Progress
citation.quote: Twelve years later, the Indians, alarmed as the English settlements kept growing in numbers, apparently decided to try to wipe them out for good. They went on a rampage and massacred 347 men, women, and children. From then on it was total war.

title: White man Hugh Davis flogged for lying with a Negro in Virginia
summary: In 1630 a Virginia court ordered Hugh Davis to be soundly whipped for defiling his body by lying with a Negro, an early documented instance of legal punishment for interracial relations.

citation.quote: The evidence, from the court records of colonial Virginia, shows that in 1630 a white man named Hugh Davis was ordered "to be soundly whipt . . . for abusing himself . . . by defiling his body in lying with a Negro."

title: "The Lawes Resolutions of Womens Rights" codifies women's legal subordination in English law
summary: An English legal document of 1632 summarized women's status under law, describing a married woman as "covert" — veiled and subsumed into her husband's legal identity, losing all independent standing.

citation.quote: English law was summarized in a document of 1632 entitled "The Lawes Resolutions of Womens Rights":

title: Puritans launch war against the Pequot Indians
summary: The murder of a white trader provided the excuse for Puritans to wage war on the Pequots in southern Connecticut and Rhode Island, beginning with a punitive expedition against the Narragansett on Block Island.

citation.chapter: Chapter 1 – Columbus, the Indians, and Human Progress
citation.quote: The murder of a white trader, Indian-kidnaper, and troublemaker became an excuse to make war on the Pequots in 1636. A punitive expedition left Boston to attack the Narragansett Indians on Block Island, who were lumped with the Pequots.

title: Fishermen mutiny against unpaid wages near Maine coast
summary: Workmen and fishermen off the coast of Maine went on a mass mutiny when their employer withheld their wages, then deserted en masse.

citation.chapter: Chapter 3 – Persons of Mean and Vile Condition
citation.quote: As early as 1636, an employer off the coast of Maine reported that his workmen and fishermen 'fell into a mutiny' because he had withheld their wages. They deserted en masse.

title: First American slave ship Desire sails from Marblehead
summary: In 1637, the Desire, the first American slave ship, sailed from Marblehead, Massachusetts, with its hold partitioned into racks fitted with leg irons and bars.

citation.quote: Some Americans in New England entered the business, and in 1637 the first American slave ship, the Desire, sailed from Marblehead. Its holds were partitioned into racks, 2 feet by 6 feet, with leg irons and bars.

title: Massacre of the Pequot tribe in New England
summary: Six hundred men, women, and children of the Pequot tribe were massacred in New England. Zinn cites this as an example of the widespread violence against indigenous peoples largely absent from orthodox American history.

citation.quote: But who learns about the massacre of 600 men, women, and children of the Pequot tribe in New England in 1637?

title: Anne Hutchinson banished from Massachusetts Bay Colony, leads followers to Rhode Island
summary: After being tried for heresy and challenging colonial authority, Anne Hutchinson was banished from the Massachusetts Bay Colony in 1638; thirty-five families followed her to Rhode Island.

citation.quote: She was banished from the colony, and when she left for Rhode Island in 1638, thirty-five families followed her.

title: Virginia law bars Negroes from receiving arms and ammunition
summary: A Virginia law passed in 1639 decreed that all persons except Negroes were to receive arms and ammunition, formally codifying racial exclusion from self-defense.

citation.quote: A law passed in 1639 decreed that "all persons except Negroes" were to get arms and ammunition—probably to fight off Indians.

title: Virginia court sentences Black runaway John Punch to lifetime servitude
summary: In 1640, when three servants tried to run away, the two white servants had their service extended, but John Punch, a Negro, was sentenced to serve his master for the rest of his natural life — an early legal codification of lifelong racial slavery.

citation.quote: When in 1640 three servants tried to run away, the two whites were punished with a lengthening of their service. But, as the court put it, "the third being a negro named John Punch shall serve his master or his assigns for the time of his natural life."

title: First lockout in American labor history at Gloucester shipyards
summary: At the Gloucester shipyards in the 1640s, colonial authorities told a group of troublesome shipwrights they could work no longer, marking what Richard Morris calls the first lockout in American labor history.

citation.chapter: Chapter 3 – Persons of Mean and Vile Condition
citation.quote: At the Gloucester shipyards in the 1640s, what Richard Morris calls the 'first lockout in American labor history' took place when the authorities told a group of troublesome shipwrights they could not 'worke a stroke of worke more.'

title: Carpenters in Maine conduct slowdown over inadequate food
summary: Five years after the fishermen's mutiny, carpenters in Maine responded to inadequate food provisions by engaging in a work slowdown.

citation.chapter: Chapter 3 – Persons of Mean and Vile Condition
citation.quote: Five years later, carpenters in Maine, protesting against inadequate food, engaged in a slowdown.

title: English settlers arrive on Martha's Vineyard; Wampanoag population documented
summary: When the English first settled Martha's Vineyard, the local Wampanoag population was about 3,000.

citation.chapter: Chapter 1 – Columbus, the Indians, and Human Progress
citation.quote: When the English first settled Martha's Vineyard in 1642, the Wampanoags there numbered perhaps three thousand.

title: Connecticut General Court orders public punishment of indentured servant Susan C.
summary: The General Court of Connecticut in 1645 sentenced an indentured servant identified as Susan C. to hard labor, coarse diet, and weekly public correction for "rebellious carriage" toward her mistress.

citation.quote: For instance, the General Court of Connecticut in 1645 ordered that a certain "Susan C., for her rebellious carriage toward her mistress, to be sent to the house of correction and be kept to hard labor and coarse diet, to be brought forth the next lecture day to be publicly corrected, and so to be corrected weekly, until order be given to the contrary."

title: Last of the original Arawak population perishes on Hispaniola
summary: A report from 1650 records no remaining original Arawaks or descendants on the island of Hispaniola.

citation.chapter: Chapter 1 – Columbus, the Indians, and Human Progress
citation.quote: A report of the year 1650 shows none of the original Arawaks or their descendants left on the island.

title: Porters and carters strike in New York City
summary: Porters refused to carry salt, and truckers, teamsters, and carriers went on strike. They were prosecuted by New York City authorities for not performing their duties.

citation.chapter: Chapter 3 – Persons of Mean and Vile Condition
citation.quote: Porters in the 1650s in New York refused to carry salt, and carters (truckers, teamsters, carriers) who went out on strike were prosecuted in New York City 'for not obeying the Command and Doing their Dutyes as becomes them in their Places.'

title: Mary Dyer hanged in Massachusetts Bay Colony for Quaker "rebellion"
summary: Twenty years after Anne Hutchinson's banishment, Mary Dyer — the one person who had defended Hutchinson at her trial — was hanged by the Massachusetts Bay government along with two other Quakers for rebellion and sedition.

citation.quote: Twenty years later, the one person back in Massachusetts Bay who had spoken up for her during her trial, Mary Dyer, was hanged by the government of the colony, along with two other Quakers, for "rebellion, sedition, and presumptuous obtruding themselves."

title: Maryland servant strikes against inadequate food
summary: Servants in Maryland went on strike over starvation-level rations, refusing to work because they were fed only beans and bread and felt too weak to labor. The court sentenced them to thirty lashes each.

citation.chapter: Chapter 3 – Persons of Mean and Vile Condition
citation.quote: One Maryland master complained to the Provincial Court in 1663 that his servants did 'peremptorily and positively refuse to goe and doe their ordinary labor.' The servants responded that they were fed only 'Beanes and Bread' and they were 'soe weake, wee are not able to perform the imploym'ts hee puts us uppon.' They were given thirty lashes by the court.

title: Virginia law penalizes white servants who run away with Negroes
summary: In 1661, Virginia passed a law requiring any English servant who ran away in company with Negroes to serve extra years for the master of the runaway Negro, reinforcing racial separation.

citation.quote: In 1661 a law was passed in Virginia that "in case any English servant shall run away in company of any Negroes" he would have to give special service for extra years to the master of the runaway Negro.

title: Isaac Friend proposes servant uprising in York County, Virginia
summary: Indentured servant Isaac Friend proposed gathering forty servants armed with guns to fight for freedom throughout the colony, declaring they would either be free or die for it.

citation.chapter: Chapter 3 – Persons of Mean and Vile Condition
citation.quote: In York County, Virginia, in 1661, a servant named Isaac Friend proposed to another, after much dissatisfaction with the food, that they 'get a matter of Forty of them together, and get Gunnes & hee would be the first & lead them and cry as they went along, 'who would be for Liberty, and free from bondage'.'

title: Block Island Indian population documented at 1,200-1,500
summary: Block Island Indians numbered between 1,200 and 1,500 in 1662; by 1774 disease had reduced them to just 51.

citation.chapter: Chapter 1 – Columbus, the Indians, and Human Progress
citation.quote: Similarly, Block Island Indians numbered perhaps 1,200 to 1,500 in 1662, and by 1774 were reduced to fifty-one.

title: White indentured servants and Black slaves form rebellion conspiracy in Virginia
summary: As early as 1663, indentured white servants and Black slaves in Gloucester County, Virginia, formed a joint conspiracy to rebel and gain their freedom; the plot was betrayed and ended with executions.

citation.quote: As early as 1663, indentured white servants and black slaves in Gloucester County, Virginia, formed a conspiracy to rebel and gain their freedom. The plot was betrayed, and ended with executions.

title: Servants' general uprising plot in Gloucester County suppressed
summary: Two years after Isaac Friend's plot, indentured servants in Gloucester County again planned a general uprising. One conspirator gave up the others, and four were executed.

citation.chapter: Chapter 3 – Persons of Mean and Vile Condition
citation.quote: The scheme was never carried out, but two years later, in Gloucester County, servants again planned a general uprising. One of them gave the plot away, and four were executed.

title: New England couple accused of servant death after mistress cut off servant's toes
summary: A New England court accused a master and mistress of causing a servant's death after the mistress had cut off the servant's toes. Despite the severity, the jury voted to acquit.

citation.chapter: Chapter 3 – Persons of Mean and Vile Condition
citation.quote: In 1666, a New England court accused a couple of the death of a servant after the mistress had cut off the servant's toes. The jury voted acquittal.

title: Virginia statute references slave "obstinacy"
summary: A Virginia statute of 1669 acknowledged the resistance of enslaved people by referring to "the obstinacy of many of them."

citation.quote: A Virginia statute of 1669 referred to "the obstinacy of many of them," and in 1680 the Assembly took note of slave meetings "under the pretense of feasts and brawls" which they considered of "dangerous consequence."

title: King Philip's War ends with Wampanoag defeat
summary: Forty years after the Pequot War, Metacom (King Philip) led the Wampanoags against the English. When the war ended in 1676, 600 English and 3,000 Indians were dead, including Metacom.

citation.chapter: Chapter 1 – Columbus, the Indians, and Human Progress
citation.quote: When it was over, in 1676, the English had won, but their resources were drained; they had lost six hundred men. Three thousand Indians were dead, including Metacom himself.

title: Bacon's Rebellion in Virginia
summary: White frontiersmen, enslaved people, and servants joined in a rebellion against the Virginia colonial government, forcing Governor Berkeley to flee Jamestown as the capital burned. England sent a thousand soldiers across the Atlantic to suppress the uprising.

citation.chapter: Chapter 3 – Persons of Mean and Vile Condition
citation.quote: In 1676, seventy years after Virginia was founded, a hundred years before it supplied leadership for the American Revolution, that colony faced a rebellion of white frontiersmen, joined by slaves and servants, a rebellion so threatening that the governor had to flee the burning capital of Jamestown, and England decided to send a thousand soldiers across the Atlantic, hoping to maintain order among forty thousand colonists.

title: Bacon issues Declaration of the People
summary: Nathaniel Bacon published a declaration indicting Governor Berkeley's administration for unjust taxes, political favoritism, monopolizing the beaver trade, and failing to protect western farmers from Indian attacks.

citation.chapter: Chapter 3 – Persons of Mean and Vile Condition
citation.quote: Bacon's 'Declaration of the People' of July 1676 shows a mixture of populist resentment against the rich and frontier hatred of the Indians. It indicted the Berkeley administration for unjust taxes, for putting favorites in high positions, for monopolizing the beaver trade, and for not protecting the western farmers from the Indians.

title: Nathaniel Bacon dies and Virginia rebellion suppressed
summary: Bacon died of illness at age twenty-nine. Captain Thomas Grantham used his armed ship as a base to disarm the remaining rebel garrisons, and twenty-three rebel leaders were subsequently hanged.

citation.chapter: Chapter 3 – Persons of Mean and Vile Condition
citation.quote: In the fall, Bacon, aged twenty-nine, fell sick and died, because of, as a contemporary put it, 'swarmes of Vermyn that bred in his body.' ... A ship armed with thirty guns, cruising the York River, became the base for securing order, and its captain, Thomas Grantham, used force and deception to disarm the last rebel forces. ... Twenty-three rebel leaders were hanged.

title: Virginia Assembly warns of dangerous slave gatherings
summary: In 1680 the Virginia Assembly took note of slave meetings held under the pretense of feasts and brawls, declaring them of dangerous consequence and moving to suppress them.

citation.quote: in 1680 the Assembly took note of slave meetings "under the pretense of feasts and brawls" which they considered of "dangerous consequence."

title: Slave plot to kill all whites discovered in Virginia's Northern Neck
summary: In 1687, a plot was discovered in Virginia's Northern Neck in which slaves had planned to kill all the whites in the area and escape during a mass funeral.

citation.quote: In 1687, in the colony's Northern Neck, a plot was discovered in which slaves planned to kill all the whites in the area and escape during a mass funeral.

title: John Locke publishes Second Treatise on Government
summary: In 1689, John Locke published his Second Treatise on Government during the English rebellion against tyrannical kings, articulating a theory of popular sovereignty that would later underpin the American Declaration of Independence.

citation.quote: The philosophy of the Declaration, that government is set up by the people to secure their life, liberty, and happiness, and is to be overthrown when it no longer does that, is often traced to the ideas of John Locke, in his Second Treatise on Government. That was published in England in 1689, when the English were rebelling against tyrannical kings and setting up parliamentary government.

title: Virginia bans intermarriage between whites and Negroes, mulattos, or Indians
summary: In 1691 Virginia provided for the banishment of any free white man or woman who intermarried with a Negro, mulatto, or Indian, legally entrenching racial separation.

citation.quote: In 1691, Virginia provided for the banishment of any "white man or woman being free who shall intermarry with a negro, mulatoo, or Indian man or woman bond or free."

title: Petition to House of Commons urging more white servants to colonies
summary: Merchants, shipmasters, and planters petitioned the British House of Commons, arguing that colonies needed more white servants to keep black slaves in subjection and to bear arms against invasion.

citation.chapter: Chapter 3 – Persons of Mean and Vile Condition
citation.quote: In 1691, the House of Commons received 'a petition of divers merchants, masters of ships, planters and others, trading to foreign plantations ... setting forth, that the plantations cannot be maintained without a considerable number of white servants, as well to keep the blacks in subjection, as to bear arms in case of invasion.'

title: Virginia has 6,000 slaves, one-twelfth of the population
summary: By 1700, Virginia had 6,000 slaves, representing one-twelfth of the colony's total population, as slavery expanded with the plantation system.

citation.quote: By 1700, in Virginia, there were 6,000 slaves, one-twelfth of the population.

title: Colonial trade with Britain valued at 500,000 pounds
summary: In 1700 colonial trade with Britain amounted to about 500,000 pounds, growing to 2,800,000 pounds by 1770, making the colonies increasingly valuable to the British economy.

citation.quote: the colonial trade had become more and more important to the British economy, and more profitable: it had amounted to about 500,000 pounds in 1700 but by 1770 was worth 2,800,000 pounds.

title: Virginia Code of 1705 provides for dismemberment of slaves
summary: The Virginia Code of 1705 legally authorized dismemberment as a punishment for enslaved people, part of an elaborate system of physical and psychological control.

citation.quote: Dismemberment was provided for in the Virginia Code of 1705.

title: Virginia passes law granting benefits to newly freed white servants
summary: In 1705, Virginia passed a law requiring masters to provide freed white indentured servants with corn, money, a gun, and 50 acres of land, helping secure poor white allegiance against slave rebellion.

citation.quote: In 1705 a law was passed requiring masters to provide white servants whose indenture time was up with ten bushels of corn, thirty shillings, and a gun, while women servants were to get 15 bushels of corn and forty shillings. Also, the newly freed servants were to get 50 acres of land.

title: Virginia Governor Spotswood warns Assembly of slave insurrection threat
summary: In 1710, Governor Alexander Spotswood warned the Virginia Assembly that the promise of freedom could call together all who longed to shake off slavery, urging preventive legislation and better defenses.

citation.quote: In 1710, warning the Virginia Assembly, Governor Alexander Spotswood said:

title: First large-scale slave revolt in North American colonies erupts in New York
summary: In 1712, about twenty-five Blacks and two Indians set fire to a building in New York and killed nine whites; soldiers captured them and twenty-one were executed by burning, hanging, breaking on the wheel, and other methods.

citation.quote: The first large-scale revolt in the North American colonies took place in New York in 1712. In New York, slaves were 10 percent of the population, the highest proportion in the northern states, where economic conditions usually did not require large numbers of field slaves. About twenty-five blacks and two Indians set fire to a building, then killed nine whites who came on the scene.

title: Joint African-Indian insurrection in New York suppressed
summary: Enslaved Africans and Native Americans joined in an insurrection in New York, which had the largest slave population in the North. The uprising was quickly put down by colonial authorities.

citation.chapter: Chapter 3 – Persons of Mean and Vile Condition
citation.quote: New York had the largest slave population in the North, and there was some contact between blacks and Indians, as in 1712 when Africans and Indians joined in an insurrection. But this was quickly suppressed.

title: Bread riot in Boston; lieutenant governor shot
summary: A severe food shortage in Boston led to a riot on the Boston Common, where around two hundred people attacked merchant Andrew Belcher's ships and warehouses looking for corn, and shot the lieutenant governor when he intervened.

citation.chapter: Chapter 3 – Persons of Mean and Vile Condition
citation.quote: A severe food shortage in Boston in 1713 brought a warning from town selectmen to the General Assembly of Massachusetts saying the 'threatening scarcity of provisions' had led to such 'extravagant prices that the necessities of the poor in the approaching winter must needs be very pressing.' ... On May 19, two hundred people rioted on the Boston Common. They attacked Belcher's ships, broke into his warehouses looking for corn, and shot the lieutenant governor when he tried to interfere.

title: British Parliament legalizes convict transportation to New World
summary: Parliament made transportation to the New World a legal punishment for crime, resulting in tens of thousands of convicts being sent to Virginia, Maryland, and other colonies.

citation.chapter: Chapter 3 – Persons of Mean and Vile Condition
citation.quote: This fear may help explain why Parliament, in 1717, made transportation to the New World a legal punishment for crime. After that, tens of thousands of convicts could be sent to Virginia, Maryland, and other colonies.

title: Slave conspiracy to destroy whites and seize Charleston exposed in South Carolina
summary: A 1720 letter from South Carolina to London reported a plot by Negroes to kill all the white people and then take Charles Town, which was discovered and suppressed with burning, hanging, and banishment.

citation.quote: A letter to London from South Carolina in 1720 reports:

title: New York City population stands at 7,000
summary: In 1720 the population of New York City was 7,000, a figure cited to contrast with the 25,000 residents present when the French and Indian War ended, illustrating the city's rapid growth and attendant social pressures.

citation.quote: There were 25,000 people living in New York (there had been 7,000 in 1720) when the French and Indian War ended.

title: English report warns slave revolt nearly succeeded in South Carolina
summary: A report to the English government noted that black slaves had nearly succeeded in overthrowing South Carolina, and recommended recruiting more white servants. The colony's militia numbered only 2,000, deemed insufficient against the threat.

citation.chapter: Chapter 3 – Persons of Mean and Vile Condition
citation.quote: A report to the English government in 1721 said that in South Carolina 'black slaves have lately attempted and were very near succeeding in a new revolution ... and therefore, it may be necessary ... to propose some new law for encouraging the entertainment of more white servants in the future. The militia of this province does not consist of above 2000 men.'

title: Maryland law authorizes cutting off ears of Blacks who strike whites
summary: Maryland passed a law in 1723 providing for cutting off the ears of Blacks who struck whites, and for hanging and quartering the body for certain serious crimes.

citation.quote: Maryland passed a law in 1723 providing for cutting off the ears of blacks who struck whites, and that for certain serious crimes, slaves should be hanged and the body quartered and exposed.

title: Virginia lieutenant governor reports armed group of Blacks seeking freedom in mountains
summary: A 1729 report from the lieutenant governor of Virginia to the British Board of Trade described about fifteen Negroes who had formed a plan to flee their master and establish themselves in the neighboring mountains, having armed and provisioned themselves.

citation.quote: In the colonial papers of England, a 1729 report from the lieutenant governor of Virginia to the British Board of Trade tells how "a number of Negroes, about fifteen . . . formed a design to withdraw from their Master and to fix themselves in the fastnesses of the neighboring Mountains."

title: Dock Square public market demolished in anti-merchant protest in Boston
summary: Boston protesters demolished the public market in Dock Square while complaining about high merchant prices and the government. When arrests were threatened, demonstrators warned five hundred more would come to destroy other markets.

citation.chapter: Chapter 3 – Persons of Mean and Vile Condition
citation.quote: In the 1730s, in Boston, people protesting the high prices established by merchants demolished the public market in Dock Square while (as a conservative writer complained) 'murmuring against the Government & the rich people.' No one was arrested, after the demonstrators warned that arrests would bring 'Five Hundred Men in Solemn League and Covenent.'

title: Anti-impressment riot in Boston against forced naval conscription
summary: Bostonians rioted against impressment—the forced drafting of men into naval service. They surrounded the governor's house, beat the sheriff, locked up a deputy sheriff, and stormed the town house where the General Court sat.

citation.chapter: Chapter 3 – Persons of Mean and Vile Condition
citation.quote: They surrounded the house of the governor, beat up the sheriff, locked up a deputy sheriff, and stormed the town house where the General Court sat. The militia did not respond when called to put them down, and the governor fled. The crowd was condemned by a merchants' group as a 'Riotous Tumultuous Assembly of Foreign Seamen, Servants, Negroes, and Other Persons of Mean and Vile Condition.'

title: William Byrd writes of fear of slave insurrection in Virginia
summary: In 1736, Virginia slaveowner William Byrd wrote expressing alarm that over 10,000 armed men of African descent could be rallied by a man of desperate fortune to spark a servile war.

citation.quote: William Byrd, a wealthy Virginia slaveowner, wrote in 1736:

title: Over 1,279 runaway slave advertisements placed in Virginia newspapers
summary: Gerald Mullin found newspaper advertisements between 1736 and 1801 for 1,138 men runaways and 141 women, documenting the persistent resistance of enslaved people in Virginia.

citation.quote: Mullin found newspaper advertisements between 1736 and 1801 for 1,138 men runaways, and 141 women.

title: Stono Rebellion: slaves revolt in South Carolina, march toward freedom
summary: At Stono, South Carolina in 1739, about twenty slaves killed two warehouse guards, seized arms, and marched south, growing to perhaps eighty, with drums beating and crying "Liberty," before the militia crushed the uprising killing roughly fifty slaves and twenty-five whites.

citation.quote: At Stono, South Carolina, in 1739, about twenty slaves rebelled, killed two warehouse guards, stole guns and gunpowder, and headed south, killing people in their way, and burning buildings.

title: Slave uprising at Stono, South Carolina
summary: A slave uprising at Stono left South Carolina insecure and forced its militia to focus on keeping slaves under control rather than fighting the British.

citation.quote: South Carolina, insecure since the slave uprising in Stono in 1739, could hardly fight against the British; her militia had to be used to keep slaves under control.

title: Child hanged in England for stealing a rag of cotton
summary: Zinn notes that as late as 1740 in England, where private property law was ascendant, a child could be hanged for stealing a rag of cotton — contrasting the brutality of European law with African communal justice.

citation.quote: In England, even as late as 1740, a child could be hanged for stealing a rag of cotton.

title: New Jersey land dispute riots; Samuel Baldwin freed from Newark jail
summary: Poor farmers occupying disputed land rioted over rent demands. When Samuel Baldwin, who held an Indian title to his land, was jailed for nonpayment, the local population stormed the Newark prison to free him and others, with soldiers refusing to intervene.

citation.chapter: Chapter 3 – Persons of Mean and Vile Condition
citation.quote: In 1745, Samuel Baldwin, who had long lived on his land and who held an Indian title to it, was arrested for nonpayment of rent to the proprietor and taken to the Newark jail. A contemporary described what happened then: 'The People in general, supposing the Design of the Proprietors was to ruin them ... went to the Prison, opened the Door, took out Baldwin.'

title: Newark jail storm after Baldwin's defenders are arrested
summary: When two men who rescued Baldwin were imprisoned, hundreds of citizens gathered around the Newark jail. Militia refused to defend it, and the crowd broke it open with axes, freeing the prisoners. The New Jersey government reported the unrest to the Lords of Trade in London.

citation.chapter: Chapter 3 – Persons of Mean and Vile Condition
citation.quote: A report sent by the New Jersey government to the Lords of Trade in London described the scene: 'The multitude ... between four and five of the clock in the afternoon lighted off their horses, and came towards the gaol, huzzaing and swinging their clubbs ... till they came within reach of the guard, struck them with their clubbs ... They then, with axes and other instruments, broke open the prison door, and took out the two prisoners.'

title: Tenant riots in New Jersey
summary: In the 1740s, tenant farmers in New Jersey staged riots that were part of long-lasting organized social movements aimed at wealthy landlords, including breaking into jails to free imprisoned associates.

citation.quote: The tenant riots in New Jersey in the 1740s, the New York tenant uprisings of the 1750s and 1760s in the Hudson Valley, and the rebellion in northeastern New York that led to the carving of Vermont out of New York State were all more than sporadic rioting.

title: New York slave conspiracy trial ends with mass executions of Blacks and whites
summary: In 1741, after mysterious fires in New York, a mass hysteria trial based on informers and forced confessions resulted in the execution of two white men, two white women, eighteen slaves hanged, and thirteen slaves burned alive.

citation.quote: In New York in 1741, there were ten thousand whites in the city and two thousand black slaves. It had been a hard winter and the poor—slave and free—had suffered greatly. When mysterious fires broke out, blacks and whites were accused of conspiring together.

title: Ship Sea-Flower departs Belfast after sixteen-week Atlantic voyage of horror
summary: The sloop Sea-Flower arrived in Boston after a harrowing sixteen-week voyage from Belfast, with forty-six of its 106 passengers dead of starvation and survivors resorting to cannibalism.

citation.chapter: Chapter 3 – Persons of Mean and Vile Condition
citation.quote: The voyage to America lasted eight, tén, or twelve weeks, and the servants were packed into ships with the same fanatic concern for profits that marked the slave ships. The sloop Sea-Flower, leaving Belfast in 1741, was at sea sixteen weeks, and when it arrived in Boston, forty-six of its 106 passengers were dead of starvation, six of them eaten by the survivors.

title: Seven slaves executed in Maryland for murdering their master
summary: In 1742, seven slaves in Maryland were put to death for murdering their master, illustrating the violent resistance that persisted despite harsh punishments.

citation.quote: In 1742, seven slaves were put to death for murdering their master.

title: Charleston grand jury condemns interracial sexual relations
summary: A grand jury in Charleston, South Carolina, denounced the common practice of white men having sexual relations with enslaved women, part of broader efforts to control interracial relationships through law.

citation.chapter: Chapter 3 – Persons of Mean and Vile Condition
citation.quote: In 1743, a grand jury in Charleston, South Carolina, denounced 'The Too Common Practice of Criminal Conversation with Negro and other Slave Wenches in this Province.' Mixed offspring continued to be produced by white-black sex relations throughout the colonial period, in spite of laws prohibiting interracial marriage.

title: Anti-impressment riot leads to burning of Thomas Hutchinson's house in Boston
summary: Crowds rioted against forced naval conscription, then turned on wealthy merchant Thomas Hutchinson, who had backed the governor in suppressing earlier riots and designed a currency plan against the poor. His house burned down mysteriously while a crowd shouted 'Let it burn!'

citation.chapter: Chapter 3 – Persons of Mean and Vile Condition
citation.quote: The forced service of seamen led to a riot against impressment in Boston in 1747. Then crowds turned against Thomas Hutchinson, a rich merchant and colonial official who had backed the governor in putting down the riot, and who also designed a currency plan for Massachusetts which seemed to discriminate against the poor. Hutchinson's house burned down, mysteriously, and a crowd gathered in the street, cursing Hutchinson and shouting, 'Let it burn!'

title: Colonial periodical publishes Benjamin Franklin's fictional "Speech of Miss Polly Baker"
summary: A colonial periodical of 1747 reprinted Benjamin Franklin's satirical fictional speech in which "Polly Baker" defends herself before a Connecticut court for the fifth time on charges of bearing a child out of wedlock.

citation.quote: A colonial periodical of 1747 reproduced a speech "of Miss Polly Baker before a Court of Judicature, at Connecticut near Boston in New England; where she was prosecuted the fifth time for having a Bastard Child." (The speech was Benjamin Franklin's ironic invention.)

title: Indentured servants advertised for sale in Virginia Gazette
summary: An advertisement in the Virginia Gazette announced the sale of about one hundred indentured servants—men, women, and boys—arriving on the ship Justitia at Leedstown.

citation.chapter: Chapter 3 – Persons of Mean and Vile Condition
citation.quote: An announcement in the Virginia Gazette, March 28, 1771, read: 'Just arrived at Leedstown, the Ship Justitia, with about one Hundred Healthy Servants, Men Women & Boys.'

title: Slaves constitute one-third of Maryland's population
summary: By 1750, slaves made up approximately one-third of Maryland's population, where slavery had been written into law since the 1660s.

citation.quote: In Maryland, where slaves were about one-third of the population in 1750, slavery had been written into law since the 1660s, and statutes for controlling rebellious slaves were passed.

title: Wealthiest urban colonists leaving estates of 20,000 pounds
summary: By 1750, court-recorded wills showed that the wealthiest people in colonial cities were leaving estates of 20,000 pounds (equivalent to about $5 million), reflecting extreme concentration of wealth.

citation.quote: Court-recorded wills showed that by 1750 the wealthiest people in the cities were leaving 20,000 pounds (equivalent to about $5 million today).

title: New York tenant uprisings in the Hudson Valley
summary: During the 1750s and 1760s, tenant farmers in the Hudson Valley staged organized uprisings against wealthy landlords, rescuing prisoners from sheriffs and at one point taking the sheriff of Albany County himself captive.

citation.quote: The tenant riots in New Jersey in the 1740s, the New York tenant uprisings of the 1750s and 1760s in the Hudson Valley, and the rebellion in northeastern New York that led to the carving of Vermont out of New York State were all more than sporadic rioting.

title: Four hundred political pamphlets published on colonial controversies
summary: From 1750 to 1776, four hundred pamphlets appeared arguing various sides of the Stamp Act, Boston Massacre, Tea Party, and broader questions of disobedience, loyalty, and rights, making pamphleteering the chief theater of colonial political debate.

citation.quote: From 1750 to 1776 four hundred pamphlets had appeared arguing one or another side of the Stamp Act or the Boston Massacre or the Tea Party or the general questions of disobedience to law, loyalty to government, rights and obligations.

title: Mohawk Chief Hendrick denounces broken Covenant Chain to New York governor
summary: Chief Hendrick of the Mohawks spoke bitterly to Governor George Clinton of New York in 1753, declaring the Covenant Chain between his people and the colonists broken over land grievances.

citation.quote: Chief Hendrick of the Mohawks is recorded speaking his bitterness to Governor George Clinton and the provincial council of New York in 1753...

title: White servants still comprise 10 percent of Maryland population
summary: Despite the growing dominance of black slavery, indentured white servants continued to make up a significant minority—10 percent—of Maryland's population as late as 1755.

citation.chapter: Chapter 3 – Persons of Mean and Vile Condition
citation.quote: More than half the colonists who came to the North American shores in the colonial period came as servants. They were mostly English in the seventeenth century, Irish and German in the eighteenth century. ... but as late as 1755, white servants made up 10 percent of the population of Maryland.

title: Massachusetts legislature declares Penobscot Indians rebels and offers scalp bounties
summary: On November 3, 1755, the Massachusetts legislature proclaimed the Penobscot Indians "rebels, enemies and traitors" and offered a bounty of forty pounds for each male scalp and twenty pounds for female or child scalps.

citation.quote: Twenty years before the Declaration, a proclamation of the legislature of Massachusetts of November 3, 1755, declared the Penobscot Indians "rebels, enemies and traitors" and provided a bounty: "For every scalp of a male Indian brought in . . . forty pounds. For every scalp of such female Indian or male Indian under the age of twelve years that shall be killed . . . twenty pounds. . . ."

title: Indentured servant Elizabeth Sprigs writes harrowing letter describing her servitude
summary: In 1756 Elizabeth Sprigs wrote to her father in England describing brutal conditions as an indentured servant in America, including whippings, near starvation, and sleeping on the ground.

citation.quote: In 1756, Elizabeth Sprigs wrote to her father about her servitude:

title: Eighteen colonial uprisings and six black rebellions recorded by 1760
summary: By 1760, starting with Bacon's Rebellion in Virginia, there had been eighteen uprisings aimed at overthrowing colonial governments, six black rebellions from South Carolina to New York, and forty riots of various origins.

citation.quote: Starting with Bacon's Rebellion in Virginia, by 1760, there had been eighteen uprisings aimed at overthrowing colonial governments. There had also been six black rebellions, from South Carolina to New York, and forty riots of various origins.

title: Regulators in Orange County organize to prevent tax collection
summary: In the 1760s, Regulators in Orange County, North Carolina organized to prevent the collection of taxes and confiscation of property, prompting officials to declare an "absolute Insurrection" and make military plans to suppress it.

citation.quote: In that county in the 1760s, the Regulators organized to prevent the collection of taxes, or the confiscation of the property of tax delinquents.

title: Impressment riots in New York and Newport, Rhode Island
summary: Through the 1760s, impressment riots broke out in New York and Newport, Rhode Island, where five hundred seamen, boys, and Negroes rioted after five weeks of British impressment.

citation.quote: There had been impressment riots through the 1760s in New York and in Newport, Rhode Island, where five hundred seamen, boys, and Negroes rioted after five weeks of impressment by the British.

title: James Otis rallies Boston mechanics against conservative colonial rulers
summary: In 1762, James Otis spoke against the conservative Massachusetts rulers represented by Thomas Hutchinson, using class-charged rhetoric to mobilize city mechanics and artisans against the entrenched colonial elite.

citation.quote: In 1762, Otis, speaking against the conservative rulers of the Massachusetts colony represented by Thomas Hutchinson, gave an example of the kind of rhetoric that a lawyer could use in mobilizing city mechanics and artisans.

title: Virginia has 170,000 slaves, about half the population
summary: By 1763, Virginia's enslaved population had grown to 170,000, representing approximately half the colony's total population.

citation.quote: By 1763, there were 170,000 slaves, about half the population.

title: British Proclamation of 1763 bars colonists from settling beyond Appalachians
summary: After England's victory over France in the Seven Years' War, the British government issued the Proclamation of 1763, declaring Indian lands beyond the Appalachians off-limits to white settlers, removing a key restraint on colonial ambitions once French power was gone.

citation.quote: After 1763, with England victorious over France in the Seven Years' War (known in America as the French and Indian War), expelling them from North America, ambitious colonial leaders were no longer threatened by the French. The British, wooing the Indians, had declared Indian lands beyond the Appalachians out of bounds to whites (the Proclamation of 1763).

title: Boston Gazette publishes critique of ruling class keeping people poor
summary: In 1763, an anonymous writer in the Boston Gazette accused a few persons in power of promoting projects "for keeping the people poor in order to make them humble," reflecting growing class anger in the city.

citation.quote: In 1763, in the Boston Gazette, someone wrote that "a few persons in power" were promoting political projects "for keeping the people poor in order to make them humble."

title: France cedes lands west of the Appalachians to Britain; Indians unite in war
summary: When the Seven Years' War ended in 1763, France ceded Indian-allied lands to Britain, prompting the Indians to unite and make war on British western forts in what the British called 'Pontiac's Conspiracy.'

citation.quote: When that war ended in 1763, the French, ignoring their old allies, ceded to the British lands west of the Appalachians. The Indians therefore united to make war on the British western forts; this is called "Pontiac's Conspiracy" by the British, but "a liberation war for independence" in the words used by Francis Jennings.

title: Royal Proclamation of 1763 establishes Appalachian boundary for settlers
summary: The Royal Proclamation of 1763 established a line at the Appalachians beyond which colonial settlements were not to encroach on Indian territory, angering American colonists.

citation.quote: A peace was made, with the British agreeing to establish a line at the Appalachians, beyond which settlements would not encroach on Indian territory. This was the Royal Proclamation of 1763, and it angered Americans...

title: Wampanoag population on Martha's Vineyard collapse to 313
summary: Despite no warfare on Martha's Vineyard, disease alone reduced the Wampanoag population from 3,000 in 1642 to just 313 by 1764.

citation.chapter: Chapter 1 – Columbus, the Indians, and Human Progress
citation.quote: There were no wars on that island, but by 1764, only 313 Indians were left there.

title: South Carolina prohibits enlisting enslaved people as mechanics in Charleston
summary: The South Carolina legislature passed a law prohibited Charleston masters from employing enslaved people as mechanics or in handicraft trades, protecting white craftsmen from black competition.

citation.chapter: Chapter 3 – Persons of Mean and Vile Condition
citation.quote: In the southern towns too, white craftsmen and traders were protected from Negro competition. In 1764 the South Carolina legislature prohibited Charleston masters from employing Negros or other slaves as mechanics or in handicraft trades.

title: Stamp Act of 1765 triggers mob attacks on Boston elite homes
summary: After the British Stamp Act of 1765, a shoemaker named Ebenezer MacIntosh led a mob that destroyed a merchant's house, and two weeks later a crowd demolished the home of Thomas Hutchinson, symbol of the ruling colonial elite.

citation.quote: This accumulated sense of grievance against the rich in Boston may account for the explosiveness of mob action after the Stamp Act of 1765. Through this Act, the British were taxing the colonial population to pay for the French war, in which colonists had suffered to expand the British Empire. That summer, a shoemaker named Ebenezer MacIntosh led a mob in destroying the house of a rich Boston merchant named Andrew Oliver.

title: Loyal Nine organizes Stamp Act procession in Boston
summary: In August 1765, the Loyal Nine—merchants, distillers, shipowners, and master craftsmen—organized a procession of two to three thousand people to protest the Stamp Act, but lost control when the crowd went beyond the planned demonstration and damaged the stampmaster's property.

citation.quote: A political group in Boston called the Loyal Nine—merchants, distillers, shipowners, and master craftsmen who opposed the Stamp Act—organized a procession in August 1765 to protest it.

title: Stamp Act takes effect; demonstrations planned and controlled
summary: As the Stamp Act was set to take effect on November 1, 1765, Boston leaders planned demonstrations but took steps to keep crowds under control, including hosting a dinner for riot leaders to co-opt them.

citation.quote: As more demonstrations were planned for November 1, 1765, when the Stamp Act was to go into effect, and for Pope's Day, November 5, steps were taken to keep things under control; a dinner was given for certain leaders of the rioters to win them over.

title: New York rebel leader trial exposes class injustice in land disputes
summary: At a rebel leader's trial in New York in 1766, a witness testified that evicted farmers had equitable title to their land but could not be defended in court because they were poor, laying bare the class bias of the legal system.

citation.quote: A witness at a rebel leader's trial in New York in 1766 said that the farmers evicted by the landlords "had an equitable Title but could not be defended in a Course of Law because they were poor and . . . poor men were always oppressed by the rich."

title: North Carolina Regulator movement organizes white farmers against corrupt officials
summary: From 1766 to 1771, class-conscious white farmers in western North Carolina organized the Regulator movement to democratize local government and resist wealthy, corrupt officials who exploited them through taxation and the courts.

citation.quote: In North Carolina, a powerful movement of white farmers was organized against wealthy and corrupt officials in the period from 1766 to 1771, exactly those years when, in the cities of the Northeast, agitation was growing against the British, crowding out class issues.

title: Tenant risings against feudal estates in Dutchess County, New York
summary: In 1766, tenants rose up against the huge feudal estates in New York, including the million-acre Rensselaerwyck holding; in Poughkeepsie, 1,700 armed tenants closed courts and broke open jails before the uprising was crushed.

citation.quote: There were tenant risings in 1766 against the huge feudal estates in New York. The Rensselaerwyck holding was a million acres. Tenants, claiming some of this land for themselves, unable to get satisfaction in the courts, turned to violence. In Poughkeepsie, 1,700 armed tenants had closed the courts and broken open the jails. But the uprising was crushed.

title: Stamp Act riots sweep Boston; General Gage analyzes mob dynamics
summary: When riots against the Stamp Act swept Boston in 1767, British commander General Thomas Gage observed that the mob had been initially incited by leading inhabitants but soon acted on its own, alarming even those who had set it in motion.

citation.quote: When riots against the Stamp Act swept Boston in 1767, they were analyzed by the commander of the British forces in North America, General Thomas Gage.

title: Regulators petition North Carolina government over class grievances
summary: In 1768, the Regulators petitioned the North Carolina government citing "the unequal chances the poor and the weak have in contentions with the rich and powerful," articulating a class-based critique of colonial governance.

citation.quote: The Regulators petitioned the government on their grievances in 1768, citing "the unequal chances the poor and the weak have in contentions with the rich and powerful."

title: Two thousand British soldiers quartered in Boston
summary: After 1768, two thousand British soldiers were quartered in Boston, creating friction with working people as soldiers competed for scarce jobs and merchants lost business due to boycotts.

citation.quote: After 1768, two thousand soldiers were quartered in Boston, and friction grew between the crowds and the soldiers.

title: England racked by riots and strikes over bread prices and wages
summary: In 1768, England experienced widespread riots and strikes by coal heavers, saw mill workers, hatters, weavers, and sailors protesting high bread prices and miserable wages, demonstrating the class conflicts underlying Locke's liberal democratic theory.

citation.quote: At the very time the American scene was becoming tense, in 1768, England was racked by riots and strikes—of coal heavers, saw mill workers, hatters, weavers, sailors—because of the high price of bread and the miserable wages.

title: Boston sets up committee to employ the growing poor
summary: In 1769, Boston established a committee to find employment for the poor, whose numbers and distress were rapidly increasing due to the loss of trade and commerce caused by the colonial boycott of British goods.

citation.quote: In 1769, Boston set up a committee "to Consider of some Suitable Methods of employing the Poor of the Town, whose Numbers and distresses are dayly increasing by the loss of its Trade and Commerce."

title: Boston wealth concentration reaches 44 percent held by top 1%
summary: Historical analysis of Boston tax records shows that by 1770 the top 1 percent of property owners controlled 44 percent of wealth, up from 25 percent held by the top 5 percent in 1687. The poverty rate among adult males doubled from 14 to 29 percent.

citation.chapter: Chapter 3 – Persons of Mean and Vile Condition
citation.quote: By 1770, the top 1 percent of property owners owned 44 percent of the wealth.

title: Colonial trade with Britain reaches 2,800,000 pounds
summary: By 1770, colonial trade with Britain had grown to 2,800,000 pounds, making the colonies economically indispensable to Britain and sharpening tensions over taxation and control.

citation.quote: the colonial trade had become more and more important to the British economy, and more profitable: it had amounted to about 500,000 pounds in 1700 but by 1770 was worth 2,800,000 pounds.

title: Regulators riot in Hillsborough, North Carolina
summary: In 1770, a large-scale riot in Hillsborough saw Regulators disrupt a court session, force the judge to flee, beat lawyers and merchants, and loot stores.

citation.quote: In 1770 there was a large-scale riot in Hillsborough, North Carolina, in which they disrupted a court, forced the judge to flee, beat three lawyers and two merchants, and looted stores.

title: New York seamen battle British soldiers; one killed
summary: Six weeks before the Boston Massacre (placing it in roughly early 1770), seamen in New York battled British soldiers who were taking their jobs, and one seaman was killed.

citation.quote: Six weeks before the Boston Massacre, there was a battle in New York of seamen against British soldiers taking their jobs, and one seaman was killed.

title: Boston Massacre: British troops kill five colonists
summary: British troops killed five colonists in what became known as the Boston Massacre. Zinn notes this event received disproportionate patriotic attention while comparable massacres of nonwhite people went largely unacknowledged.

citation.quote: my talk was not about the killing of five colonists by British troops in 1770. I thought that had been given an inordinate amount of attention for over two hundred years, because it served a certain patriotic function.

title: Boston Massacre: British soldiers kill Crispus Attucks and others
summary: On March 5, 1770, a crowd gathered before the customhouse and provoked British soldiers, who fired and killed Crispus Attucks—a mulatto worker—and others, an event that became known as the Boston Massacre.

citation.quote: On March 5, 1770, grievances of ropemakers against British soldiers taking their jobs led to a fight. A crowd gathered in front of the customhouse and began provoking the soldiers, who fired and killed first Crispus Attucks, a mulatto worker, then others. This became known as the Boston Massacre.

title: Sheriff of Albany County leads posse to Bennington
summary: In 1771, the sheriff of Albany County led a posse composed of the local power elite to Bennington to suppress tenant rebels, who were seen as "the dregs of the People."

citation.quote: The tenants were seen as "chiefly the dregs of the People," and the posse that the sheriff of Albany County led to Bennington in 1771 included the privileged top of the local power structure.

title: Battle of Alamance crushes Regulator movement; six hanged
summary: In May 1771, a disciplined government army using cannon defeated several thousand Regulators in a decisive battle, and six Regulators were subsequently hanged, ending the movement.

citation.quote: In May of 1771 there was a decisive battle in which several thousand Regulators were defeated by a disciplined army using cannon. Six Regulators were hanged.

title: Boston Tea Party carried out under tight committee control
summary: In December 1773, the Boston Committee of Correspondence organized and controlled crowd action against the tea from the start, and the resulting Tea Party led Parliament to pass the Coercive Acts imposing near-martial law on Massachusetts.

citation.quote: In the Boston Tea Party of December 1773, the Boston Committee of Correspondence, formed a year before to organize anti-British actions, "controlled crowd action against the tea from the start," Dirk Hoerder says.

title: Block Island Indian population collapses to 51
summary: Disease alone reduced the Block Island Indian population from 1,200-1,500 in 1662 to just 51 by 1774.

citation.chapter: Chapter 1 – Columbus, the Indians, and Human Progress
citation.quote: Similarly, Block Island Indians numbered perhaps 1,200 to 1,500 in 1662, and by 1774 were reduced to fifty-one.

title: Continental Congress established as illegal forerunner of independent government
summary: In 1774, colonial leaders set up the Continental Congress, an illegal body that served as a forerunner to an independent government, bringing together the colonial resistance movement at the institutional level.

citation.quote: in 1774, the setting up of a Continental Congress—an illegal body, forerunner of a future independent government.

title: Tom Paine arrives in Philadelphia
summary: Tom Paine, a staymaker, tax official, teacher, and poor emigrant from England, arrived in Philadelphia in 1774, when agitation against England was already strong and artisan mechanics were forming into a politically conscious militia.

citation.quote: He arrived in Philadelphia in 1774, when agitation against England was already strong in the colonies.

title: Virginia lower classes alarmed by Boston reports; fear impressment
summary: In the spring of 1774, a Virginia diarist recorded that the lower class was in tumult over reports from Boston, with many fearing they would be pressed and compelled to fight the British, illustrating the fear that class interests would be overridden.

citation.quote: One Virginian wrote in his diary in the spring of 1774: "The lower Class of People here are in tumult on account of Reports from Boston, many of them expect to be press'd & compell'd to go and fight the Britains!"

title: Poor and obscure fighters bear the burden of the Revolutionary War
summary: John Shy's study found that prominent citizens served only briefly in the Revolutionary War, while large numbers of the poor did much of the actual fighting and suffering.

citation.quote: Revolutionary America may have been a middle-class society, happier and more prosperous than any other in its time, but it contained a large and growing number of fairly poor people, and many of them did much of the actual fighting and suffering between 1775 and 1783: A very old story.

title: Military clash at Lexington and Concord triggers decision for independence
summary: After the military clash between colonial Minutemen and British troops at Lexington and Concord in April 1775, the Continental Congress decided on separation from Britain and organized a committee to draft the Declaration of Independence.

citation.quote: It was after the military clash at Lexington and Concord in April 1775, between colonial Minutemen and British troops, that the Continental Congress decided on separation.

title: Colonial elites discover the utility of national unity
summary: Around 1776, important people in the English colonies realized that creating a unified nation called the United States would allow them to seize land, profits, and power from British favorites while containing potential rebellions.

citation.quote: Around 1776, certain important people in the English colonies made a discovery that would prove enormously useful for the next two hundred years. They found that by creating a nation, a symbol, a legal unity called the United States, they could take over land, profits, and political power from favorites of the British Empire.

title: Tom Paine's Common Sense published and sells hundreds of thousands of copies
summary: Common Sense, published in early 1776, became the most popular pamphlet in the American colonies, going through twenty-five editions that year and making the first bold public argument for independence in language accessible to ordinary literate colonists.

citation.quote: Tom Paine's Common Sense, which appeared in early 1776 and became the most popular pamphlet in the American colonies, did this. It made the first bold argument for independence, in words that any fairly literate person could understand.

title: Pennsylvania Constitution of 1776 adopted
summary: In 1776, Pennsylvania adopted a progressive state constitution that James Wilson and conservatives opposed, and that militia members associated with lower-class interests defended.

citation.quote: Wilson was a Revolutionary leader who opposed price controls and wanted a more conservative government than was given by the Pennsylvania Constitution of 1776.

title: Democratic constitution adopted in Pennsylvania
summary: Pennsylvania adopted a democratic constitution in 1776 that abolished property qualifications for voting, unlike most other states.

citation.quote: In October came the "Fort Wilson riot," in which a militia group marched into the city and to the house of James Wilson, a wealthy lawyer and Revolutionary official who had opposed price controls and the democratic constitution adopted in Pennsylvania in 1776.

title: New state constitutions drawn up across America with limited democratic reforms
summary: New constitutions drawn up in all states from 1776 to 1780 were not much different from the old ones; property qualifications for voting were lowered in some states but raised in Massachusetts, and only Pennsylvania abolished them entirely.

citation.quote: In general, throughout the states, concessions were kept to a minimum. The new constitutions that were drawn up in all states from 1776 to 1780 were not much different from the old ones.

title: Abigail Adams writes to John Adams urging women's rights in the new legal code
summary: In March 1776, before the Declaration of Independence, Abigail Adams wrote to her husband John Adams urging that the new laws "remember the ladies" and warning that women would "foment a rebellion" if denied representation.

citation.quote: Abigail Adams, even before the Declaration of Independence, in March of 1776, wrote to her husband:

title: North Carolina resolutions declare independence from England
summary: In May 1776, resolutions adopted in North Carolina and sent to the Continental Congress declared independence from England, asserted all British law null and void, and urged military preparations.

citation.quote: Resolutions adopted in North Carolina in May of 1776, and sent to the Continental Congress, declared independence of England, asserted that all British law was null and void, and urged military preparations.

title: Laborers, artisans, and tradesmen take command in Philadelphia
summary: By mid-1776, laborers, artisans, and small tradesmen in Philadelphia—aided by Thomas Paine and Thomas Young—had seized clear command of the city through extralegal measures and launched a full-scale attack on concentrated wealth and unlimited private property.

citation.quote: "By mid-1776, laborers, artisans, and small tradesmen, employing extralegal measures when electoral politics failed, were in clear command in Philadelphia." Helped by some middle-class leaders (Thomas Paine, Thomas Young, and others), they "launched a full-scale attack on wealth and even on the right to acquire unlimited private property."

title: Declaration of Independence officially proclaimed
summary: The Declaration of Independence, drafted by Thomas Jefferson, was adopted by the Continental Congress on July 2 and officially proclaimed on July 4, 1776, establishing the legal basis for American independence.

citation.quote: It was adopted by the Congress on July 2, and officially proclaimed July 4, 1776.

title: Battle of Saratoga turns the tide of the Revolutionary War
summary: After early losses, the Americans won a decisive battle at Saratoga, New York, in 1777, marking a turning point in the war.

citation.quote: The Americans lost the first battles of the war: Bunker Hill, Brooklyn Heights, Harlem Heights, the Deep South; they won small battles at Trenton and Princeton, and then in a turning point, a big battle at Saratoga, New York, in 1777.

title: Dutchess County landowner proposes freeholder promises to recruit tenant soldiers
summary: A prominent landowner of Dutchess County wrote in 1777 that promising tenants freehold land would instantly bring six thousand able farmers into military service.

citation.quote: A prominent landowner of Dutchess County wrote in 1777 that a promise to make tenants freeholders "would instantly bring you at least six thousand able farmers into the field."

title: Women's "coffee party" in Boston: merchants' warehouse stormed to seize hoarded goods
summary: In 1777, a group of roughly a hundred women marched on a Boston merchant's warehouse, seized him, took his keys, and helped themselves to hoarded coffee he refused to sell at a fair price — a women's counterpart to the Boston Tea Party.

citation.quote: In 1777 there was a women's counterpart to the Boston Tea Party—a "coffee party," described by Abigail Adams in a letter to her husband John:

title: Philadelphia militia attack home of James Wilson
summary: In 1779, lower-class militia members attacked the house of James Wilson, a Revolutionary leader who opposed price controls and favored a more conservative government, reflecting ongoing class conflict within the revolutionary movement.

citation.quote: Once the Revolution was under way, Paine more and more made it clear that he was not for the crowd action of lower-class people—like those militia who in 1779 attacked the house of James Wilson.

title: American navy begins impressing seamen by 1779
summary: By 1779, the American navy was impressing seamen into service, drawing comparisons to the British impressment practices that had sparked colonial riots and resistance.

citation.quote: With the impressment riots against the British still remembered, impressment of seamen by the American navy was taking place by 1779.

title: Philadelphia Artillery petitions Assembly over hardships of the poor
summary: In May 1779, the First Company of Philadelphia Artillery petitioned the Assembly about the troubles of 'the midling and poor' and threatened violence against those amassing wealth.

citation.quote: In May of 1779, the First Company of Philadelphia Artillery petitioned the Assembly about the troubles of "the midling and poor" and threatened violence against "those who are avariciously intent upon amassing wealth by the destruction of the more virtuous part of the community."

title: Philadelphia mass meeting calls for price reductions and investigates Robert Morris
summary: A mass extralegal gathering in Philadelphia in May 1779 called for price reductions and initiated an investigation of wealthy merchant Robert Morris, accused of hoarding food.

citation.quote: That same month, there was a mass meeting, an extralegal gathering, which called for price reductions and initiated an investigation of Robert Morris, a rich Philadelphian who was accused of holding food from the market.

title: Fort Wilson riot in Philadelphia
summary: In October 1779, a militia group marched to the house of wealthy lawyer James Wilson, who had opposed price controls, but was driven off by a 'silk stocking brigade' of well-off citizens.

citation.quote: In October came the "Fort Wilson riot," in which a militia group marched into the city and to the house of James Wilson, a wealthy lawyer and Revolutionary official who had opposed price controls and the democratic constitution adopted in Pennsylvania in 1776.

title: Seven Black residents of Dartmouth, Massachusetts petition for voting rights
summary: In 1780, seven blacks in Dartmouth, Massachusetts petitioned the legislature for the right to vote, arguing that taxation without representation was unjust especially for those who had fought in the war.

citation.quote: In 1780, seven blacks in Dartmouth, Massachusetts, petitioned the legislature for the right to vote, linking taxation to representation...

title: Massachusetts raises property qualifications for voting under new constitution
summary: The new Massachusetts Constitution of 1780 raised property qualifications for voting and set high wealth requirements for holding state office, concentrating political power among the wealthy.

citation.quote: The new Constitution of 1780 had raised the property qualifications for voting. No one could hold state office without being quite wealthy.

title: Americans win final victory of the Revolutionary War at Yorktown
summary: Aided by French forces on land and sea, the Americans won the final victory of the Revolutionary War at Yorktown, Virginia, in 1781.

citation.quote: ...the Americans, aided by a large French army, with the French navy blocking off the British from supplies and reinforcements, won the final victory of the war at Yorktown, Virginia, in 1781.

title: Pennsylvania troops mutiny near Morristown, march on Continental Congress
summary: On New Year's Day 1781, Pennsylvania troops near Morristown, New Jersey dispersed their officers, killed one captain, and marched armed with cannon toward the Continental Congress in Philadelphia.

citation.quote: On New Year's Day, 1781, the Pennsylvania troops near Morristown, New Jersey, perhaps emboldened by rum, dispersed their officers, killed one captain, wounded others, and were marching, fully armed, with cannon, toward the Continental Congress at Philadelphia.
