title: Shays' Rebellion begins in western Massachusetts
summary: An uprising in the summer of 1786 in western Massachusetts, known as Shays' Rebellion, was sparked by the legislature's refusal to issue paper money and its foreclosure actions against debt-ridden farmers.

citation.quote: By 1787 there was not only a positive need for strong central government to protect the large economic interests, but also immediate fear of rebellion by discontented farmers. The chief event causing this fear was an uprising in the summer of 1786 in western Massachusetts, known as Shays' Rebellion.

title: New Hampshire farmers surround the legislature demanding tax relief
summary: In September 1786, several hundred men surrounded the legislature in Exeter, New Hampshire, demanding that taxes be returned and paper money issued; they dispersed only when military action was threatened.

citation.quote: In New Hampshire, several hundred men, in September of 1786, surrounded the legislature in Exeter, asking that taxes be returned and paper money issued; they dispersed only when military action was threatened.

title: Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court indicts eleven Shays' Rebellion leaders
summary: On September 19, 1786, the Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts met in Worcester and indicted eleven leaders of the rebellion as 'disorderly, riotous and seditious persons,' prompting Daniel Shays to organize armed resistance.

citation.quote: What brought Shays fully into the situation was that on September 19, the Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts met in Worcester and indicted eleven leaders of the rebellion, including three of his friends, as "disorderly, riotous and seditious persons" who "unlawfully and by force of arms" prevented "the execution of justice and the laws of the commonwealth."

title: Constitutional Convention meets in Philadelphia
summary: Fifty-five men gathered in Philadelphia in 1787 to draft the Constitution; Charles Beard found that most were wealthy lawyers, landowners, slaveholders, or bondholders with direct economic interests in a strong federal government.

citation.quote: Beard applied this general idea to the Constitution, by studying the economic backgrounds and political ideas of the fifty-five men who gathered in Philadelphia in 1787 to draw up the Constitution.

title: New York ratifies the Constitution after anti-Federalist leaders switch sides
summary: In 1788, Melancton Smith and other anti-Federalist leaders in New York switched to support the Constitution, and with New York ratifying, adoption was ensured.

citation.quote: Once the new landholders were brought into the privileged circle of the Revolution and seemed politically under control, their leaders, Melancton Smith and others, at first opposed to adoption of the Constitution, switched to support, and with New York ratifying, adoption was ensured.

title: Daniel Shays pardoned and returns to Massachusetts
summary: Daniel Shays, who had fled to Vermont after the suppression of his rebellion, was pardoned in 1788 and returned to Massachusetts, where he died poor and obscure in 1825.

citation.quote: Shays, in Vermont, was pardoned in 1788 and returned to Massachusetts, where he died, poor and obscure, in 1825.

title: Samuel Slater introduces industrial spinning machinery to New England
summary: Samuel Slater introduced industrial spinning machinery in New England in 1789, creating demand for young women — "spinsters" — to operate the new factory equipment.

citation.quote: Samuel Slater had introduced industrial spinning machinery in New England in 1789, and now there was a demand for young girls—literally, "spinsters"—to work the spinning machinery in factories.

title: A thousand tons of cotton produced annually in the South
summary: In 1790, the South produced a thousand tons of cotton per year, supported by roughly 500,000 enslaved people. Over the following seventy years both cotton output and the enslaved population would grow dramatically.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: In 1790, a thousand tons of cotton were being produced every year in the South. By 1860, it was a million tons. In the same period, 500,000 slaves grew to 4 million.

title: First Amendment passed by Congress
summary: Congress passed the First Amendment in 1791, providing that Congress shall make no law abridging freedom of speech or the press, though this protection would prove weaker than it appeared.

citation.quote: Passed in 1791 by Congress, it provided that "Congress shall make no law . . . abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press. . . ."

title: Young woman writes of her dread at approaching marriage
summary: In 1791 a young woman wrote expressing deep anxiety about her impending marriage, describing it as a decision that would "determine the future happiness or misery" of her life with the solemnity of death.

citation.quote: One girl wrote in 1791: "The die is about to be cast which will probably determine the future happiness or misery of my life. . . . I have always anticipated the event with a degree of solemnity almost equal to that which will terminate my present existence."

title: Whiskey Rebellion: western Pennsylvania farmers take up arms against whiskey tax
summary: In 1794, farmers in western Pennsylvania took up arms and rebelled against the collection of the Whiskey Tax; Secretary of the Treasury Alexander Hamilton led troops to put them down.

citation.quote: In 1794 the farmers of western Pennsylvania took up arms and rebelled against the collection of this tax. Secretary of the Treasury Hamilton led the troops to put them down.

title: Liverpool dominates European slave trade with over a hundred ships
summary: By 1795, Liverpool had more than a hundred ships carrying slaves and accounted for half of all European slave trade.

citation.quote: By 1795 Liverpool had more than a hundred ships carrying slaves and accounted for half of all the European slave trade.

title: Death of William Scott, Revolutionary War veteran
summary: William Scott, the Bunker Hill lieutenant from Peterborough, New Hampshire who fought throughout the Revolutionary War and sold his farm for a note that became worthless with inflation, died in 1796 after catching a fever while surveying western lands.

citation.quote: He then got a job surveying western lands with the army, but caught a fever and died in 1796.

title: Sedition Act of 1798 criminalizes criticism of the government
summary: The Sedition Act of 1798, passed under John Adams's administration, made it a crime to say or write anything 'false, scandalous and malicious' against the government, Congress, or the President; ten Americans were imprisoned under it.

citation.quote: This was the Sedition Act of 1798, passed under John Adams's administration, at a time when Irishmen and Frenchmen in the United States were looked on as dangerous revolutionaries because of the recent French Revolution and the Irish rebellions.

title: 103 U.S. armed interventions abroad recorded
summary: A State Department list presented to the Senate in 1962 documented 103 instances of U.S. armed forces used abroad between 1798 and 1895.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: A State Department list, "Instances of the Use of United States Armed Forces Abroad 1798–1945" (presented by Secretary of State Dean Rusk to a Senate committee in 1962 to cite precedents for the use of armed force against Cuba), shows 103 interventions in the affairs of other countries between 1798 and 1895.

title: Ten to fifteen million Africans transported as slaves to the Americas
summary: By 1800, an estimated 10 to 15 million Black Africans had been transported as slaves to the Americas, representing perhaps one-third of those originally seized in Africa.

citation.quote: By 1800, 10 to 15 million blacks had been transported as slaves to the Americas, representing perhaps one-third of those originally seized in Africa.

title: Gabriel Prosser slave conspiracy
summary: Gabriel Prosser's slave conspiracy in 1800 was one of a series of rebellions and plots that forced Southern states to build an elaborate network of controls backed by law, courts, and armed force.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: A system harried by slave rebellions and conspiracies (Gabriel Prosser, 1800; Denmark Vesey, 1822; Nat Turner, 1831) developed a network of controls in the southern states, backed by the laws, courts, armed forces, and race prejudice of the nation's political leaders.

title: Slave conspiracy in Virginia involving white participants
summary: A report to the governor of Virginia in 1802 revealed a slave conspiracy in which three white persons were also involved, with arms and ammunition concealed under their houses. The incident rekindled slaveowner fears about cross-racial resistance.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: Herbert Aptheker quotes a report to the governor of Virginia on a slave conspiracy in 1802: "I have just received information that three white persons are concerned in the plot; and they have arms and ammunition concealed under their houses, and were to give aid when the negroes should begin."

title: Haitian revolution against France produces first Black republic
summary: Haiti's revolution against France in 1803 led to the first nation run by Black people in the New World, a precedent invoked in U.S. and Spanish debates over Cuban independence.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: The reference to "another" black republic meant Haiti, whose revolution against France in 1803 had led to the first nation run by blacks in the New World.

title: New Jersey rescinds women's right to vote
summary: After the American Revolution, New Jersey was the only state to grant women the right to vote; that right was rescinded in 1807, leaving no state constitution that permitted women's suffrage.

citation.quote: And after the Revolution, none of the new state constitutions granted women the right to vote, except for New Jersey, and that state rescinded the right in 1807.

title: New York sermon prescribes woman's duty as devoted helpmate to her husband
summary: A sermon preached in New York in 1808 defined women's role entirely in relation to their husbands — as counsellor, comforter, and guardian angel devoted to making him more virtuous and happy.

citation.quote: A sermon preached in 1808 in New York:

title: Slave importation made illegal
summary: In 1808 the importation of enslaved people became illegal in the United States, but the law went largely unenforced; John Hope Franklin estimates that perhaps 250,000 slaves were still smuggled in before the Civil War.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: But slave importation became illegal in 1808. Therefore, "from the beginning, the law went unenforced," says John Hope Franklin *(From Slavery to Freedom).*

title: Thirty thousand blacks remain enslaved in the northern states
summary: As late as 1810, thirty thousand blacks—one-fourth of the black population of the North—remained enslaved, showing how slowly emancipation progressed even after the Revolution.

citation.quote: As late as 1810, thirty thousand blacks, one-fourth of the black population of the North, remained slaves.

title: Largest US slave revolt near New Orleans
summary: Four to five hundred enslaved people gathered near New Orleans after a rising at the plantation of Major Andry, marching from plantation to plantation before being attacked by US army and militia forces; sixty-six were killed on the spot and sixteen were tried and shot.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: Probably the largest slave revolt in the United States took place near New Orleans in 1811. Four to five hundred slaves gathered after a rising at the plantation of a Major Andry. Armed with cane knives, axes, and clubs, they wounded Andry, killed his son, and began marching from plantation to plantation, their numbers growing. They were attacked by U.S. army and militia forces; sixty-six were killed on the spot, and sixteen were tried and shot by a firing squad.

title: Woman writes of distress at facing her third childbirth
summary: In 1813, a woman wrote of the despair she felt at the prospect of giving birth to her third child and the burdens of motherhood, expressing that the duty "distresses me so I feel as if I should sink."

citation.quote: One woman, writing in 1813: "The idea of soon giving birth to my third child and the consequent duties I shall be called to discharge distresses me so I feel as if I should sink."

title: Power loom introduced in Waltham, Massachusetts, centralizing textile production
summary: In 1814 the power loom was introduced in Waltham, Massachusetts, bringing all textile operations under one roof and rapidly expanding factories where women made up 80 to 90 percent of the workforce.

citation.quote: In 1814, the power loom was introduced in Waltham, Massachusetts, and now all the operations needed to turn cotton fiber into cloth were under one roof.

title: Emma Willard addresses New York legislature on women's education
summary: In 1819, Emma Willard addressed the New York legislature arguing that women's education had been too narrowly directed toward displaying beauty and conforming to men's tastes rather than developing women as rational, independent beings.

citation.quote: When Emma Willard addressed the New York legislature in 1819 on the subject of education for women, she was contradicting the statement made just the year before by Thomas Jefferson (in a letter) in which he suggested women should not read novels "as a mass of trash" with few exceptions.

title: Emma Willard founds Troy Female Seminary, first recognized school for girls' education
summary: In 1821 Emma Willard founded the Troy Female Seminary in New York, the first recognized institution for the education of girls, where she taught anatomy and other subjects that shocked Victorian sensibilities.

citation.quote: In 1821, Willard founded the Troy Female Seminary, the first recognized institution for the education of girls.

title: Mexico wins independence from Spain
summary: Mexico won its independence in a revolutionary war against Spain, establishing a large country that included Texas and what are now New Mexico, Utah, Nevada, Arizona, California, and part of Colorado.

citation.chapter: Chapter 8 – We Take Nothing by Conquest, Thank God
citation.quote: To the southwest was Mexico, which had won its independence in a revolutionary war against Spain in 1821—a large country which included Texas and what are now New Mexico, Utah, Nevada, Arizona, California, and part of Colorado.

title: Denmark Vesey conspiracy thwarted in Charleston
summary: The conspiracy of Denmark Vesey, a free Black man, was betrayed before it could be carried out. The plan was to burn Charleston and initiate a general slave revolt; thirty-five Black people including Vesey were hanged.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: The conspiracy of Denmark Vesey, himself a free Negro, was thwarted before it could be carried out in 1822. The plan was to burn Charleston, South Carolina, then the sixth-largest city in the nation, and to initiate a general revolt of slaves in the area.

title: Monroe Doctrine issued
summary: The Monroe Doctrine was issued in 1823 as Latin American nations were winning independence from Spain, asserting U.S. hegemony over Latin America as its sphere of influence.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: Issued in 1823 when the countries of Latin America were winning independence from Spanish control, it made plain to European nations that the United States considered Latin America its sphere of influence.

title: First known strike of women factory workers in Pawtucket, Rhode Island
summary: In 1824 in Pawtucket, Rhode Island, 202 women joined men in striking against a wage cut and longer hours — the first known strike of women factory workers — though the women met separately from the men.

citation.quote: In Pawtucket, Rhode Island, in 1824, came the first known strike of women factory workers; 202 women joined men in protesting a wage cut and longer hours, but they met separately.

title: Frances Wright immigrates from Scotland, becomes advocate for women's rights and abolition
summary: Frances Wright, a Scottish writer and founder of a utopian community, immigrated to America in 1824 where she advocated for abolition, birth control, sexual freedom, and free public education for all children.

citation.quote: Frances Wright was a writer, founder of a utopian community, immigrant from Scotland in 1824, a fighter for the emancipation of slaves, for birth control and sexual freedom.

title: Death of Daniel Shays
summary: Daniel Shays died poor and obscure in Massachusetts in 1825, decades after leading the famous rebellion that bore his name.

citation.quote: Shays, in Vermont, was pardoned in 1788 and returned to Massachusetts, where he died, poor and obscure, in 1825.

title: United Tailoresses of New York stage first women's strike
summary: Women struck independently for the first time in 1825: the United Tailoresses of New York demanded higher wages in what Zinn identifies as the first strike of women on their own.

citation.quote: Women struck by themselves for the first time in 1825. They were the United Tailoresses of New York, demanding higher wages.

title: "Address before the Mechanics and Working Classes of Philadelphia" published
summary: In 1827 an "Unlettered Mechanic," probably a young shoemaker, wrote an address to the mechanics and working classes of Philadelphia describing their oppression and dependence on employers' will.

citation.quote: In 1827 an "Address . . . before the Mechanics and Working Classes . . . of Philadelphia" was recorded, written by an "Unlettered Mechanic," probably a young shoemaker...

title: Women in Dover, New Hampshire, strike alone at textile mill
summary: Four years after the 1824 Pawtucket strike, women in Dover, New Hampshire, conducted an all-women strike at a textile mill — one of the earliest independent strikes by women workers in America.

citation.quote: Four years later, women in Dover, New Hampshire, struck alone.

title: First strike of mill women in Dover, New Hampshire
summary: In 1828 the first strike of mill women on their own took place in Dover, New Hampshire, when several hundred women paraded with banners and fired off gunpowder to protest new factory rules imposing fines, forbidding talk, and requiring church attendance.

citation.quote: In 1828, the first strike of mill women on their own took place in Dover, New Hampshire, when several hundred women paraded with banners and flags.

title: David Walker publishes his Appeal
summary: David Walker, a free Black man from North Carolina living in Boston, wrote and printed Walker's Appeal, a militant pamphlet denouncing American slavery. It so enraged Southern slaveholders that Georgia offered $10,000 for his capture alive.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: In 1829, David Walker, son of a slave, but born free in North Carolina, moved to Boston, where he sold old clothes. The pamphlet he wrote and printed, *Walker's Appeal,* became widely known.

title: George Henry Evans writes "Working Men's Declaration of Independence"
summary: Later in 1829, George Henry Evans, editor of the Workingman's Advocate, wrote the "Working Men's Declaration of Independence," denouncing tax laws, private incorporation laws, and property-based political inequality.

citation.quote: Later that year, George Henry Evans, a printer, editor of the Workingman's Advocate, wrote "The Working Men's Declaration of Independence."

title: Frances Wright addresses first city-wide labor union association in Philadelphia
summary: Frances Wright of Scotland, feminist and utopian socialist, was invited by Philadelphia workingmen to speak on the Fourth of July 1829 to one of the first city-wide associations of labor unions in the United States.

citation.quote: Frances Wright of Scotland, an early feminist and utopian socialist, was invited by Philadelphia workingmen to speak on the Fourth of July 1829 to one of the first city-wide associations of labor unions in the United States.

title: The Young Lady's Book published, prescribing female obedience and submission
summary: The Young Lady's Book of 1830 instructed women that "a spirit of obedience and submission, pliability of temper, and humility of mind" were required of them in every situation from cradle to grave.

citation.quote: In *The Young Lady's Book* of 1830: ". . . in whatever situation of life a woman is placed from her cradle to her grave, a spirit of obedience and submission, pliability of temper, and humility of mind, are required from her."

title: Death of David Walker
summary: One summer day in 1830, David Walker was found dead near the doorway of his shop in Boston, under mysterious circumstances.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: One summer day in 1830, David Walker was found dead near the doorway of his shop in Boston.

title: Nat Turner's rebellion in Southampton County, Virginia
summary: Nat Turner led roughly seventy enslaved people on a violent rebellion through Southampton County, Virginia, killing at least fifty-five people. The revolt threw the slaveholding South into panic; Turner and about eighteen others were hanged.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: Nat Turner's rebellion in Southampton County, Virginia, in the summer of 1831, threw the slaveholding South into a panic, and then into a determined effort to bolster the security of the slave system.

title: Garrison publishes The Liberator
summary: William Lloyd Garrison published his abolitionist newspaper The Liberator in Boston in 1831. Of its first twenty-five subscribers, most were Black, and it became a central organ of the antislavery movement.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: Before Garrison published his famous *Liberator* in Boston in 1831, the first national convention of Negroes had been held, David Walker had already written his "Appeal," and a black abolitionist magazine named *Freedom's Journal* had appeared.

title: Slavery abolished in British West Indies
summary: Britain abolished slavery in its West Indies colonies in 1833. When the enslaved crew of the American ship Creole sailed to the British West Indies in 1841 after overpowering their captors, England refused to return them on this basis.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: Slaves being transported on a ship, the *Creole,* overpowered the crew, killed one of them, and sailed into the British West Indies (where slavery had been abolished in 1833).

title: Lowell, Massachusetts mill girls strike and one gives "Mary Wollstonecraft speech" on women's rights
summary: In Lowell, Massachusetts in 1834, when a young woman was fired, her fellow mill workers left their looms in protest; one climbed the town pump and delivered a public speech on women's rights and the injustice of the "moneyed aristocracy."

citation.quote: And in Lowell, Massachusetts, in 1834, when a young woman was fired from her job, other girls left their looms, one of them then climbing the town pump and making, according to a newspaper report, "a flaming Mary Wollstonecraft speech on the rights of women and the iniquities of the 'moneyed aristocracy' which produced a powerful effect on her auditors and they determined to have their own way, if they died for it."

title: Boston Trades' Union formed, citing Declaration of Independence
summary: A city-wide Trades' Union formed in Boston in 1834, including mechanics from Charlestown and women shoe binders from Lynn, invoked the Declaration of Independence to condemn laws favoring the wealthy and the underfunding of common schools.

citation.quote: A city-wide "Trades' Union" in Boston in 1834, including mechanics from Charlestown and women shoe binders from Lynn, referred to the Declaration of Independence:

title: Lowell women workers strike against wage cut
summary: In 1834, a cut in wages led Lowell women to strike, proclaiming "Union is power." The threat of replacement workers eventually drove them back at reduced wages, with their leaders fired.

citation.quote: In 1834, a cut in wages led the Lowell women to strike, proclaiming: "Union is power. Our present object is to have union and exertion, and we remain in possession of our own unquestionable rights. . . ."

title: Dr. Harriot Hunt begins medical practice, later twice refused admission to Harvard Medical School
summary: Dr. Harriot Hunt began practicing medicine in 1835, focusing on women and children and emphasizing diet, hygiene, and mental health, despite being twice refused admission to Harvard Medical School.

citation.quote: Dr. Harriot Hunt, a woman physician who began to practice in 1835, was twice refused admission to Harvard Medical School.

title: Baltimore riot after Bank of Maryland collapse
summary: In the summer of 1835, the Bank of Maryland collapsed and depositors lost their savings. A crowd convinced of fraud attacked the homes of officials associated with the bank; militia killed some twenty people and wounded a hundred.

citation.quote: Such was the riot in Baltimore in the summer of 1835, when the Bank of Maryland collapsed and its depositors lost their savings.

title: General strike for ten-hour day in Philadelphia
summary: In 1835, fifty different trades organized unions in Philadelphia and staged a successful general strike of laborers, factory workers, bookbinders, jewelers, coal heavers, butchers, cabinet workers and others demanding the ten-hour day.

citation.quote: In 1835, fifty different trades organized unions in Philadelphia, and there was a successful general strike of laborers, factory workers, bookbinders, jewelers, coal heavers, butchers, cabinet workers—for the ten-hour day.

title: Twenty New Hampshire mills strike for eleven-hour workday
summary: In 1835, twenty mills went on strike to reduce the workday from thirteen and a half hours to eleven hours and to obtain cash wages instead of company scrip. Fifteen hundred children and parents struck for six weeks, winning a twelve-hour day.

citation.quote: In 1835, twenty mills went on strike to reduce the workday from thirteen and a half hours to eleven hours, to get cash wages instead of company scrip, and to end fines for lateness.

title: Texas breaks from Mexico and declares itself the Lone Star Republic
summary: After agitation and aid from the United States, Texas broke off from Mexico in 1836 and declared itself the "Lone Star Republic."

citation.chapter: Chapter 8 – We Take Nothing by Conquest, Thank God
citation.quote: After agitation, and aid from the United States, Texas broke off from Mexico in 1836 and declared itself the "Lone Star Republic."

title: Factory Girls' Association strike at Lowell mills
summary: In 1836, 1,500 Lowell women went on strike through the Factory Girls' Association against a raise in boardinghouse charges. Eleven-year-old Harriet Hanson led her floor out; the strikers held out a month before returning, their leaders fired.

citation.quote: The young women, determined to do better next time, organized a Factory Girls' Association, and 1,500 went on strike in 1836 against a raise in boardinghouse charges.

title: Flour Riot of 1837 in New York City
summary: During the crisis of 1837, a crowd in New York responding to soaring flour prices stormed Eli Hart's flour store, rolling barrels into the street and destroying thousands of bushels of flour. Troops and police eventually restored order.

citation.quote: This was the Flour Riot of 1837. During the crisis of that year, 50,000 persons (one-third of the working class) were without work in New York City alone, and 200,000 (of a population of 500,000) were living, as one observer put it, "in utter and hopeless distress."

title: Angelina Grimké becomes first woman to address a Massachusetts state legislative committee
summary: In 1838 Angelina Grimké became the first woman to address a committee of the Massachusetts state legislature, speaking on antislavery petitions before a huge crowd, nearly fainting from the emotional intensity.

citation.quote: Angelina was the first woman (in 1838) to address a committee of the Massachusetts state legislature on antislavery petitions.

title: Frederick Douglass escapes slavery
summary: Frederick Douglass, enslaved and working in Baltimore as a servant and shipyard laborer, escaped to the North in 1838 at age twenty-one. He went on to become the most famous Black man of his era as a lecturer, newspaper editor, and writer.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: Frederick Douglass, a slave, sent to Baltimore to work as a servant and as a laborer in the shipyard, somehow learned to read and write, and at twenty-one, in the year 1838, escaped to the North, where he became the most famous black man of his time, as lecturer, newspaper editor, writer.

title: Anti-Rent tenants defy Hudson Valley sheriff
summary: Tenants on the Rensselaer estate in the Hudson Valley organized to resist rent collection, threatening the sheriff sent to serve writs. A deputy who arrived was met by farmers who seized and burned his writs.

citation.quote: A sheriff in the Hudson River Valley near Albany, New York, about to go into the hills in the fall of 1839 to collect back rents from tenants on the enormous Rensselaer estate, was handed a letter:

title: Hudson Valley tenants hold first mass meeting
summary: By the summer of 1839 Hudson Valley tenants held their first mass meeting, driven by the economic crisis of 1837 and unemployment from completed canal and railroad construction. They resolved to carry forward the Revolution to freedom for the masses.

citation.quote: By the summer of 1839, the tenants were holding their first mass meeting. The economic crisis of 1837 had filled the area with unemployed seeking land, on top of the layoffs accompanying the completion of the Erie Canal, after the first wave of railroad building ended.

title: Eighteen hundred armed farmers block sheriff's posse in Hudson Valley
summary: A sheriff and mounted posse of five hundred rode into the Anti-Rent farm country and were blocked by eighteen hundred armed farmers, with six hundred more at the rear, forcing the posse to retreat.

citation.quote: That December, a sheriff and a mounted posse of five hundred rode into the farm country, but found themselves in the midst of shrieking tin horns, eighteen hundred farmers blocking their path, six hundred more blocking their rear, all mounted, armed with pitchforks and clubs.

title: A thousand slaves still held in the North
summary: In 1840, there were still a thousand slaves in the northern states, demonstrating the prolonged and incomplete nature of northern emancipation.

citation.quote: In 1840 there were still a thousand slaves in the North.

title: World Anti-Slavery Society Convention in London votes to exclude women delegates
summary: In 1840, the World Anti-Slavery Society Convention in London voted to exclude women from participation, relegating them to a curtained gallery; Elizabeth Cady Stanton met Lucretia Mott there, sparking plans for a women's rights convention.

citation.quote: In 1840, a World Anti-Slavery Society Convention met in London. After a fierce argument, it was voted to exclude women, but it was agreed they could attend meetings in a curtained enclosure. The women sat in silent protest in the gallery, and William Lloyd Garrison, one abolitionist who had fought for the rights of women, sat with them.

title: Enslaved people seize the ship Creole and sail to freedom
summary: In 1841, enslaved people being transported on the American ship Creole overpowered the crew, killed one of them, and sailed to the British West Indies where slavery had been abolished. England refused to return them, provoking angry Congressional talk of war with Britain.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: But that year, 1841, one incident took place which kept alive the idea of rebellion. Slaves being transported on a ship, the *Creole,* overpowered the crew, killed one of them, and sailed into the British West Indies (where slavery had been abolished in 1833). England refused to return the slaves...

title: Thousands parade in Providence for electoral reform
summary: Working people formed the Rhode Island Suffrage Association, and in the spring of 1841 thousands paraded in Providence carrying banners for electoral reform, going outside the legal system to organize a People's Convention.

citation.quote: Working people formed the Rhode Island Suffrage Association, and in the spring of 1841 thousands paraded in Providence carrying banners and signs for electoral reform.

title: Rhode Island People's Constitution ratified by popular vote
summary: In early 1842, fourteen thousand people voted for the People's Constitution drafted outside the legal system, including about five thousand who held property—a majority even of those legally entitled to vote.

citation.quote: In early 1842, they invited votes on the constitution; fourteen thousand voted for it, including about five thousand with property—therefore a majority even of those legally entitled to vote by the charter.

title: Thomas Dorr elected governor in unofficial Rhode Island election
summary: In April 1842 the Dorr forces held an unofficial election in which Dorr ran unopposed for governor and six thousand people voted for him, while the regular governor secured a federal promise of troops in case of rebellion.

citation.quote: In April they held an unofficial election, in which Dorr ran unopposed for governor, and six thousand people voted for him.

title: Dorr forces hold inauguration parade in Providence
summary: On May 3, 1842, the Dorr forces held an inauguration with a great parade of artisans, shopkeepers, mechanics, and militia through Providence. The newly elected People's Legislature was convened, though Dorr's subsequent attack on the state arsenal failed.

citation.quote: Ignoring this, on May 3, 1842, the Dorr forces held an inauguration with a great parade of artisans, shopkeepers, mechanics, and militia marching through Providence.

title: Dr. Harriot Hunt organizes Ladies Physiological Society in Boston
summary: In 1843, Dr. Harriot Hunt organized a Ladies Physiological Society where she gave monthly talks on health, diet, hygiene, and the body — part of her effort to advance women's medical knowledge and autonomy.

citation.quote: She organized a Ladies Physiological Society in 1843 where she gave monthly talks.

title: Dorothea Dix addresses Massachusetts legislature on conditions in prisons and almshouses
summary: In 1843, Dorothea Dix addressed the Massachusetts legislature with a detailed account of the horrific treatment of insane persons she had witnessed in prisons and almshouses — chained, naked, and beaten into obedience.

citation.quote: Speaking out on other issues prepared the way for speaking on the situation of women: Dorothea Dix, in 1843, addressed the legislature of Massachusetts on what she saw in the prisons and almshouses in the Boston area:

title: William Cullen Bryant witnesses enslaved people's corn-shucking mockery
summary: In 1843 the poet William Cullen Bryant attended a corn-shucking in South Carolina and described enslaved people turning their dances into a burlesque parody of militia training, illustrating how cultural forms served as covert resistance.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: The poet William Cullen Bryant, after attending a corn shucking in 1843 in South Carolina, told of slave dances turned into a pretended military parade, "a sort of burlesque of our militia trainings. . . ."

title: Thomas Dorr arrested and tried for treason
summary: Dorr returned to Rhode Island in the fall of 1843, was arrested on the streets of Providence, tried for treason, and sentenced to life imprisonment at hard labor by a judge who instructed the jury to ignore political arguments.

citation.quote: Dorr returned to Rhode Island in the fall of 1843. He was arrested on the streets of Providence and tried for treason.

title: Women workers march through Chicopee, Massachusetts in labor protest
summary: On May 2, 1843, women textile workers in Chicopee, Massachusetts marched through the streets in a labor protest, with their numbers growing from sixteen to over forty during the day's procession.

citation.quote: A journal kept by an unsympathetic resident of Chicopee, Massachusetts, recorded an event of May 2, 1843:

title: Lynn Awl newspaper articulates capital-labor antagonism
summary: In 1844, four years before Marx and Engels's Communist Manifesto, the Awl newspaper of Lynn shoe factory workers analyzed the division between producing and non-producing classes and declared labor a commodity in antagonism with capital.

citation.quote: In 1844, four years before Marx and Engels's Communist Manifesto appeared, the Awl wrote: The division of society into the producing and the non-producing classes, and the fact of the unequal distribution of value between the two, introduces us at once to another distinction—that of capital and labor.

title: Protestant-Catholic riots in Kensington, Philadelphia
summary: In May 1844, nativist rioters attacked Irish Catholic weavers' neighborhoods in Kensington, destroying homes and attacking a Catholic church, fragmenting the Philadelphia working class along religious and ethnic lines.

citation.quote: In May 1844 there were Protestant-Catholic riots in Kensington, a suburb of Philadelphia; nativist (anti-immigrant) rioters destroyed the weavers' neighborhoods and attacked a Catholic church.

title: New York Sun publishes call for mass meeting of working women
summary: In 1845, the New York Sun published a notice calling working women to a mass meeting in the park, with the organizers specifically requesting that men not attend so women could deliberate by themselves.

citation.quote: In 1845, the New York *Sun* carried this item:

title: U.S. Congress annexes Texas as a state
summary: In 1845, the U.S. Congress brought Texas into the Union as a state, setting the stage for conflict with Mexico over the disputed Rio Grande border.

citation.chapter: Chapter 8 – We Take Nothing by Conquest, Thank God
citation.quote: In 1845, the U.S. Congress brought it into the Union as a state.

title: John O'Sullivan coins the phrase "manifest destiny"
summary: In the summer of 1845, John O'Sullivan, editor of the Democratic Review, coined the phrase "manifest destiny," declaring it was America's destiny to overspread the continent.

citation.chapter: Chapter 8 – We Take Nothing by Conquest, Thank God
citation.quote: It was shortly after that, in the summer of 1845, that John O'Sullivan, editor of the Democratic Review, used the phrase that became famous, saying it was "Our manifest destiny to overspread the continent allotted by Providence for the free development of our yearly multiplying millions."

title: Anti-Rent petitions presented to New York legislature
summary: Petitions signed by 25,000 tenants were put before the legislature in 1845 calling for an antirent bill, but the bill was defeated. Fourth of July meetings that year, attended by thousands of farmers, pledged continued resistance.

citation.quote: Petitions for an antirent bill, signed by 25,000 tenants, were put before the legislature in 1845. The bill was defeated.

title: Anti-Renters elect fourteen members to New York state legislature
summary: In 1845 the Anti-Renters elected fourteen members to the state legislature. Governor Silas Wright commuted death sentences and asked the legislature to end the feudal system, leading to partial reforms though proposals to break up large estates were defeated.

citation.quote: In 1845, the Anti-Renters elected fourteen members to the state legislature. Governor Silas Wright now commuted to life imprisonment the two death sentences and asked the legislature to give relief to the tenants, to end the feudal system in the Hudson Valley.

title: Female Labor Reform Association formed in Lowell
summary: The crisis following the 1837 panic stimulated the formation in 1845 of the Female Labor Reform Association in Lowell, which sent thousands of petitions to the Massachusetts legislature asking for a ten-hour day. The legislature held the first governmental investigation of labor conditions in the country.

citation.quote: The crisis that followed the 1837 panic stimulated the formation in 1845 of the Female Labor Reform Association in Lowell, which sent thousands of petitions to the Massachusetts legislature asking for a ten-hour day.

title: Colonel Hitchcock receives orders to move troops toward the Rio Grande
summary: Colonel Ethan Allen Hitchcock records in his diary that orders arrived directing General Taylor to move troops to the Rio Grande and expel any Mexican armed forces that cross it, predicting the move would lead to bloodshed.

citation.chapter: Chapter 8 – We Take Nothing by Conquest, Thank God
citation.quote: Fort Jesup, La., June 30, 1845. Orders came last evening by express from Washington City directing General Taylor to move without any delay to some point on the coast near the Sabine or elsewhere, and as soon as he shall hear of the acceptance by the Texas convention of the annexation resolutions of our Congress he is immediately to proceed with his whole command to the extreme western border of Texas and take up a position on the banks of or near the Rio Grande...

title: Henry David Thoreau refuses to pay his poll tax and is jailed to protest the Mexican War
summary: In the summer of 1846, Henry David Thoreau refused to pay his Massachusetts poll tax to denounce the Mexican War, was put in jail for one night, and was released after friends paid his tax without his consent.

citation.chapter: Chapter 8 – We Take Nothing by Conquest, Thank God
citation.quote: The war had barely begun, the summer of 1846, when a writer, Henry David Thoreau, who lived in Concord, Massachusetts, refused to pay his Massachusetts poll tax, denouncing the Mexican war. He was put in jail and spent one night there.

title: Mid-term elections show anti-Polk sentiment; Abraham Lincoln elected to Congress
summary: The 1846 elections showed much anti-Polk sentiment; among those elected was Abraham Lincoln of Illinois, who would later challenge Polk with his "spot resolutions" over where American blood was shed.

citation.chapter: Chapter 8 – We Take Nothing by Conquest, Thank God
citation.quote: The 1846 elections showed much anti-Polk sentiment, but who could tell how much of this was due to the war?

title: U.S. Army lowers physical requirements for recruits as enlistment falls off
summary: By late 1846, recruitment was falling off so badly that physical requirements were lowered and a $2 bounty was paid for each acceptable recruit brought in, but dissatisfaction with the war continued.

citation.chapter: Chapter 8 – We Take Nothing by Conquest, Thank God
citation.quote: By late 1846, recruitment was falling off, so physical requirements were lowered, and anyone bringing in acceptable recruits would get $2 a head.

title: New York governor elected with Anti-Rent support pardons prisoners
summary: The governor elected in 1846 with Anti-Rent support pardoned the Anti-Rent prisoners upon taking office. Throngs of farmers greeted them on their release.

citation.quote: The next governor, elected in 1846 with Anti-Rent support, had promised to pardon the Anti-Rent prisoners, and he did. Throngs of farmers greeted them on their release.

title: Taylor receives orders to march his army to the Rio Grande
summary: General Taylor received orders in February 1846 to march his army down the Gulf Coast to the Rio Grande, moving into disputed territory inhabited by Mexicans.

citation.chapter: Chapter 8 – We Take Nothing by Conquest, Thank God
citation.quote: They came in February 1846—to go down the Gulf Coast to the Rio Grande.

title: Taylor's army arrives at the Rio Grande opposite Matamoros
summary: Taylor's army arrived on March 28, 1846, in fields abandoned by Mexican inhabitants who had fled across the river, and set up camp with cannons facing the city of Matamoros.

citation.chapter: Chapter 8 – We Take Nothing by Conquest, Thank God
citation.quote: Then, along a narrow road, through a belt of thick chaparral, they arrived, March 28, 1846, in cultivated fields and thatched-roof huts hurriedly abandoned by the Mexican occupants, who had fled across the river to the city of Matamoros.

title: Colonel Cross disappears while riding up the Rio Grande
summary: In April 1846, General Taylor's quartermaster Colonel Cross disappeared while riding up the Rio Grande; his body was found eleven days later with his skull smashed, assumed killed by Mexican guerrillas.

citation.chapter: Chapter 8 – We Take Nothing by Conquest, Thank God
citation.quote: It came in April, when General Taylor's quartermaster, Colonel Cross, while riding up the Rio Grande, disappeared. His body was found eleven days later, his skull smashed by a heavy blow.

title: Mexican forces attack and wipe out a U.S. patrol, triggering the Mexican-American War
summary: On April 25, a patrol of Taylor's soldiers was surrounded and attacked by Mexicans—sixteen dead, others wounded, the rest captured—prompting Taylor to declare hostilities commenced.

citation.chapter: Chapter 8 – We Take Nothing by Conquest, Thank God
citation.quote: The next day (April 25), a patrol of Taylor's soldiers was surrounded and attacked by Mexicans, and wiped out: sixteen dead, others wounded, the rest captured.

title: Congress passes war resolution 174 to 14; Senate passes 40 to 2
summary: After Congress acted in May 1846, Whigs joined Democrats in voting overwhelmingly for the war resolution (174 to 14 in the House, 40 to 2 in the Senate), followed by war rallies in New York, Baltimore, Indianapolis, Philadelphia, and other cities.

citation.chapter: Chapter 8 – We Take Nothing by Conquest, Thank God
citation.quote: After Congress acted in May of 1846, there were rallies and demonstrations for the war in New York, Baltimore, Indianapolis, Philadelphia, and many other places.

title: New York workingmen hold meeting to oppose the Mexican War
summary: In May, when the war against Mexico began, New York workingmen called a meeting to oppose the war, with many Irish workers attending; the meeting called the war a plot by slaveowners and demanded withdrawal of American troops.

citation.chapter: Chapter 8 – We Take Nothing by Conquest, Thank God
citation.quote: In May, when the war against Mexico began, New York workingmen called a meeting to oppose the war, and many Irish workers came. The meeting called the war a plot by slaveowners and asked for the withdrawal of American troops from disputed territory.

title: Polk proposes war declaration to his cabinet before news of any battle
summary: On May 9, before news of any battles had arrived, President Polk was already suggesting to his cabinet a declaration of war against Mexico, based on money claims and Mexico's rejection of negotiator John Slidell.

citation.chapter: Chapter 8 – We Take Nothing by Conquest, Thank God
citation.quote: On May 9, before news of any battles, Polk was suggesting to his cabinet a declaration of war, based on certain money claims against Mexico, and on Mexico's recent rejection of an American negotiator named John Slidell.

title: Polk sends war recommendations to Congress
summary: Polk sent his May 11 war recommendations to Congress; the Democratic majority responded with efficiency, limiting debate to two hours and passing the war measure 174 to 14.

citation.chapter: Chapter 8 – We Take Nothing by Conquest, Thank God
citation.quote: The disciplined Democratic majority in the House responded with alacrity and high-handed efficiency to Polk's May 11 war recommendations.

title: Horace Greeley publishes antiwar editorial in the New York Tribune
summary: Horace Greeley wrote in the New York Tribune on May 12, 1846, questioning whether military victory over Mexico would bring more liberty or prosperity, and asking whether the country needed to resort to "the hideous enginery of War."

citation.chapter: Chapter 8 – We Take Nothing by Conquest, Thank God
citation.quote: Horace Greeley wrote in the New York Tribune, May 12, 1846: We can easily defeat the armies of Mexico, slaughter them by thousands, and pursue them perhaps to their capital; we can conquer and "annex" their territory; but what then?

title: General Kearney takes Santa Fe without battle; New Mexico occupied
summary: That was in August — General Kearney moved easily into New Mexico and Santa Fe was taken without battle, with the Mexican population reacting with a mixture of watchfulness, grief, and suppressed emotion.

citation.chapter: Chapter 8 – We Take Nothing by Conquest, Thank God
citation.quote: That was in August. In December, Mexicans in Taos, New Mexico, rebelled against American rule.

title: Mexicans in Los Angeles force U.S. garrison to surrender
summary: In Los Angeles, Mexicans revolted and forced the American garrison to surrender in September 1846; the United States did not retake Los Angeles until January, after a bloody battle.

citation.chapter: Chapter 8 – We Take Nothing by Conquest, Thank God
citation.quote: In Los Angeles, too, there was a revolt. Mexicans forced the American garrison there to surrender in September 1846. The United States did not retake Los Angeles until January, after a bloody battle.

title: Mexicans in Taos, New Mexico rebel against American rule
summary: In December 1846, Mexicans in Taos, New Mexico rebelled against American rule; the revolt was put down and arrests made, but many rebels fled and carried on sporadic attacks before a final battle left 150 of six to seven hundred rebels dead.

citation.chapter: Chapter 8 – We Take Nothing by Conquest, Thank God
citation.quote: In December, Mexicans in Taos, New Mexico, rebelled against American rule. As a report to Washington put it, "many of the most influential persons in the northern part of this territory were engaged in the rebellion."

title: Lucy Stone begins lecturing on women's rights in Gardner, Massachusetts
summary: In 1847, Lucy Stone began lecturing on women's rights at her brother's church in Gardner, Massachusetts; she went on to face violent mobs as a lecturer for the American Anti-Slavery Society.

citation.quote: Lucy Stone began lecturing on women's rights in 1847 in a church in Gardner, Massachusetts, where her brother was a minister.

title: Reverend Theodore Parker urges active resistance to the Mexican War
summary: In 1847, Unitarian minister Theodore Parker urged active resistance to the war, calling it infamous for New England men to enlist or loan money to support it.

citation.chapter: Chapter 8 – We Take Nothing by Conquest, Thank God
citation.quote: Parker urged active resistance to the war in 1847: "Let it be infamous for a New England man to enlist; for a New England merchant to loan his dollars, or to let his ships in aid of this wicked war; let it be infamous for a manufacturer to make a cannon, a sword, or a kernel of powder to kill our brothers. . . ."

title: Congress authorizes ten new army regiments with land bounties for service
summary: In early 1847, Congress authorized ten new regiments of regulars to serve for the duration of the war, promising 100 acres of public land upon honorable discharge, but dissatisfaction among soldiers continued.

citation.chapter: Chapter 8 – We Take Nothing by Conquest, Thank God
citation.quote: Congress in early 1847 authorized ten new regiments of regulars, to serve for the duration of the war, promising them 100 acres of public land upon honorable discharge.

title: Frederick Douglass starts his own newspaper, North Star
summary: In 1847 Frederick Douglass started his own newspaper in Rochester, the North Star, breaking with Garrison and asserting Black independence in the abolitionist movement.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: Douglass wrote for *The Liberator,* but in 1847 started his own newspaper in Rochester, *North Star,* which led to a break with Garrison.

title: North Carolina woman records poor turnout of volunteers at a general muster
summary: A woman in Greensboro, North Carolina, recorded in her diary on January 5, 1847 that at a general muster only six or seven "bad looking persons" volunteered to follow General Logan, lamenting the sacrifices of poor men for pride and ambition.

citation.chapter: Chapter 8 – We Take Nothing by Conquest, Thank God
citation.quote: Tuesday, January 5, 1847 . . . today was a general muster and speeches by Mr. Gorrell and Mr. Henry. General Logan received them in this street and requested all the Volunteers to follow after; as he walked up and down the street, I saw some 6 or 7, bad looking persons following, with poor Jim Laine in front.

title: Mr. Giles of Maryland advocates continental expansion in Congress
summary: The Congressional Globe of February 11, 1847 reported Representative Giles of Maryland declaring that Anglo-Saxon destiny required marching from Texas straight to the Pacific Ocean.

citation.chapter: Chapter 8 – We Take Nothing by Conquest, Thank God
citation.quote: The Congressional Globe of February 11, 1847, reported: Mr. Giles, of Maryland—I take it for granted, that we shall gain territory, and must gain territory, before we shut the gates of the temple of Janus. . . . We must march from ocean to ocean. . . . We must march from Texas straight to the Pacific ocean, and be bounded only by its roaring wave. . . . It is the destiny of the white race, it is the destiny of the Anglo-Saxon race. . . .

title: U.S. Army reports over a thousand deserters
summary: In March 1847 the army reported over a thousand deserters; the total number of deserters during the entire war reached 9,207, including both regulars and volunteers.

citation.chapter: Chapter 8 – We Take Nothing by Conquest, Thank God
citation.quote: In March 1847 the army reported over a thousand deserters. The total number of deserters during the war was 9,207: 5,331 regulars, 3,876 volunteers.

title: Ship Urania from Cork quarantined at Grosse Isle with typhus
summary: On May 18, 1847, the Urania from Cork, carrying hundreds of Irish immigrants many sick with ship-fever, was the first plague-stricken ship of that year to be quarantined at Grosse Isle. By early June, eighty-four ships had arrived, none free of malignant typhus, and some 10,000 Irish died on the island.

citation.quote: On the 18th of May, 1847, the "Urania", from Cork, with several hundred immigrants on board, a large proportion of them sick and dying of the ship-fever, was put into quarantine at Grosse Isle.

title: New York Commercial Advertiser warns soldiers' land warrants are being bought by speculators
summary: The New York Commercial Advertiser said in June 1847 that speculators were preying on poor soldiers by buying up their 160-acre land warrants for less than $50, drawing a parallel to similar exploitation after the Revolutionary War.

citation.chapter: Chapter 8 – We Take Nothing by Conquest, Thank God
citation.quote: The New York Commercial Advertiser said in June 1847: "It is a well-known fact that immense fortunes were made out of the poor soldiers who shed their blood in the revolutionary war by speculators who preyed upon their distresses."

title: Virginia, Mississippi, and North Carolina volunteer regiments mutiny in northern Mexico
summary: On the night of August 15, 1847, volunteer regiments from Virginia, Mississippi, and North Carolina rebelled against Colonel Robert Treat Paine in northern Mexico; Paine killed a mutineer, but his lieutenants refused to help him, and the rebels were ultimately exonerated.

citation.chapter: Chapter 8 – We Take Nothing by Conquest, Thank God
citation.quote: On the night of August 15, 1847, volunteer regiments from Virginia, Mississippi, and North Carolina rebelled in northern Mexico against Colonel Robert Treat Paine.

title: Anglo-American troops capture Mexico City
summary: In September 1847, Anglo-American troops took the height of Chapultepec and entered Mexico City, the capital of 200,000 people, with General Santa Anna having fled northward.

citation.chapter: Chapter 8 – We Take Nothing by Conquest, Thank God
citation.quote: In the final battle for Mexico City, Anglo-American troops took the height of Chapultepec and entered the city of 200,000 people, General Santa Anna having moved northward. This was September 1847.

title: Thoreau publishes "Civil Disobedience" essay
summary: Two years after his jailing (in 1848), Thoreau gave a lecture called "Resistance to Civil Government," which was then printed as the famous essay "Civil Disobedience."

citation.chapter: Chapter 8 – We Take Nothing by Conquest, Thank God
citation.quote: Two years later, he gave a lecture, "Resistance to Civil Government," which was then printed as an essay, "Civil Disobedience."

title: Frederick Douglass condemns the Mexican War in the North Star
summary: Frederick Douglass wrote in his Rochester newspaper the North Star on January 21, 1848, denouncing the "present disgraceful, cruel, and iniquitous war" and scorning opponents of the war for their unwillingness to take real action.

citation.chapter: Chapter 8 – We Take Nothing by Conquest, Thank God
citation.quote: Frederick Douglass, former slave, extraordinary speaker and writer, wrote in his Rochester newspaper the North Star, January 21, 1848, of "the present disgraceful, cruel, and iniquitous war with our sister republic."

title: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo signed, ending the Mexican-American War
summary: The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, signed in February 1848, ended the war: Mexico ceded New Mexico and California, the Texas boundary was set at the Rio Grande, and the United States paid Mexico $15 million—prompting the Whig Intelligencer to remark "we take nothing by conquest. . . . Thank God."

citation.chapter: Chapter 8 – We Take Nothing by Conquest, Thank God
citation.quote: The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, signed February 1848, just took half. The Texas boundary was set at the Rio Grande; New Mexico and California were ceded. The United States paid Mexico $15 million, which led the Whig Intelligencer to conclude that "we take nothing by conquest. . . . Thank God."

title: Lincoln speaks in the House in support of General Zachary Taylor for President
summary: Speaking in the House on July 27, 1848, Abraham Lincoln defended the Whig position on the Mexican War while supporting General Zachary Taylor's presidential candidacy, arguing the war was unconstitutionally commenced but that Whigs had still funded it.

citation.chapter: Chapter 8 – We Take Nothing by Conquest, Thank God
citation.quote: Speaking in the House on July 27, 1848, in support of the candidacy of General Zachary Taylor for President, he said...

title: Elizabeth Blackwell receives medical degree from Geneva College, first woman in the US
summary: Elizabeth Blackwell received her medical degree in 1849 from Geneva College after overcoming repeated rejections, then established the New York Dispensary for Poor Women and Children to provide women access to female physicians.

citation.quote: Elizabeth Blackwell got her medical degree in 1849, having overcome many rebuffs before being admitted to Geneva College.

title: Lincoln proposes abolishing slavery in DC while requiring return of fugitives
summary: In 1849, as a congressman, Lincoln proposed a resolution to abolish slavery in the District of Columbia, but paired it with a requirement that local authorities arrest and return fugitive slaves entering Washington—a contradictory stance that earned him the nickname 'that slavehound from Illinois.'

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: And when he did propose, in 1849, as a Congressman, a resolution to abolish slavery in the District of Columbia, he accompanied this with a section requiring local authorities to arrest and return fugitive slaves coming into Washington.

title: Supreme Court decides Luther v. Borden
summary: In Luther v. Borden (1849) the Supreme Court established a lasting doctrine refusing to interfere in certain "political" questions, deferring to the executive and legislature on issues of war and revolution.

citation.quote: In its decision, the Supreme Court established (Luther v. Borden, 1849) a long-lasting doctrine: it would not interfere in certain "political" questions, to be left to executive and legislature.

title: Astor Place Opera House riot in New York City
summary: In New York in 1849, a mob largely of Irish workers stormed the fashionable Astor Place Opera House, shouting "Burn the damn den of aristocracy." The militia was called out and about two hundred people were killed or wounded.

citation.quote: In New York in 1849 a mob, largely Irish; stormed the fashionable Astor Place Opera House, where an English actor, William Charles Macready, was playing Macbeth... The crowd, shouting "Burn the damn den of aristocracy," charged, throwing bricks. The militia were called out, and in the violence that followed about two hundred people were killed or wounded.

title: Antoinette Brown graduates from Oberlin theology school but is omitted from class list
summary: In 1850, Antoinette Brown became the first woman to complete Oberlin College's theology program, but the college left her name off the class list; Lucy Stone, another Oberlin resister, refused to write her commencement address after being told it would be read by a man.

citation.quote: But the first girl admitted to the theology school there, Antoinette Brown, who graduated in 1850, found that her name was left off the class list.

title: Fugitive Slave Act passed
summary: The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 was a concession to Southern states in return for admitting Mexican war territories as non-slave states. It made it easy for slaveholders to recapture escaped enslaved people and prompted fierce resistance from Northern Black communities.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: The Fugitive Slave Act passed in 1850 was a concession to the southern states in return for the admission of the Mexican war territories (California, especially) into the Union as nonslave states.

title: Amelia Bloomer proposes reform dress for women in her feminist publication
summary: In 1851, Amelia Bloomer suggested in her feminist publication that women wear a short skirt over pants to free themselves from restrictive traditional dress; the proposal was attacked in popular women's literature as connected to "socialism and agrarian radicalism."

citation.quote: When Amelia Bloomer in 1851 suggested in her feminist publication that women wear a kind of short skirt and pants, to free themselves from the encumbrances of traditional dress, this was attacked in the popular women's literature.

title: Sojourner Truth delivers "Ain't I a Woman" speech at women's convention
summary: In 1851, at a women's convention following the one at Seneca Falls, the formerly enslaved Sojourner Truth rose to challenge male ministers dominating the discussion, powerfully linking the oppression of race and sex in her famous speech.

citation.quote: A series of women's conventions in various parts of the country followed the one at Seneca Falls. At one of these, in 1851, an aged black woman, who had been born a slave in New York, tall, thin, wearing a gray dress and white turban, listened to some male ministers who had been dominating the discussion. This was Sojourner Truth.

title: Runaway slave Jerry rescued from Syracuse courthouse
summary: The year after J. W. Loguen's 1850 defiance speech, a runaway slave named Jerry was captured and put on trial in Syracuse. A crowd used crowbars and a battering ram to break into the courthouse, defying marshals with drawn guns, and freed Jerry.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: The following year, Syracuse had its chance. A runaway slave named Jerry was captured and put on trial. A crowd used crowbars and a battering ram to break into the courthouse, defying marshals with drawn guns, and set Jerry free.

title: U.S. Marines land in Buenos Aires to protect American interests
summary: Marines were landed and maintained in Buenos Aires during a revolution to protect American interests.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: **1852–53—Argentina.** Marines were landed and maintained in Buenos Aires to protect American interests during a revolution.

title: Frederick Douglass delivers Independence Day address
summary: On the Fourth of July 1852, Frederick Douglass delivered a searing Independence Day speech condemning the hypocrisy of American freedom, asking "What to the American slave is your Fourth of July?" and declaring the United States guilty of practices more shocking than any nation on earth.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: Frederick Douglass knew that the shame of slavery was not just the South's, that the whole nation was complicit in it. On the Fourth of July, 1852, he gave an Independence Day address:

title: Sojourner Truth speaks at Fourth National Woman's Rights Convention
summary: In 1853 in New York City, Sojourner Truth rose to speak at the Fourth National Woman's Rights Convention in the face of a hostile mob shouting and jeering, combining her stands against slavery, racism, and patriarchy in a single defiant address.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: When Sojourner Truth rose to speak in 1853 in New York City at the Fourth National Woman's Rights Convention, it all came together.

title: U.S. intervention in Nicaragua to protect American interests
summary: U.S. forces intervened in Nicaragua to protect American lives and interests during political disturbances.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: **1853—Nicaragua**—to protect American lives and interests during political disturbances.

title: Perry Expedition forces Japan to open its ports
summary: The Perry Expedition used warships to force Japan to open its ports to the United States.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: **1853–54—Japan**—The "Opening of Japan" and the Perry Expedition. [The State Department does not give more details, but this involved the use of warships to force Japan to open its ports to the United States.]

title: Perry makes naval demonstrations in Ryukyu and Bonin Islands
summary: Commodore Perry landed marines twice in Ryukyu and demonstrated in the Bonin Islands, securing a coaling concession from the ruler of Naha on Okinawa.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: **1853–54—Ryukyu and Bonin Islands**—Commodore Perry on three visits before going to Japan and while waiting for a reply from Japan made a naval demonstration, landing marines twice, and secured a coaling concession from the ruler of Naha on Okinawa.

title: U.S. destroys Greytown, Nicaragua
summary: San Juan del Norte (Greytown) was destroyed to avenge an insult to the American Minister to Nicaragua.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: **1854—Nicaragua**—San Juan del Norte [Greytown was destroyed to avenge an insult to the American Minister to Nicaragua.]

title: U.S. and European naval forces land in Montevideo
summary: U.S. and European naval forces landed in Uruguay to protect American interests during an attempted revolution in Montevideo.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: **1855—Uruguay**—U.S. and European naval forces landed to protect American interests during an attempted revolution in Montevideo.

title: Frederick Douglass speech on struggle and reform
summary: In 1857 Frederick Douglass delivered a speech articulating his philosophy that "power concedes nothing without a demand," arguing that all progress for human liberty had been born of struggle and that those who want freedom without agitation want crops without plowing.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: Frederick Douglass spoke in 1857: Let me give you a word of the philosophy of reforms. . . . Power concedes nothing without a demand. It never did and it never will. . . .

title: Supreme Court rules Dred Scott is property, not a person
summary: In 1857 the Supreme Court declared that the enslaved man Dred Scott could not sue for his freedom because he was not a person but property, cementing federal support for the slave system.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: It was the Supreme Court of the United States that declared in 1857 that the slave Dred Scott could not sue for his freedom because he was not a person, but property.

title: Economic crisis of 1857 leaves 200,000 unemployed
summary: Another economic crisis struck in 1857, driven by railroad speculation, immigration surges, stock manipulation, and corruption. By October, 200,000 were unemployed and thousands of recent immigrants crowded eastern ports hoping to work passage back to Europe.

citation.quote: Another economic crisis came in 1857. The boom in railroads and manufacturing, the surge of immigration, the increased speculation in stocks and bonds, the stealing, corruption, manipulation, led to wild expansion and then crash. By October of that year, 200,000 were unemployed...

title: Lincoln's contradictory statements on race during Illinois Senate campaign
summary: During his 1858 Illinois Senate campaign, Lincoln told northern audiences that all men are created equal while telling southern Illinois audiences that he had never favored social or political equality of the races and supported white superiority.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: In his 1858 campaign in Illinois for the Senate against Stephen Douglas, Lincoln spoke differently depending on the views of his listeners...

title: Slave Abream Scriven writes farewell letter to wife after being sold
summary: In 1858 an enslaved man named Abream Scriven was sold away from his wife and wrote her a letter expressing his love and his hope to meet her in heaven, illustrating the brutal tearing apart of Black families under slavery.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: In 1858, a slave named Abream Scriven was sold by his master, and wrote to his wife: "Give my love to my father and mother and tell them good Bye for me, and if we Shall not meet in this world I hope to meet in heaven."

title: John Brown hanged after Harpers Ferry raid
summary: John Brown was hanged in 1859 with federal complicity after his attempt to seize the federal arsenal at Harpers Ferry, Virginia, and spark a slave rebellion. His last written statement declared that the crimes of the nation would never be purged away but with blood.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: In 1859, John Brown was hanged, with federal complicity, for attempting to do by small-scale violence what Lincoln would do by large-scale violence several years later—end slavery.

title: U.S. forces deploy to Shanghai
summary: U.S. forces deployed to Shanghai for the protection of American interests.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: **1859—China**—For the protection of American interests in Shanghai.

title: Lincoln elected President; southern states begin to secede
summary: Lincoln was elected President in the fall of 1860 as the candidate of the new Republican Party, triggering the secession of seven southern states and then four more after he tried to repossess Fort Sumter, leading to the Civil War.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: Behind the secession of the South from the Union, after Lincoln was elected President in the fall of 1860 as candidate of the new Republican party, was a long series of policy clashes between South and North.

title: New York proposal to abolish Black property requirement for voting defeated
summary: A proposal put on the ballot in 1860 to abolish New York's requirement that Black men own $250 in property to vote (a qualification not applied to whites) was defeated two to one, even as Lincoln carried New York by 50,000 votes.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: A proposal to abolish this, put on the ballot in 1860, was defeated two to one (although Lincoln carried New York by 50,000 votes).

title: Wendell Phillips speaks at Tremont Temple the day after Lincoln's election
summary: The day after Lincoln's election in 1860, Wendell Phillips spoke at the Tremont Temple in Boston, calling Lincoln 'a pawn on the political chessboard' whose antislavery value lay in his position and who could, with effort, be moved toward more radical action.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: Speaking at the Tremont Temple in Boston the day after the election, Phillips said: If the telegraph speaks truth, for the first time in our history the slave has chosen a President of the United States. . . . Not an Abolitionist, hardly an antislavery man, Mr. Lincoln consents to represent an antislavery idea.

title: Lynn shoemakers call great strike on Washington's Birthday
summary: In early 1860, three thousand shoemakers met in Lyceum Hall in Lynn and launched a strike on Washington's Birthday against wage cuts of $3 a week for men and $1 for women. Shoeworkers across New England joined within days, with twenty thousand on strike in twenty-five towns.

citation.quote: In early 1860, a mass meeting of the newly formed Mechanics Association demanded higher wages. When the manufacturers refused to meet with their committees, the workers called a strike for Washington's Birthday. That morning three thousand shoemakers met in the Lyceum Hall in Lynn...

title: Procession of ten thousand workers marches through Lynn
summary: Ten days after the women's procession, a procession of ten thousand striking workers including delegations from Salem, Marblehead, and other towns marched through Lynn in what was the greatest labor demonstration in New England up to that time.

citation.quote: Ten days after that, a procession of ten thousand striking workers, including delegations from Salem, Marblehead, and other towns, men and women, marched through Lynn, in what was the greatest demonstration of labor to take place in New England up to that time.

title: Pemberton Mill collapses in Lawrence, Massachusetts, killing 88
summary: In Lawrence, Massachusetts in 1860, the Pemberton Mill collapsed on a winter day with nine hundred workers inside, mostly women; eighty-eight died. Despite evidence the structure was never adequate, a jury found no criminal intent.

citation.quote: In Lawrence, Massachusetts, in 1860, on a winter day, the Pemberton Mill collapsed, with nine hundred workers inside, mostly women. Eighty-eight died, and although there was evidence that the structure had never been adequate to support the heavy machinery inside, and that this was known to the construction engineer, a jury found "no evidence of criminal intent."

title: U.S. coal production reaches 14 million tons
summary: In 1860, 14 million tons of coal were mined in the United States; by 1884 this had grown to 100 million tons, fueling the industrial expansion of the era.

citation.quote: In 1860, 14 million tons of coal were mined; by 1884 it was 100 million tons.

title: U.S. forces land at Kissembo, Angola
summary: U.S. forces landed at Kissembo in Portuguese West Africa to protect American lives and property.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: **1860—Angola, Portuguese West Africa**—To protect American lives and property at Kissembo when the natives became troublesome.

title: Congress resolution: war is not to end slavery but to preserve the Union
summary: In the summer of 1861, Congress passed a resolution with only a few dissenting votes declaring that the war was not waged to overthrow or interfere with established institutions of Southern states, but only to preserve the Union.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: The spirit of Congress, even after the war began, was shown in a resolution it passed in the summer of 1861, with only a few dissenting votes: ". . . this war is not waged . . . for any purpose of . . . overthrowing or interfering with the rights of established institutions of those states, but . . . to preserve the Union."

title: Morrill Tariff passed by Congress
summary: Congress passed the Morrill Tariff in 1861, making foreign goods more expensive, allowing American manufacturers to raise prices, and forcing consumers to pay more—a key business-interest benefit under Republican legislation.

citation.quote: Now Congress in 1861 passed the Morrill Tariff. This made foreign goods more expensive, allowed American manufacturers to raise their prices, and forced American consumers to pay more.

title: Lincoln's first Inaugural Address promises not to touch slavery
summary: In his first Inaugural Address in March 1861, Lincoln was conciliatory toward the seceded Southern states, explicitly stating he had no purpose, direct or indirect, to interfere with slavery where it existed.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: Lincoln's first Inaugural Address, in March 1861, was conciliatory toward the South and the seceded states: "I have no purpose, directly or indirectly, to interfere with the institution of slavery in the States where it exists."

title: Homestead Act passed
summary: In 1862 the Homestead Act gave 160 acres of western land to anyone who would cultivate it for five years, but few ordinary people had the funds to buy; speculators acquired much of the land. During the Civil War, over 100 million acres were also given to railroads free of charge.
