citation.quote: The following year a Homestead Act was passed. It gave 160 acres of western land, unoccupied and publicly owned, to anyone who would cultivate it for five years.

title: Rockefeller buys his first oil refinery
summary: John D. Rockefeller bought his first oil refinery in 1862, beginning his path to controlling the oil industry through Standard Oil.

citation.quote: He bought his first oil refinery in 1862, and by 1870 set up Standard Oil Company of Ohio, made secret agreements with railroads to ship his oil with them if they gave him rebates—discounts—on their prices, and thus drove competitors out of business.

title: Congress passes Confiscation Act enabling freeing of rebel-owned slaves
summary: In July 1862 Congress passed a Confiscation Act enabling the freeing of slaves owned by those fighting against the Union, but Lincoln ignored its nonenforcement by Union generals.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: In July Congress passed a Confiscation Act, which enabled the freeing of slaves of those fighting the Union.

title: Lincoln–Greeley exchange of letters on slavery and the Union
summary: In August 1862 Lincoln responded to editor Horace Greeley's open letter demanding enforcement of emancipation measures, stating that his paramount object was to save the Union and not to save or destroy slavery, distinguishing his 'official duty' from his 'personal wish.'

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: An exchange of letters between Lincoln and Horace Greeley, editor of the New York *Tribune,* in August of 1862, gave Lincoln a chance to express his views.

title: Lincoln issues preliminary Emancipation Proclamation
summary: In September 1862 Lincoln issued his preliminary Emancipation Proclamation as a military move, giving the South four months to stop rebelling and threatening to emancipate their slaves if they continued fighting while promising to leave slavery untouched in states that rejoined the Union.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: When in September 1862, Lincoln issued his preliminary Emancipation Proclamation, it was a military move, giving the South four months to stop rebelling, threatening to emancipate their slaves if they continued to fight, promising to leave slavery untouched in states that came over to the North...

title: Draft riots in northern cities target Black people
summary: The draft riots of 1863 erupted as angry white working-class men in northern cities rebelled against a draft law that allowed rich men to buy their way out for $300; their violence was directed not at the wealthy but at nearby Black communities.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: And so the draft riots of 1863 took place, uprisings of angry whites in northern cities, their targets not the rich, far away, but the blacks, near at hand.

title: Strikes break out across the country during the Civil War
summary: During 1863, strikes spread widely across the United States. The Springfield Republican reported that workmen of almost every branch of trade had struck within the last few months, and Philadelphia shoemakers announced that high prices made organization imperative.

citation.quote: The Springfield Republican in 1863 said that "the workmen of almost every branch of trade have had their strikes within the last few months," and the San Francisco Evening Bulletin said "striking for higher wages is now the rage among the working people of San Francisco."

title: New York working women form Working Women's Protective Union
summary: In late 1863, New York working women held a mass meeting and formed a Working Women's Protective Union. A strike of women umbrella workers followed in New York and Brooklyn, and a Ladies Cigar Makers Union was organized in Providence.

citation.quote: In late 1863, New York working women held a mass meeting to find a solution to their problems. A Working Women's Protective Union was formed, and there was a strike of women umbrella workers in New York and Brooklyn.

title: Confederate bread riot in Richmond
summary: In April 1863, there was a bread riot in Richmond. That summer, draft riots occurred in various southern cities, and in September a bread riot erupted in Mobile, Alabama, revealing widespread disaffection beneath Confederate unity.

citation.quote: In April 1863, there was a bread riot in Richmond. That summer, draft riots occurred in various southern cities. In September, a bread riot in Mobile, Alabama.

title: Emancipation Proclamation takes effect
summary: On January 1, 1863, the Emancipation Proclamation declared slaves free only in areas still in rebellion against the Union, leaving slavery untouched behind Union lines. Critics noted it had, as Hofstadter put it, 'all the moral grandeur of a bill of lading.'

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: Thus, when the Emancipation Proclamation was issued January 1, 1863, it declared slaves free in those areas still fighting against the Union (which it listed very carefully), and said nothing about slaves behind Union lines.

title: South Carolina Sea Islands land sale; freedmen buy only 2,000 of 16,000 acres
summary: In March 1863, 16,000 acres in the South Carolina Sea Islands were put up for sale; freedmen who pooled their money could afford only 2,000 acres, while the rest were bought by northern investors and speculators.
location: South Carolina Sea Islands, South Carolina

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: In the South Carolina Sea Islands, out of 16,000 acres up for sale in March of 1863, freedmen who pooled their money were able to buy 2,000 acres, the rest being bought by northern investors and speculators.

title: New York City draft riots: four hundred killed
summary: When army recruiting began in July 1863, a mob wrecked the main recruiting station in New York City. For three days, white workers attacked draft headquarters, wealthy homes, factories, and Black residents. On the fourth day, Union troops from Gettysburg stopped the rioting; perhaps four hundred people were killed.

citation.quote: When recruiting for the army began in July 1863, a mob in New York wrecked the main recruiting station. Then, for three days, crowds of white workers marched through the city, destroying buildings, factories, streetcar lines, homes.

title: Fincher's Trades' Review headlines labor upheaval in New York
summary: The headline in Fincher's Trades' Review of November 21, 1863, "THE REVOLUTION IN NEW YORK," catalogued sweeping labor activities—machinists, railroad employees, house painters, carpenters, safe-makers, printers, and many other trades striking or winning wage increases.

citation.quote: The headline in Fincher's Trades' Review of November 21, 1863, "THE REVOLUTION IN NEW YORK," was an exaggeration, but its list of labor activities was impressive evidence of the hidden resentments of the poor during the war:

title: 400,000 signatures for legislation to end slavery sent to Congress
summary: By the summer of 1864, an unprecedented 400,000 signatures petitioning for legislation to end slavery had been gathered and sent to Congress. That April, the Senate had adopted the Thirteenth Amendment.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: By the summer of 1864, 400,000 signatures asking legislation to end slavery had been gathered and sent to Congress, something unprecedented in the history of the country. That April, the Senate had adopted the Thirteenth Amendment, declaring an end to slavery, and in January 1865, the House of Representatives followed.

title: 200,000 workers in trade unions across the country
summary: By 1864, about 200,000 workers, men and women, were in trade unions, with national unions forming in some trades and labor newspapers being published.

citation.quote: All together, by 1864, about 200,000 workers, men and women, were in trade unions, forming national unions in some of the trades, putting out labor newspapers.

title: Contract Labor Law of 1864 enables strikebreaking with imported workers
summary: The Contract Labor Law of 1864 allowed companies to sign contracts with foreign workers who pledged twelve months of wages to pay emigration costs, giving employers cheap labor and strikebreakers during the Civil War.

citation.quote: The Contract Labor Law of 1864 made it possible for companies to sign contracts with foreign workers whenever the workers pledged to give twelve months of their wages to pay the cost of emigration.

title: Confederate troops massacre Union soldiers at Fort Pillow
summary: In April 1864 Confederate troops at Fort Pillow, Kentucky, massacred Union soldiers who had surrendered—Black and white—along with women and children in an adjoining camp.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: They suffered the fate of soldiers, as in April 1864, when Confederate troops at Fort Pillow, Kentucky, massacred Union soldiers who had surrendered—black and white, along with women and children in an adjoining camp.

title: Congress grants equal pay to Black soldiers
summary: In June 1864 Congress passed a law granting equal pay to Black soldiers, after Black sergeant William Walker had been court-martialed and shot for leading a protest against unequal pay.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: Finally, in June 1864, Congress passed a law granting equal pay to Negro soldiers.

title: Sherman's Special Field Order No. 15 reserves coastal land for Black settlement
summary: In early 1865 General William T. Sherman issued Special Field Order No. 15, designating the entire southern coastline thirty miles inland for exclusive Black settlement, allowing families up to forty acres. By June 1865, forty thousand freedmen had settled, but President Andrew Johnson reversed the order in August 1865.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: In early 1865, General William T. Sherman held a conference in Savannah, Georgia, with twenty Negro ministers and church officials, mostly former slaves, at which one of them expressed their need: "The way we can best take care of ourselves is to have land, and till it by our labor. . . ." Four days later Sherman issued "Special Field Order No. 15," designating the entire southern coastline 30 miles inland for exclusive Negro settlement.

title: Mississippi enacts black codes restricting freedmen
summary: In 1865 Mississippi enacted Black Codes making it illegal for freedmen to rent or lease farmland, subjecting them to unbreakable labor contracts with penalty of prison, and allowing courts to assign Black children to forced 'apprenticeships'—effectively re-enslaving freed people.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: During his presidency, these returned southern states enacted "black codes," which made the freed slaves like serfs, still working the plantations. For instance, Mississippi in 1865 made it illegal for freedmen to rent or lease farmland, and provided for them to work under labor contracts which they could not break under penalty of prison.

title: House of Representatives adopts Thirteenth Amendment
summary: In January 1865 the House of Representatives followed the Senate in adopting the Thirteenth Amendment, constitutionally abolishing slavery in the United States.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: That April, the Senate had adopted the Thirteenth Amendment, declaring an end to slavery, and in January 1865, the House of Representatives followed.

title: Confederate President Davis signs Negro Soldier Law
summary: In March 1865, under mounting desperation, Confederate President Davis signed a 'Negro Soldier Law' authorizing the enlistment of enslaved people as soldiers to be freed with owner consent, but the war ended before it had any significant effect.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: By early 1865, the pressure had mounted, and in March President Davis of the Confederacy signed a "Negro Soldier Law" authorizing the enlistment of slaves as soldiers, to be freed by consent of their owners and their state governments.

title: Fincher's Trades' Review reports veterans flooding the streets seeking work
summary: In June 1865, Fincher's Trades' Review reported that returned soldiers were "flooding the streets already, unable to find employment," as disbanded armies returned to cities marked by typhus, tuberculosis, and desperate poverty.

citation.quote: In June 1865, Fincher's Trades' Review reported: "As was to be expected, the returned soldiers are flooding the streets already, unable to find employment."

title: President Johnson restores Sherman's land grant to Confederate owners
summary: In August 1865 President Andrew Johnson restored to Confederate owners the land that Sherman had set aside for Black settlement, forcing forty thousand freedmen off their new farms, some at bayonet point.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: But President Andrew Johnson, in August of 1865, restored this land to the Confederate owners, and the freedmen were forced off, some at bayonet point.

title: New Orleans riot kills thirty-five Black people and three whites
summary: In the summer of 1866 a riot against Black people in New Orleans killed thirty-five Black people and three whites, part of a wave of white supremacist violence accompanying Reconstruction.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: In New Orleans, in the summer of 1866, another riot against blacks killed thirty-five Negroes and three whites.

title: Mill fire in Providence kills workers who jump from upper stories
summary: At a mill in Providence, Rhode Island, a fire broke out one night in 1866 with six hundred workers, mostly women, inside. Many jumped to their deaths from upper-story windows in the ensuing panic.

citation.quote: At a mill in Providence, Rhode Island, fire broke out one night in 1866. There was panic among the six hundred workers, mostly women, and many jumped to their deaths from upper-story windows.

title: Memphis massacre: whites kill forty-six Black people
summary: In May 1866 in Memphis, Tennessee, white rioters killed forty-six Black people, most of them Union army veterans, as well as two white sympathizers, and raped five Black women; ninety homes, twelve schools, and four churches were burned.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: In Memphis, Tennessee, in May of 1866, whites on a rampage of murder killed forty-six Negroes, most of them veterans of the Union army, as well as two white sympathizers. Five Negro women were raped. Ninety homes, twelve schools, and four churches were burned.

title: Black levee workers strike in Mobile, Alabama
summary: Black workers found the National Labor Union reluctant to organize them, so they formed their own unions and carried on their own strikes—including the levee workers in Mobile, Alabama, in 1867, Negro longshoremen in Charleston, and dockworkers in Savannah.

citation.quote: So they formed their own unions and carried on their own strikes—like the levee workers in Mobile, Alabama, in 1867, Negro longshoremen in Charleston, dockworkers in Savannah.

title: Georgia legislature expels all its Black members
summary: In 1868 the Georgia legislature voted to expel all its Black members—two senators and twenty-five representatives—prompting Henry MacNeal Turner's powerful speech demanding his rights and condemning the unprecedented act of expelling men solely for the color of their skin.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: In 1868, the Georgia legislature voted to expel all its Negro members—two senators, twenty-five representatives—and Turner spoke to the Georgia House of Representatives...

title: Andrew Johnson impeached; Ulysses Grant elected President
summary: Congress impeached Andrew Johnson in 1868 but fell one vote short of removing him; that same year Republican Ulysses Grant won the presidential election by 300,000 votes, aided by 700,000 Black voters, ending Johnson's obstruction of Reconstruction.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: These members of Congress succeeded in impeaching Johnson in 1868, using as an excuse that he had violated some minor statute, but the Senate fell one vote short of the two-thirds required to remove him from office. In the presidential election of that year, Republican Ulysses Grant was elected, winning by 300,000 votes, with 700,000 Negroes voting...

title: Anti-Rent "Indians" still resisting in Hudson Valley
summary: As late as 1869, bands of Anti-Rent "Indians" were still assembling to thwart sheriffs acting for wealthy landowner Walter Church in the Hudson Valley.

citation.quote: As late as 1869, bands of "Indians" were still assembling to thwart sheriffs acting for a rich valley landowner named Walter Church.

title: Collar laundresses of Troy, New York strike
summary: In 1869, the collar laundresses of Troy, New York, working in extreme heat for $2–$3 a week, went on strike. Their leader Kate Mullaney was second vice-president of the National Labor Union; seven thousand people rallied in support but the strike ultimately failed.

citation.quote: In 1869, the collar laundresses of Troy, New York, whose work involved standing "over the wash tub and over the ironing table with furnaces on either side, the thermometer averaging 100 degrees, for wages averaging $2.00 and $3.00 a week" (according to a contemporary account), went on strike.

title: National Labor Union convention resolves to organize women and Negroes
summary: At its 1869 convention, the National Labor Union resolved to organize women and Negroes, declaring it recognized "neither color nor sex on the question of the rights of labor," a remarkable show of racial unity noted by a journalist.

citation.quote: This probably stimulated the National Labor Union, at its 1869 convention, to resolve to organize women and Negroes, declaring that it recognized "neither color nor sex on the question of the rights of labor."

title: Pennsylvania legislature passes mine safety act
summary: The Pennsylvania legislature passed a mine safety act in 1869 providing for regulation and ventilation of mines and protection of miners' lives, though a hundred years of continuing accidents would demonstrate how insufficient the law proved in practice.

citation.quote: The Pennsylvania legislature in 1869 passed a mine safety act providing for the "regulation and ventilation of mines, and for the protection of the lives of the miners."

title: Transcontinental railroad lines meet in Utah
summary: The Union Pacific and Central Pacific railroads met in Utah in 1869, completing the first transcontinental railroad built through bribery, government subsidies, and the labor of thousands of Irish and Chinese workers.

citation.quote: In 1869, amid music and speeches, the two crooked lines met in Utah.

title: Wan Lee stoned to death in San Francisco
summary: A Chinese man named Wan Lee was stoned to death in the streets of San Francisco in 1869 by a mob of youths and children, as described in Bret Harte's obituary for him.

citation.quote: Dead, my revered friends, dead. Stoned to death in the streets of San Francisco, in the year of grace 1869 by a mob of halfgrown boys and Christian school children.

title: Rockefeller sets up Standard Oil Company of Ohio
summary: By 1870, John D. Rockefeller had set up the Standard Oil Company of Ohio and began making secret agreements with railroads to drive competitors out of business.

citation.quote: He bought his first oil refinery in 1862, and by 1870 set up Standard Oil Company of Ohio, made secret agreements with railroads to ship his oil with them if they gave him rebates—discounts—on their prices, and thus drove competitors out of business.

title: U.S. cavalry destroys sleeping Piegan Indian camp in Montana
summary: Two hundred U.S. cavalrymen attacked and wiped out a sleeping camp of Piegan Indians in Montana. Zinn cites this alongside other massacres of nonwhite people suppressed in mainstream American historical memory.

citation.quote: Or the military attack by 200 U.S. cavalrymen in 1870 which wiped out a sleeping camp of Piegan Indians in Montana?

title: Carnegie travels to London and sees Bessemer steel process
summary: Andrew Carnegie went to London in 1872, observed the new Bessemer method of producing steel, and returned to the United States to build a million-dollar steel plant.

citation.quote: He went to London in 1872, saw the new Bessemer method of producing steel, and returned to the United States to build a million-dollar steel plant.

title: 150,000 workers parade in New York City after eight-hour-day victory
summary: A three-month strike of 100,000 workers in New York won the eight-hour day, and at a victory celebration in June 1872, 150,000 workers paraded through the city. The New York Times questioned what proportion were "thoroughly American."

citation.quote: A three-month strike of 100,000 workers in New York won the eight-hour day, and at a victory celebration in June 1872, 150,000 workers paraded through the city.

title: United States enters economic depression
summary: The country had been in economic depression since 1873, and by 1877 farmers and workers were beginning to rebel against the new capitalist order, creating conditions that pushed northern business interests to ally with the white South against Black rights.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: The country had been in economic depression since 1873, and by 1877 farmers and workers were beginning to rebel.

title: Jay Cooke locks his bank, triggering financial panic
summary: On September 18, 1873, while President Grant slept in Cooke's Philadelphia mansion, banker Jay Cooke rode downtown and locked the door on his bank, triggering a wave of financial panic in which five thousand businesses closed.

citation.quote: It was the closing of the banking house of Jay Cooke—the banker who during the war had made $3 million a year in commissions alone for selling government bonds—that started the wave of panic. While President Grant slept in Cooke's Philadelphia mansion on September 18, 1873, the banker rode downtown to lock the door on his bank.

title: Ninety thousand workers sleep in New York police stations
summary: During the first three months of 1874, ninety thousand workers, almost half of them women, had to sleep in police stations in New York. Known as "revolvers," they were limited to one or two days per station and had to keep moving as people were evicted and roamed cities looking for food.

citation.quote: During the first three months of 1874, ninety thousand workers, almost half of them women, had to sleep in police stations in New York.

title: Police attack workers' demonstration at Tompkins Square in New York
summary: In January 1874, a huge parade of workers in New York City was barred from approaching City Hall and moved to Tompkins Square, where police told them they couldn't meet. When they stayed, police attacked with clubs, riding down bystanders and beating women and children.

citation.quote: In January 1874, in New York City, a huge parade of workers, kept by the police from approaching City Hall, went to Tompkins Square, and there were told by the police they couldn't have the meeting. They stayed, and the police attacked.

title: Civil Rights Act of 1875 outlaws exclusion of Black people from public accommodations
summary: In 1875 Congress passed a Civil Rights Act outlawing the exclusion of Black people from hotels, theaters, railroads, and other public accommodations, a measure that was later struck down by the Supreme Court in 1883.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: And in 1875, a Civil Rights Act outlawed the exclusion of Negroes from hotels, theaters, railroads, and other public accommodations.

title: J. P. Morgan appears as director of southern railroad lines
summary: By 1875 J. P. Morgan appears in directories as director of several railroad lines in Alabama and Georgia, marking the penetration of northern finance capital into the post-Reconstruction South.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: J. P. Morgan appears by 1875 as director for several lines in Alabama and Georgia.

title: Charles Caldwell shot to death by white gang in Mississippi
summary: On Christmas Day 1875, Charles Caldwell—a formerly enslaved blacksmith, Mississippi state senator, and the first Black man acquitted in Mississippi for killing a white man in self-defense—was shot to death by a white gang, signaling the violent reversal of Reconstruction in the state.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: But on Christmas Day 1875, Caldwell was shot to death by a white gang. It was a sign. The old white rulers were taking back political power in Mississippi, and everywhere else in the South.

title: Centennial declarations by Negro and labor organizations denounce inequality
summary: In the centennial year of 1876, a "Negro Declaration of Independence" denounced the Republican party and proposed independent political action by colored voters, while the Workingmen's party of Illinois at a July 4 German socialist gathering in Chicago issued its own Declaration of Independence condemning capitalist rule.

citation.quote: The centennial year of 1876—one hundred years after the Declaration of Independence—brought forth a number of new declarations... the Workingmen's party of Illinois, at a July 4 celebration organized by German socialists in Chicago, said in its Declaration of Independence:

title: Popular vote winner loses presidency due to Electoral College
summary: As in the 2000 election, the winner of the popular vote failed to win the presidency because of the Electoral College system. Zinn notes this had happened twice before—in 1876 and 1888.

citation.chapter: Chapter 25 – The 2000 Election and the "War on Terrorism"
citation.quote: This difference between popular vote and electoral vote had happened twice before, in 1876 and 1888.

title: Compromise of 1877 ends Reconstruction
summary: The disputed presidential election of 1876–77 was resolved by the Compromise of 1877, awarding the presidency to Republican Rutherford Hayes in exchange for removing Union troops from the South, effectively ending Reconstruction and restoring white supremacist rule.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: It was the year 1877 that spelled out clearly and dramatically what was happening. When the year opened, the presidential election of the past November was in bitter dispute. The Democratic candidate, Samuel Tilden, had 184 votes and needed one more to be elected: his popular vote was greater by 250,000.

title: Great Railroad Strike of 1877 begins in Martinsburg, West Virginia
summary: The great railroad strike of 1877 began at the Baltimore & Ohio station in Martinsburg, West Virginia, when workers struck against a wage cut, ran engines into the roundhouse, and stopped all trains. A striker was shot and later died; federal troops were eventually sent in.

citation.quote: At the Baltimore & Ohio station in Martinsburg, West Virginia, workers determined to fight the wage cut went on strike, uncoupled the engines, ran them into the roundhouse, and announced no more trains would leave Martinsburg until the 10 percent cut was canceled.

title: Railroad strike violence in Baltimore: ten killed
summary: In Baltimore, thousands surrounded the National Guard armory called out at the B&O Railroad's request. Soldiers fired on the rock-throwing crowd, and in the running battle ten men or boys were killed and more badly wounded. Fifteen thousand surrounded the depot before federal troops restored order.

citation.quote: In Baltimore, a crowd of thousands sympathetic to the railroad strikers surrounded the armory of the National Guard, which had been called out by the governor at the request of the B. & O. Railroad... When the evening was over, ten men or boys were dead, more badly wounded, one soldier wounded.

title: Pittsburgh railroad strike: twenty-four killed, seventy-nine buildings burned
summary: The railroad strike spread to Pittsburgh where crowds fought Philadelphia militia troops; at least ten workers were killed in initial gunfire. The whole city rose, buildings and rail cars were set afire, and in a few days twenty-four people were dead and seventy-nine buildings burned to the ground.

citation.quote: In a few days, twenty-four people had been killed (including four soldiers). Seventy-nine buildings had been burned to the ground. Something like a general strike was developing in Pittsburgh: mill workers, car workers, miners, laborers, and the employees at the Carnegie steel plant.

title: Chicago Workingmen's Party rally draws six thousand; Albert Parsons blacklisted
summary: During the railroad strikes in the summer of 1877, the Chicago Workingmen's Party called a rally attended by six thousand people demanding nationalization of the railroads. Speaker Albert Parsons was fired from his Chicago Times job and blacklisted the next day after young workers shut down the city.

citation.quote: In the midst of the railroad strikes, that summer of 1877, it called a rally. Six thousand people came and demanded nationalization of the railroads. Albert Parsons gave a fiery speech.

title: St. Louis general strike: Workingmen's Party leads near-total shutdown
summary: In St. Louis during the 1877 railroad strikes, the Workingmen's Party led a near-complete shutdown of all industry. Five thousand attended an open-air meeting calling for nationalization of railroads and mines. A black man's appeal for solidarity was cheered. Historian Burbank called it the closest any American city came to being ruled by a workers' soviet.

citation.quote: In St. Louis, itself, the Workingmen's party called an open-air mass meeting to which five thousand people came. The party was clearly in the leadership of the strike.

title: Railroad strikes of 1877 end: a hundred dead, thousand jailed, 100,000 strikers
summary: When the great railroad strikes of 1877 were over, a hundred people were dead, a thousand had gone to jail, and 100,000 workers had struck. More than half the freight on 75,000 miles of track had stopped running at the height of the strikes.

citation.quote: When the great railroad strikes of 1877 were over, a hundred people were dead, a thousand people had gone to jail, 100,000 workers had gone on strike, and the strikes had roused into action countless unemployed in the cities.

title: Supreme Court approves state laws regulating grain elevator prices
summary: In 1877, the Supreme Court ruled in Munn v. Illinois that grain elevators were invested with a 'public interest' and thus could be regulated by state law, rejecting the argument that such regulation violated the Fourteenth Amendment.

citation.quote: However, in 1877, a Supreme Court decision (Munn v. Illinois) approved state laws regulating the prices charged to farmers for the use of grain elevators.

title: Socialist Labor Party formed
summary: The Socialist Labor Party was formed in 1877; though small and internally divided, it had some influence organizing unions among foreign workers.

citation.quote: The Socialist Labor party, formed in 1877, was tiny, and torn by internal arguments, but it had some influence in organizing unions among foreign workers.

title: Farmers Alliance formed in Texas during depression
summary: In the height of the 1877 depression, white farmers in Texas gathered on a farm and formed the first Farmers Alliance; within a few years it spread across the state and eventually grew into the Populist movement.

citation.quote: In the height of the 1877 Depression, a group of white farmers gathered together on a farm in Texas and formed the first "Farmers Alliance." In a few years, it was across the state.

title: SS Metropolis sinks with laborers bound for South America
summary: In 1878, the SS Metropolis, filled with laborers leaving the United States for South America in desperation, sank with all aboard. An hour after news reached Philadelphia, hundreds of hungry men besieged the office begging for the places of the drowned.

citation.quote: In 1878, the SS Metropolis, filled with laborers, left the United States for South America and sank with all aboard.

title: Henry George publishes Progress and Poverty
summary: Henry George, a self-educated workingman turned economist, published Progress and Poverty in 1879, arguing that land was the basis of wealth, was being monopolized, and that a single land tax could solve poverty. The book sold millions of copies worldwide.

citation.quote: Henry George, a self-educated workingman from a poor Philadelphia family, who became a newspaperman and an economist, wrote a book that was published in 1879 and sold millions of copies, not only in the United States, but all over the world.

title: Henry Adams testifies before Senate on why Black people fled the South
summary: In 1880 Henry Adams, a Black veteran of the Union army, told a Senate committee why he left Shreveport, Louisiana, explaining that the whole South had gotten back into the hands of the very men who had held his people as slaves.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: Henry Adams, another black migrant, illiterate, a veteran of the Union army, told a Senate committee in 1880 why he left Shreveport, Louisiana: "We seed that the whole South—every state in the South—had got into the hands of the very men that held us slaves."

title: Black sugar field workers strike for a dollar a day in Louisiana
summary: In 1880, Black sugar field workers in Louisiana struck for a dollar a day instead of 75 cents, threatening to leave the state; strikers were repeatedly arrested but marched carrying banners reading 'a dollar a day or kansas.'

citation.quote: In 1880, they had struck to get a dollar a day instead of 75 cents, threatening to leave the state. Strikers were arrested and jailed, but they walked the roads along the sugar fields, carrying banners: "a dollar a day or kansas."

title: Supreme Court nullifies Civil Rights Act of 1875
summary: In 1883 the Supreme Court nullified the Civil Rights Act of 1875, ruling that the Fourteenth Amendment applied only to state action and not to individual discrimination, effectively ending federal protection against private racial discrimination.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: In 1883, the Civil Rights Act of 1875, outlawing discrimination against Negroes using public facilities, was nullified by the Supreme Court, which said: "Individual invasion of individual rights is not the subject-matter of the amendment."

title: Thomas Fortune testifies before Senate on conditions of Black Americans
summary: In 1883 Thomas Fortune, a young Black editor of the New York Globe, testified before a Senate committee describing widespread poverty, government betrayal, debt-peonage enforced by planter-controlled stores, chain-gang terror, and the systematic swindling of Black farm laborers earning about fifty cents a day.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: Thomas Fortune, a young black editor of the New York *Globe,* testified before a Senate committee in 1883 about the situation of the Negro in the United States. He spoke of "widespread poverty," of government betrayal, of desperate Negro attempts to educate themselves.

title: Anarchist congress held in Pittsburgh
summary: In 1883, an anarchist congress took place in Pittsburgh and drew up a manifesto calling for worker liberation, condemning the church, press, and capitalist parties, and quoting the Communist Manifesto.

citation.quote: In 1883, an anarchist congress took place in Pittsburgh. It drew up a manifesto:

title: Grover Cleveland elected President
summary: Grover Cleveland, a Democrat, was elected President in 1884, defeating Republican James Blaine. Despite a public image of opposing monopolies, Cleveland reassured industrialists that their interests would be safe under his administration.

citation.quote: When Grover Cleveland, a Democrat, ran for President in 1884, the general impression in the country was that he opposed the power of monopolies and corporations, and that the Republican party, whose candidate was James Blaine, stood for the wealthy. But when Cleveland defeated Blaine, Jay Gould wired him: "I feel . . . that the vast business interests of the country will be entirely safe in your hands."

title: Women textile workers and hatmakers go on strike
summary: In 1884, women's assemblies of textile workers and hatmakers went on strike, part of a wave of labor action by women workers affiliated with the Knights of Labor.

citation.quote: In 1884, women's assemblies of textile workers and hatmakers went on strike.

title: Gustavus Swift forms first national meatpacking company
summary: Gustavus Swift combined the ice-cooled railway car with the ice-cooled warehouse to create the first national meatpacking company in 1885.

citation.quote: Gustavus Swift, a Chicago butcher who put together the ice-cooled railway car with the ice-cooled warehouse to make the first national meatpacking company in 1885.

title: Massacre of Chinese miners at Rock Springs, Wyoming
summary: In the summer of 1885, whites attacked five hundred Chinese miners in Rock Springs, Wyoming, massacring twenty-eight of them.

citation.quote: In Rock Springs, Wyoming, in the summer of 1885, whites attacked five hundred Chinese miners, massacring twenty-eight of them in cold blood.

title: Henry Grady's 'New South' speech in New York
summary: In 1886 Henry Grady, editor of the Atlanta Constitution, spoke at a New York dinner attended by J. P. Morgan and other financiers, urging reconciliation between North and South under a 'New South' framework that glossed over continued racial oppression. He received a standing ovation.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: In the year 1886, Henry Grady, an editor of the Atlanta *Constitution,* spoke at a dinner in New York. In the audience were J. P. Morgan, H. M. Flagler (an associate of Rockefeller), Russell Sage, and Charles Tiffany.

title: Supreme Court strikes down 230 state laws regulating corporations
summary: In 1886, the Supreme Court in Wabash v. Illinois ruled that states could not regulate railroad rates, striking down 230 state laws that had been passed to regulate corporations.

citation.quote: By 1886, they succeeded. State legislatures, under the pressure of aroused farmers, had passed laws to regulate the rates charged farmers by the railroads. The Supreme Court that year (Wabash v. Illinois) said states could not do this, that this was an intrusion on federal power. That year alone, the Court did away with 230 state laws that had been passed to regulate corporations.

title: Knights of Labor has fifty thousand women members in 192 assemblies
summary: By 1886, the Knights of Labor had fifty thousand women members organized in 192 women's assemblies, and Leonora Barry was appointed as general investigator to educate and organize women workers.

citation.quote: She joined the Knights of Labor, which had fifty thousand women members in 192 women's assemblies by 1886.

title: Texas & Pacific Railroad strike spreads across Southwest
summary: In early 1886, the Texas & Pacific Railroad fired a Knights of Labor assembly leader, triggering a strike that spread throughout the Southwest, tying up traffic as far as St. Louis and Kansas City.

citation.quote: In early 1886, the Texas & Pacific Railroad fired a leader of the district assembly of the Knights of Labor, and this led to a strike which spread throughout the Southwest, tying up traffic as far as St. Louis and Kansas City.

title: Henry George runs for mayor of New York City
summary: In the fall of 1886, trade unions formed an Independent Labor party and nominated radical economist Henry George for mayor of New York City. George came second with 31% of the vote; Democrat Abram Hewitt won with 41%, and Republican Theodore Roosevelt came third.

citation.quote: Some of the energy of resentment in late 1886 was poured into the electoral campaign for mayor of New York that fall. Trade unions formed an Independent Labor party and nominated for mayor Henry George, the radical economist, whose Progress and Poverty had been read by tens of thousands of workers.

title: Over 1,400 strikes involving 500,000 workers — year of the great labor uprising
summary: The year 1886 became known as 'the year of the great uprising of labor,' with over 1,400 strikes involving 500,000 workers, compared to an average of about 500 strikes per year from 1881–1885.

citation.quote: The year 1886 became known to contemporaries as "the year of the great uprising of labor." From 1881 to 1885, strikes had averaged about 500 each year, involving perhaps 150,000 workers each year. In 1886 there were over 1,400 strikes, involving 500,000 workers.

title: Farmers Alliance issues Cleburne Demands — first document of Populist movement
summary: In the summer of 1886 in Cleburne, Texas, the Farmers Alliance drew up the 'Cleburne Demands,' calling for regulation of railroad rates, taxation of speculative land, and an increase in the money supply — the first document of the Populist movement.

citation.quote: In the summer of 1886, in the town of Cleburne, near Dallas, the Alliance gathered and drew up what came to be known as the "Cleburne Demands"—the first document of the Populist movement, asking "such legislation as shall secure to our people freedom from the onerous and shameful abuses that the industrial classes are now suffering at the hands of arrogant capitalists and powerful corporations."

title: Nationwide strikes for eight-hour day involving 350,000 workers
summary: On May 1, 1886, the American Federation of Labor called for nationwide strikes wherever the eight-hour day was refused; 350,000 workers in 11,562 establishments went out on strike across the country.

citation.quote: So, 350,000 workers in 11,562 establishments all over the country went out on strike.

title: Police fire on strikers at McCormick Harvester Works, killing four
summary: On May 3, 1886, police fired into a crowd of strikers and sympathizers fleeing from fighting outside the McCormick Harvester Works in Chicago, wounding many and killing four. August Spies responded by printing a circular calling workers to arms.

citation.quote: On May 3, a series of events took place which were to put Parsons and Spies in exactly the position that the Chicago Mail had suggested . . . . That day, in front of the McCormick Harvester Works, where strikers and sympathizers fought scabs, the police fired into a crowd of strikers running from the scene, wounded many of them, and killed four.

title: Haymarket Square bombing kills police and workers in Chicago
summary: On May 4, 1886, a meeting at Haymarket Square in Chicago was interrupted when police advanced on the crowd; a bomb exploded among the police, wounding 66 (seven later died), and police fired into the crowd, killing several and wounding two hundred.

citation.quote: A meeting was called for Haymarket Square on the evening of May 4, and about three thousand persons assembled. . . . A bomb then exploded in the midst of the police, wounding sixty-six policemen, of whom seven later died. The police fired into the crowd, killing several people, wounding two hundred.

title: Cleveland vetoes relief for Texas drought farmers
summary: In 1887, President Cleveland vetoed a bill appropriating $100,000 to help Texas farmers buy seed grain during a drought, saying federal aid weakened national character, while that same year using a treasury surplus to pay wealthy bondholders $45 million above face value.

citation.quote: In 1887, with a huge surplus in the treasury, Cleveland vetoed a bill appropriating $100,000 to give relief to Texas farmers to help them buy seed grain during a drought.

title: Interstate Commerce Act passed
summary: The Interstate Commerce Act of 1887 was ostensibly designed to regulate railroads on behalf of consumers, but railroad lawyer and future Attorney General Richard Olney noted it could be made to serve railroad interests while pacifying public criticism.

citation.quote: The Interstate Commerce Act of 1887 was supposed to regulate the railroads on behalf of the consumers.

title: Four Haymarket anarchists hanged; Louis Lingg dies in cell
summary: A year after the Haymarket trial, four convicted anarchists — Albert Parsons, August Spies, Adolph Fischer, and George Engel — were hanged. Louis Lingg, 21, killed himself in his cell by exploding a dynamite tube in his mouth.

citation.quote: A year after the trial, four of the convicted anarchists—Albert Parsons, a printer, August Spies, an upholsterer, Adolph Fischer, and George Engel—were hanged. Louis Lingg, a twenty-one-year-old carpenter, blew himself up in his cell by exploding a dynamite tube in his mouth.

title: Ten thousand sugar laborers strike in Louisiana; militia arrives and Thibodaux massacre follows
summary: In the fall of 1887, close to ten thousand sugar laborers in Louisiana — 90% Black and members of the Knights of Labor — went on strike for a dollar a day; the militia arrived, and on November 22 thirty Black workers were killed in the Thibodaux massacre.

citation.quote: The following year, in the fall, close to ten thousand sugar laborers went on strike, 90 percent of them Negroes and members of the Knights. The militia arrived and gun battles began.

title: Allotment Act attempts to break up Indian reservations
summary: In 1887 the Allotment Act tried to dissolve Indian reservations into individually owned small plots, but much of the land was seized by white speculators and the reservations largely remained.

citation.quote: In 1887, an Allotment Act tried to break up the reservations into small plots of land owned by individual Indians, to turn them into American-type small farmers—but much of this land was taken by white speculators, and the reservations remained.

title: Thibodaux massacre: thirty Black strikers killed
summary: On the night of November 22, 1887, shooting broke out in Thibodaux, Louisiana, where striking sugar workers had gathered; by the next day thirty Black workers were dead or dying and hundreds were wounded, while only two whites were wounded.

citation.quote: On the night of November 22, shooting broke out, each side claiming the other was at fault; by noon the next day, thirty Negroes were dead or dying, and hundreds wounded. Two whites were wounded.

title: Popular vote winner again loses presidency to Electoral College
summary: For the second time in U.S. history, the Electoral College produced a president who had lost the popular vote. This precedent was cited when the same outcome occurred in 2000.

citation.chapter: Chapter 25 – The 2000 Election and the "War on Terrorism"
citation.quote: This difference between popular vote and electoral vote had happened twice before, in 1876 and 1888.

title: 22,000 railroad workers killed or injured in one year
summary: Interstate Commerce Commission records for 1889 showed that 22,000 railroad workers were killed or injured that year, highlighting the deadly human cost of the railroad industry's rapid expansion.

citation.quote: That year, 1889, records of the Interstate Commerce Commission showed that 22,000 railroad workers were killed or injured.

title: Average of two Black Americans lynched per week
summary: In the years between 1889 and 1903, on average every week two Black Americans were lynched by mobs—hanged, burned, or mutilated.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: In the years between 1889 and 1903, on the average, every week, two Negroes were lynched by mobs—hanged, burned, mutilated.

title: Morgan hosts secret railroad magnates meeting to form anti-competitive combination
summary: On January 2, 1889, banking houses Drexel Morgan, Brown Brothers, and Kidder Peabody issued a confidential circular inviting railroad magnates to Morgan's home to form a compact eliminating competition among railroads.

citation.quote: On January 2, 1889, as Gustavus Myers reports: . . . a circular marked "Private and Confidential" was issued by the three banking houses of Drexel, Morgan & Company, Brown Brothers & Company, and Kidder, Peabody & Company.

title: James Duke forms American Tobacco Company
summary: James Duke combined the four biggest cigarette producers in 1890 to form the American Tobacco Company, using a new cigarette-rolling machine capable of producing 100,000 cigarettes a day.

citation.quote: James Duke used a new cigarette-rolling machine that could roll, paste, and cut tubes of tobacco into 100,000 cigarettes a day; in 1890 he combined the four biggest cigarette producers to form the American Tobacco Company.

title: Sherman Anti-Trust Act passed
summary: The Sherman Anti-Trust Act was passed in 1890, making illegal any combination or conspiracy to restrain interstate trade. Senator Sherman explained it as a way to appease critics of monopoly and prevent more radical responses.

citation.quote: The Sherman Anti-Trust Act, passed in 1890, called itself "An Act to protect trade and commerce against unlawful restraints" and made it illegal to form a "combination or conspiracy" to restrain trade in interstate or foreign commerce.

title: People's Party (Populist) convention in Topeka; Alliance elects 38 to Congress
summary: In 1890, the Farmers Alliances became the People's party and held a convention in Topeka, Kansas; that year the Alliance elected thirty-eight members to Congress and won governors' races in Georgia and Texas.

citation.quote: Now, as a political party, they became the People's party (or Populist party), and met in convention in 1890 in Topeka, Kansas.

title: Mississippi draws up new constitution to disenfranchise Black voters
summary: Starting with Mississippi in 1890, southern states began drawing up new constitutions to prevent Black voters from voting through devices such as poll taxes, literacy tests, and property qualifications — mechanisms that also disenfranchised many poor whites.

citation.quote: Southern states were drawing up new constitutions, starting with Mississippi in 1890, to prevent blacks from voting by various devices, and to maintain ironclad segregation in every aspect of life.

title: U.S. Census Bureau declares internal frontier closed
summary: The year of the Wounded Knee massacre, the Bureau of the Census officially declared the internal frontier closed, spurring American expansionist ambitions overseas.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: The year of the massacre at Wounded Knee, 1890, it was officially declared by the Bureau of the Census that the internal frontier was closed.

title: Women in the labor force doubles from 4 million to 8 million
summary: The number of women workers doubled from 4 million in 1890 to 8 million in 1910, making women one-fifth of the labor force, yet only one in a hundred belonged to a union.

citation.quote: Although the number of women workers kept growing—it doubled from 4 million in 1890 to 8 million in 1910, and women were one-fifth of the labor force—only one in a hundred belonged to a union.

title: Massacre at Wounded Knee Creek kills up to 300 Sioux
summary: In the last days of 1890, shortly after Christmas, U.S. cavalry surrounded 350 Sioux men, women, and children at Pine Ridge, South Dakota. When one Indian fired his rifle, soldiers opened fire; between 200 and 300 Sioux were killed.

citation.quote: In the last days of the year 1890, shortly after Christmas, the last massacre of Indians took place at Pine Ridge, South Dakota, near Wounded Knee Creek. Sitting Bull, the great Sioux leader, had just been assassinated by Indian police in the pay of the United States, and the remaining Sioux sought refuge at Pine Ridge, 120 men and 230 women and children, surrounded by U.S. cavalry...

title: U.S. Army massacre at Wounded Knee kills three hundred Lakota
summary: On a cold winter day in 1890, U.S. Army soldiers attacked Indians camped at Wounded Knee, South Dakota, and killed three hundred men, women, and children, marking the final bloody chapter of four centuries of violence against Native peoples.

citation.quote: on a cold winter day in 1890, U.S. army soldiers attacked Indians camped at Wounded Knee, South Dakota, and killed three hundred men, women, and children.

title: Colored Alliance cotton pickers strike for a dollar a day; Ben Patterson leads and is killed
summary: In 1891, the Colored Alliance declared a strike in the cotton fields for a dollar a day for cotton pickers; in Arkansas, thirty-year-old cotton picker Ben Patterson led the strike, engaging in gun battles with a white posse; Patterson and fifteen others were shot to death.

citation.quote: When the Colored Alliance declared a strike in the cotton fields in 1891 for a dollar a day wages for cotton pickers, Leonidas Polk, head of the white Alliance, denounced it as hurting the Alliance farmer . . . . In Arkansas, a thirty-year-old black cotton picker named Ben Patterson led the strike, traveling from plantation to plantation to get support, his band growing, engaging in gun battles with a white posse.

title: Standard Oil controls 70 percent of world kerosene market
summary: By 1891, the Rockefeller family's Standard Oil Company accounted for 90 percent of American kerosene exports and controlled 70 percent of the world market.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: by 1891, the Rockefeller family's Standard Oil Company accounted for 90 percent of American exports of kerosene and controlled 70 percent of the world market.

title: Armed miners seize Tennessee coal mines and free convict laborers
summary: On the night of October 31, 1891, a thousand armed miners in Tennessee took control of the Tennessee Coal Mine Company area, freed five hundred convicts used as strikebreakers, and burned the stockades; the companies surrendered and agreed not to use convict labor.

citation.quote: On the night of October 31, 1891, a thousand armed miners took control of the mine area, set five hundred convicts free, and burned down the stockades in which the convicts were kept.

title: Supreme Court Justice Brewer declares the United States a Christian nation
summary: Supreme Court Justice David Brewer stated in 1892 that 'this is a Christian nation,' cited by historian William G. McLoughlin to argue that the separation of church and state was never truly implemented after the Revolution.

citation.quote: William G. McLoughlin, quoting Supreme Court Justice David Brewer in 1892 that "this is a Christian nation," says of the separation of church and state in the Revolution that it "was neither conceived of nor carried out. . . ."

title: General strike in New Orleans involving forty-two unions and twenty thousand members
summary: In 1892, forty-two union locals with over twenty thousand members, mostly white but including some blacks, called a general strike in New Orleans that brought work in the city to a halt; it ended after three days in a compromise gaining hours and wages but without union recognition.

citation.quote: That same year, in New Orleans, forty-two union locals, with over twenty thousand members, mostly white but including some blacks (there was one black on the strike committee), called a general strike, involving half the population of the city.

title: Alexander Berkman shoots Henry Clay Frick
summary: In the midst of the Homestead strike, anarchist Alexander Berkman entered the office of Carnegie Steel manager Henry Clay Frick and wounded him in an assassination attempt; Berkman was convicted of attempted murder and sentenced to fourteen years in prison.

citation.quote: In the midst of the Homestead strike, a young anarchist from New York named Alexander Berkman, in a plan prepared by anarchist friends in New York, including his lover Emma Goldman, came to Pittsburgh and entered the office of Henry Clay Frick, determined to kill him. Berkman's aim was poor; he wounded Frick and was overwhelmed, then was tried and found guilty of attempted murder.

title: Populist Congressman Simpson calls for foreign markets for farm surplus
summary: Kansas Populist Congressman Jerry Simpson told Congress in 1892 that with a huge agricultural surplus, farmers must seek a foreign market.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: Populist Congressman Jerry Simpson of Kansas told Congress in 1892 that with a huge agricultural surplus, farmers "must of necessity seek a foreign market."

title: Populist Party nominates James Weaver for President at Omaha convention
summary: In July 1892, the People's party nominating convention in Omaha nominated James Weaver, an Iowa Populist and former Union general, for President; Weaver received over a million votes but lost the election.

citation.quote: A People's party nominating convention in Omaha in July of 1892 nominated James Weaver, an Iowa Populist and former general in the Union army, for President. . . . Weaver got over a million votes, but lost.

title: Battle of Homestead: Pinkerton guards attack steel strikers
summary: On the night of July 5, 1892, hundreds of Pinkerton guards moved by barge toward the Carnegie Steel plant at Homestead, Pennsylvania; in the confrontation that followed seven workers were killed, the Pinkertons were forced to surrender and beaten by the crowd.

citation.quote: On the night of July 5, 1892, hundreds of Pinkerton guards boarded barges 5 miles down the river from Homestead and moved toward the plant, where ten thousand strikers and sympathizers waited.

title: Battle at Coeur d'Alene copper mine: five dead, mill destroyed
summary: On July 11, 1892, gun battles between strikers and strikebreakers at the Coeur d'Alene copper mines in Idaho left five men dead, sixteen hospitalized, and the Frisco mill in ruins; the National Guard and federal troops subsequently imprisoned 600 miners.

citation.quote: A newspaper account of July 11, 1892, reported: . . . The long-dreaded conflict between the forces of the strikers and the nonunion men who have taken their places has come at last. As a result five men are known to be dead and 16 are already in the hospital; the Frisco mill on Canyon Creek is in ruins . . .

title: Largest economic crisis in U.S. history: 642 banks fail, 16,000 businesses close
summary: The year 1893 saw the biggest economic crisis in U.S. history to that point — 642 banks failed, 16,000 businesses closed, and out of a labor force of 15 million, 3 million were unemployed.

citation.quote: The year 1893 saw the biggest economic crisis in the country's history. After several decades of wild industrial growth, financial manipulation, uncontrolled speculation and profiteering, it all collapsed: 642 banks failed and 16,000 businesses closed down.

title: Emma Goldman arrested for 'inciting to riot' at New York unemployment rally
summary: During the 1893 depression, Emma Goldman addressed a huge meeting of the unemployed at Union Square in New York and urged those whose children needed food to take it from stores; she was arrested for 'inciting to riot' and sentenced to two years in prison.

citation.quote: In New York City, in Union Square, Emma Goldman addressed a huge meeting of the unemployed and urged those whose children needed food to go into the stores and take it. She was arrested for "inciting to riot" and sentenced to two years in prison.

title: American Railway Union founded by Eugene Debs
summary: In the midst of the 1893 economic crisis, Eugene Debs and a small group of railroad workers formed the American Railway Union to unite all railway workers regardless of craft, seeking to eliminate the 'aristocracy of labor.'

citation.quote: In the midst of the economic crisis of 1893, a small group of railroad workers, including Debs, formed the American Railway Union, to unite all railway workers.

title: Severe economic depression begins
summary: A severe depression beginning in 1893 intensified the push among the political and financial elite to seek overseas markets to relieve underconsumption and prevent further class conflict.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: The severe depression that began in 1893 strengthened an idea developing within the political and financial elite of the country: that overseas markets for American goods might relieve the problem of underconsumption at home and prevent the economic crises that in the 1890s brought class war.

title: U.S. military promotes provisional government in Hawaii
summary: U.S. forces intervened in Hawaii ostensibly to protect American lives and property but actually to promote a provisional government under Sanford B. Dole; the action was later disavowed.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: **1893—Hawaii**—Ostensibly to protect American lives and property; actually to promote a provisional government under Sanford B. Dole. This action was disavowed by the United States.

title: American trade exceeds all nations except England
summary: By 1893, American trade had exceeded that of every country in the world except England, reflecting rapid industrial and commercial expansion.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: Walter Lafeber writes (The New Empire): "By 1893, American trade exceeded that of every country in the world except England."

title: Thirteen killed and hundreds arrested as Pullman strike crushed in Chicago
summary: During the Pullman strike, thirteen people were killed and fifty-three seriously wounded in Chicago in one day; seven hundred were arrested before the strike. Eugene Debs was arrested for contempt of court for violating an injunction against the strike.

citation.quote: In Chicago that day, thirteen people were killed, fifty-three seriously wounded, seven hundred arrested. Before the strike was over, perhaps thirty-four were dead.

title: U.S. intervention in Bluefields, Nicaragua
summary: U.S. forces intervened at Bluefields, Nicaragua, to protect American interests following a revolution.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: **1894—Nicaragua**—To protect American interests at Bluefields following a revolution.

title: Pullman Palace Car Company workers go on strike
summary: In June 1894, workers at the Pullman Palace Car Company went on strike after wage cuts of nearly 30% while rents in the company town were not reduced; the American Railway Union soon joined the boycott, turning it into a nationwide railroad strike.

citation.quote: In June 1894, workers at the Pullman Palace Car Company went on strike.

title: Hundreds of railroad cars burned during Pullman strike
summary: On July 6, 1894, hundreds of railroad cars were burned by strikers during the Pullman strike, as federal troops dispatched by President Cleveland moved into Chicago to enforce an injunction against the strike.

citation.quote: When the strikers ignored the injunction, President Cleveland ordered federal troops to Chicago. On July 6, hundreds of cars were burned by strikers.

title: Morgan syndicate profits $18 million from U.S. gold bond deal
summary: In 1895, with the U.S. gold reserve depleted, a syndicate headed by J. P. Morgan offered the government gold in exchange for bonds, then immediately resold the bonds at higher prices, making $18 million in profit.

citation.quote: In 1895 the gold reserve of the United States was depleted, while twenty-six New York City banks had $129 million in gold in their vaults. A syndicate of bankers headed by J. P. Morgan & Company, August Belmont & Company, the National City Bank, and others offered to give the government gold in exchange for bonds. President Grover Cleveland agreed. The bankers immediately resold the bonds at higher prices, making $18 million profit.

title: Supreme Court limits Sherman Act to exclude manufacturing monopolies
summary: In 1895, the Supreme Court ruled in U.S. v. E. C. Knight Co. that a monopoly of sugar refining was a manufacturing monopoly rather than a commerce monopoly, effectively gutting the Sherman Anti-Trust Act; the same year it ruled the act could be used against striking railroad workers.

citation.quote: In 1895 the Court interpreted the Sherman Act so as to make it harmless. It said a monopoly of sugar refining was a monopoly in manufacturing, not commerce, and so could not be regulated by Congress through the Sherman Act (U.S. v. E. C. Knight Co.).

title: Cuban rebels begin revolt against Spain
summary: By 1898, Cuban rebels had been fighting their Spanish conquerors for three years, meaning the revolt against Spain began in 1895.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: By 1898, Cuban rebels had been fighting their Spanish conquerors for three years in an attempt to win independence.

title: Boston Transcript reports arrest and clubbing of Black man
summary: The Boston Transcript of September 25, 1895 reported that a Black man named Henry W. Turner was arrested on suspicion of robbery, taken to be photographed for the 'Rogue's Gallery,' and clubbed by police when he resisted—illustrating Northern racism contemporaneous with the Jim Crow South.

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: An item in the Boston *Transcript,* September 25, 1895: A colored man who gives his name as Henry W. Turner was arrested last night on suspicion of being a highway robber. He was taken this morning to Black's studio, where he had his picture taken for the "Rogue's Gallery". That angered him, and he made himself as disagreeable as he possibly could. Several times along the way to the photographer's he resisted the police with all his might, and had to be clubbed.

title: Plessy v. Ferguson: Supreme Court upholds railroad segregation
summary: In 1896 the Supreme Court ruled in Plessy v. Ferguson that a railroad could segregate Black and white passengers if the facilities were equal, enshrining the 'separate but equal' doctrine. Justice John Harlan dissented: 'Our Constitution is color-blind.'

citation.chapter: Chapter 9 – Slavery Without Submission, Emancipation Without Freedom
citation.quote: The culmination of this mood came in the decision of 1896, *Plessy* v. *Ferguson,* when the Court ruled that a railroad could segregate black and white if the segregated facilities were equal...

title: William McKinley defeats Bryan; Populist movement collapses into Democratic Party
summary: In the election of 1896, the Populist movement had allied itself with the Democratic Party behind William Jennings Bryan's candidacy; Bryan was defeated by William McKinley, whose campaign was backed by corporations, effectively ending Populism as an independent force.

citation.quote: In the election of 1896, with the Populist movement enticed into the Democratic party, Bryan, the Democratic candidate, was defeated by William McKinley, for whom the corporations and the press mobilized, in the first massive use of money in an election campaign.

title: President Cleveland describes U.S. investment in Cuba
summary: President Cleveland estimated in 1896 that at least $30–50 million of American capital was invested in Cuba and that trade between the U.S. and Cuba reached $103 million in 1893.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: There already was a substantial economic interest in the island, which President Grover Cleveland summarized in 1896: It is reasonably estimated that at least from $30,000,000 to $50,000,000 of American capital are invested in the plantations and in railroad, mining, and other business enterprises on the island.

title: Winston Churchill argues Spain should retain control of Cuba
summary: In a 1896 Saturday Review article, Churchill warned that Cuban rebel success would result in a 'black republic' given that two-fifths of insurgents were Black, and argued Spain should maintain control.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: This idea was expressed in 1896 in an article in The Saturday Review by a young and eloquent imperialist, whose mother was American and whose father was English—Winston Churchill.

title: Jack London preaches socialism in Alaskan gold camps
summary: Jack London, before becoming a world-famous writer, preached socialism in the Alaskan gold camps during the winter of 1896 and then sailed 2,000 miles back through the Bering Sea.

citation.quote: preached socialism in the Alaskan gold camps in the winter of 1896, sailed 2,000 miles back through the Bering Sea, and became a world-famous writer of adventure books.

title: Theodore Roosevelt expresses desire for war
summary: Roosevelt wrote to a friend that he would welcome almost any war, believing the country needed one.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: Theodore Roosevelt wrote to a friend in the year 1897: "In strict confidence . . . I should welcome almost any war, for I think this country needs one."

title: AFL convention defeats resolution calling for U.S. intervention in Cuba
summary: Despite sympathy for Cuban rebels, a resolution calling for U.S. intervention was defeated at the 1897 AFL convention, reflecting labor's opposition to expansionism.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: Both the Knights of Labor and the American Federation of Labor spoke against the idea of annexing Hawaii, which McKinley proposed in 1897. Despite the feeling for the Cuban rebels, a resolution calling for U.S. intervention was defeated at the 1897 convention of the AFL.

title: US private foreign investments reach $700 million
summary: In 1897 the private foreign investments of the United States amounted to $700 million, growing to $3.5 billion by 1914, illustrating the expanding role of overseas capital in driving American foreign policy.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: In 1897, the private foreign investments of the United States amounted to $700 million dollars. By 1914 they were $3½ billion.

title: Lattimer Massacre: sheriff kills nineteen striking miners
summary: During a coal strike in Pennsylvania, the sheriff and deputies opened fire on immigrant miners marching to the Lattimer mine, killing nineteen, most shot in the back.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: It pointed to the Lattimer Massacre of September 10, 1897, during a coal strike in Pennsylvania. Miners marching on a highway to the Lattimer mine—Austrians, Hungarians, Italians, Germans—who had originally been imported as strikebreakers but then organized themselves, refused to disperse, whereupon the sheriff and his deputies opened fire, killing nineteen of them, most shot in the back, with no outcry in the press.

title: Anti-Imperialist League formed
summary: Prominent American businessmen, politicians, and intellectuals formed the Anti-Imperialist League in 1898 and campaigned to educate the public about the horrors of the Philippine war.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: William James was part of a movement of prominent American businessmen, politicians, and intellectuals who formed the Anti-Imperialist League in 1898 and carried on a long campaign to educate the American public about the horrors of the Philippine war and the evils of imperialism.

title: USS Maine destroyed in Havana harbor
summary: The U.S. battleship Maine was destroyed by a mysterious explosion in Havana harbor, killing 268 men; despite no evidence of cause, the event rapidly escalated calls for war with Spain.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: In February 1898, the U.S. battleship Maine, in Havana harbor as a symbol of American interest in the Cuban events, was destroyed by a mysterious explosion and sank, with the loss of 268 men.

title: Lodge writes McKinley that conservatives want Cuban question solved
summary: Henry Cabot Lodge wrote McKinley a long letter reporting that businessmen, editors, and 'the most conservative classes' in Boston and vicinity wanted the Cuban question resolved, even if it meant war.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: On March 21, 1898, Henry Cabot Lodge wrote McKinley a long letter, saying he had talked with "bankers, brokers, businessmen, editors, clergymen and others" in Boston, Lynn, and Nahant, and "everybody," including "the most conservative classes," wanted the Cuban question "solved."

title: McKinley adviser telegraphs that big corporations welcome war
summary: On March 25, a telegram to the White House from a McKinley adviser reported that big corporations now believed war was coming and would welcome it as relief from economic suspense.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: On March 25, a telegram arrived at the White House from an adviser to McKinley, saying: "Big corporations here now believe we will have war. Believe all would welcome it as relief to suspense."

title: Congress authorizes U.S. intervention in Cuba
summary: Nine days after McKinley's war message, Congress passed a joint resolution giving McKinley the power to intervene in Cuba.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: Nine days later, Congress, by joint resolution, gave McKinley the power to intervene.

title: McKinley asks Congress for war with Spain
summary: McKinley asked Congress for war on April 11, without recognizing Cuban rebels as belligerents or requesting Cuban independence.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: Indeed, when McKinley asked Congress for war on April 11, he did not recognize the rebels as belligerents or ask for Cuban independence.

title: Armour sells army 500,000 pounds of rotted beef
summary: In May 1898, Armour and Company sold the army 500,000 pounds of beef that had been previously returned from Liverpool; two months later an army inspector found 751 cases containing rotten meat.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: In May of 1898, Armour and Company, the big meatpacking company of Chicago, sold the army 500,000 pounds of beef which had been sent to Liverpool a year earlier and had been returned.

title: Authorities ban Socialist Labor Party antiwar parade in New York
summary: On May Day 1898, the Socialist Labor Party organized an antiwar parade in New York City, but authorities would not allow it to take place, while a pro-war Jewish Daily Forward parade was permitted.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: On May Day, 1898, the Socialist Labor party organized an antiwar parade in New York City, but the authorities would not allow it to take place, while a May Day parade called by the Jewish Daily Forward, urging Jewish workers to support the war, was permitted.

title: Western Labor Union founded in Salt Lake City
summary: The Western Labor Union was founded at Salt Lake City on May 10, 1898, because the AFL had failed to organize unskilled workers, aiming to unite all workers regardless of occupation, nationality, creed, or color.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: The Western Labor Union was founded at Salt Lake City on May 10, 1898, because the AFL had not organized unskilled workers.

title: Hawaii annexed by joint resolution of Congress
summary: The Hawaiian Islands, already penetrated by American missionaries and plantation owners, were annexed by joint resolution of Congress in July 1898.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: The Hawaiian Islands, one-third of the way across the Pacific, which had already been penetrated by American missionaries and pineapple plantation owners, and had been described by American officials as "a ripe pear ready to be plucked," was annexed by joint resolution of Congress in July of 1898.

title: Peace treaty with Spain cedes Guam, Puerto Rico, and Philippines to U.S.
summary: In December 1898, the peace treaty was signed with Spain, officially turning over Guam, Puerto Rico, and the Philippines to the United States for a payment of $20 million.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: In December of 1898, the peace treaty was signed with Spain, officially turning over to the United States Guam, Puerto Rico, and the Philippines, for a payment of $20 million.

title: Filipinos rise in revolt against American rule
summary: In February 1899, Filipinos rose in revolt against American rule under Emilio Aguinaldo, who had earlier been brought back from China by U.S. warships to fight the Spanish.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: In February 1899, they rose in revolt against American rule, as they had rebelled several times against the Spanish. Emilio Aguinaldo, a Filipino leader, who had earlier been brought back from China by U.S. warships to lead soldiers against Spain, now became leader of the insurrectos fighting the United States.

title: Boston banquet celebrates Senate ratification of peace treaty with Spain
summary: Two thousand diners attended the biggest banquet in the nation's history in Boston in February 1899 to celebrate Senate ratification of the peace treaty; McKinley denied imperial designs while his Postmaster General called for foreign markets.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: In February 1899, a banquet took place in Boston to celebrate the Senate's ratification of the peace treaty with Spain.

title: General strike for eight-hour day in Havana
summary: In September 1899, thousands of workers in Havana launched a general strike for the eight-hour day; U.S. General Ludlow ordered the arrest of eleven strike leaders and U.S. troops occupied railroad stations and docks.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
