citation.quote: In September 1899, a gathering of thousands of workers in Havana launched a general strike for the eight-hour day, saying, ". . . we have determined to promote the struggle between the worker and the capitalist."

title: 500,000 women office workers in the United States
summary: In 1900 there were 500,000 women office workers — compared to only 19,000 in 1870 — along with half a million women teachers, signaling a dramatic expansion of women in the paid workforce.

citation.quote: In 1900 there were 500,000 women office workers—in 1870 there had been 19,000.

title: Repeated US military interventions in Central America and the Caribbean
summary: Between 1900 and 1933, the United States intervened militarily in Cuba four times, Nicaragua twice, Panama six times, Guatemala once, and Honduras seven times.

citation.quote: Between 1900 and 1933, the United States intervened in Cuba four times, in Nicaragua twice, in Panama six times, in Guatemala once, in Honduras seven times.

title: Senator Beveridge delivers speech advocating retention of the Philippines
summary: Senator Albert Beveridge of Indiana delivered a Senate speech on January 9, 1900, calling the Philippines 'ours forever' and arguing for American commercial empire in Asia.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: In the Senate, Albert Beveridge spoke, January 9, 1900, for the dominant economic and political interests of the country: Mr. President, the times call for candor. The Philippines are ours forever. . . .

title: General Leonard Wood writes that Cuba has 'little or no independence' under Platt Amendment
summary: General Leonard Wood wrote to Theodore Roosevelt in 1901 that the Platt Amendment left Cuba with little or no independence.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: General Leonard Wood wrote in 1901 to Theodore Roosevelt: "There is, of course, little or no independence left Cuba under the Platt Amendment."

title: Platt Amendment passed by Congress
summary: Congress passed the Platt Amendment in February 1901, giving the United States the right to intervene in Cuba for preservation of Cuban independence and to obtain naval stations; Cuba was required to incorporate it into its constitution.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: a Cuban Constitutional Convention was told that the United States army would not leave Cuba until the Platt Amendment, passed by Congress in February 1901, was incorporated into the new Cuban Constitution.

title: Black infantryman Fulbright calls Philippine war 'gigantic scheme of robbery'
summary: William Fulbright, a Black infantryman, wrote from Manila in June 1901 to an Indianapolis newspaper that the Philippine struggle had been 'naught but a gigantic scheme of robbery and oppression.'

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: A black infantryman named William Fulbright wrote from Manila in June 1901 to the editor of a paper in Indianapolis: "This struggle on the islands has been naught but a gigantic scheme of robbery and oppression."

title: Philadelphia Ledger reports U.S. soldiers exterminating Filipino civilians
summary: In November 1901, the Manila correspondent of the Philadelphia Ledger reported that American soldiers had been killing men, women, children, prisoners, and captives indiscriminately.

citation.chapter: Chapter 12 – The Empire and The People
citation.quote: In November 1901, the Manila correspondent of the Philadelphia Ledger reported: The present war is no bloodless, opera bouffe engagement; our men have been relentless, have killed to exterminate men, women, children, prisoners and captives, active insurgents and suspected people from lads of ten up...

title: Riot during Jewish community funeral in New York leads to police clubbing
summary: On July 30, 1902, a mass funeral in New York's Jewish community was met by a riot led by Irish residents; the official investigation found police had helped the rioters, with officers receiving only minor penalties.

citation.quote: On July 30, 1902, New York's Jewish community held a mass funeral for an important rabbi, and a riot took place, led by Irish who resented Jews coming into their neighborhood.

title: Mother Jones organizes children's march from Kensington, Pennsylvania
summary: In the spring of 1903, Mother Jones organized a children's march from Kensington, Pennsylvania, where seventy-five thousand textile workers were on strike, to draw national attention to child labor. The children marched through New Jersey and New York toward President Roosevelt at Oyster Bay, who refused to see them.

citation.quote: In the spring of 1903, I went to Kensington, Pennsylvania, where seventy-five thousand textile workers were on strike. Of this number at least ten thousand were little children.

title: Children in Philadelphia textile mills strike for shorter hours
summary: In 1903, children working sixty hours a week in textile mills in Philadelphia went on strike, carrying signs: 'We want to go to school!' and '55 hours or nothing!'

citation.quote: That same year, children working sixty hours a week in textile mills in Philadelphia went on strike, carrying signs: "we want to go to school!" "55 hours or nothing!"

title: National Afro-American Council formed to protest lynching and discrimination
summary: A National Afro-American Council was formed in 1903 to protest against lynching, peonage, discrimination, and disfranchisement, alongside the National Association of Colored Women which condemned segregation and lynchings.

citation.quote: Blacks began to organize: a National Afro-American Council formed in 1903 to protest against lynching, peonage, discrimination, disfranchisement;

title: United States engineers Panamanian revolution and signs canal treaty
summary: In 1903, the United States engineered a revolution against Colombia, established the new republic of Panama, and dictated a treaty giving the U.S. military bases, control of the Panama Canal, and sovereignty 'in perpetuity.'

citation.quote: Back in 1903 the United States had engineered a revolution against Colombia, set up the new tiny republic of Panama in Central America, and dictated a treaty giving the United States military bases, control of the Panama Canal, and sovereignty "in perpetuity."

title: Booker T. Washington speech disrupted by William Monroe Trotter in Boston
summary: In the summer of 1903, Booker T. Washington spoke to an audience of two thousand at a Boston church, where Trotter and his supporters prepared nine provocative questions causing a commotion, fistfights, and ultimately Trotter's arrest.

citation.quote: When, in the summer of 1903, Washington spoke to an audience of two thousand at a Boston church, Trotter and his supporters prepared nine provocative questions, which caused a commotion and led to fistfights. Trotter and a friend were arrested.

title: Henry James tours the United States and condemns the money passion
summary: The novelist Henry James toured the United States in 1904 and described the country as a 'huge Rappacini garden, rank with each variety of the poison-plant of the money passion.'

citation.quote: the novelist Henry James—could tour the United States in 1904 and see the country as a "huge Rappacini garden, rank with each variety of the poison-plant of the money passion."

title: Railroad consolidation: over a thousand lines absorbed into six combinations
summary: By 1904, more than a thousand railroad lines had been consolidated into six great combinations, each allied with either Morgan or Rockefeller interests.

citation.quote: By 1904, more than a thousand railroad lines had been consolidated into six great combinations, each allied with either Morgan or Rockefeller interests.

title: 27,000 workers killed on the job in one year
summary: In the year 1904, 27,000 workers were killed on the job in manufacturing, transport, and agriculture, while in one year alone 50,000 accidents took place in New York factories.

citation.quote: In the year 1904, 27,000 workers were killed on the job, in manufacturing, transport, and agriculture.

title: Number of strikes rises to four thousand per year
summary: Around the turn of the century, strike struggles were multiplying — in the 1890s there had been about a thousand strikes a year, but by 1904 there were four thousand strikes a year.

citation.quote: Around the turn of the century, strike struggles were multiplying—in the 1890s there had been about a thousand strikes a year; by 1904 there were four thousand strikes a year.

title: Debs writes on the need for revolutionary unionism
summary: In 1904, three years after the formation of the Socialist party, Debs wrote that the 'pure and simple' trades union did not answer the requirements of today and that the labor movement's higher object was to overthrow the capitalist system.

citation.quote: Debs wrote in 1904, three years after the formation of the Socialist party:

title: Only 3 percent of Socialist party members are women; eight women delegates at national convention
summary: In 1904, only 3 percent of the Socialist party's members were women, and there were only eight women delegates at that year's national convention.

citation.quote: Only 3 percent of the Socialist party's members were women in 1904. At the national convention that year, there were only eight women delegates.

title: 318 trusts control 40 percent of U.S. manufacturing
summary: By 1904, 318 trusts with capital of more than seven billion dollars controlled 40 percent of U.S. manufacturing, illustrating the enormous concentration of economic power.

citation.quote: By 1904, 318 trusts, with capital of more than seven billion dollars, controlled 40% of the U.S. manufacturing.

title: W. E. B. Du Bois calls conference near Niagara Falls — start of the Niagara Movement
summary: In 1905, W. E. B. Du Bois, teaching in Atlanta, Georgia, sent out a letter calling Negro leaders to a conference just across the Canadian border from Buffalo, near Niagara Falls — the start of the 'Niagara Movement.'

citation.quote: W. E. B. Du Bois, teaching in Atlanta, Georgia, in 1905, sent out a letter to Negro leaders throughout the country, calling them to a conference just across the Canadian border from Buffalo, near Niagara Falls. It was the start of the "Niagara Movement."

title: Founding convention of the Industrial Workers of the World (IWW)
summary: One morning in June 1905, two hundred socialists, anarchists, and radical trade unionists from across the United States met in a hall in Chicago to found the IWW — the Industrial Workers of the World — with Big Bill Haywood presiding.

citation.quote: One morning in June 1905, there met in a hall in Chicago a convention of two hundred socialists, anarchists, and radical trade unionists from all over the United States. They were forming the I. W. W.—the Industrial Workers of the World.

title: Strike at Federman's bakery on the Lower East Side turns violent
summary: The New York Tribune reported on August 10, 1905 that strikers or sympathizers wrecked Philip Federman's bake shop on Orchard Street when he used scab labor, and police smashed heads with nightsticks after two officers were roughly handled by the crowd.

citation.quote: On August 10, 1905, the New York Tribune reported that a strike at Federman's bakery on the Lower East Side led to violence when Federman used scab labor to continue producing:

title: Upton Sinclair publishes The Jungle
summary: Sinclair's novel exposed conditions in Chicago meatpacking plants and depicted immigrant labor, stimulating demand for meat-industry regulation. It was first published in the Socialist newspaper Appeal to Reason and then translated into seventeen languages.

citation.quote: Upton Sinclair's novel The Jungle, published in 1906, brought the conditions in the meatpacking plants of Chicago to the shocked attention of the whole country, and stimulated demand for laws regulating the meat industry.

title: Jack London publishes The Iron Heel
summary: London wrote his novel The Iron Heel in 1906, warning of a fascist America and presenting an ideal of socialist brotherhood.

citation.quote: In 1906, he wrote his novel The Iron Heel, with its warning of a fascist America, its ideal of a socialist brotherhood of man.

title: Debs writes flaming article after Haywood and other miners' officers imprisoned in Idaho
summary: In 1906, after Big Bill Haywood and two other officers of the Western Federation of Miners were imprisoned in Idaho on an apparently faked murder charge, Debs wrote a fiery article in the Appeal to Reason warning of revolution if they were killed.

citation.quote: In 1906, after the imprisonment in Idaho of Bill Haywood and two other officers of the Western Federation of Miners on an apparently faked murder charge, Debs wrote a flaming article in the Appeal to Reason:

title: Equal Rights Convention in Georgia protests 260 lynchings since 1885
summary: In Georgia in 1906, an Equal Rights Convention pointed to 260 Georgia Negroes lynched since 1885 and demanded the right to vote, to enter the militia, and to serve on juries.

citation.quote: In Georgia in 1906 there was an Equal Rights Convention, which pointed to 260 Georgia Negroes lynched since 1885.

title: Financial panic and economic crisis
summary: In 1907 there was a panic, financial collapse, and crisis. The very big businesses were not hurt, but profits fell and industrialists began to look for ways to cut costs.

citation.quote: In 1907, there was a panic, financial collapse, and crisis. True, the very big businesses were not hurt, but profits after 1907 were not as high as capitalists wanted, industry was not expanding as fast as it might, and industrialists began to look for ways to cut costs.

title: Carnegie plants in Allegheny County employ large Eastern European immigrant workforce
summary: In the Carnegie plants of Allegheny County in 1907, of 14,359 common laborers, 11,694 were Eastern Europeans, making Taylorism with its simplified unskilled jobs more feasible.

citation.quote: With immigrants a larger proportion of the labor force (in the Carnegie plants of Allegheny County in 1907, of the 14,359 common laborers, 11,694 were Eastern Europeans), Taylorism, with its simplified unskilled jobs, became more feasible.

title: New Orleans general strike on the levees involving ten thousand workers
summary: In New Orleans in 1907, a general strike on the levees involving ten thousand workers — longshoremen, teamsters, freight handlers, black and white — lasted twenty days, exemplifying rare interracial labor solidarity.

citation.quote: In New Orleans in 1907 a general strike on the levees, involving ten thousand workers (longshoremen, teamsters, freight handlers), black and white, lasted twenty days.

title: Wilson lectures at Columbia on forcibly opening foreign markets
summary: Back in 1907, Woodrow Wilson said in a lecture at Columbia University that concessions obtained by financiers must be safeguarded by ministers of state, "even if the sovereignty of unwilling nations be outraged in the process."

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: Back in 1907, Woodrow Wilson had said in a lecture at Columbia University: "Concessions obtained by financiers must be safeguarded by ministers of state, even if the sovereignty of unwilling nations be outraged in the process. . . . the doors of the nations which are closed must be battered down."

title: Edwin Markham describes sweatshop conditions in Cosmopolitan magazine
summary: Poet Edwin Markham wrote about child and family labor in home sweatshops, published in Cosmopolitan magazine in January 1907, describing the brutal conditions facing immigrant families on the East Side of New York City.

citation.quote: The poet Edwin Markham wrote in Cosmopolitan magazine, January 1907:

title: Ford sells 10,607 autos
summary: In 1909, Ford sold 10,607 autos; by 1913 that number reached 168,000, and by 1914 had grown to 248,000 — 45 percent of all autos produced — yielding $30 million in profit.

citation.quote: In 1909, Ford sold 10,607 autos; in 1913, 168,000; in 1914, 248,000 (45 percent of all autos produced). The profit: $30 million.

title: Triangle Shirtwaist workers organize and launch general strike
summary: In the winter of 1909, women at the Triangle Shirtwaist Company organized and went on strike. Clara Lemlich called for a general strike at a mass meeting; the union had hoped three thousand would join but twenty thousand walked out.

citation.quote: At the Triangle Shirtwaist Company, in the winter of 1909, women organized and decided to strike.

title: IWW leads strike of six thousand workers in McKees Rocks, Pennsylvania
summary: In McKees Rocks, Pennsylvania, in 1909, the IWW led a strike of six thousand workers against a U.S. Steel affiliate, defied state troopers, promised a trooper's life for every worker killed, and ultimately won the strike.

citation.quote: In McKees Rocks, Pennsylvania, they led a strike of six thousand workers in 1909 against an affiliate of the U.S. Steel Company, defied the state troopers, and battled with them.

title: IWW free-speech fight in Spokane, Washington
summary: In Spokane, Washington in 1909, an ordinance was passed to stop street meetings and an IWW organizer was arrested. Thousands of Wobblies flooded in to speak; six hundred were jailed before the IWW won the right to speak.

citation.quote: In Spokane, Washington, in 1909, an ordinance was passed to stop street meetings, and an IWW organizer who insisted on speaking was arrested.

title: Herbert Croly publishes The Promise of American Life
summary: In 1909, Herbert Croly, editor of the New Republic and admirer of Theodore Roosevelt, published The Promise of American Life, a manifesto of the new Progressivism calling for government discipline and regulation to stabilize the American system.

citation.quote: In 1909, a manifesto of the new Progressivism appeared—a book called The Promise of American Life by Herbert Croly, editor of the New Republic and an admirer of Theodore Roosevelt.

title: AFL leaders vacationing at Atlantic City; John Mitchell loses diamond ring
summary: A 1910 press dispatch from Atlantic City described AFL president Samuel Gompers, secretary Frank Morrison, and former mine workers head John Mitchell playing beach baseball, with Mitchell losing a $1,000 diamond ring from a roll of cash in his pocket.

citation.quote: A press dispatch from Atlantic City, New Jersey, the fashionable seaside resort, in the summer of 1910:

title: Mother Mary Jones describes conditions in Milwaukee brewery
summary: Mother Mary Jones, who worked briefly in a Milwaukee brewery in 1910 at nearly eighty years of age, described girls condemned to slave in wet clothes in the wash-room, lifting heavy cases, suffering rheumatism and consumption for $3.00 a week.

citation.quote: The conditions of women working in a Milwaukee brewery were described by Mother Mary Jones, who worked there briefly in 1910 (she was close to eighty at this time):

title: Kate Richards O'Hare runs for Congress in Kansas City
summary: In 1910, Socialist leader Kate Richards O'Hare ran for Congress in Kansas City, expressing her belief in domestic life while arguing that socialism was needed to restore the home.

citation.quote: When she ran for Congress in 1910 in Kansas City she said: "I long for domestic life, home and children with every fiber of my being. . . . Socialism is needed to restore the home."

title: NAACP formed after race riot in Springfield, Illinois
summary: A race riot in Springfield, Illinois prompted the formation of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People in 1910. Whites dominated the leadership; W. E. B. Du Bois was the only black officer and first editor of The Crisis.

citation.quote: A race riot in Springfield, Illinois, prompted the formation of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People in 1910.

title: Victor Berger becomes first Socialist elected to Congress
summary: In 1910, Victor Berger became the first member of the Socialist party elected to Congress; that same year, seventy-three Socialist mayors were elected and twelve hundred lesser officials in 340 cities and towns.

citation.quote: In 1910, Victor Berger became the first member of the Socialist party elected to Congress; in 1911, seventy-three Socialist mayors were elected, and twelve hundred lesser officials in 340 cities and towns.

title: National Civic Federation draws up model workmen's compensation bill
summary: The National Civic Federation drew up a model workmen's compensation bill in 1910, and the following year twelve states passed laws for compensation or accident insurance.

citation.quote: Thus, the Federation drew up a model workmen's compensation bill in 1910, and the following year twelve states passed laws for compensation or accident insurance.

title: Frederick W. Taylor publishes book on scientific management
summary: In 1911, Taylor published a book on 'scientific management' that became powerfully influential in the business world, enabling management to control every detail of the worker's energy and time in the factory.

citation.quote: In 1911, he published a book on "scientific management" that became powerfully influential in the business world.

title: IWW free-speech fight in Fresno, California
summary: In Fresno, California in 1911, there was another IWW free-speech fight. Wobblies who filled the jails lectured about the class struggle and sang songs; when city officials heard thousands more were coming, they lifted the ban and released prisoners.

citation.quote: In Fresno, California, in 1911, there was another free speech fight.

title: IWW free-speech fight in Aberdeen, Washington
summary: In Aberdeen, Washington in 1911, the IWW again faced laws against free speech, arrests, and prison, but unexpectedly won the right to speak.

citation.quote: That same year in Aberdeen, Washington, once again laws against free speech, arrests, prison, and, unexpectedly, victory.

title: Helen Keller writes to a suffragist in England criticizing electoral democracy
summary: In 1911, Helen Keller wrote to a suffragist in England arguing that voting only allows choosing between two bodies of autocrats and that land inequality in Great Britain made votes for women an insufficient remedy.

citation.quote: And Helen Keller, writing in 1911 to a suffragist in England:

title: Triangle Shirtwaist Company fire kills 146 workers
summary: A fire at the Triangle Shirtwaist Company swept through the eighth, ninth, and tenth floors, killing 146 workers — mostly women — who were trapped behind locked and inward-opening doors. A memorial parade down Broadway drew 100,000 marchers.

citation.quote: On the afternoon of March 25, 1911, a fire at the Triangle Shirtwaist Company that began in a rag bin swept through the eighth, ninth, and tenth floors, too high for fire ladders to reach.

title: New York State Factory Investigation Commission reports on lead poisoning of workers
summary: A New York State Factory Investigation Commission reported in 1912 on the case of 'Sadie,' an embroidery worker who suffered lead poisoning after her employer secretly switched from chalk to lead powder without the workers' knowledge.

citation.quote: A New York State Factory Investigation Commission reported in 1912:

title: Jack White arrested in San Diego free-speech fight
summary: In San Diego in 1912, Wobbly Jack White was arrested in a free-speech fight and sentenced to six months in the county jail on bread and water. He delivered a defiant speech to the court denouncing the legal system.

citation.quote: In San Diego, Jack White, a Wobbly arrested in a free-speech fight in 1912, sentenced to six months in the county jail on a bread and water diet, was asked if he had anything to say to the court.

title: IWW-led textile strike in Lawrence, Massachusetts
summary: In 1912, the IWW became involved in a dramatic strike in Lawrence, Massachusetts, where eleven thousand immigrant workers at the American Woolen Company mills struck against low pay, dangerous conditions, and company domination of their lives.

citation.quote: The IWW became involved in a set of dramatic events in Lawrence, Massachusetts, in the year 1912, where the American Woolen Company owned four mills.

title: Debs receives 900,000 votes in presidential election
summary: In the 1912 presidential election, Debs received 900,000 votes — double what he had received in 1908 — as the Socialist party candidate.

citation.quote: As the Socialists became more successful at the polls (Debs got 900,000 votes in 1912, double what he had in 1908), and more concerned with increasing that appeal, they became more critical of IWW tactics of "sabotage" and "violence," and in 1913 removed Bill Haywood from the Socialist Party Executive Committee.

title: Women's suffrage parade up Fifth Avenue in New York
summary: In 1912, thousands lined Fifth Avenue from Washington Square to 57th Street as an impressive column of women — doctors, lawyers, architects, industrial workers — marched five abreast with striking intensity and purpose.

citation.quote: Every spring in New York, the parades for women's suffrage kept growing. In 1912, a news report:

title: Over a hundred Lawrence strikers' children sent to New York City
summary: On February 10, 1912, over a hundred children aged four to fourteen left Lawrence for New York City, where they were greeted at Grand Central Station by five thousand Italian Socialists singing the 'Marseillaise' and the 'Internationale.'

citation.quote: On February 10, over a hundred children, aged four to fourteen, left Lawrence for New York City. They were greeted at Grand Central Station by five thousand Italian Socialists singing the "Marseillaise" and the "Internationale."

title: Police attack children and mothers at Lawrence railroad station
summary: On February 24, 1912, police at the Lawrence railroad station clubbed a group of forty children and their mothers who had assembled to travel to Philadelphia, dragging them into military trucks despite their screams.

citation.quote: Despite the city edict, a group of forty children assembled on February 24 to go to Philadelphia.

title: Lawrence textile strike ends with workers' victory
summary: On March 14, 1912, ten thousand strikers gathered on the Lawrence Common and, with Bill Haywood presiding, voted to end the strike after the American Woolen Company offered raises of 5 to 11 percent and other concessions.

citation.quote: On March 14, 1912, ten thousand strikers gathered on the Lawrence Common and, with Bill Haywood presiding, voted to end the strike.

title: Fifteen thousand Lawrence workers strike to support Ettor and Giovanitti
summary: On September 30, 1912, fifteen thousand Lawrence workers struck for twenty-four hours to demonstrate support for IWW organizers Joseph Ettor and Arturo Giovanitti, who were on trial for murder in connection with the Lawrence strike.

citation.quote: on September 30, fifteen thousand Lawrence workers struck for twenty-four hours to show their support for the two men.

title: W. E. B. Du Bois writes on AFL exclusion of Black workers
summary: W. E. B. Du Bois wrote in 1913 that the net result of AFL exclusion had been to convince the American Negro that his greatest enemy was not the employer but his fellow white workingman.

citation.quote: W. E. B. Du Bois wrote in 1913: "The net result of all this has been to convince the American Negro that his greatest enemy is not the employer who robs him, but his fellow white workingman."

title: Bill Haywood removed from Socialist Party Executive Committee
summary: In 1913, the Socialist party removed Bill Haywood from its Executive Committee, claiming he advocated violence — even though some of Debs's own writings were far more inflammatory.

citation.quote: in 1913 removed Bill Haywood from the Socialist Party Executive Committee, claiming he advocated violence (although some of Debs's writings were far more inflammatory).

title: Women reach 15 percent of Socialist party membership
summary: By 1913, 15 percent of the Socialist party's membership was women, up from 3 percent in 1904, driven by local socialist women's organizations and the national magazine Socialist Woman.

citation.quote: But in a few years, local socialist women's organizations, and a national magazine, Socialist Woman, began bringing more women into the party, so that by 1913, 15 percent of the membership was women.

title: Women's suffrage parade in Washington, D.C. draws 500,000 spectators
summary: In the spring of 1913, Washington saw the greatest parade of women in its history, with over 5,000 women marching down Pennsylvania Avenue as an estimated 500,000 persons watched.

citation.quote: From Washington, in the spring of 1913, came a New York Times report: In a woman's suffrage demonstration to-day the capital saw the greatest parade of women in its history.

title: Pujo Committee studies banking power concentration; Commission on Industrial Relations holds hearings
summary: In 1913, the Pujo Committee of Congress studied the concentration of power in the banking industry, and the Commission on Industrial Relations of the Senate held hearings on labor-management conflict.

citation.quote: In 1913 the Pujo Committee of Congress studied the concentration of power in the banking industry, and the Commission on Industrial Relations of the Senate held hearings on labor-management conflict.

title: Colorado coal strike begins
summary: In September 1913, eleven thousand miners in southern Colorado, mostly foreign-born workers for the Colorado Fuel & Iron Corporation owned by the Rockefellers, went on strike against low pay, dangerous conditions, and feudal domination of their lives in company towns.

citation.quote: This was the Colorado coal strike that began in September 1913 and culminated in the "Ludlow Massacre" of April 1914.

title: Commission on Industrial Relations reports 35,000 workers killed in industrial accidents
summary: According to a 1914 report of the Commission on Industrial Relations, 35,000 workers were killed in industrial accidents and 700,000 were injured. That same year the income of 44 families making $1 million or more equaled the total income of 100,000 families earning $500 a year.

citation.quote: According to a report of the Commission on Industrial Relations, in 1914, 35,000 workers were killed in industrial accidents and 700,000 injured.

title: Socialist party in Oklahoma has twelve thousand dues-paying members
summary: By 1914 the Socialist party in Oklahoma had twelve thousand dues-paying members — more than New York State — elected over a hundred Socialists to local office including six to the state legislature, and had fifty-five weekly Socialist newspapers.

citation.quote: The strongest Socialist state organization was in Oklahoma, which in 1914 had twelve thousand dues-paying members (more than New York State), and elected over a hundred Socialists to local office, including six to the Oklahoma state legislature.

title: Nations of Europe go to war
summary: As European nations entered the First World War in 1914, governments flourished and patriotism bloomed while class struggle was suppressed and millions of young men died on the battlefields.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: Indeed, as the nations of Europe went to war in 1914, the governments flourished, patriotism bloomed, class struggle was stilled, and young men died in frightful numbers on the battlefields—often for a hundred yards of land, a line of trenches.

title: Henry James laments outbreak of World War I
summary: One day after England declared war, Henry James wrote to a friend expressing profound disillusionment that civilization had plunged into an abyss of blood and darkness.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: One day after the English declared war, Henry James wrote to a friend: "The plunge of civilization into this abyss of blood and darkness . . . is a thing that so gives away the whole long age during which we have supposed the world to be . . . gradually bettering."

title: US economic recession begins; war orders stimulate recovery by 1915
summary: In 1914 a serious recession had begun in the United States, with depressed business, deflated farm prices, and unemployment. By 1915, war orders for the Allies had stimulated the economy, and by April 1917 more than $2 billion worth of goods had been sold to the Allies.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: In 1914 a serious recession had begun in the United States. J. P. Morgan later testified: "The war opened during a period of hard times. . . . Business throughout the country was depressed, farm prices were deflated, unemployment was serious, the heavy industries were working far below capacity and bank clearings were off."

title: American warships bombard and occupy Vera Cruz, Mexico
summary: On the morning the bodies were discovered at Ludlow, American warships were attacking Vera Cruz on the coast of Mexico — bombarding and occupying it, leaving a hundred Mexicans dead — because Mexico had arrested American sailors and refused to salute with twenty-one guns.

citation.quote: On the morning that the bodies were discovered in the tent pit at Ludlow, American warships were attacking Vera Cruz, a city on the coast of Mexico—bombarding it, occupying it, leaving a hundred Mexicans dead—because Mexico had arrested American sailors and refused to apologize to the United States with a twenty-one-gun salute.

title: Ludlow Massacre: National Guard machine-guns strikers' tent colony
summary: On the morning of April 20, 1914, two National Guard companies opened machine-gun fire on the Ludlow tent colony housing a thousand striking miners, women, and children. At dusk, Guard soldiers torched the tents; thirteen were killed by gunfire and the following day eleven children and two women were found charred in a pit.

citation.quote: In April 1914, two National Guard companies were stationed in the hills overlooking the largest tent colony of strikers, the one at Ludlow, housing a thousand men, women, children. On the morning of April 20, a machine gun attack began on the tents.

title: Secretary of State Bryan praises Wilson for opening weaker nations to US capital
summary: In May 1914, Secretary of State William Jennings Bryan praised Wilson as one who had "opened the doors of all the weaker countries to an invasion of American capital and American enterprise," revealing the economic imperialism underlying American foreign policy.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: in May of 1914 he praised the President as one who had "opened the doors of all the weaker countries to an invasion of American capital and American enterprise."

title: British army recruitment standards lowered as casualties mount
summary: In August 1914 a volunteer for the British army had to be 5 feet 8 inches to enlist; by October the requirement dropped to 5 feet 5 inches as casualties reached thirty thousand, and then to 5 feet 3 inches. In the first three months of war, almost the entire original British army was wiped out.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: In August 1914, a volunteer for the British army had to be 5 feet 8 inches to enlist. By October, the requirement was lowered to 5 feet 5 inches. That month there were thirty thousand casualties, and then one could be 5 feet 3.

title: New York women socialists campaign for women's suffrage referendum
summary: During the 1915 campaign in New York for a referendum on women's suffrage, New York women socialists in a single day at the campaign's climax distributed 110,000 leaflets in English and Yiddish, held 100 meetings, and sold thousands of books.

citation.quote: During the 1915 campaign in New York for a referendum on women's suffrage, in one day at the climax of the campaign, they distributed 60,000 English leaflets, 50,000 Yiddish leaflets, sold 2,500 one-cent books and 1,500 five-cent books, put up 40,000 stickers, and held 100 meetings.

title: British liner Lusitania torpedoed and sunk; 1,198 die including 124 Americans
summary: In early 1915, a German submarine torpedoed and sank the British liner Lusitania. It sank in eighteen minutes, killing 1,198 people including 124 Americans. The U.S. government claimed it carried an innocent cargo, but its manifests had been falsified to conceal war materials.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: In early 1915, the British liner Lusitania was torpedoed and sunk by a German submarine. She sank in eighteen minutes, and 1,198 people died, including 124 Americans.

title: Wilson lifts ban on private bank loans to Allied powers
summary: In 1915 Wilson lifted the ban on private bank loans to the Allies, allowing J. P. Morgan to begin lending money in great amounts, tying American finance closely to the interest of a British victory over Germany.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: when, in 1915, Wilson lifted the ban on private bank loans to the Allies, Morgan could now begin lending money in such great amounts as to both make great profit and tie American finance closely to the interest of a British victory in the war against Germany.

title: US intervenes in Haiti for the second time
summary: The United States intervened in Haiti for the second time in 1915 and kept troops there for nineteen years.

citation.quote: It intervened for the second time in Haiti in 1915 and kept troops there for nineteen years.

title: W. E. B. Du Bois publishes "The African Roots of War" in the Atlantic Monthly
summary: In May 1915, W. E. B. Du Bois published "The African Roots of War" in the Atlantic Monthly, arguing that the war was fundamentally a struggle for empire and that Africa's resources were a prime cause of the conflict.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: A remarkably perceptive article on the nature of the First World War appeared in May 1915 in the Atlantic Monthly. Written by W. E. B. Du Bois, it was titled "The African Roots of War."

title: Joe Hill executed by firing squad in Salt Lake City
summary: In November 1915, IWW organizer and songwriter Joe Hill was accused of killing a grocer in Salt Lake City in a robbery and was found guilty without direct evidence. Despite ten thousand letters of protest to the governor, he was executed by firing squad.

citation.quote: In November 1915, Joe Hill was accused of killing a grocer in Salt Lake City, Utah, in a robbery. There was no direct evidence presented to the court that he had committed the murder, but there were enough pieces of evidence to persuade a jury to find him guilty.

title: Five Wobblies shot dead by vigilantes in Everett, Washington
summary: In Everett, Washington in 1916, a boatload of Wobblies was fired on by two hundred armed vigilantes gathered by the sheriff. Five Wobblies were shot to death and thirty-one wounded; two vigilantes were killed and nineteen wounded.

citation.quote: In 1916, in Everett, Washington, a boatload of Wobblies was fired on by two hundred armed vigilantes gathered by the sheriff, and five Wobblies were shot to death, thirty-one wounded.

title: Preparedness Day bombing in San Francisco kills nine
summary: During a Preparedness Day parade in San Francisco in the summer of 1916, a bomb exploded killing nine people. Two local radicals, Tom Mooney and Warren Billings, were arrested and would spend twenty years in prison.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: In the summer of 1916, during a Preparedness Day parade in San Francisco, a bomb exploded, killing nine people; two local radicals, Tom Mooney and Warren Billings, were arrested and would spend twenty years in prison.

title: Battle of Verdun and Somme offensive: 600,000 Allied casualties
summary: In 1916 the Germans tried to break through at Verdun; the British and French counterattacked along the Somme, moved forward a few miles, and lost 600,000 men.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: In 1916 the Germans tried to break through at Verdun; the British and French counterattacked along the Seine, moved forward a few miles, and lost 600,000 men.

title: U.S. Steel profits reach $348 million
summary: In 1916 alone, U.S. Steel made $348 million in profit, illustrating how the war enriched industrialists while workers in the steel plants gained comparatively little.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: did the workers in the steel plants gain as much as U.S. Steel, which made $348 million in profit in 1916 alone?

title: US intervenes in Dominican Republic for the fourth time
summary: The United States intervened in the Dominican Republic for the fourth time in 1916, keeping troops there for eight years.

citation.quote: It intervened in the Dominican Republic for the fourth time in 1916 and kept troops there for eight years.

title: General Haig orders mass attack; 60,000 British soldiers killed or wounded in one day
summary: In July 1916, British General Douglas Haig ordered eleven divisions to advance on German lines. Of the 110,000 who attacked, 20,000 were killed and 40,000 wounded in a single day.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: In July 1916, British General Douglas Haig ordered eleven divisions of English soldiers to climb out of their trenches and move toward the German lines. The six German divisions opened up with their machine guns. Of the 110,000 who attacked, 20,000 were killed, 40,000 more wounded—all those bodies strewn on no man's land...

title: Vigilantes in Montana seize and hang IWW organizer Frank Little
summary: The year the United States entered World War I, vigilantes in Montana seized IWW organizer Frank Little, tortured him, and hanged him, leaving his body dangling from a railroad trestle.

citation.quote: The following year—the year the United States entered World War I—vigilantes in Montana seized IWW organizer Frank Little, tortured him, and hanged him, leaving his body dangling from a railroad trestle.

title: United States enters World War I amid French army mutinies
summary: The United States entered the war in the spring of 1917 when mutinies were beginning to occur in the French army. Out of 112 French divisions, 68 would eventually have mutinies, with 629 men tried and condemned and 50 shot by firing squads.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: Into this pit of death and deception came the United States, in the spring of 1917. Mutinies were beginning to occur in the French army. Soon, out of 112 divisions, 68 would have mutinies; 629 men would be tried and condemned, 50 shot by firing squads.

title: Only 73,000 volunteers in first six weeks after US war declaration; Congress institutes draft
summary: Despite Wilson's war rhetoric, Americans did not rush to enlist — only 73,000 volunteered in the first six weeks after the declaration of war when a million men were needed. Congress voted overwhelmingly for a draft.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: Americans did not rush to enlist. A million men were needed, but in the first six weeks after the declaration of war only 73,000 volunteered. Congress voted overwhelmingly for a draft.

title: National Civic Federation member reports workers and farmers indifferent to war preparedness
summary: At the beginning of 1917, a member of the National Civic Federation complained that "neither workingmen nor farmers" were taking "any part or interest in the efforts of the security or defense leagues or other movements for national preparedness."

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: At the beginning of 1917, a member of the National Civic Federation had complained that "neither workingmen nor farmers" were taking "any part or interest in the efforts of the security or defense leagues or other movements for national preparedness."

title: Socialist Party emergency convention condemns war declaration as "a crime against the people"
summary: The day after Congress declared war, the Socialist Party met in emergency convention in St. Louis and called the declaration "a crime against the people of the United States."

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: The day after Congress declared war, the Socialist party met in emergency convention in St. Louis and called the declaration "a crime against the people of the United States."

title: Socialist antiwar meetings draw tens of thousands of farmers in Minnesota
summary: In the summer of 1917, Socialist antiwar meetings in Minnesota drew large crowds of five thousand, ten thousand, and twenty thousand farmers protesting the war, the draft, and profiteering.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: In the summer of 1917, Socialist antiwar meetings in Minnesota drew large crowds—five thousand, ten thousand, twenty thousand farmers—protesting the war, the draft, profiteering.

title: Socialists make sweeping gains in 1917 municipal elections
summary: In the 1917 municipal elections, Socialist candidates made remarkable gains across major cities: their New York mayoral candidate Morris Hillquit got 22 percent of the vote, ten Socialists were elected to the New York State legislature, and the party vote in Chicago leaped from 3.6 to 34.7 percent.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: In the municipal elections of 1917, against the tide of propaganda and patriotism, the Socialists made remarkable gains. Their candidate for mayor of New York, Morris Hillquit, got 22 percent of the vote, five times the normal Socialist vote there. Ten Socialists were elected to the New York State legislature. In Chicago, the party vote went from 3.6 percent in 1915 to 34.7 percent in 1917.

title: Socialist Charles Schenck arrested in Philadelphia for distributing antiwar leaflets
summary: Two months after the Espionage Act passed, Socialist Charles Schenck was arrested in Philadelphia for printing and distributing fifteen thousand leaflets denouncing the draft law and the war, arguing conscription violated the Thirteenth Amendment.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: Two months after the law passed, a Socialist named Charles Schenck was arrested in Philadelphia for printing and distributing fifteen thousand leaflets that denounced the draft law and the war.

title: American Defense Society formed and deploys Vigilante Patrol to suppress antiwar speech
summary: In the summer of 1917, the American Defense Society was formed and enrolled over one hundred men in an American Vigilante Patrol "to put an end to seditious street oratory."

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: In the summer of 1917, the American Defense Society was formed. The New York Herald reported: "More than one hundred men enrolled yesterday in the American Vigilante Patrol at the offices of the American Defense Society. . . . The Patrol was formed to put an end to seditious street oratory."

title: Green Corn Rebellion: Oklahoma tenant farmers and IWW members plan armed resistance to draft
summary: In Oklahoma, the Socialist Party and IWW organized tenant farmers and sharecroppers into a "Working Class Union" that planned to destroy a railroad bridge and march on Washington to resist the draft. Before they could act, 450 members were arrested; leaders received three to ten years in prison.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: In Oklahoma, the Socialist party and the IWW had been active among tenant farmers and sharecroppers who formed a "Working Class Union." At a mass meeting of the Union, plans were made to destroy a railroad bridge and cut telegraph wires in order to block military enlistments.

title: The Masses socialist magazine banned from the US mails
summary: In the summer of 1917, The Masses, a socialist magazine of politics, literature, and art, was banned from the mails by the Post Office Department for printing antiwar articles including an editorial by Max Eastman.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: The Post Office Department began taking away the mailing privileges of newspapers and magazines that printed antiwar articles. The Masses, a socialist magazine of politics, literature, and art, was banned from the mails. It had carried an editorial by Max Eastman in the summer of 1917...

title: Filmmaker prosecuted under Espionage Act for depicting British atrocities in American Revolution film
summary: In Los Angeles, a filmmaker was prosecuted under the Espionage Act for a film depicting British atrocities against American colonists during the Revolution, because the judge ruled it tended to "question the good faith of our ally, Great Britain." He was sentenced to ten years in prison.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: The man who made the film was prosecuted under the Espionage Act because, the judge said, the film tended "to question the good faith of our ally, Great Britain." He was sentenced to ten years in prison.

title: Socialist Kate Richards O'Hare sentenced to five years for antiwar speech in North Dakota
summary: In July 1917, Socialist Kate Richards O'Hare spoke in North Dakota and was subsequently arrested, tried, found guilty, and sentenced to five years in the Missouri state penitentiary under the Espionage Act.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: Socialist Kate Richards O'Hare, speaking in North Dakota in July of 1917, said, it was reported, that "the women of the United States were nothing more nor less than brood sows, to raise children to get into the army and be made into fertilizer." She was arrested, tried, found guilty, and sentenced to five years in the Missouri state penitentiary.

title: Emma Goldman and Alexander Berkman sentenced to prison for opposing the draft
summary: Emma Goldman and her fellow anarchist Alexander Berkman were sentenced to prison for opposing the draft. Goldman addressed the jury, arguing that a democracy "conceived in the military servitude of the masses" is not democracy at all but despotism.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: Emma Goldman and her fellow anarchist, Alexander Berkman (he had already been locked up fourteen years in Pennsylvania; she had served a year on Blackwell's Island), were sentenced to prison for opposing the draft.

title: US exchanges notes with Japan recognizing Japan's special interests in China
summary: The United States exchanged diplomatic notes with Japan in 1917 recognizing that Japan had special interests in China, reflecting the US acceptance of Japanese imperialism in Asia.

citation.quote: It had exchanged notes with Japan in 1917 saying "the Government of the United States recognizes that Japan has special interests in China."

title: East St. Louis race massacre kills approximately 200 Black residents
summary: White workers in East St. Louis, angered by the influx of Black workers, killed approximately 200 people in what was called a race riot. W. E. B. Du Bois wrote an angry article titled "The Massacre of East St. Louis" in response.

citation.quote: in East St. Louis in 1917 there occurred one of the many "race riots" that took place in what our white-oriented history books called the "Progressive Era." There, white workers, angered by the influx of black workers, killed perhaps 200 people, provoking an angry article by W. E. B. Du Bois called "The Massacre of East St. Louis"

title: Haig promoted to field marshal after catastrophic Somme offensive
summary: On January 1, 1917, General Haig was promoted to field marshal despite having ordered the disastrous July 1916 attack that resulted in 60,000 British casualties in a single day.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: On January 1, 1917, Haig was promoted to field marshal.

title: Wilson cites German submarine warfare as justification for US entry into WWI
summary: In April 1917, after Germany announced its submarines would sink any ship bringing supplies to its enemies and had already sunk several merchant vessels, Wilson declared he must stand by the right of Americans to travel on merchant ships in the war zone.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: But in April of 1917, the Germans had announced they would have their submarines sink any ship bringing supplies to their enemies; and they had sunk a number of merchant vessels.

title: New York Times quotes Elihu Root calling for executions of antiwar dissenters
summary: In April 1917, the New York Times quoted former Secretary of War Elihu Root saying "We must have no criticism now," and a few months later quoted him saying that men spreading dissent "ought to be taken out at sunrise tomorrow and shot for treason."

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: In April of 1917, the New York Times quoted Elihu Root (former Secretary of War, a corporation lawyer) as saying: "We must have no criticism now."

title: Espionage Act passed and signed into law
summary: Congress passed and Wilson signed the Espionage Act in June 1917, which despite its name was used to imprison Americans who spoke or wrote against the war, carrying penalties of up to twenty years in prison.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: Congress passed, and Wilson signed, in June of 1917, the Espionage Act.

title: American Protective League expands to 600 cities with nearly 100,000 members
summary: By June 1917, the Department of Justice–sponsored American Protective League had units in six hundred cities and towns with a membership of nearly 100,000, engaged in illegal surveillance, mail opening, and breaking and entering to uncover alleged disloyalty.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: The Department of Justice sponsored an American Protective League, which by June of 1917 had units in six hundred cities and towns, a membership of nearly 100,000.

title: Antiwar parade in Boston draws eight thousand marchers and is attacked by soldiers
summary: On July 1, 1917, radicals organized an antiwar parade in Boston carrying banners demanding peace and questioning conscription. The New York Call reported eight thousand people marched, and the parade was attacked by soldiers and sailors on orders from their officers.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: On July 1, 1917, radicals organized a parade in Boston against the war, with banners: IS THIS A POPULAR WAR, WHY CONSCRIPTION? . . . The parade was attacked by soldiers and sailors, on orders from their officers.

title: Minneapolis Journal reports draft opposition spreading rapidly in Minnesota
summary: Headlines in the Minneapolis Journal of August 6 and 7, 1917 read "Draft Opposition Fast Spreading in State" and "Conscripts Give False Addresses," reflecting widespread resistance to the war draft in Minnesota.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: In Minnesota, headlines in the Minneapolis Journal of August 6 and 7 read: "Draft Opposition Fast Spreading in State," and "Conscripts Give False Addresses."

title: Ninety of first hundred draftees in New York City claim exemption
summary: On August 1, 1917, the New York Herald reported that in New York City ninety of the first hundred draftees had claimed exemption, evidence of the widespread resistance to the draft.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: On August 1, 1917, the New York Herald reported that in New York City ninety of the first hundred draftees claimed exemption.

title: Department of Justice raids 48 IWW halls simultaneously across the country
summary: In early September 1917, Department of Justice agents made simultaneous raids on forty-eight IWW meeting halls across the country, seizing correspondence and literature to use as courtroom evidence.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: In early September 1917, Department of Justice agents made simultaneous raids on forty-eight IWW meeting halls across the country, seizing correspondence and literature that would become courtroom evidence.

title: 165 IWW leaders arrested for conspiring to hinder the draft
summary: Later in September 1917, 165 IWW leaders were arrested for conspiring to hinder the draft, encourage desertion, and intimidate others in connection with labor disputes, leading to what would become the longest criminal trial in American history up to that time.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: Later that month, 165 IWW leaders were arrested for conspiring to hinder the draft, encourage desertion, and intimidate others in connection with labor disputes.

title: IWW defendants found guilty; Haywood sentenced to twenty years, fines total $2.5 million
summary: The jury found all 101 IWW defendants guilty. The judge sentenced Haywood and fourteen others to twenty years in prison; thirty-three received ten-year sentences; fines totaled $2,500,000. The IWW was shattered as an organization.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: The jury found them all guilty. The judge sentenced Haywood and fourteen others to twenty years in prison; thirty-three were given ten years, the rest shorter sentences. They were fined a total of $2,500,000. The IWW was shattered.

title: American force of seven thousand lands at Vladivostok as part of Allied intervention in Russia
summary: Just before World War I ended, seven thousand American troops landed at Vladivostok as part of an Allied intervention against the Bolshevik revolution, remaining until early 1920.

citation.quote: Just before World War I ended, in 1918, an American force of seven thousand landed at Vladivostok as part of an Allied intervention in Russia, and remained until early 1920.

title: IWW mass trial begins: 101 defendants in longest US criminal trial to date
summary: One hundred and one IWW members went on trial in April 1918; the trial lasted five months and was the longest criminal trial in American history up to that time. John Reed covered the trial for The Masses.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: One hundred and one went on trial in April 1918; it lasted five months, the longest criminal trial in American history up to that time.

title: Eugene Debs delivers antiwar speech in Canton, Ohio and is arrested
summary: In June 1918, Eugene Debs visited three Socialists imprisoned for opposing the draft, then delivered a two-hour speech across the street from the jail in which he denounced the war and declared solidarity with all working people, leading to his arrest for violating the Espionage Act.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: In June of 1918, Debs visited three Socialists who were in prison for opposing the draft, and then spoke, across the street from the jail, to an audience he kept enthralled for two hours.

title: World War I ends; 50,000 American soldiers dead
summary: The war ended in November 1918 with fifty thousand American soldiers dead, soon followed by widespread bitterness and disillusionment reflected in the literature of the postwar decade.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: The war ended in November 1918. Fifty thousand American soldiers had died, and it did not take long, even in the case of patriots, for bitterness and disillusionment to spread through the country.

title: Supreme Court unanimously upholds Debs's Espionage Act conviction
summary: In 1919, after the war had ended, the Supreme Court heard Debs's appeal and unanimously affirmed his guilt under the Espionage Act. Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote that Debs's speech naturally would have the effect of obstructing recruiting.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: Debs's appeal was not heard by the Supreme Court until 1919. The war was over. Oliver Wendell Holmes, for a unanimous court, affirmed Debs's guilt.

title: Wilson adviser George Record urges economic reform as alternative to socialism and Bolshevism
summary: In early 1919, George L. Record, one of Wilson's friends, wrote to him urging that Wilson become "the real leader of the radical forces in America" and present a program of fundamental reform as an alternative to socialism and Bolshevism.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: The first was suggested by George L. Record, one of Wilson's friends, who wrote to him in early 1919 that something would have to be done for economic democracy, "to meet this menace of socialism."

title: Bomb explodes at home of Attorney General Palmer
summary: In the summer of 1919, a bomb exploded in front of the home of Wilson's Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer, which Wilson's adviser Joseph Tumulty cited as a symptom of the "terrible unrest" spreading across the country.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: "What happened in Washington last night" was the explosion of a bomb in front of the home of Wilson's Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer.

title: Palmer deports 249 Russian-born aliens including Emma Goldman and Alexander Berkman
summary: On December 21, 1919, Palmer's agents picked up 249 aliens of Russian birth, including Emma Goldman and Alexander Berkman, put them on a transport, and deported them to Soviet Russia.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: Palmer's men, on December 21, 1919, picked up 249 aliens of Russian birth (including Emma Goldman and Alexander Berkman), put them on a transport, and deported them to what had become Soviet Russia.

title: Anarchist Andrea Salsedo found dead after eight weeks of secret FBI detention
summary: In the spring of 1920, anarchist typesetter Andrea Salsedo was arrested in New York by FBI agents and held for eight weeks in their offices without access to family, friends, or lawyers. His crushed body was then found on the pavement below the building; the FBI claimed suicide.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: In the spring of 1920, a typesetter and anarchist named Andrea Salsedo was arrested in New York by FBI agents and held for eight weeks in the FBI offices on the fourteenth floor of the Park Row Building, not allowed to contact family or friends or lawyers. Then his crushed body was found on the pavement below the building and the FBI said he had committed suicide by jumping from the fourteenth floor window.

title: Sacco and Vanzetti arrested and charged with robbery and murder
summary: Two friends of Salsedo — anarchists Nicola Sacco and Bartolomeo Vanzetti — began carrying guns after learning of his death and were arrested on a streetcar in Brockton, Massachusetts, charged with a holdup and murder at a shoe factory that had taken place two weeks before.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: Two friends of Salsedo, anarchists and workingmen in the Boston area, having just learned of his death, began carrying guns. They were arrested on a streetcar in Brockton, Massachusetts, and charged with a holdup and murder that had taken place two weeks before at a shoe factory. These were Nicola Sacco and Bartolomeo Vanzetti.

title: Claude McKay writes militant poem entered into Congressional Record
summary: In the 1920s, McKay wrote "If we must die," a poem so alarming to whites that Senator Henry Cabot Lodge read it into the Congressional Record as evidence of dangerous currents among young Black Americans.

citation.quote: In the 1920s, Claude McKay, one of the figures of what came to be called the "Harlem Renaissance," wrote a poem that Henry Cabot Lodge put in the *Congressional Record* as an example of dangerous currents among young blacks:

title: Palmer Raids: 4,000 arrested nationwide; 600 in Boston rounded up in early-morning raids
summary: In January 1920, four thousand persons were rounded up all over the country in secret hearings and ordered deported. In Boston, 600 people were arrested by raiding meeting halls and invading homes in the early morning, with those arrested handcuffed in pairs and chained together.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: In January 1920, four thousand persons were rounded up all over the country, held in seclusion for long periods of time, brought into secret hearings, and ordered deported. In Boston, Department of Justice agents, aided by local police, arrested six hundred people by raiding meeting halls or by invading their homes in the early morning.

title: President Harding releases Debs from federal penitentiary
summary: Debs spent thirty-two months in federal penitentiary before President Harding released him in 1921 at the age of sixty-six.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: Debs was locked up in the West Virginia state penitentiary, and then in the Atlanta federal penitentiary, where he spent thirty-two months until, at the age of sixty-six, he was released by President Harding in 1921.

title: US directs finances of half of Latin American states
summary: By 1924 the United States was directing to some extent the finances of half of the twenty Latin American states.

citation.quote: By 1924 the finances of half of the twenty Latin American states were being directed to some extent by the United States.

title: United States sends five thousand marines to Nicaragua
summary: The U.S. sent five thousand marines to Nicaragua to counter a revolution and maintained a force there for seven years.

citation.quote: It sent five thousand marines to Nicaragua in 1926 to counter a revolution, and kept a force there for seven years.

title: Sacco and Vanzetti executed after seven years of appeals
summary: After seven years in jail during which people around the world became involved in their case, Sacco and Vanzetti were electrocuted in August 1927. The trial record and surrounding circumstances suggested they were sentenced to death because they were anarchists and foreigners.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: They went on trial, were found guilty, and spent seven years in jail while appeals went on, and while all over the country and the world, people became involved in their case. The trial record and the surrounding circumstances suggested that Sacco and Vanzetti were sentenced to death because they were anarchists and foreigners. In August 1927, as police broke up marches and picket lines with arrests and beatings, and troops surrounded the prison, they were electrocuted.

title: Langston Hughes writes "Lenox Avenue Mural"
summary: In the 1930s, Hughes composed the poem that asks "What happens to a dream deferred?" — a defining meditation on Black American frustration and latent revolt.

citation.quote: In the 1930s, Langston Hughes wrote a poem, "Lenox Avenue Mural":

title: Angelo Herndon joins Communist Party and organizes unemployed in Birmingham
summary: In 1932, nineteen-year-old Angelo Herndon joined an Unemployment Council organized by the Communist Party in Birmingham and then joined the party, becoming an organizer in Atlanta who secured relief for hundreds of jobless people.

citation.quote: And in Georgia, in 1932, a nineteen-year-old black youth named Angelo Herndon, whose father died of miner's pneumonia, who had worked in mines as a boy in Kentucky, joined an Unemployment Council in Birmingham organized by the Communist party, and then joined the party.

title: Herndon organizes Atlanta demonstration; city grants $6,000 in relief
summary: Herndon and fellow Communists organized block committees in 1932 that got rent relief, then mounted a demonstration of a thousand people — including six hundred whites — that moved the city to grant $6,000 to the jobless. Herndon was soon arrested and charged with insurrection.

citation.quote: Herndon became a Communist party organizer in Atlanta. He and his fellow Communists organized block committees of Unemployment Councils in 1932 which got rent relief for needy people. They organized a demonstration to which a thousand people came, six hundred of them white, and the next day the city voted \$6,000 in relief to the jobless.

title: Chief Luther Standing Bear publishes From the Land of the Spotted Eagle
summary: In his 1933 autobiography, Lakota chief Luther Standing Bear criticized the "varied fruits" of white civilization as sickening and deadening, and celebrated the spiritual wisdom of traditional Indian ways of life.

citation.quote: Chief Luther Standing Bear, in his 1933 autobiography, *From the Land of the Spotted Eagle,* wrote: True, the white man brought great change. But the varied fruits of his civilization, though highly colored and inviting, are sickening and deadening.

title: Senate resolution expressing concern over Nazi persecution of Jews buried in committee
summary: A Senate resolution asking Congress and the President to express 'surprise and pain' at German persecution of Jews was buried in committee at the State Department's instigation.

citation.quote: when a resolution was introduced in the Senate in January 1934 asking the Senate and the President to express "surprise and pain" at what the Germans were doing to the Jews, and to ask restoration of Jewish rights, the State Department "caused this resolution to be buried in committee," according to Arnold Offner (American Appeasement).

title: Italy invades Ethiopia; US allows oil exports to continue
summary: When Mussolini's Italy invaded Ethiopia in 1935, the U.S. declared an embargo on munitions but allowed American businesses to ship oil to Italy in large quantities essential to the war effort.

citation.quote: When Mussolini's Italy invaded Ethiopia in 1935, the U.S. declared an embargo on munitions but let American businesses send oil to Italy in huge quantities, which was essential to Italy's carrying on the war.

title: Fascist rebellion in Spain; Roosevelt sponsors neutrality act blocking aid to Spanish Republic
summary: When a Fascist rebellion broke out in Spain in 1936 against the elected socialist-liberal government, the Roosevelt administration sponsored a neutrality act that cut off help to the Spanish Republic while Hitler and Mussolini aided Franco.

citation.quote: When a Fascist rebellion took place in Spain in 1936 against the elected socialist-liberal government, the Roosevelt administration sponsored a neutrality act that had the effect of shutting off help to the Spanish government while Hitler and Mussolini gave critical aid to Franco.

title: Japan bombs civilians at Nanking; US does not respond with war
summary: Japan's attack on China in 1937 and the bombing of civilians at Nanking did not provoke the United States to enter the war, demonstrating that US entry was driven by strategic interests rather than humanitarian concern.

citation.quote: Surely it was not the humane concern for Japan's bombing of civilians that led to Roosevelt's outraged call for war—Japan's attack on China in 1937, her bombing of civilians at Nanking, had not provoked the United States to war.

title: Richard Wright publishes autobiography Black Boy
summary: Wright's autobiography, published in 1937, documented the daily humiliations of Black life in the South and expressed unapologetically the rage that lay beneath forced subservience.

citation.quote: By the 1940s there was Richard Wright, a gifted novelist, a black man. His autobiography of 1937, *Black Boy,* gave endless insights: for instance, how blacks were set against one another, when he told how he was prodded to fight another black boy for the amusement of white men.

title: Supreme Court strikes down Georgia insurrection statute; Herndon freed
summary: After five years in prison, Angelo Herndon was freed in 1937 when the Supreme Court ruled unconstitutional the Georgia statute under which he had been convicted of insurrection.

citation.quote: Herndon was convicted and spent five years in prison until in 1937 the Supreme Court ruled unconstitutional the Georgia statute under which he was found guilty.

title: American Communist Party performs anti-imperialist war skit
summary: The U.S. Communist Party performed a skit satirizing Allied claims that the war was not imperialist, listing the many colonial territories represented by Britain and the United States.

citation.quote: Thus went a skit put on in the United States in the year 1939 by the Communist party.

title: US begins sending large amounts of war supplies to England and France
summary: In 1940 the United States began sending large amounts of war supplies to England and France; by 1941 three-fourths of the value of military contracts were handled by fifty-six large corporations.

citation.quote: In 1940 the United States had begun sending large amounts of war supplies to England and France. By 1941 three-fourths of the value of military contracts were handled by fifty-six large corporations.

title: Congress passes the Smith Act extending Espionage Act prohibitions to peacetime
summary: In 1940, with the United States not yet at war, Congress passed the Smith Act, making it a crime in peacetime to advocate the overthrow of the government by force or to join any group advocating such ideas.

citation.quote: But in 1940, with the United States not yet at war, Congress passed the Smith Act.

title: ACLU expels Elizabeth Gurley Flynn for Communist Party membership
summary: In 1940 the American Civil Liberties Union expelled charter member Elizabeth Gurley Flynn because she was a member of the Communist Party, beginning the ACLU's capitulation to Cold War anti-Communist pressure.

citation.quote: It had already started in this direction back in 1940 when it expelled one of its charter members, Elizabeth Gurley Flynn, because she was a member of the Communist party.

title: Twenty percent of Americans identify as political independents
summary: Back in 1940, only 20 percent of those polled called themselves "independents," a figure that would rise to 34 percent by 1974.

citation.quote: Back in 1940, 20 percent of those polled called themselves "independents." In 1974, 34 percent called themselves "independents."

title: Germany invades Soviet Russia; American Communist Party reverses its anti-war position
summary: When Germany invaded Soviet Russia, the American Communist Party abandoned its characterization of the war as imperialist and instead called it a 'people's war' against Fascism.

citation.quote: Two years later, Germany invaded Soviet Russia, and the American Communist party, which had repeatedly described the war between the Axis Powers and the Allied Powers as an imperialist war, now called it a "people's war" against Fascism.

title: US imposes total embargo on scrap iron and oil against Japan
summary: The United States imposed a total embargo on scrap iron and a total embargo on oil in the summer of 1941, measures widely recognized in Washington as carrying grave risks of provoking Japan to war.

citation.quote: a total embargo on scrap iron, a total embargo on oil in the summer of 1941.

title: Roosevelt and Churchill release the Atlantic Charter
summary: Roosevelt and Churchill met off the coast of Newfoundland in August 1941 and released the Atlantic Charter, declaring their countries sought no territorial aggrandizement and respected the right of all peoples to choose their form of government.

citation.quote: In August 1941, Roosevelt and Churchill met off the coast of Newfoundland and released to the world the Atlantic Charter, setting forth noble goals for the postwar world, saying their countries "seek no aggrandizement, territorial or other," and that they respected "the right of all peoples to choose the form of government under which they will live."

title: Roosevelt misrepresents facts in incidents involving German submarines and American destroyers
summary: In September and October 1941, Roosevelt misstated the facts in two incidents involving German submarines and American destroyers, deceiving the American public in the lead-up to war.

citation.quote: In September and October 1941, he misstated the facts in two incidents involving German submarines and American destroyers.

title: Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor brings United States into World War II
summary: Japan attacked the American naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, prompting Roosevelt's call for war and bringing the United States fully into World War II.

citation.quote: What brought the United States fully into the war was the Japanese attack on the American naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, on December 7, 1941.

title: Roosevelt's representative assures French General Giraud that French sovereignty will be restored
summary: In late 1942, Roosevelt's personal representative assured French General Henri Giraud that French sovereignty would be re-established throughout all territory over which the French flag had flown in 1939, contradicting Atlantic Charter principles.

citation.quote: In late 1942, Roosevelt's personal representative assured French General Henri Giraud: "It is thoroughly understood that French sovereignty will be re-established as soon as possible throughout all the territory, metropolitan or colonial, over which flew the French flag in 1939."

title: Allied invasion of North Africa
summary: Allied forces invaded North Africa in 1942 as part of the major military operations of World War II.

citation.quote: the invasion of North Africa in 1942, Italy in 1943, the massive, dramatic cross-Channel invasion of German-occupied France in 1944

title: Roosevelt signs Executive Order 9066 authorizing Japanese-American internment
summary: Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066 in February 1942, giving the army power to arrest 110,000 Japanese Americans on the West Coast without warrants, indictments, or hearings and confine them in inland camps.

citation.quote: Franklin D. Roosevelt did not share this frenzy, but he calmly signed Executive Order 9066, in February 1942, giving the army the power, without warrants or indictments or hearings, to arrest every Japanese-American on the West Coast—110,000 men, women, and children—to take them from their homes, transport them to camps far into the interior, and keep them there under prison conditions.

title: Allied invasion of Italy
summary: Allied forces invaded Italy in 1943 as part of the campaign to defeat the Axis powers in Europe.

citation.quote: the invasion of North Africa in 1942, Italy in 1943, the massive, dramatic cross-Channel invasion of German-occupied France in 1944
