title: "Draftee's Prayer" published in Negro newspaper
summary: In January 1943, a Negro newspaper published the 'Draftee's Prayer,' a poem expressing the anger and alienation of Black Americans asked to fight in a war for a country that denied them basic rights.

citation.quote: In January 1943, there appeared in a Negro newspaper this "Draftee's Prayer":

title: Eighteen members of Socialist Workers Party convicted under Smith Act in Minneapolis
summary: In Minneapolis in 1943, eighteen members of the Socialist Workers Party were convicted for belonging to a party whose principles were said to violate the Smith Act; they were sentenced to prison and the Supreme Court refused to review the case.

citation.quote: In Minneapolis in 1943, eighteen members of the Socialist Workers party were convicted for belonging to a party whose ideas, expressed in its Declaration of Principles, and in the Communist Manifesto, were said to violate the Smith Act.

title: Allies meet at Casablanca and agree on area bombing of German cities
summary: The Allies met at Casablanca in January 1943 and agreed on large-scale air attacks aimed at destroying the German military, industrial and economic system and undermining the morale of the German people, launching the saturation bombing campaign.

citation.quote: In January 1943 the Allies met at Casablanca and agreed on large-scale air attacks to achieve "the destruction and dislocation of the German military, industrial and economic system and the undermining of the morale of the German people to the point where their capacity for armed resistance is fatally weakened."

title: Massive cross-Channel invasion of German-occupied France
summary: The Allies launched the massive cross-Channel invasion of German-occupied France in 1944, while simultaneously the Soviet Union drove the Germans out of Russia.

citation.quote: the invasion of North Africa in 1942, Italy in 1943, the massive, dramatic cross-Channel invasion of German-occupied France in 1944

title: Britain and US sign oil pact agreeing on principle of equal opportunity in Middle East
summary: In 1944 Britain and the United States signed an oil pact agreeing on the principle of equal opportunity, effectively extending Open Door Policy to the Middle East and consolidating US dominance in the region.

citation.quote: In 1944 Britain and the U.S. signed a pact on oil agreeing on "the principle of equal opportunity,"

title: Supreme Court upholds forced evacuation of Japanese Americans
summary: In 1944 the Supreme Court upheld the forced evacuation of Japanese Americans on the grounds of military necessity.

citation.quote: In 1944 the Supreme Court upheld the forced evacuation on the grounds of military necessity.

title: One million workers on strike in mines, steel mills, and auto industries
summary: In 1944 alone, a million workers were on strike in the mines, steel mills, and auto and transportation equipment industries, demonstrating widespread worker discontent despite the wartime no-strike pledges of union leadership.

citation.quote: In 1944 alone, a million workers were on strike, in the mines, in the steel mills, in the auto and transportation equipment industries.

title: US Strategic Bombing Survey set up by War Department to study aerial attacks
summary: The United States Strategic Bombing Survey was set up by the War Department in 1944 to study the results of aerial attacks; after the war it concluded that Japan would have surrendered even without the atomic bombs.

citation.quote: The United States Strategic Bombing Survey, set up by the War Department in 1944 to study the results of aerial attacks in the war, interviewed hundreds of Japanese civilian and military leaders after Japan surrendered

title: State Department official acknowledges need for greatly increased foreign markets after the war
summary: In April 1944 a State Department official stated that the US would need greatly increased foreign markets to absorb its enormously increased postwar production, revealing the economic aims behind US wartime diplomacy.

citation.quote: In April 1944 a State Department official said: "As you know, we've got to plan on enormously increased production in this country after the war, and the American domestic market can't absorb all that production indefinitely. There won't be any question about our needing greatly increased foreign markets."

title: Simone Weil's essay on the Apparatus published in Dwight Macdonald's magazine Politics
summary: In early 1945, Dwight Macdonald's wartime magazine Politics published an essay by French philosopher Simone Weil arguing that the true adversary of human freedom was the bureaucratic Apparatus — regardless of whether it called itself Fascism, Democracy, or Proletarian Dictatorship.

citation.quote: A few voices continued to insist that the real war was inside each nation: Dwight Macdonald's wartime magazine Politics presented, in early 1945, an article by the French worker-philosopher Simone Weil:

title: Firebombing of Dresden kills more than 100,000
summary: Allied bombing of Dresden in early 1945 created a massive firestorm that killed more than 100,000 people, representing the climax of the terror bombing campaign against German cities.

citation.quote: The climax of this terror bombing was the bombing of Dresden in early 1945, in which the tremendous heat generated by the bombs created a vacuum into which fire leaped swiftly in a great firestorm through the city. More than 100,000 died in Dresden.

title: Nighttime firebombing of Tokyo kills 80,000
summary: A nighttime fire-bombing of Tokyo as part of the Allied strategy of saturation bombing to destroy civilian morale killed 80,000 people.

citation.quote: one nighttime fire-bombing of Tokyo took 80,000 lives.

title: Du Bois's warning about the color line gains new prominence
summary: What W. E. B. Du Bois had long said — "The problem of the 20th century is the problem of the color line" — loomed large in 1945 as the United States confronted postwar decolonization and Cold War rivalry.

citation.quote: What Du Bois had said long ago, unnoticed, now loomed large in 1945: "The problem of the 20th century is the problem of the color line."

title: Japan withdraws from Indochina; Ho Chi Minh declares independence
summary: Defeated Japan was forced to leave Indochina in the fall of 1945. Ho Chi Minh's revolutionary movement held a massive celebration in Hanoi and issued a Declaration of Independence.

citation.quote: In the fall of 1945 Japan, defeated, was forced to leave Indochina, the former French colony it had occupied at the start of the war. In the meantime, a revolutionary movement had grown there, determined to end colonial control and to achieve a new life for the peasants of Indochina. Led by a Communist named Ho Chi Minh, the revolutionists fought against the Japanese, and when they were gone held a spectacular celebration in Hanoi in late 1945, with a million people in the streets, and issued a Declaration of Independence.

title: Roosevelt entertains King Ibn Saud on cruiser Quincy after Yalta
summary: On his way back from Yalta in February 1945, Roosevelt entertained Saudi King Ibn Saud on the cruiser Quincy, cementing the US-Saudi relationship driven by oil interests.

citation.quote: Roosevelt, on his way back from Yalta in February 1945, entertained the King on the cruiser Quincy, together with his entourage of fifty, including two sons, a prime minister, an astrologer and flocks of sheep for slaughter.

title: Roosevelt dies; Truman becomes President
summary: Franklin D. Roosevelt died in April 1945, and Harry Truman assumed the presidency and proceeded to create an atmosphere of cold war and anti-Communism.

citation.quote: the Truman administration (Roosevelt had died in April 1945) worked to create an atmosphere of crisis and cold war.

title: Truman assures France he does not question her sovereignty over Indochina
summary: In May 1945, President Truman assured the French he did not question France's sovereignty over Indochina, completing the U.S. reversal from Atlantic Charter self-determination principles.

citation.quote: In May, Truman assured the French he did not question her "sovereignty over Indochina."

title: Japanese Emperor begins to suggest alternatives to fighting to the end
summary: In June 1945, the Japanese Emperor himself began to suggest that alternatives to fighting to the end be considered, indicating Japan's readiness to surrender before the atomic bombs were dropped.

citation.quote: Japanese leaders had begun talking of surrender a year before this, and the Emperor himself had begun to suggest, in June 1945, that alternatives to fighting to the end be considered.

title: Harry Gold meets David Greenglass in New Mexico and receives atomic secrets
summary: In June 1945, Harry Gold allegedly appeared at the Los Alamos area with the other half of a Jell-O box top and received sketches Greenglass had drawn from memory of atomic bomb lens experiments.

citation.quote: in June 1945, Harry Gold appeared with the other half of the box top, and Greenglass gave him information he had memorized.

title: Japanese Foreign Minister Togo cables that unconditional surrender is the only obstacle to peace
summary: On July 13, 1945, Japanese Foreign Minister Shigenori Togo wired his ambassador in Moscow that unconditional surrender was the only obstacle to peace, a message decoded by US intelligence and relayed to the President with no effect on war planning.

citation.quote: On July 13, Foreign Minister Shigenori Togo wired his ambassador in Moscow: "Unconditional surrender is the only obstacle to peace. . . ."

title: Potsdam demand for Japan's unconditional surrender issued
summary: The Potsdam demand for Japan's unconditional surrender was issued on July 26, 1945; a New York Times military analyst later concluded Japan was already in a hopeless strategic position by this date.

citation.quote: The enemy, in a military sense, was in a hopeless strategic position by the time the Potsdam demand for unconditional surrender was made on July 26.

title: Forrestal diary entry records Byrnes anxious to end war with Japan before Russia enters
summary: A diary entry for July 28, 1945 by Secretary of the Navy James Forrestal records Secretary of State James F. Byrnes as 'most anxious to get the Japanese affair over with before the Russians got in,' supporting the argument that the atomic bomb was the first act of Cold War diplomacy.

citation.quote: Blackett is supported by American historian Gar Alperovitz (Atomic Diplomacy), who notes a diary entry for July 28, 1945, by Secretary of the Navy James Forrestal, describing Secretary of State James F. Byrnes as "most anxious to get the Japanese affair over with before the Russians got in."

title: State Department officer notes petroleum's dominant role in US external relations
summary: In August 1945, a State Department officer stated that petroleum had historically played a larger part in US external relations than any other commodity over the preceding 35 years, illustrating the oil-driven motives behind US Middle East policy.

citation.quote: In August 1945 a State Department officer said that "a review of the diplomatic history of the past 35 years will show that petroleum has historically played a larger part in the external relations of the United States than any other commodity."

title: Ho Chi Minh establishes the Democratic Republic of Vietnam
summary: In August–September 1945 Ho Chi Minh overthrew Japanese rule and established the Democratic Republic of Vietnam, giving Vietnam its only period of unity and freedom from foreign domination in its modern history.

citation.quote: He was the only Vietnamese wartime leader with a national following, and he assured himself wider fealty among the Vietnamese people when in August-September, 1945, he overthrew the Japanese . . . established the Democratic Republic of Vietnam, and staged receptions for in-coming allied occupation forces. . . . For a few weeks in September, 1945, Vietnam was—for the first and only time in its modern history—free of foreign domination, and united from north to south under Ho Chi Minh. . . .

title: United States drops first atomic bomb on Hiroshima
summary: The United States dropped the first atomic bomb on Hiroshima on August 6, 1945, killing perhaps 100,000 Japanese and leaving tens of thousands more slowly dying from radiation poisoning.

citation.quote: And then, on August 6, 1945, came the lone American plane in the sky over Hiroshima, dropping the first atomic bomb, leaving perhaps 100,000 Japanese dead, and tens of thousands more slowly dying from radiation poisoning.

title: Soviet Union declares war on Japan
summary: The Soviet Union entered the war against Japan on August 8, 1945, as secretly agreed — ninety days after the end of the European war on May 8 — but by then the atomic bomb had already been dropped on Hiroshima.

citation.quote: That turned out to be May 8, and so, on August 8, the Russians were due to declare war on Japan.

title: Second atomic bomb dropped on Nagasaki
summary: Three days after Hiroshima, a second atomic bomb was dropped on the city of Nagasaki, killing perhaps 50,000 people.

citation.quote: Three days later, a second atomic bomb was dropped on the city of Nagasaki, with perhaps 50,000 killed.

title: Harper's Magazine publishes article calling Japanese evacuation 'our worst wartime mistake'
summary: In September 1945, the month the war ended in Asia, Yale Law Professor Eugene V. Rostow published an article in Harper's Magazine calling the Japanese evacuation 'our worst wartime mistake.'

citation.quote: The month the war ended in Asia, September 1945, an article appeared in Harper's Magazine by Yale Law Professor Eugene V. Rostow, calling the Japanese evacuation "our worst wartime mistake."

title: Ho Chi Minh writes eight letters to President Truman seeking support
summary: Between October 1945 and February 1946, Ho Chi Minh wrote eight letters to President Truman invoking the self-determination promises of the Atlantic Charter; Truman never replied.

citation.quote: Between October 1945 and February 1946, Ho Chi Minh wrote eight letters to President Truman, reminding him of the self-determination promises of the Atlantic Charter.

title: Three million workers on strike in postwar labor upsurge
summary: When the war ended, strikes continued in record numbers with three million workers on strike in the first half of 1946, nearly approaching a general confrontation between workers and government.

citation.quote: When the war ended, the strikes continued in record numbers—3 million on strike in the first half of 1946.

title: 100,000 South African gold mine workers strike
summary: In 1946, 100,000 gold mine workers in South Africa stopped work in the greatest strike in the country's history, demanding ten shillings a day; the strike was broken by a military attack.

citation.quote: The year before in South Africa, 100,000 gold mine workers stopped work, demanding ten shillings (about $2.50) a day in wages, the greatest strike in the history of South Africa, and it took a military attack to get them back to work.

title: Truman appoints Committee on Civil Rights
summary: In late 1946, President Truman appointed a Committee on Civil Rights that recommended expanding federal civil rights enforcement and passing laws against lynching and voting discrimination.

citation.quote: President Harry Truman, in late 1946, appointed a Committee on Civil Rights, which recommended that the civil rights section of the Department of Justice be expanded, that there be a permanent Commission on Civil Rights, that Congress pass laws against lynching and to stop voting discrimination, and suggested new laws to end racial discrimination in jobs.

title: Total U.S. military aid to El Salvador reaches $16.7 million
summary: From 1946 to 1979, total U.S. military aid to El Salvador was $16.7 million; in Reagan's first year in office alone, this figure rose to $82 million.

citation.quote: From 1946 to 1979, total military aid to El Salvador was $16.7 million. In Reagan's first year in office, the figure rose to $82 million.

title: France bombards Haiphong, starting eight-year war with Vietminh
summary: In October 1946 the French bombarded the port of Haiphong in northern Vietnam, beginning the eight-year war between the Vietminh movement and France over control of Vietnam.

citation.quote: In October of 1946, the French bombarded Haiphong, a port in northern Vietnam, and there began the eight-year war between the Vietminh movement and the French over who would rule Vietnam.

title: Truman Doctrine announced: $400 million in aid to Greece and Turkey
summary: Truman gave a speech to Congress in the spring of 1947 requesting $400 million in military and economic aid to Greece and Turkey, establishing the Truman Doctrine of intervention against left-wing movements.

citation.quote: The United States responded with the Truman Doctrine, the name given to a speech Truman gave to Congress in the spring of 1947, in which he asked for $400 million in military and economic aid to Greece and Turkey.

title: US sends 74,000 tons of military equipment to right-wing Greek government
summary: In the last five months of 1947 the United States sent 74,000 tons of military equipment including artillery, dive bombers, and napalm to the right-wing government in Athens, along with 250 army advisers, to defeat the Greek leftist guerrilla movement.

citation.quote: In the last five months of 1947, 74,000 tons of military equipment were sent by the United States to the right-wing government in Athens, including artillery, dive bombers, and stocks of napalm.

title: 19,000 railwaymen in French West Africa strike for 160 days
summary: In 1947, 19,000 railwaymen in French West Africa staged the longest recorded strike in African history — 160 days — issuing a militant ultimatum to the governor general and signaling a new mood of anti-colonial resistance.

citation.quote: Basil Davidson (Let Freedom Come) tells of the longest recorded strike (160 days) in African history, of 19,000 railwaymen in French West Africa in 1947

title: Truman issues Executive Order 9835 launching federal loyalty program
summary: Two weeks after announcing the Truman Doctrine, Truman issued Executive Order 9835 on March 22, 1947, initiating a program to search out 'disloyal persons' in the US government; by December 1952, 6.6 million persons had been investigated.

citation.quote: Truman issued, on March 22, 1947, Executive Order 9835, initiating a program to search out any "infiltration of disloyal persons" in the U.S. government.

title: Communist Party ousts non-Communists from Czechoslovak government
summary: In 1948, the Communist party in Czechoslovakia ousted non-Communists from the government and established Communist rule, one of several postwar events used to build public support for the US anti-Communist crusade.

citation.quote: In 1948, the Communist party in Czechoslovakia ousted non-Communists from the government and established their own rule.

title: Soviet Union blockades Berlin
summary: The Soviet Union blockaded Berlin in 1948, forcing the United States to airlift supplies into the jointly occupied city isolated inside the Soviet sphere.

citation.quote: The Soviet Union that year blockaded Berlin, which was a jointly occupied city isolated inside the Soviet sphere of East Germany, forcing the United States to airlift supplies into Berlin.

title: Marshall Plan provides $16 billion in economic aid to Western Europe
summary: The Marshall Plan of 1948 gave $16 billion in economic aid to Western European countries over four years, aimed both at building markets for American exports and at preventing Communist parties from gaining power in Italy and France.

citation.quote: The Marshall Plan of 1948, which gave $16 billion in economic aid to Western European countries in four years, had an economic aim: to build up markets for American exports.

title: Truman issues executive order desegregating the armed forces
summary: Four months before the 1948 presidential election, Truman issued an executive order requiring the armed forces to institute policies of racial equality "as rapidly as possible," though full desegregation took over a decade to complete.

citation.quote: But Truman—four months before the presidential election of 1948, and challenged from the left in that election by Progressive party candidate Henry Wallace—issued an executive order asking that the armed forces, segregated in World War II, institute policies of racial equality "as rapidly as possible."

title: Greek left-wing rebellion defeated with US aid
summary: With US military aid, the Greek leftist rebellion was defeated by 1949 and a right-wing military dictatorship remained in power, while US investment capital flowed into the country.

citation.quote: With that aid, the rebellion was defeated by 1949.

title: Soviet Union explodes its first atomic bomb
summary: In 1949 the Soviet Union exploded its first atomic bomb, intensifying Cold War tensions and helping the Truman administration build public support for anti-Communist policies at home and abroad.

citation.quote: in that year also, the Soviet Union exploded its first atomic bomb.

title: Communist victory in China prompts US military aid to France in Indochina
summary: After the Communist victory in China in 1949 and the Korean War the following year, the United States began giving large amounts of military aid to the French fighting in Vietnam.

citation.quote: After the Communist victory in China in 1949 and the Korean war the following year, the United States began giving large amounts of military aid to the French.

title: Chinese Communist forces move into Peking; civil war ends
summary: In January 1949, Chinese Communist forces moved into Peking, ending the civil war and establishing a people's government independent of outside control despite $2 billion in US aid to Chiang Kai-shek.

citation.quote: In January 1949, Chinese Communist forces moved into Peking, the civil war was over, and China was in the hands of a revolutionary movement, the closest thing, in the long history of that ancient country, to a people's government, independent of outside control.

title: Kennedy blames White House and State Department for 'loss' of China
summary: In January 1949, Representative John F. Kennedy gave a House speech blaming the White House and State Department for the 'failure' of US foreign policy that allowed Communist forces to take over China.

citation.quote: expressed in the House of Representatives, January 1949, when the Chinese Communists took over Peking. Kennedy said: Mr. Speaker, over this weekend we have learned the extent of the disaster that has befallen China and the United States.

title: General strike against starvation wages in Kenya
summary: In 1950, Kenya saw a general strike against starvation wages, part of the worldwide wave of anti-imperialist insurrection that threatened US and European interests after World War II.

citation.quote: In 1950, in Kenya, there was a general strike against starvation wages.

title: Senator McCarthy claims 205 Communists in the State Department
summary: In early 1950, speaking to a Women's Republican Club in Wheeling, West Virginia, Senator Joseph McCarthy held up papers claiming to have a list of 205 Communist Party members still shaping policy in the State Department.

citation.quote: Speaking to a Women's Republican Club in Wheeling, West Virginia, in early 1950, he held up some papers and shouted: "I have here in my hand a list of 205—a list of names that were made known to the Secretary of State as being members of the Communist Party and who nevertheless are still working and shaping policy in the State Department."

title: Prosecution of Julius and Ethel Rosenberg
summary: In the summer of 1950, Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were charged with espionage for allegedly passing atomic bomb secrets to the Soviets; their prosecution intensified the nation's anti-Communist mood.

citation.quote: The most important of these was the prosecution of Julius and Ethel Rosenberg in the summer of 1950.

title: US military budget was about $12 billion at start of 1950
summary: At the start of 1950 the total US budget was about $40 billion and the military portion was about $12 billion; by 1955 the military budget alone reached $40 billion, reflecting the dramatic militarization of the postwar economy.

citation.quote: At the start of 1950, the total U.S. budget was about $40 billion, and the military part of it was about $12 billion. But by 1955, the military part alone was $40 billion out of a total of $62 billion.

title: NSC secret memo articulates "domino theory" for Southeast Asia
summary: In 1950, secret National Security Council memoranda articulated what became known as the "domino theory," warning that if one Southeast Asian country fell to Communism the next would follow.

citation.quote: In the secret memoranda of the National Security Council (which advised the President on foreign policy) there was talk in 1950 of what came to be known as the "domino theory"—that, like a row of dominoes, if one country fell to Communism, the next one would do the same and so on.

title: More than fifty major riots occur in American prisons
summary: Between 1950 and 1953, more than fifty major riots erupted in American prisons, reflecting widespread grievances over conditions and treatment.

citation.quote: Between 1950 and 1953 more than fifty major riots occurred in American prisons.

title: North Korea invades South Korea; Truman orders US armed forces to intervene
summary: On June 25, 1950, North Korean armies moved southward across the 38th parallel in an invasion of South Korea; Truman ordered American armed forces to intervene under the UN flag.

citation.quote: when on June 25, 1950, North Korean armies moved southward across the 38th parallel in an invasion of South Korea, the United Nations, dominated by the United States, asked its members to help "repel the armed attack."

title: Mickey Spillane's One Lonely Night sells three million copies
summary: Three million copies were sold of Mickey Spillane's 1951 novel One Lonely Night, whose hero boasts about killing Communists in cold blood, reflecting the widespread anti-Communist culture of the era.

citation.quote: Three million copies were sold of the book by Mickey Spillane published in 1951, One Lonely Night

title: NSC memo warns Communist control of Southeast Asia threatens US Pacific security
summary: A secret NSC memo in June 1952 warned that Communist control of Southeast Asia would jeopardize US security in the Pacific and endanger access to the region's natural rubber, tin, and petroleum.

citation.quote: A secret memo of the National Security Council in June 1952 also pointed to the chain of U.S. military bases along the coast of China, the Philippines, Taiwan, Japan, South Korea

title: Korean War ends; boundary between North and South restored
summary: Peace negotiations restored the old boundary between North and South Korea in 1953, ending a war that killed perhaps 2 million Koreans after the US had advanced deep into North Korea and provoked Chinese intervention.

citation.quote: until peace negotiations restored, in 1953, the old boundary between North and South.

title: CIA overthrows government of Iran that nationalized the oil industry
summary: In 1953, the CIA succeeded in overthrowing the Iranian government that had nationalized the oil industry, a prime example of US military intervention under the guise of opposing Communist expansion.

citation.quote: In Iran, in 1953, the Central Intelligence Agency succeeded in overthrowing a government which nationalized the oil industry.

title: Castro leads unsuccessful attack on army barracks in Santiago
summary: In 1953, Fidel Castro led an unsuccessful attack on an army barracks in Santiago, was imprisoned, later released, and went to Mexico before returning to Cuba to launch the guerrilla campaign that would eventually succeed.

citation.quote: Fidel Castro had spent time in prison after he led an unsuccessful attack in 1953 on an army barracks in Santiago.

title: Congressional study mission declares Indochina a strategic resource prize
summary: In 1953, a congressional study mission reported that Indochina was immensely wealthy in rice, rubber, coal, and iron ore, and a State Department memo warned that French defeat could mean Communist domination of all Southeast Asia.

citation.quote: In 1953, a congressional study mission reported: "The area of Indochina is immensely wealthy in rice, rubber, coal and iron ore. Its position makes it a strategic key to the rest of Southeast Asia."

title: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg executed
summary: The Rosenbergs were executed in the electric chair on June 19, 1953, after Chief Justice Vinson recalled vacationing Supreme Court justices to cancel a last-minute stay of execution granted by Justice William O. Douglas.

citation.quote: They canceled Douglas's stay in time for the Rosenbergs to be executed June 19, 1953.

title: Samuel Eliot Morison publishes Christopher Columbus, Mariner
summary: Harvard historian Morison released a popular Columbus biography that acknowledged 'the cruel policy initiated by Columbus and pursued by his successors resulted in complete genocide' while largely burying it within a romanticized narrative.

citation.chapter: Chapter 1 – Columbus, the Indians, and Human Progress
citation.quote: In his popular book Christopher Columbus, Mariner, written in 1954, he tells about the enslavement and the killing: 'The cruel policy initiated by Columbus and pursued by his successors resulted in complete genocide.'

title: McCarthy begins hearings to investigate subversives in the military
summary: In the spring of 1954, Senator McCarthy began hearings to investigate supposed subversives in the military, eventually attacking generals and alienating both Republicans and Democrats.

citation.quote: In the spring of 1954 he began hearings to investigate supposed subversives in the military.

title: CIA-backed mercenary invasion overthrows elected government of Guatemala
summary: In 1954, the CIA trained and supported a mercenary force that overthrew Guatemala's legally elected government, replacing it with Colonel Carlos Castillo Armas who promptly returned land to United Fruit and abolished the secret ballot.

citation.quote: In Guatemala, in 1954, a legally elected government was overthrown by an invasion force of mercenaries trained by the CIA at military bases in Honduras and Nicaragua and supported by four American fighter planes flown by American pilots.

title: Supreme Court rules in Brown v. Board of Education
summary: In 1954 the Supreme Court struck down the "separate but equal" doctrine, ruling in Brown v. Board of Education that segregated schools generated a feeling of inferiority in Black children unlikely ever to be undone.

citation.quote: In 1954, the Court finally struck down the "separate but equal" doctrine that it had defended since the 1890s. The NAACP brought a series of cases before the Court to challenge segregation in the public schools, and now in *Brown* v. *Board of Education* the Court said the separation of schoolchildren "generates a feeling of inferiority . . . that may affect their hearts and minds in a way unlikely ever to be undone."

title: France withdraws from Vietnam after failing to win popular support
summary: By 1954 the United States had given France $1 billion and 300,000 weapons, financing 80 percent of the French war effort, but France still had to withdraw after failing to win Vietnamese popular support.

citation.quote: In 1954, the French, having been unable to win Vietnamese popular support, which was overwhelmingly behind Ho Chi Minh and the revolutionary movement, had to withdraw.

title: Geneva Accords set terms for French withdrawal and Vietnamese elections
summary: An international conference in Geneva produced a peace agreement under which the French would withdraw to southern Vietnam and elections would be held within two years to let the Vietnamese choose their own government.

citation.quote: An international assemblage at Geneva presided over the peace agreement between the French and the Vietminh. It was agreed that the French would temporarily withdraw into the southern part of Vietnam, that the Vietminh would remain in the north, and that an election would take place in two years in a unified Vietnam to enable the Vietnamese to choose their own government.

title: Joint Chiefs memo concludes free elections would hand Vietnam to Communists
summary: A Joint Chiefs of Staff memo in early 1954 concluded that a settlement based on free elections would almost certainly result in Communist control of Laos, Cambodia, and Vietnam.

citation.quote: A memo in early 1954 of the Joint Chiefs of Staff said that intelligence estimates showed "a settlement based on free elections would be attended by almost certain loss of the Associated States [Laos, Cambodia, and Vietnam—the three parts of Indochina created by the Geneva Conference] to Communist control."

title: Senate votes to censure Senator McCarthy
summary: In December 1954, the Senate voted overwhelmingly to censure McCarthy for 'conduct unbecoming a Member of the United States Senate,' focusing on procedural breaches rather than his anti-Communist fabrications.

citation.quote: in December 1954, the Senate voted overwhelmingly to censure him for "conduct . . . unbecoming a Member of the United States Senate."

title: Rosa Parks arrested; Montgomery Bus Boycott begins
summary: At the end of 1955 in Montgomery, Alabama, Rosa Parks refused to obey the city's bus segregation law. Montgomery Blacks responded with a mass meeting and a boycott of all city buses that lasted over eighty days.

citation.quote: Those events came, at the end of 1955, in the capital city of Alabama—Montgomery.

title: Castro returns to Cuba and begins guerrilla campaign
summary: After going to Mexico and meeting Che Guevara, Castro returned to Cuba in 1956 with a tiny force that fought guerrilla warfare against Batista's army, gradually drawing more popular support.

citation.quote: Out of prison, he went to Mexico, met Argentine revolutionary Che Guevara, and returned in 1956 to Cuba.

title: FBI COINTELPRO targets 295 Black organizations
summary: Between 1956 and 1971 the FBI conducted its massive Counterintelligence Program (COINTELPRO), taking 295 actions against Black groups in a sustained effort to harass and destroy Black militant organizations.

citation.quote: Between 1956 and 1971 the FBI concluded a massive Counterintelligence Program (known as COINTELPRO) that took 295 actions against black groups.

title: Kennedy praises Diem's Vietnam as a model of political liberty
summary: In 1956 Kennedy publicly praised President Diem and called South Vietnam's political liberty an inspiration, before later facilitating Diem's overthrow.

citation.quote: Back in 1956, he had spoken of "the amazing success of President Diem" and said of Diem's Vietnam: "Her political liberty is an inspiration."

title: Supreme Court outlaws segregation on local bus lines
summary: In November 1956, the Supreme Court ruled that segregation on local bus lines was unconstitutional, vindicating the Montgomery Bus Boycott after months of Black resistance.

citation.quote: But the black people of Montgomery persisted, and in November 1956, the Supreme Court outlawed segregation on local bus lines.

title: Civil Rights Act of 1957 passed
summary: Congress passed civil rights laws in 1957, 1960, and 1964 that promised voting and employment equality but were poorly enforced or ignored.

citation.quote: Civil rights laws were passed in 1957, 1960, and 1964. They promised much, on voting equality, on employment equality, but were enforced poorly or ignored.

title: Eisenhower sends thousands of marines to Lebanon
summary: In 1958 the Eisenhower government sent thousands of marines to Lebanon to prevent the pro-American government from being toppled by revolution and to maintain an armed presence in the oil-rich area.

citation.quote: In 1958, the Eisenhower government sent thousands of marines to Lebanon to make sure the pro-American government there was not toppled by a revolution, and to keep an armed presence in that oil-rich area.

title: Robert Williams advocates armed self-defense for Monroe NAACP
summary: Two years after the Montgomery boycott, ex-marine Robert Williams, president of the Monroe, North Carolina, NAACP, became known for his view that Blacks should defend themselves with guns if necessary; when Klansmen attacked a leader's home, Williams and armed Blacks fired back and drove them off.

citation.quote: Two years after the Montgomery boycott, in Monroe, North Carolina, an ex-marine named Robert Williams, the president of the local NAACP, became known for his view that blacks should defend themselves against violence, with guns if necessary.

title: Cuban revolution overthrows Batista; Fidel Castro comes to power
summary: In 1959, a rebel force led by Fidel Castro overthrew the American-backed dictator Fulgencio Batista on New Year's Day, establishing a revolutionary government that threatened extensive American business interests in Cuba.

citation.quote: the American-backed dictator, Fulgencio Batista, was overthrown. . . . Fidel Castro had spent time in prison after he led an unsuccessful attack in 1953 on an army barracks in Santiago. . . . The Batista government fell apart on New Year's Day 1959.

title: Betty Friedan records suburban women naming "the problem"
summary: In an anecdote from The Feminine Mystique, Friedan describes a morning in 1959 when a mother of four and her friends finally articulated a shared sense of dissatisfaction and emptiness with their domestic lives.

citation.quote: But on an April morning in 1959, I heard a mother of four, having coffee with four other mothers in a suburban development fifteen miles from New York, say in a tone of quiet desperation, "the problem."

title: Eisenhower secretly authorizes CIA to arm and train anti-Castro Cuban exiles
summary: In the spring of 1960, President Eisenhower secretly authorized the CIA to arm and train anti-Castro Cuban exiles in Guatemala in preparation for a future invasion of Cuba.

citation.quote: In the spring of 1960, President Eisenhower secretly authorized the Central Intelligence Agency to arm and train anti-Castro Cuban exiles in Guatemala for a future invasion of Cuba.

title: Military budget reaches $45.8 billion; Kennedy elected and increases defense spending
summary: In 1960 the military budget was $45.8 billion — 49.7 percent of the total US budget. Kennedy was elected that year and in fourteen months added $9 billion to defense funds.

citation.quote: In 1960, the military budget was $45.8 billion—49.7 percent of the budget. That year John F. Kennedy was elected President, and he immediately moved to increase military spending.

title: Sit-ins spread to fifteen cities; lunch counters desegregated in Greensboro
summary: Within two weeks of the Greensboro sit-in, protests spread to fifteen cities in five southern states; by the end of 1960 more than fifty thousand people had participated in demonstrations and over 3,600 had been jailed, but lunch counters in Greensboro and many other cities were opened to Blacks.

citation.quote: There was violence against the sit-inners. But the idea of taking the initiative against segregation took hold. In the next twelve months, more than fifty thousand people, mostly black, some white, participated in demonstrations of one kind or another in a hundred cities, and over 3,600 people were put in jail. But by the end of 1960, lunch counters were open to blacks in Greensboro and many other places.

title: National Liberation Front formed in South Vietnam
summary: In 1960 the National Liberation Front was formed in South Vietnam, uniting various opposition strands against the Diem regime and drawing its strength primarily from South Vietnamese peasants.

citation.quote: In 1960, the National Liberation Front was formed in the South. It united the various strands of opposition to the regime; its strength came from South Vietnamese peasants, who saw it as a way of changing their daily lives.

title: ITT makes illegal contributions to Bobby Baker linked to Democratic senators
summary: In 1960, International Telephone and Telegraph made illegal contributions to Bobby Baker, who worked with Democratic senators including Lyndon Johnson, demonstrating ITT's practice of funding both political parties.

citation.quote: In 1960 it had made illegal contributions to Bobby Baker, who worked with Democratic Senators, including Lyndon Johnson.

title: FBI admits to ninety-two illegal break-ins of radical and left-wing groups
summary: Congressional investigations revealed that the FBI admitted to ninety-two illegal burglaries between 1960 and 1966, as well as sending forged letters, opening mail illegally, and, in the case of Fred Hampton, apparently conspiring in murder.

citation.quote: The FBI had sent forged letters, engaged in burglaries (it admitted to ninety-two between 1960 and 1966), opened mail illegally, and, in the case of Black Panther leader Fred Hampton, seems to have conspired in murder.

title: Federal budget devotes 53.7 percent to foreign affairs, 22.3 percent to social spending
summary: In 1960, foreign affairs spending represented 53.7 percent of the federal budget while social spending was only 22.3 percent; by 1974 foreign affairs had dropped to 33 percent and social spending had risen to 31 percent, reflecting the impact of 1960s democratic demands.

citation.quote: In 1960 foreign affairs spending was 53.7 percent of the budget, and social spending was 22.3 percent. By 1974 foreign affairs took 33 percent and social spending 31 percent.

title: Only eight U.S. banks have foreign branches with $3.5 billion in assets
summary: In 1960 only eight United States banks had foreign branches, with assets of $3.5 billion; by 1974 there were 129 such banks with $155 billion in overseas assets, demonstrating the massive growth of international U.S. banking.

citation.quote: In 1960 there were eight United States banks with foreign branches; in 1974 there were 129. The assets of these overseas branches amounted to $3.5 billion in 1960, $155 billion in 1974.

title: Voter turnout reaches 63 percent in the presidential election
summary: In 1960, 63 percent of eligible voters cast ballots in the presidential election, a figure that would fall sharply over the following decades as public disillusionment with politics grew.

citation.quote: In 1960, 63 percent of those eligible to vote voted in the presidential election. By 1976, this figure had dropped to 53 percent.

title: Greensboro sit-in at Woolworth's lunch counter
summary: On February 1, 1960, four Black freshmen at a North Carolina college sat down at the whites-only Woolworth's lunch counter in Greensboro, were refused service, and refused to leave, sparking a wave of sit-ins across the South.

citation.quote: On February 1, 1960, four freshmen at a Negro college in Greensboro, North Carolina, decided to sit down at the Woolworth's lunch counter downtown, where only whites ate.

title: Mass demonstrations in Albany, Georgia; over a thousand jailed
summary: In the winter of 1961 and again in 1962, mass demonstrations swept Albany, Georgia, where more than a thousand of the city's 22,000 Black residents went to jail protesting segregation and discrimination.

citation.quote: In Albany, Georgia, a small deep-South town where the atmosphere of slavery still lingered, mass demonstrations took place in the winter of 1961 and again in 1962. Of 22,000 black people in Albany, over a thousand went to jail for marching, assembling, to protest segregation and discrimination.

title: Kennedy approves secret military operations in Vietnam and Laos
summary: Shortly after taking office in early 1961, Kennedy approved a secret plan for military actions in Vietnam and Laos, including dispatching agents to North Vietnam for sabotage and harassment.

citation.quote: When Kennedy took office in early 1961 he continued the policies of Truman and Eisenhower in Southeast Asia. Almost immediately, he approved a secret plan for various military actions in Vietnam and Laos, including the "dispatch of agents to North Vietnam" to engage in "sabotage and light harassment," according to the Pentagon Papers.

title: Five hundred Indian leaders convene in Chicago; National Indian Youth Council formed
summary: In 1961, five hundred tribal and urban Indian leaders met in Chicago, out of which university-educated young Indians formed the National Indian Youth Council to advance Indian rights and resistance.

citation.quote: In 1961, five hundred tribal and urban Indian leaders met in Chicago. Out of this came another gathering of university-educated young Indians who formed the National Indian Youth Council.

title: E. Howard Hunt leads CIA-organized invasion of Cuba
summary: Hunt had been the CIA man in charge of the 1961 invasion of Cuba, and three of the Watergate burglars were veterans of that invasion.

citation.quote: Hunt had been the CIA man in charge of the invasion of Cuba in 1961, and three of the Watergate burglars were veterans of the invasion.

title: Eisenhower wonders aloud to Kennedy why Communist forces always have better morale
summary: When Eisenhower met with President-elect Kennedy in January 1961, he wondered aloud why US-backed forces always seemed to have lower morale than Communist forces in such interventions.

citation.quote: The Pentagon historians wrote that when Eisenhower met with President-elect Kennedy in January 1961, he "wondered aloud why, in interventions of this kind, we always seemed to find that the morale of the Communist forces was better than that of the democratic forces."

title: CIA-trained force lands at Bay of Pigs and is crushed
summary: On April 17, 1961, the CIA-trained force of 1,400 Cuban exiles, with some American participation, landed at the Bay of Pigs expecting a popular uprising against Castro; within three days the invasion was crushed by Castro's army.

citation.quote: on April 17, 1961, the CIA-trained force, with some Americans participating, landed at the Bay of Pigs on the south shore of Cuba, 90 miles from Havana. They expected to stimulate a general rising against Castro. But it was a popular regime. There was no rising. In three days, the CIA forces were crushed by Castro's army.

title: CORE Freedom Riders depart Washington; beaten and buses burned in the South
summary: On May 4, 1961, two buses of Freedom Riders organized by CORE left Washington bound for New Orleans. They were beaten in South Carolina, had a bus set afire in Alabama, and were attacked with fists and iron bars — while federal agents watched and did nothing.

citation.quote: The two buses that left Washington, D.C., on May 4, 1961, headed for New Orleans, never got there. In South Carolina, riders were beaten. In Alabama, a bus was set afire. Freedom Riders were attacked with fists and iron bars.

title: NLF membership reaches approximately 300,000
summary: By early 1962, US government analyst Douglas Pike estimated NLF membership stood at around 300,000, with the Pentagon Papers acknowledging that only the Viet Cong had real broad-based popular support.

citation.quote: Pike estimated that the NLF membership by early 1962 stood at around 300,000. The Pentagon Papers said of this period: "Only the Viet Cong had any real support and influence on a broad base in the countryside."

title: SDS issues the Port Huron Statement, a manifesto for participatory democracy
summary: Students for a Democratic Society, which began at the University of Michigan, issued the Port Huron Statement in 1962, a manifesto for participatory democracy that became an important organizer of antiwar protest.

citation.quote: Students for a Democratic Society (SDS), which began at the University of Michigan, and which issued the Port Huron Statement in 1962, a manifesto for participatory democracy, played an important part in organizing anti-war protest.

title: Kennedy publicly claims US has assisted Vietnam's independence for a decade
summary: At a February 14, 1962 press conference, Kennedy publicly stated that the United States had been assisting Vietnam in maintaining its independence for more than a decade, using freedom rhetoric that obscured the actual US strategic interests.

citation.quote: In a news conference February 14, 1962, he said: "Yes, as you know, the U.S. for more than a decade has been assisting the government, the people of Vietnam, to maintain their independence."

title: Kennedy administration pushes bill to apply Espionage Act to Americans abroad
summary: In 1963 the Kennedy administration pushed a bill — unsuccessfully — to apply the Espionage Act to statements uttered by Americans abroad, concerned about journalists in Vietnam writing critical articles about the Diem government.

citation.chapter: Chapter 14 – War is the Health of the State
citation.quote: In 1963, the Kennedy administration pushed a bill [unsuccessfully] to apply the Espionage Act to statements uttered by Americans abroad; it was concerned, in the words of a cable from Secretary of State Rusk to Ambassador Lodge in Vietnam, about journalists in Vietnam writing "critical articles . . . on Diem and his government" that were "likely to impede the war effort."

title: Birmingham campaign: thousands fill streets facing police dogs and fire hoses
summary: In 1963, thousands of Black demonstrators took to the streets of Birmingham, Alabama, confronting police clubs, tear gas, attack dogs, and high-powered water hoses. The Justice Department recorded 1,412 demonstrations across the country in three months of that year.

citation.quote: In Birmingham in 1963, thousands of blacks went into the streets, facing police clubs, tear gas, dogs, high-powered water hoses. And meanwhile, all over the deep South, the young people of SNCC, mostly black, a few white, were moving into communities in Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, Arkansas.

title: March on Washington draws 200,000; King delivers "I Have a Dream" speech
summary: In the summer of 1963, Black civil rights leaders planned a mass march on Washington to protest the race problem. Kennedy embraced it, turning it into a friendly assemblage; King's "I have a dream" speech thrilled 200,000, but militant SNCC leader John Lewis was censored.

citation.quote: Martin Luther King's speech there thrilled 200,000 black and white Americans—"I have a dream. . . ." It was magnificent oratory, but without the anger that many blacks felt.

title: Birmingham church bombing kills four girls
summary: Eighteen days after the March on Washington, a bomb exploded in the basement of a Black church in Birmingham, killing four girls attending Sunday school — an act of white supremacist terror that underscored the limits of the moderate march.

citation.quote: Eighteen days after the Washington gathering, almost as if in deliberate contempt for its moderation, a bomb exploded in the basement of a black church in Birmingham and four girls attending a Sunday school class were killed.

title: Kennedy assassinated three weeks after Diem's execution; Johnson takes office
summary: Three weeks after the November 1963 execution of Diem, President Kennedy was assassinated and Vice-President Lyndon Johnson assumed the presidency.

citation.quote: Three weeks after the execution of Diem, Kennedy himself was assassinated, and his Vice-President, Lyndon Johnson, took office.

title: Ron Kovic enlists in the marines at age seventeen
summary: In 1963, Ron Kovic, whose father worked in a Long Island supermarket, enlisted in the marines at age seventeen; two years later in Vietnam, his spine was shattered and he was paralyzed, later becoming a prominent antiwar veteran.

citation.quote: One of those who stayed, fought, but then turned against the war was Ron Kovic. His father worked in a supermarket on Long Island. In 1963, at the age of seventeen, he enlisted in the marines.

title: McNamara declares "Victory is in sight" in Vietnam
summary: Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara declared on February 19, 1963, that "Victory is in sight" in Vietnam, one of a series of official proclamations of imminent success that proved false.

citation.quote: Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara, February 19, 1963: "Victory is in sight."

title: Buddhist monk self-immolates in Saigon to protest Diem regime
summary: In June 1963 a Buddhist monk set himself afire in a Saigon public square, triggering a wave of monk suicides by fire and mass protests against the Diem government's repression of Buddhists.

citation.quote: One day in June 1963, a Buddhist monk sat down in the public square in Saigon and set himself afire. More Buddhist monks began committing suicide by fire to dramatize their opposition to the Diem regime.

title: Ambassador Lodge reports to McGeorge Bundy on coup plotting against Diem
summary: On October 25, 1963, Ambassador Henry Cabot Lodge reported to Kennedy's assistant McGeorge Bundy that he had personally approved meetings between General Tran Van Don and CIA operative Lucien Conein to plan the coup against Diem.

citation.quote: Lodge reported to Kennedy's assistant, McGeorge Bundy, on October 25 (Pentagon Papers): "I have personally approved each meeting between General Tran Van Don and Conein who has carried out my orders in each instance explicitly."

title: A. Philip Randolph addresses AFL-CIO convention on the Black revolt
summary: In November 1963, A. Philip Randolph spoke to an AFL-CIO convention, warning that the Black protest movement was only the "first rumbling of the 'under-class'" and predicting that the unemployed of all races would follow Blacks into the streets.

citation.quote: Back in November 1963, A. Philip Randolph had spoken to an AFL-CIO convention about the civil rights movement, and foreseen its direction: "The Negro's protest today is but the first rumbling of the 'under-class.' As the Negro has taken to the streets, so will the unemployed of all races take to the streets."

title: South Vietnamese generals overthrow and execute President Diem
summary: On November 1, 1963, South Vietnamese generals attacked the presidential palace. Diem fled but was captured, taken out in a truck, and executed along with his brother.

citation.quote: When, on November 1, 1963, the generals attacked the presidential palace, Diem phoned Ambassador Lodge, and the conversation went as follows:

title: Murder of Chaney, Goodman, and Schwerner in Philadelphia, Mississippi
summary: Twelve days after the public hearing, three civil rights workers — James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner — were arrested in Philadelphia, Mississippi, released at night, then seized, beaten with chains, and shot to death.

citation.quote: Twelve days after the public hearing, three civil rights workers, James Chaney, a young black Mississippian, and two white volunteers, Andrew Goodman and Michael Schwerner, were arrested in Philadelphia, Mississippi, released from jail late at night, then seized, beaten with chains, and shot to death.

title: Mississippi Freedom Democrats denied seats at Democratic National Convention
summary: Later in the summer of 1964, Black Mississippians asked to be seated as part of the state delegation to the Democratic National Convention to represent the 40 percent of the state who were Black. The liberal Democratic leadership, including Hubert Humphrey, turned them down.

citation.quote: Dissatisfaction with the national government intensified. Later that summer, during the Democratic National Convention in Washington, Mississippi, blacks asked to be seated as part of the state delegation to represent the 40 percent of the state's population who were black. They were turned down by the liberal Democratic leadership, including vice-presidential candidate Hubert Humphrey.

title: Black uprisings in Florida, Cleveland, New York, and other cities
summary: In precisely the years when civil rights legislation peaked — 1964 and 1965 — Black urban uprisings erupted across the country, including in Florida, Cleveland, New York, Rochester, Jersey City, Chicago, and Philadelphia.

citation.quote: In precisely those years when civil rights legislation coming out of Congress reached its peak, 1964 and 1965, there were black outbreaks in every part of the country: in Florida, set off by the killing of a Negro woman and a bomb threat against a Negro high school; in Cleveland, set off by the killing of a white minister who sat in the path of a bulldozer to protest discrimination against blacks in construction work; in New York, set off by the fatal shooting of a fifteen-year-old Negro boy during a fight with an off-duty policeman.

title: US military campaign in Vietnam fails against revolutionary movement
summary: From 1964 to 1972 the United States conducted a maximum military effort in Vietnam, short of atomic bombs, and failed to defeat the nationalist revolutionary movement there.

citation.quote: From 1964 to 1972, the wealthiest and most powerful nation in the history of the world made a maximum military effort, with everything short of atomic bombs, to defeat a nationalist revolutionary movement in a tiny, peasant country—and failed.

title: Congress passes Tonkin Resolution authorizing Johnson to wage war in Southeast Asia
summary: The Gulf of Tonkin incident triggered a congressional resolution—passed unanimously in the House and with only two Senate dissents—giving Johnson the power to take military action in Southeast Asia without a formal declaration of war.

citation.quote: The Tonkin "attack" brought a congressional resolution, passed unanimously in the House, and with only two dissenting votes in the Senate, giving Johnson the power to take military action as he saw fit in Southeast Asia.

title: Women strike at McComb Freedom House over domestic labor
summary: Women at a civil rights Freedom House in McComb, Mississippi went on strike against male colleagues who expected them to cook and make beds while the men organized.

citation.quote: In the summer of 1964, in McComb, Mississippi, at a Freedom House (a civil rights headquarters where people worked and lived together) the women went on strike against the men who wanted them to cook and make beds while the men went around in cars organizing.

title: Indian fish-ins on Nisqually River defy state court closures
summary: When state courts closed river areas to Indian fishermen in 1964, Indians staged fish-ins on the Nisqually River in defiance of court orders, going to jail to publicize their fight for treaty rights.

citation.quote: When state courts closed river areas to Indian fishermen, in 1964, Indians had "fish-ins" on the Nisqually River, in defiance of the court orders, and went to jail, hoping to publicize their protest.

title: Young Indians briefly occupy Alcatraz Island
summary: In 1964 a group of young Indians occupied Alcatraz Island in San Francisco Bay to establish an Indian university, but were driven off with no publicity.

citation.quote: In 1964 some young Indians had occupied it to establish an Indian university, but they were driven off and there was no publicity.

title: University of Michigan poll finds 26 percent believe government serves big interests
summary: In 1964, 26 percent of respondents answered "yes" when asked if the government was run by a few big interests looking out for themselves.

citation.quote: The answer in 1964 had been "yes" from 26 percent of those polled; by 1972 the answer was "yes" from 53 percent of those polled.

title: US drops over 75,000 tons of bombs on Laos's Plain of Jars
summary: From May 1964 through September 1969, over 25,000 attack sorties were flown against the Plain of Jars in Laos, dropping over 75,000 tons of bombs and destroying the entire aboveground society.

citation.quote: Over 25,000 attack sorties were flown against the Plain of Jars from May, 1964, through September, 1969; over 75,000 tons of bombs were dropped on it; on the ground, thousands were killed and wounded, tens of thousands driven underground, and the entire aboveground society leveled.

title: "We Won't Go" draft resistance slogan widely publicized
summary: As early as May 1964, the slogan "We Won't Go" was widely publicized as young men began refusing to register for the draft or be inducted.

citation.quote: As early as May 1964 the slogan "We Won't Go" was widely publicized.

title: Mississippi Summer public hearing near the White House
summary: In early June 1964, on the eve of Mississippi Summer, civil rights organizers brought Black Mississippians to Washington to testify publicly about violence they faced. They presented the transcript to President Johnson and Attorney General Kennedy and requested a federal protective presence — and received no response.

citation.quote: On the eve of the Mississippi Summer, in early June 1964, the civil rights movement rented a theater near the White House, and a busload of black Mississippians traveled to Washington to testify publicly about the daily violence, the dangers facing the volunteers coming into Mississippi.

title: US officials meet in Honolulu to plan congressional resolution on Southeast Asia
summary: Two months before the Gulf of Tonkin incident, US government leaders met in Honolulu and discussed obtaining a congressional resolution affirming support for the administration's Southeast Asia policy.

citation.quote: Two months before the Gulf of Tonkin incident, U.S. government leaders met in Honolulu and discussed such a resolution. Rusk said, in this meeting, according to the Pentagon Papers, that "public opinion on our Southeast Asia policy was badly divided in the United States at the moment and that, therefore, the President needed an affirmation of support."

title: Gulf of Tonkin incident used to launch full-scale US war on Vietnam
summary: In early August 1964 President Johnson used a fabricated Gulf of Tonkin incident—claiming an unprovoked North Vietnamese torpedo attack on the USS Maddox—to launch full-scale war on Vietnam.

citation.quote: In early August 1964, President Johnson used a murky set of events in the Gulf of Tonkin, off the coast of North Vietnam, to launch full-scale war on Vietnam. Johnson and Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara told the American public there was an attack by North Vietnamese torpedo boats on American destroyers.

title: Civil rights activists at Mississippi memorial connect Gulf of Tonkin to racial violence
summary: On the very day Johnson announced the Gulf of Tonkin bombing of North Vietnam in early August 1964, black and white activists gathering near Philadelphia, Mississippi for a civil rights memorial drew a direct parallel between US force in Asia and racist violence at home.

citation.quote: On the very day that Lyndon Johnson was telling the nation in early August 1964 about the Gulf of Tonkin incident, and announcing the bombing of North Vietnam, black and white activists were gathering near Philadelphia, Mississippi, at a memorial service for the three civil rights workers killed there that summer.

title: Voting Rights Act of 1965 signed into law
summary: In 1965, President Johnson sponsored and Congress passed a strong Voting Rights Law ensuring on-the-spot federal protection of the right to register and vote, dramatically increasing Black voter registration across the South.

citation.quote: In 1965, President Johnson sponsored and Congress passed an even stronger Voting Rights Law, this time ensuring on-the-spot federal protection of the right to register and vote.

title: Over 200,000 US soldiers sent to South Vietnam
summary: During 1965, over 200,000 American soldiers were sent to South Vietnam, and another 200,000 followed in 1966, with the US Air Force dropping bombs at a historically unprecedented rate.

citation.quote: During 1965, over 200,000 American soldiers were sent to South Vietnam, and in 1966, 200,000 more. By early 1968, there were more than 500,000 American troops there, and the U.S. Air Force was dropping bombs at a rate unequaled in history.

title: Black youths in McComb, Mississippi distribute antiwar leaflet
summary: In mid-1965, young Black activists in McComb, Mississippi who had just lost a classmate in Vietnam distributed a leaflet urging Black men not to fight for white freedom abroad when they were not free at home.

citation.quote: In mid-1965, in McComb, Mississippi, young blacks who had just learned that a classmate of theirs was killed in Vietnam distributed a leaflet: No Mississippi Negroes should be fighting in Viet Nam for the White man's freedom, until all the Negro People are free in Mississippi.

title: Alice Herz burns herself to death in Detroit to protest the Indochina war
summary: In 1965, an 82-year-old woman named Alice Herz burned herself to death in Detroit to make a statement against the horrors of Indochina.

citation.quote: Also that year, in Detroit, an eighty-two-year-old woman named Alice Herz burned herself to death to make a statement against the horror of Indochina.

title: Hundred people gather on Boston Common as bombing of North Vietnam begins
summary: When the bombing of North Vietnam began in early 1965, only a hundred people gathered on the Boston Common to protest, a number that grew to 100,000 by October 1969.

citation.quote: In early 1965, when the bombing of North Vietnam began, a hundred people gathered on the Boston Common to voice their indignation.

title: Judge rules Puyallup tribe does not exist and cannot fish its own river
summary: The year after the fish-ins, a local judge ruled that the Puyallup tribe did not legally exist and barred its members from fishing on the Puyallup River; police raided fishing groups, destroying boats and arresting seven Indians.

citation.quote: A local judge the following year ruled that the Puyallup tribe did not exist, and its members could not fish on the river named for them, the Puyallup River. Policemen raided Indian fishing groups, destroyed boats, slashed nets, manhandled people, arrested seven Indians.

title: Malcolm X assassinated
summary: In February 1965, Malcolm X was assassinated as he spoke on a public platform, in a plan whose origins remain obscure. He became the martyr of the Black Power movement and was more influential in death than in life.

citation.quote: After he was assassinated as he spoke on a public platform in February 1965, in a plan whose origins are still obscure, he became the martyr of this movement.

title: CIA director recommends intensified bombing of North Vietnam before public opinion hardens
summary: On April 2, 1965, CIA director John McCone sent a memo suggesting the bombing of North Vietnam be increased quickly for a fast knockout before mounting US and world public opinion against the bombing could build up.

citation.quote: On April 2, 1965, a memo from CIA director John McCone suggested that the bombing of North Vietnam be increased because it was "not sufficiently severe" to change North Vietnam's policy. "On the other hand . . . we can expect increasing pressure to stop the bombing . . . from various elements of the American public, from the press, the United Nations and world opinion."

title: West Point graduate Richard Steinke refuses combat posting in Vietnam and is court-martialed
summary: As early as June 1965, Richard Steinke, a West Point graduate serving in Vietnam, refused to board an aircraft to a remote Vietnamese village, saying the war was not worth a single American life; he was court-martialed and dismissed.

citation.quote: As early as June 1965, Richard Steinke, a West Point graduate in Vietnam, refused to board an aircraft taking him to a remote Vietnamese village. "The Vietnamese war," he said, "is not worth a single American life." Steinke was court-martialed and dismissed from the service.

title: New York Times reports US jet bombers kill up to 500 Vietnamese near Quangngai
summary: A June 5, 1965 New York Times dispatch from Saigon reported that US jet bombers killed an estimated 500 people near Quangngai, with three out of four hospital patients burned by napalm being village women.

citation.quote: On June 5, 1965, the New York Times carried a dispatch from Saigon: As the Communists withdrew from Quangngai last Monday, United States jet bombers pounded the hills into which they were headed. Many Vietnamese—one estimate is as high as 500—were killed by the strikes.

title: First Washington antiwar march draws a few hundred; marchers splattered with red paint
summary: In the summer of 1965, a few hundred people marched in Washington against the war; those first in line—Staughton Lynd, Bob Moses, and David Dellinger—were splattered with red paint by hecklers.

citation.quote: In the summer of 1965, a few hundred people had gathered in Washington to march in protest against the war: the first in line, historian Staughton Lynd, SNCC organizer Bob Moses, and long-time pacifist David Dellinger, were splattered with red paint by hecklers.

title: Watts uprising in Los Angeles
summary: In August 1965, as Johnson signed the Voting Rights Act, the Watts ghetto in Los Angeles erupted in the most violent urban uprising since World War II. Police and National Guardsmen were called in; thirty-four people were killed, most of them Black, and four thousand were arrested.

citation.quote: In August 1965, just as Lyndon Johnson was signing into law the strong Voting Rights Act, providing for federal registration of black voters to ensure their protection, the black ghetto in Watts, Los Angeles, erupted in the most violent urban outbreak since World War II.

title: 61 percent of Americans believe US involvement in Vietnam is not wrong
summary: In August 1965, 61 percent of the American population thought US involvement in Vietnam was not wrong; by May 1971 those numbers had exactly reversed, with 61 percent calling involvement wrong.

citation.quote: In August of 1965, 61 percent of the population thought the American involvement in Vietnam was not wrong. By May 1971 it was exactly reversed; 61 percent thought our involvement was wrong.

title: US aircraft accidentally bombs Buddhist pagoda and Catholic church in Bien Hoa
summary: On August 15, 1965, US aircraft accidentally bombed a Buddhist pagoda and a Catholic church in Bien Hoa province, the third time that pagoda had been bombed that year.

citation.quote: In Bien Hoa province south of Saigon on August 15 United States aircraft accidentally bombed a Buddhist pagoda and a Catholic church . . . it was the third time their pagoda had been bombed in 1965.

title: State agents attack nineteen women and children at Frank's Landing
summary: Nineteen women and children were brutalized by more than forty-five armed state agents of Washington at Frank's Landing on the Nisqually River during an assault on Indian fishing protesters.

citation.quote: Just three years ago today, on October 13, 1965, 19 women and children were brutalized by more than 45 armed agents of the State of Washington at Frank's Landing on the Nisqually river in a vicious, unwarranted attack. . . .

title: Norman Morrison self-immolates outside Pentagon in protest against Vietnam War
summary: On November 2, 1965, Norman Morrison, a 32-year-old pacifist and father of three, stood below Robert McNamara's Pentagon office windows, doused himself with kerosene, and set himself afire in protest against the war.

citation.quote: On November 2, 1965, in front of the Pentagon in Washington, as thousands of employees were streaming out of the building in the late afternoon, Norman Morrison, a thirty-two-year-old pacifist, father of three, stood below the third-floor windows of Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara, doused himself with kerosene, and set himself afire, giving up his life in protest against the war.

title: Urban rebellions in Chicago and Cleveland
summary: In the summer of 1966, Black uprisings in Chicago and Cleveland brought National Guard shootings; three Blacks were killed in Chicago — including a thirteen-year-old boy and a fourteen-year-old pregnant girl — and four were shot dead in Cleveland.

citation.quote: In the summer of 1966, there were more outbreaks, with rock throwing, looting, and fire bombing by Chicago blacks and wild shootings by the National Guard; three blacks were killed, one a thirteen-year-old boy, another a fourteen-year-old pregnant girl. In Cleveland, the National Guard was summoned to stop a commotion in the black community; four Negroes were shot to death, two by troopers, two by white civilians.

title: Poor Black Mississippians occupy Greenville air force barracks
summary: In 1966, seventy poor Black people in Greenville, Mississippi, occupied an unused air force barracks to protest the federal government's failure to address poverty, and were eventually evicted by the military.

citation.quote: In 1966, seventy poor black people in Greenville, Mississippi, occupied an unused air force barracks, until they were evicted by the military.

title: McNaughton proposes flooding rice fields via dam destruction to starve North Vietnam
summary: In early 1966, Assistant Secretary of Defense John McNaughton suggested destroying locks and dams to flood rice fields and create widespread starvation in North Vietnam as a more covert strategy than direct village bombing.

citation.quote: Assistant Secretary of Defense John McNaughton in early 1966, seeing that large-scale bombing of North Vietnam villages was not producing the desired result, suggested a different strategy.

title: CIA recommends intensified bombing to break North Vietnamese regime's will
summary: The CIA recommended a "bombing program of greater intensity" in 1966, targeting the will of the North Vietnamese regime as a system, according to the Pentagon Papers.

citation.quote: The CIA at one point in 1966 recommended a "bombing program of greater intensity," according to the Pentagon Papers, directed against, in the CIA's words, "the will of the regime as a target system."

title: SNCC declares US is pursuing aggressive illegal policy in Vietnam
summary: In early 1966, the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee declared that the United States was pursuing an aggressive policy in violation of international law and called for withdrawal from Vietnam.

citation.quote: The Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee declared in early 1966 that "the United States is pursuing an aggressive policy in violation of international law" and called for withdrawal from Vietnam.

title: Six SNCC members arrested for invading induction center in Atlanta
summary: In the summer of 1966, six SNCC members were arrested for invading an induction center in Atlanta to protest the Vietnam War; they were convicted and sentenced to several years in prison.

citation.quote: That summer, six members of SNCC were arrested for an invasion of an induction center in Atlanta. They were convicted and sentenced to several years in prison.

title: 191,749 college students enrolled in ROTC
summary: In 1966, 191,749 college students enrolled in ROTC; by 1973 that number had fallen to 72,459 as student protest and antimilitarism severely eroded officer pipeline programs.

citation.quote: In 1966, 191,749 college students enrolled in ROTC. By 1973, the number was 72,459.

title: Three army privates court-martialed for refusing to embark for Vietnam
summary: In 1966, three army privates—one Black, one Puerto Rican, one Lithuanian-Italian, all poor—refused to embark for Vietnam, denouncing the war as immoral, illegal, and unjust; they were court-martialed and imprisoned.

citation.quote: The following year, three army privates, one black, one Puerto Rican, one Lithuanian-Italian—all poor—refused to embark for Vietnam, denouncing the war as "immoral, illegal, and unjust." They were court-martialed and imprisoned.

title: National Organization for Women (NOW) founded
summary: NOW was founded in 1966 and subsequently initiated over a thousand suits against U.S. corporations charging sex discrimination.

citation.quote: Over a thousand suits were initiated by NOW (National Organization for Women, formed in 1966) against U.S. corporations charging sex discrimination.

title: American Correctional Association president boasts of progress at annual address
summary: The president of the American Correctional Association delivered a self-congratulatory annual address in 1966, describing correctional "Valhalla," even as the most intense series of prison uprisings in U.S. history was underway.

citation.quote: The president of the American Correctional Association, delivering the annual address in 1966, described the new edition of the *Manual of Correctional Standards*: "It permits us to linger, if we will, at the gates of correctional Valhalla—with an abiding pride in the sense of a job superbly done!"

title: Lou Harris poll documents collapse in public confidence in military, business, and government
summary: The Lou Harris poll found that from 1966 to 1975, public confidence in the military dropped from 62 to 29 percent, in business from 55 to 18 percent, and in both the President and Congress from 42 to 13 percent.

citation.quote: That July the Lou Harris poll, looking at the public's confidence in the government from 1966 to 1975, reported that confidence in the military during that period had dropped from 62 percent to 29 percent, in business from 55 percent to 18 percent, in both President and Congress from 42 percent to 13 percent.

title: Americans feeling "alienated" rises from 29 to over 50 percent by 1973
summary: According to a Harris poll, the number of Americans feeling "alienated" and "disaffected" climbed from 29 percent in 1966 to over 50 percent in 1973, with inflation cited as the primary concern.

citation.quote: Inflation and unemployment had been rising steadily since 1973, which was the year when, according to a Harris poll, the number of Americans feeling "alienated" and "disaffected" with the general state of the country climbed (from 29 percent in 1966) to over 50 percent.

title: University of Michigan survey: 41 percent of grade-school educated favor immediate Vietnam withdrawal
summary: A June 1966 University of Michigan survey found that 41 percent of people with only a grade school education favored immediate withdrawal from Vietnam, compared to only 27 percent of college-educated people.

citation.quote: In June 1966, of people with a college education, 27 percent were for immediate withdrawal from Vietnam; of people with only a grade school education, 41 percent were for immediate withdrawal.

title: Greatest urban riots in American history sweep Black ghettos
summary: In 1967, the National Advisory Commission on Urban Disorders recorded eight major uprisings, thirty-three serious outbreaks, and 123 minor disorders across the country. Eighty-three people died of gunfire, mostly in Newark and Detroit, with the overwhelming majority of casualties being Black civilians.

citation.quote: In 1967, in the black ghettos of the country, came the greatest urban riots of American history. According to the report of the National Advisory Committee on Urban Disorders, they "involved Negroes acting against local symbols of white American society."
