title: Three Black teens killed at Algiers Motel during Detroit riots; police acquitted
summary: During the 1967 Detroit riots, three Black teenagers were killed in the Algiers Motel by Detroit policemen and a Black private guard. The defense conceded the four men had shot two of the victims; a jury nonetheless exonerated them.

citation.quote: In the 1967 riots in Detroit, three black teen-agers were killed in the Algiers Motel. Three Detroit policemen and a black private guard were tried for this triple murder. The defense conceded, a UPI dispatch said, that the four men had shot two of the blacks. A jury exonerated them.

title: League of Revolutionary Black Workers founded in Detroit
summary: Out of the 1967 Detroit riots came the League of Revolutionary Black Workers, an organization devoted to organizing Black workers for revolutionary change; it lasted until 1971 and influenced thousands of Detroit workers.

citation.quote: Out of the 1967 riots in Detroit came an organization devoted to organizing black workers for revolutionary change. This was the League of Revolutionary Black Workers, which lasted until 1971 and influenced thousands of black workers in Detroit during its period of activity.

title: Martin Luther King Jr. speaks against the Vietnam War at Riverside Church
summary: In 1967, Martin Luther King Jr. spoke out against the Vietnam War at Riverside Church in New York, calling on America to stop the madness and speaking as a voice for the poor of both Vietnam and the United States.

citation.quote: Martin Luther King, Jr., spoke out in 1967 at Riverside Church in New York: Somehow this madness must cease. We must stop now.

title: Dearborn poll shows 41 percent favor withdrawal from Vietnam
summary: As early as 1967, a poll in Dearborn, Michigan—an automobile manufacturing town—showed that 41 percent of the population favored withdrawal from the Vietnam War, countering the media narrative that the working class was uniformly prowar.

citation.quote: For instance, in Dearborn, Michigan, an automobile manufacturing town, a poll as early as 1967 showed 41 percent of the population favored withdrawal from the Vietnam war.

title: Captain Howard Levy court-martialed for refusing to train Green Berets
summary: In early 1967, Captain Howard Levy, an army doctor at Fort Jackson, refused to teach Green Berets, calling them murderers of women and children; he was court-martialed for trying to promote disaffection among enlisted men.

citation.quote: In early 1967, Captain Howard Levy, an army doctor at Fort Jackson, South Carolina, refused to teach Green Berets, a Special Forces elite in the military. He said they were "murderers of women and children" and "killers of peasants." He was court-martialed on the grounds that he was trying to promote disaffection among enlisted men by his statements.

title: Johnson signs executive order banning sex discrimination in federal employment
summary: After lobbying by women's groups, President Johnson signed an executive order prohibiting sex discrimination in federally connected employment.

citation.quote: In 1967, after lobbying by women's groups, President Johnson signed an executive order banning sex discrimination in federally connected employment, and in the years that followed, women's groups demanded that this be enforced.

title: Race riot at San Quentin prison
summary: A race riot erupted at San Quentin prison in California in 1967, the first in a series of revolts at the facility in the late 1960s.

citation.quote: At San Quentin prison in California, which housed four thousand prisoners, there was a series of revolts in the late sixties: a race riot in 1967, a united black-white general strike in early 1968 that shut down almost all the prison industries, and then a second strike that summer.

title: CIA produces, subsidizes, or sponsors over 1,000 books as strategic propaganda
summary: In 1961 the chief of the CIA's Covert Action Staff wrote that books were "the most important weapon of strategic propaganda"; the Church Committee found that more than a thousand books were produced, subsidized, or sponsored by the CIA before the end of 1967.

citation.quote: In 1961 the chief of the CIA's Covert Action Staff wrote that books were "the most important weapon of strategic propaganda." The Church Committee found that more than a thousand books were produced, subsidized, or sponsored by the CIA before the end of 1967.

title: George Ball tells International Chamber of Commerce that nation-states are too narrow for modern business
summary: In 1967, George Ball, former Undersecretary of State and director of Lehman Brothers, told the International Chamber of Commerce that national political boundaries were "too narrow and constricted" for the scope of modern business, articulating the ideology behind multinational corporate expansion.

citation.quote: Back in 1967, George Ball, who had been Undersecretary of State for economic affairs in the Kennedy administration and who was director of Lehman Brothers, a large investment banking firm, told members of the International Chamber of Commerce: "In these twenty postwar years, we have come to recognize in action, though not always in words, that the political boundaries of nation-states are too narrow and constricted to define the scope and activities of modern business."

title: McNaughton warns antiwar dissent could provoke domestic crisis of unprecedented proportions
summary: In May 1967, Pentagon historian John McNaughton warned that growing public unrest and dissatisfaction with the war—especially among young people, the poor, and women—risked provoking a domestic crisis of unprecedented proportions.

citation.quote: In May 1967, the Pentagon historians write: "McNaughton was also very deeply concerned about the breadth and intensity of public unrest and dissatisfaction with the war . . . especially with young people, the underprivileged, the intelligentsia and the women."

title: Organized draft-card turn-ins held across the US; 300 cards returned in San Francisco
summary: In October 1967, organized draft-card turn-ins took place across the country; in San Francisco alone three hundred draft cards were returned to the government, and a sack of collected cards was presented to the Justice Department before a Pentagon demonstration.

citation.quote: In October of 1967 there were organized draft-card "turn-ins" all over the country; in San Francisco alone, three hundred draft cards were returned to the government. Just before a huge demonstration at the Pentagon that month, a sack of collected draft cards was presented to the Justice Department.

title: Father Philip Berrigan and others drench Baltimore draft records with blood
summary: In the fall of 1967, Father Philip Berrigan, artist Tom Lewis, and two others went to a Baltimore draft board, drenched the records with blood, and waited to be arrested; they were sentenced to two to six years in prison.

citation.quote: In the fall of 1967, Father Philip Berrigan (a Josephite priest who was a veteran of World War II), joined by artist Tom Lewis and friends David Eberhardt and James Mengel, went to the office of a draft board in Baltimore, Maryland, drenched the draft records with blood, and waited to be arrested. They were put on trial and sentenced to prison terms of two to six years.

title: General Westmoreland claims he has never been more encouraged in Vietnam
summary: General William Westmoreland declared on November 15, 1967, that he had never been more encouraged in his four years in Vietnam, another in a series of optimistic official statements about the war.

citation.quote: General William Westmoreland, November 15, 1967: "I have never been more encouraged in my four years in Vietnam."

title: Civil Rights Act of 1968 passed; H. Rap Brown first person prosecuted
summary: Congress responded to the 1967 riots by passing the Civil Rights Act of 1968, which added penalties for those depriving people of civil rights but exempted law enforcement and also criminalized interstate travel to organize a riot. H. Rap Brown of SNCC was the first person prosecuted under the new law.

citation.quote: Congress responded to the riots of 1967 by passing the Civil Rights Act of 1968. Presumably it would make stronger the laws prohibiting violence against blacks; it increased the penalties against those depriving people of their civil rights.

title: Martin Luther King speaks out against the Vietnam War
summary: In the spring of 1968, King began speaking out against the Vietnam War despite warnings from other Negro leaders that it would cost him allies in Washington, connecting the war to poverty and misplaced national priorities.

citation.quote: In the spring of 1968, he began speaking out, against the advice of some Negro leaders who feared losing friends in Washington, against the war in Vietnam.

title: Martin Luther King assassinated in Memphis
summary: King was shot and killed by an unseen marksman while standing on a balcony outside his hotel room in Memphis, Tennessee, where he had gone to support a strike of garbage workers. His killing sparked urban uprisings across the country in which thirty-nine people died.

citation.quote: And he went to Memphis, Tennessee, to support a strike of garbage workers in that city. There, standing on a balcony outside his hotel room, he was shot to death by an unseen marksman.

title: Three Black delegates admitted to Mississippi delegation at Democratic Convention
summary: In the 1968 Democratic Convention, three Black delegates were admitted into the Mississippi delegation — a token concession following the exclusion of the Mississippi Freedom Democrats four years earlier.

citation.quote: Blacks were voting in large numbers in the South, and in the 1968 Democratic Convention three blacks were admitted into the Mississippi delegation.

title: Nixon elected president on pledge to end the Vietnam War
summary: In the fall of 1968, Richard Nixon was elected president after pledging to get the United States out of Vietnam; he subsequently began withdrawing troops while continuing the bombing.

citation.quote: In the fall of 1968, Richard Nixon, pledging that he would get the United States out of Vietnam, was elected President.

title: Army lieutenant arrested for picketing White House against the war
summary: In early 1968, an army lieutenant was arrested in Washington D.C. for picketing the White House with a sign that read "120,000 American Casualties—Why?"

citation.quote: An army lieutenant was arrested in Washington, D.C., in early 1968 for picketing the White House with a sign that said: "120,000 American Casualties—Why?"

title: Presidio stockade prisoners sit down and sing after guard shoots inmate; sentenced for mutiny
summary: In 1968, at the Presidio stockade in California, after a guard shot an emotionally disturbed prisoner for walking away from a work detail, twenty-seven prisoners sat down singing "We Shall Overcome" and were court-martialed for mutiny with sentences up to fourteen years.

citation.quote: In 1968, at the Presidio stockade in California, a guard shot to death an emotionally disturbed prisoner for walking away from a work detail. Twenty-seven prisoners then sat down and refused to work, singing "We Shall Overcome." They were court-martialed, found guilty of mutiny, and sentenced to terms of up to fourteen years, later reduced after much public attention and protest.

title: "Burial of Traditional Womanhood" staged at Arlington National Cemetery
summary: At a women's antiwar meeting in Washington, hundreds of women carrying torches paraded to Arlington National Cemetery and symbolically buried traditional womanhood.

citation.quote: in early 1968, at a women's antiwar meeting in Washington, hundreds of women carrying torches paraded to the Arlington National Cemetery and staged "The Burial of Traditional Womanhood."

title: Radical Women protest Miss America pageant
summary: A group called Radical Women protested the Miss America pageant, tossing bras, girdles, and other items into a Freedom Trash Can, calling the pageant an image that oppresses women.

citation.quote: In the fall of 1968, a group called Radical Women attracted national attention when they protested the selection of Miss America, which they called "an image that oppresses women." They all threw bras, girdles, curlers, false eyelashes, wigs, and other things they called "women's garbage" into a Freedom Trash Can.

title: Dorothy Bolden begins organizing National Domestic Workers Union
summary: Dorothy Bolden, a laundry worker in Atlanta, began organizing women doing housework into the National Domestic Workers Union, arguing that women in the slums deserved a voice in community decisions.

citation.quote: In 1970, Dorothy Bolden, a laundry worker in Atlanta and mother of six, told why in 1968 she began organizing women doing housework, into the National Domestic Workers Union.

title: San Quentin prisoners stage interracial general strike
summary: In early 1968, a united black-white general strike at San Quentin shut down almost all the prison industries, marking an unprecedented moment of interracial solidarity among inmates.

citation.quote: a united black-white general strike in early 1968 that shut down almost all the prison industries, and then a second strike that summer.

title: Mohawk Nation begins publishing Akwesasne Notes newspaper
summary: In 1968, members of the Mohawk Nation at Akwesasne on the St. Lawrence River began publishing Akwesasne Notes, a newspaper filled with news, editorials, poetry, and defiant Native American voices.

citation.quote: In 1968, members of the Mohawk Nation at Akwesasne, on the St. Lawrence River between the United States and Canada, began a remarkable newspaper, *Akwesasne Notes,* with news, editorials, poetry, all flaming with the spirit of defiance.

title: Martin Luther King assassinated
summary: By the time King was assassinated in 1968, he had come to believe that the economic system was fundamentally unjust and needed radical transformation, speaking of "the evils of capitalism."

citation.quote: By the time King was assassinated in 1968, he had come to believe that our economic system was fundamentally unjust and needed radical transformation. He spoke of "the evils of capitalism" and asked for "a radical redistribution of economic and political power."

title: US soldiers massacre civilians at My Lai
summary: On March 16, 1968, a company of US soldiers entered the hamlet of My Lai 4 in Quang Ngai province, rounded up inhabitants including women, children, and the elderly, and methodically shot them in a ditch.

citation.quote: On March 16, 1968, a company of American soldiers went into the hamlet of My Lai 4, in Quang Ngai province. They rounded up the inhabitants, including old people and women with infants in their arms. These people were ordered into a ditch, where they were methodically shot to death by American soldiers.

title: Johnson announces he will not seek re-election and begins Paris peace negotiations
summary: In the spring of 1968, as his popularity collapsed, Lyndon Johnson announced he would not run for president again and that peace negotiations would begin with the Vietnamese in Paris.

citation.quote: In the spring of 1968 Johnson announced he would not run again for President, and that negotiations for peace would begin with the Vietnamese in Paris.

title: French publications report My Lai massacre while American press ignores it
summary: The story of the My Lai massacre appeared in May 1968 in two French publications, but the American press paid no attention until Seymour Hersh broke the story through an antiwar news agency.

citation.quote: The story of the massacre had appeared in May 1968 in two French publications, one called Sud Vietnam en Lutte, and another published by the North Vietnamese delegation to the peace talks in Paris—but the American press did not pay any attention.

title: Catonsville Nine burn draft records outside the draft board office
summary: In May 1968, Philip Berrigan, his brother Daniel Berrigan, and seven others entered a Catonsville, Maryland draft board, removed records, and set them afire outside in the presence of reporters; they became famous as the Catonsville Nine.

citation.quote: The following May, Philip Berrigan—out on bail in the Baltimore case—was joined in a second action by his brother Daniel, a Jesuit priest who had visited North Vietnam and seen the effects of U.S. bombing. They and seven other people went into a draft board office in Catonsville, Maryland, removed records, and set them afire outside in the presence of reporters and onlookers. They were convicted and sentenced to prison, and became famous as the "Catonsville Nine."

title: Boston University student Philip Supina writes to draft board refusing induction
summary: On May 1, 1968, Boston University graduate student Philip Supina wrote to his Tucson draft board declaring he had no intention of reporting for induction or aiding the American war effort; he was convicted and sentenced to four years in prison.

citation.quote: A Boston University graduate student in history, Philip Supina, wrote on May 1, 1968, to his draft board in Tucson, Arizona: I am enclosing the order for me to report for my pre-induction physical exam for the armed forces. I have absolutely no intention to report for that exam, or for induction, or to aid in any way the American war effort against the people of Vietnam. . . .

title: American Sociological Review study finds educated, high-income groups most favor aggressive Vietnam policy
summary: An article in the American Sociological Review in June 1968 found that preferences for tough policy alternatives in Vietnam were most common among the highly educated, high-status occupations, and high-income groups.

citation.quote: In an article in the American Sociological Review (June 1968), Richard F. Hamilton found in his survey of public opinion: "Preferences for 'tough' policy alternatives are most frequent among the following groups, the highly educated, high status occupations, those with high incomes, younger persons, and those paying much attention to newspapers and magazines."

title: Sid Mills arrested at fish-in and renounces U.S. Army service
summary: Yakima and Cherokee veteran Sid Mills was arrested at a fish-in at Frank's Landing, Washington, and issued a statement renouncing further military service, declaring his first obligation lay with his people fighting for treaty fishing rights.

citation.quote: One was Sid Mills, who was arrested in a fish-in at Frank's Landing on the Nisqually River in Washington on October 13, 1968. He made a statement:

title: West Virginia mine explosion kills 78 miners, prompting congressional action
summary: After a mine explosion in West Virginia killed seventy-eight miners in November 1968, angry protest in the mine district prompted Congress to pass the Coal Mine Health and Safety Act of 1969.

citation.quote: After a mine explosion in West Virginia killed seventy-eight miners in November 1968 there had been angry protest in the mine district, and Congress passed the Coal Mine Health and Safety Act of 1969.

title: At least 215,000 students participate in campus protests in first six months of 1969
summary: A survey by the Urban Research Corporation found that in just the first six months of 1969, at 232 institutions, at least 215,000 students participated in campus protests, with 3,652 arrested and 956 suspended or expelled.

citation.quote: A survey by the Urban Research Corporation, for the first six months of 1969 only, and for only 232 of the nation's two thousand institutions of higher education, showed that at least 215,000 students had participated in campus protests, that 3,652 had been arrested, that 956 had been suspended or expelled.

title: FBI lists 1,785 student demonstrations including occupation of 313 buildings
summary: During the school year of 1969–1970, the FBI listed 1,785 student demonstrations, including the occupation of 313 buildings, as campus protest against the Vietnam War reached a peak.

citation.quote: During that school year of 1969–1970, the FBI listed 1,785 student demonstrations, including the occupation of 313 buildings.

title: First Convocation of American Indian Scholars held; Indian Historian Press founded
summary: In 1969 the First Convocation of American Indian Scholars convened, where Indians protested the inaccurate depiction of Native peoples in textbooks; the same year the Indian Historian Press was founded and evaluated four hundred textbooks.

citation.quote: In 1969, at the First Convocation of American Indian Scholars, Indians spoke indignantly of either the ignoring or the insulting of Indians in textbooks given to little children all over the United States. That year the Indian Historian Press was founded.

title: U.S. conducts secret massive bombing of Cambodia
summary: For over a year in 1969–1970 the United States engaged in a secret, massive bombing of Cambodia, concealed from the American public and even from Congress.

citation.quote: It was disclosed that for over a year in 1969–1970 the U.S. had engaged in a secret, massive bombing of Cambodia, which it kept from the American public and even from Congress.

title: Congress passes the Coal Mine Health and Safety Act
summary: In 1969, following angry protests after a mine explosion in West Virginia that killed seventy-eight miners, Congress passed the Coal Mine Health and Safety Act.

citation.quote: After a mine explosion in West Virginia killed seventy-eight miners in November 1968 there had been angry protest in the mine district, and Congress passed the Coal Mine Health and Safety Act of 1969.

title: Harris poll finds 64 percent support women's right to choose abortion
summary: A Harris poll in spring 1969 showed that 64 percent of those surveyed believed the decision on abortion was a private matter.

citation.quote: In the spring of 1969 a Harris poll showed that 64 percent of those polled thought the decision on abortion was a private matter.

title: 150 Navajos meet to oppose Peabody Coal strip mining on Black Mesa
summary: One hundred and fifty Navajos gathered in spring 1969 to declare that Peabody Coal Company's strip mining on their land would pollute the water and air, destroy grazing land, and deplete scarce water resources.

citation.quote: One hundred and fifty Navajos met in the spring of 1969 to declare that the strip mining would pollute the water and the air, destroy the grazing land for livestock, use up their scarce water resources.

title: More than half of men ordered to Oakland induction center fail to appear
summary: In May 1969, the Oakland induction center—serving all of northern California—reported that of 4,400 men ordered to report, 2,400 did not show up.

citation.quote: In May 1969 the Oakland induction center, where draftees reported from all of northern California, reported that of 4,400 men ordered to report for induction, 2,400 did not show up.

title: Nixon announces antiwar protests will not affect his decisions
summary: On September 26, 1969, President Nixon announced that "under no circumstance will I be affected whatever" by growing antiwar activity—yet later in his Memoirs admitted the movement caused him to drop plans for escalation.

citation.quote: Back on September 26, 1969, President Richard Nixon, noting the growing antiwar activity all over the country, announced that "under no circumstance will I be affected whatever by it."

title: Newton College and Boston College mark Moratorium Day with antiwar displays
summary: On Moratorium Day 1969, the Newton College of the Sacred Heart displayed a giant red fist on its front door, and at Boston College six thousand people gathered in the gymnasium to denounce the war.

citation.quote: On Moratorium Day 1969, at the Newton College of the Sacred Heart near Boston, a sanctuary of bucolic quiet and political silence, the great front door of the college displayed a huge painted red fist.

title: 100,000 gather on Boston Common for Vietnam Moratorium; 2 million protest nationwide
summary: On October 15, 1969, the Vietnam Moratorium brought 100,000 people to the Boston Common and perhaps 2 million people across the country to towns and villages that had never seen an antiwar meeting.

citation.quote: On October 15, 1969, the number of people assembled on the Boston Common to protest the war was 100,000. Perhaps 2 million people across the nation gathered that day in towns and villages that had never seen an antiwar meeting.

title: Army investigators find mass graves of 450–500 victims at My Lai
summary: When Army investigators reached My Lai in November 1969, they found mass graves at three sites and a ditch full of bodies, with an estimated 450 to 500 people—mostly women, children, and old men—killed.

citation.quote: When Army investigators reached the barren area in November, 1969, in connection with the My Lai probe in the United States, they found mass graves at three sites, as well as a ditch full of bodies. It was estimated that between 450 and 500 people—most of them women, children and old men—had been slain and buried there.

title: Seventy-eight Indians occupy Alcatraz Island
summary: Before dawn on November 9, 1969, seventy-eight Indians landed on Alcatraz Island in San Francisco Bay and occupied the abandoned federal prison, launching a celebrated occupation that drew hundreds more and forced national attention to Native American grievances.

citation.quote: In 1969, November 9, there took place a dramatic event which focused attention on Indian grievances as nothing else had. It burst through the invisibility of previous local Indian protests and declared to the entire world that the Indians still lived and would fight for their rights. On that day, before dawn, seventy-eight Indians landed on Alcatraz Island in San Francisco Bay and occupied the island.

title: Draft delinquents reach 33,960 nationwide
summary: By the end of 1969, there were 33,960 draft delinquents nationwide, up from 380 prosecutions in mid-1965 and 3,305 in mid-1968.

citation.quote: By mid-1965, 380 prosecutions were begun against men refusing to be inducted; by mid-1968 that figure was up to 3,305. At the end of 1969, there were 33,960 delinquents nationwide.

title: Chicago police raid kills Black Panther leader Fred Hampton
summary: On December 4, 1969, a squad of Chicago police armed with a submachine gun and shotguns raided an apartment where Black Panthers lived, firing at least eighty-two rounds. They killed twenty-one-year-old Panther leader Fred Hampton in his bed and another Panther, Mark Clark. It later emerged the FBI had provided police with a floor plan marking where Hampton slept.

citation.quote: On December 4, 1969, a little before five in the morning, a squad of Chicago police, armed with a submachine gun and shotguns, raided an apartment where Black Panthers lived. They fired at least eighty-two and perhaps two hundred rounds into the apartment, killing twenty-one-year-old Black Panther leader Fred Hampton as he lay in his bed, and another Black Panther, Mark Clark.

title: Police open fire at Jackson State College; two Black students killed
summary: In the spring of 1970, police laid down a 28-second barrage of gunfire at Jackson State College in Mississippi, firing hundreds of rounds into a girls' dormitory and killing two Black students. A grand jury found the attack "justified."

citation.quote: In Jackson, Mississippi, in the spring of 1970, on the campus of Jackson State College, a Negro college, police laid down a 28-second barrage of gunfire, using shotguns, rifles, and a submachine gun. Four hundred bullets or pieces of buckshot struck the girls' dormitory and two black students were killed.

title: San Francisco and Marin County referenda support US withdrawal from Vietnam
summary: In 1970, referenda placed on the ballot in San Francisco County and Marin County, California—petitioned by citizens—voted for withdrawal of US forces from Vietnam, demonstrating significant antiwar sentiment even in working-class communities.

citation.quote: In 1970, in two counties in California where petitioners placed the issue on the ballot—San Francisco County and Marin County—referenda asking withdrawal of the U.S. forces from Vietnam received a majority vote.

title: Gallup poll shows 65 percent support full troop withdrawal from Vietnam by end of 1971
summary: In late 1970, a Gallup poll found that 65 percent of Americans agreed the United States should withdraw all troops from Vietnam by the end of the following year.

citation.quote: In late 1970, when a Gallup poll presented the statement: "The United States should withdraw all troops from Vietnam by the end of next year," 65 percent of those questioned said, "Yes."

title: Pentagon reports 209 fraggings of officers in Vietnam
summary: The Pentagon reported 209 fragging incidents in Vietnam in 1970 alone, reflecting the widespread low morale and open hostility among US servicemen toward officers ordering them into combat.

citation.quote: The Pentagon reported 209 fraggings in Vietnam in 1970 alone.

title: Prisoners take over Queens House of Detention
summary: Prisoners at the Queens House of Detention took over the jail, seized hostages, and demanded immediate bail hearings in cases they said reflected racism, winning some paroles before police stormed the facility.

citation.quote: At the Queens House of Detention on Long Island in New York in the fall of 1970, prisoners took over the jail, took hostages, issued demands.

title: Pit River Indians occupy ancestral land and defy federal orders to leave
summary: Sixty Pit River Indians occupied land they claimed as their own in northern California, defying the Forest Service when ordered to leave and citing a federal statute that placed the burden of proof on the white man in land disputes.

citation.quote: In the fall of 1970, a magazine called *La Raza,* one of the countless local publications coming out of the movements of those years to supply information ignored in the regular media, told about the Pit River Indians of northern California. Sixty Pit Indians occupied land they said belonged to them; they defied the Forest Services when ordered to leave.

title: Wampanoag Frank James barred from delivering anti-colonial Thanksgiving speech at Plymouth
summary: On Thanksgiving Day 1970, authorities invited Wampanoag Indian Frank James to speak at the Pilgrims' landing celebration in Plymouth, Massachusetts, but canceled his invitation when they saw his speech denouncing Pilgrim colonialism.

citation.quote: On Thanksgiving Day 1970, at the annual celebration of the landing of the Pilgrims, the authorities decided to do something different: invite an Indian to make the celebratory speech. They found a Wampanoag Indian named Frank James and asked him to speak. But when they saw the speech he was about to deliver, they decided they did not want it.

title: University of Michigan survey finds low trust in government across all classes
summary: A Survey Research Center poll found that "trust in government" was low in every section of the population, with 40 percent of professional people and 66 percent of unskilled blue-collar workers reporting "low" political trust.

citation.quote: As early as 1970, according to the University of Michigan's Survey Research Center, "trust in government" was low in every section of the population.

title: ITT director offers CIA $1 million to help overthrow Allende government in Chile
summary: In 1970, ITT director John McCone, who had also been head of the CIA, told Henry Kissinger and CIA director Richard Helms that ITT was willing to give $1 million to help overthrow the Allende government in Chile.

citation.quote: And in 1970, an ITT director, John McCone, who also had been head of the CIA, told Henry Kissinger, Secretary of State, and Richard Helms, CIA director, that ITT was willing to give $1 million to help the U.S. government in its plans to overthrow the Allende government in Chile.

title: Nixon signs the Occupational Safety and Health Act
summary: In 1970, President Nixon signed the Occupational Safety and Health Act, establishing a universal right to a safe and healthy workplace and creating an enforcement machinery, in response to strong demands from the labor movement and consumer groups.

citation.quote: The following year, yielding to strong demands from the labor movement and consumer groups, but also seeing it as an opportunity to win the support of working-class voters, President Nixon had signed the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970.

title: Police attack Chicano antiwar march in Los Angeles, leaving three dead
summary: In 1970, a large march in Los Angeles against the Vietnam war — described as a Chicano march — was attacked by police, leaving three Chicanos dead.

citation.quote: In 1970 a great march in Los Angeles against the Vietnam war, which had been attacked by police, left three Chicanos dead.

title: Boston policeman kills unarmed Black patient at City Hospital
summary: In April 1970, a Boston policeman shot and killed an unarmed Black man — a hospital patient — firing five shots after the man snapped a towel at him. The chief judge of the municipal court exonerated the officer.

citation.quote: In Boston in April 1970, a policeman shot and killed an unarmed black man, a patient in a ward in the Boston City Hospital, firing five shots after the black man snapped a towel at him. The chief judge of the municipal court of Boston exonerated the policeman.

title: Nixon and Kissinger launch invasion of Cambodia
summary: In the spring of 1970, Nixon and Kissinger launched an invasion of Cambodia following a secret undisclosed bombardment; the invasion failed militarily and triggered massive antiwar protests in the US.

citation.quote: In the spring of 1970, Nixon and Secretary of State Henry Kissinger launched an invasion of Cambodia, after a long bombardment that the government never disclosed to the public.

title: Six Black men shot dead in Augusta, Georgia
summary: In May 1970, six Black men were shot to death during looting and disorder in Augusta, Georgia. A confidential police report indicated that at least five were killed by police, who shot one man nine times in the back without warning.

citation.quote: In Augusta, Georgia, in May 1970, six Negroes were shot to death during looting and disorder in the city.

title: National Guard kills four students at Kent State University
summary: On May 4, 1970, when students gathered at Kent State University in Ohio to protest Nixon's invasion of Cambodia, National Guardsmen fired into the crowd, killing four students and paralyzing one for life.

citation.quote: At Kent State University in Ohio, on May 4, when students gathered to demonstrate against the war, National Guardsmen fired into the crowd. Four students were killed. One was paralyzed for life.

title: 28 commissioned officers announce the Concerned Officers Movement against the war
summary: In the summer of 1970, twenty-eight commissioned officers, including Vietnam veterans and claiming to represent about 250 others, announced the formation of the Concerned Officers Movement against the war.

citation.quote: In the summer of 1970, twenty-eight commissioned officers of the military, including some veterans of Vietnam, saying they represented about 250 other officers, announced formation of the Concerned Officers Movement against the war.

title: Folsom prison strike becomes longest in U.S. history
summary: In November 1970, most of the 2,400 prisoners at Folsom prison in California held out in their cells for nineteen days without food in what became the longest prison strike in U.S. history.

citation.quote: Around the same time, in November 1970, in Folsom prison in California, a work stoppage began which became the longest prison strike in the history of the United States. Most of the 2,400 prisoners held out in their cells for nineteen days, without food, in the face of threats and intimidation.

title: Vietnam Veterans Against the War hold Winter Soldier investigations in Detroit
summary: In December 1970, hundreds of Vietnam veterans went to Detroit for the Winter Soldier investigations, testifying publicly about atrocities they had participated in or witnessed in Vietnam.

citation.quote: In December 1970, hundreds of them went to Detroit to what was called the "Winter Soldier" investigations, to testify publicly about atrocities they had participated in or seen in Vietnam, committed by Americans against Vietnamese.

title: Two thousand Black and white woodworkers strike together in Mississippi
summary: In 1971, two thousand woodworkers in Mississippi — Black and white — joined together to protest a new method of measuring wood that had led to lower wages, demonstrating the potential for interracial working-class solidarity.

citation.quote: In 1971, two thousand woodworkers in Mississippi, black and white, joined together to protest a new method of measuring wood that led to lower wages.

title: Colonel Henderson tells reporters every brigade-size unit has its own hidden My Lai
summary: In early 1971, Colonel Oran Henderson, charged with covering up the My Lai killings, told reporters that every unit of brigade size had its own My Lai hidden somewhere.

citation.quote: Colonel Oran Henderson, who had been charged with covering up the My Lai killings, told reporters in early 1971: "Every unit of brigade size has its My Lai hidden someplace."

title: US drops 800,000 tons of bombs on Laos, Cambodia, and Vietnam
summary: In 1971, the United States dropped 800,000 tons of bombs on Laos, Cambodia, and Vietnam, while supporting a failed South Vietnamese invasion of Laos.

citation.quote: In 1971, 800,000 tons of bombs were dropped by the United States on Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam.

title: 20,000 war protesters arrested in Washington in largest mass arrest in US history
summary: In 1971, twenty thousand antiwar protesters came to Washington to commit civil disobedience, trying to tie up traffic; 14,000 were arrested, the largest mass arrest in American history.

citation.quote: In 1971, twenty thousand came to Washington to commit civil disobedience, trying to tie up Washington traffic to express their revulsion against the killing still going on in Vietnam. Fourteen thousand of them were arrested, the largest mass arrest in American history.

title: Public opinion surveys show unwillingness to intervene militarily for allied nations
summary: After seven years of intervention in Vietnam, polls showed Americans were unwilling to send troops to aid even NATO allies or Mexico if attacked, with only 12 percent of whites and 4 percent of nonwhites willing to send troops to Thailand.

citation.quote: Public opinion surveys in 1971—after seven years of intervention in Vietnam—showed an unwillingness to come to the aid of other countries, assuming they were attacked by Communist-backed forces.

title: ITT secretly donates $400,000 to Republican Party to secure Hartford Fire Insurance merger
summary: In 1971 ITT planned to take over Hartford Fire Insurance in what would have been the largest merger in corporate history; the Justice Department's antitrust prosecution was dropped after ITT agreed to donate $400,000 to the Republican Party.

citation.quote: In 1971 ITT planned to take over the $1½ billion Hartford Fire Insurance Company—the largest merger in corporate history. The antitrust division of the Justice Department moved to prosecute ITT for violating the antitrust laws.

title: Milk producers donate over $400,000 to Nixon campaign in exchange for higher price supports
summary: In early 1971, after initially being denied higher price supports, the Associated Milk Producers began donating to the Nixon campaign; following White House meetings and more donations totaling over $400,000, price supports were raised, adding $500 million in profits for dairy corporations.

citation.quote: In early 1971 the Secretary of Agriculture announced the government would not increase its price supports for milk—the regular subsidy to the big milk producers.

title: CIA introduces African swine fever virus into Cuba, forcing slaughter of 500,000 pigs
summary: The CIA introduced African swine fever virus into Cuba in 1971, bringing disease and then the slaughter of 500,000 pigs; a CIA operative told a reporter he had delivered the virus from an army base in the Canal Zone to anti-Castro Cubans.

citation.quote: The CIA had also been involved in assassination plots against Castro of Cuba and other heads of state. It had introduced African swine fever virus into Cuba in 1971, bringing disease and then slaughter to 500,000 pigs.

title: Contaminated drinking water causes over 100,000 illnesses in the U.S.
summary: According to an EPA report, contaminated drinking water caused over 100,000 illnesses between 1971 and 1985; despite this, in Bush's first year in office only one in a hundred of the 80,000 complaints received was investigated.

citation.quote: Contaminated drinking water had caused over 100,000 illnesses between 1971 and 1985, according to an EPA report.

title: Madison, Wisconsin referendum votes 31,000 to 16,000 for immediate US withdrawal from Southeast Asia
summary: In the spring of 1971, Madison, Wisconsin voted 31,000 to 16,000 in favor of immediate withdrawal of US forces from Southeast Asia, reversing a similar measure that had failed in 1968.

citation.quote: In Madison, Wisconsin, in the spring of 1971, a resolution calling for an immediate withdrawal of U.S. forces from Southeast Asia won by 31,000 to 16,000 (in 1968 such a resolution had lost).

title: Vietnam veterans throw medals over White House fence in Washington protest
summary: In April 1971, more than a thousand Vietnam veterans marched to Washington D.C., went up to a fence around the Capitol, and threw over their war medals one by one with brief statements of protest against the war.

citation.quote: In April 1971 more than a thousand of them went to Washington, D.C., to demonstrate against the war. One by one, they went up to a wire fence around the Capitol, threw over the fence the medals they had won in Vietnam, and made brief statements about the war, sometimes emotionally, sometimes in icy, bitter calm.

title: 61 percent of Americans say US involvement in Vietnam was wrong
summary: By May 1971, polls showed that 61 percent of Americans believed US involvement in Vietnam was wrong, a complete reversal from the 61 percent who had thought it was not wrong back in August 1965.

citation.quote: By May 1971 it was exactly reversed; 61 percent thought our involvement was wrong.

title: New York Times begins publishing the Pentagon Papers
summary: In June 1971, the New York Times began printing selections from the secret Pentagon Papers, documents that Daniel Ellsberg and Anthony Russo had duplicated and made public, creating a national sensation.

citation.quote: Then Ellsberg gave copies to various Congressmen and to the New York Times. In June 1971 the Times began printing selections from what came to be known as the Pentagon Papers. It created a national sensation.

title: Camden 28 raid New Jersey draft board; jury acquits all defendants
summary: In August 1971, the Camden 28—priests, nuns, and laypeople—raided a draft board in Camden, New Jersey; unlike the Baltimore Four four years earlier, they were acquitted by the jury on all counts.

citation.quote: The last group of draft board raiders, the "Camden 28," were priests, nuns, and laypeople who raided a draft board in Camden, New Jersey, in August 1971.

title: George Jackson shot and killed at San Quentin
summary: George Jackson, author of Soledad Brother and a prominent revolutionary prisoner, was shot in the back by guards at San Quentin prison, allegedly while trying to escape. Prisoners across the country viewed it as a political assassination.

citation.quote: In August 1971 he was shot in the back by guards at San Quentin prison while he was allegedly trying to escape. The state's story (analyzed by Eric Mann in *Comrade George*) was full of holes.

title: Nixon aides burglarize office of Daniel Ellsberg's psychiatrist
summary: Shortly after the New York Times published the Pentagon Papers, the Nixon administration ordered a burglary of the office of Ellsberg's psychiatrist, carried out by Howard Hunt and Gordon Liddy, searching for Ellsberg's records.

citation.quote: In September of 1971, shortly after the New York Times printed Daniel Ellsberg's copies of the top-secret Pentagon Papers, the administration planned and carried out—Howard Hunt and Gordon Liddy themselves doing it—the burglary of the office of Ellsberg's psychiatrist, looking for Ellsberg's records.

title: Attica prison uprising begins
summary: On September 9, 1971, prisoners at Attica broke through a defective gate and took over a prison yard with forty guards as hostages, then established a remarkable interracial community inside the besieged territory for five days.

citation.quote: On September 9, 1971, a series of conflicts between prisoners and guards ended with a group of inmates breaking through a gate with a defective weld and taking over one of the four prison yards, with forty guards as hostages.

title: Armed raid removes prisoners from Norfolk, Massachusetts prison
summary: Two months after Attica, armed guards and state troopers carried out a surprise raid at Norfolk prison in Massachusetts, pulling sixteen men from their cells and shipping them out to disrupt organizing efforts.

citation.quote: On November 8, 1971, armed guards and state troopers, in a surprise raid, moved into the cells at Norfolk, pulled out sixteen men, and shipped them out.

title: Virgil Vogel documents Pequot near-extinction
summary: A footnote in Virgil Vogel's This Land Was Ours reports the official Pequot population in Connecticut as just 21 persons.

citation.chapter: Chapter 1 – Columbus, the Indians, and Human Progress
citation.quote: A footnote in Virgil Vogel's book This Land Was Ours (1972) says: 'The official figure on the number of Pequots now in Connecticut is twenty-one persons.'

title: Vietnam veterans disrupt Republican National Convention in Miami and are expelled
summary: In 1972, Ron Kovic and other veterans drove to Miami for the Republican National Convention, wheeled into the hall, and shouted "Stop the bombing! Stop the war!" as Nixon gave his acceptance speech before being hustled out by Secret Service.

citation.quote: Kovic and the other veterans drove to Miami to the Republican National Convention in 1972, went into the Convention Hall, wheeled themselves down the aisles, and as Nixon began his acceptance speech shouted, "Stop the bombing! Stop the war!"

title: US agrees to Vietnam peace settlement but Saigon refuses; final B-52 bombing campaign launched
summary: In the fall of 1972 the United States agreed to accept a settlement that would leave revolutionary troops in place pending new elections, but Saigon refused; the US then launched a devastating B-52 bombing campaign on Hanoi and Haiphong before ultimately signing essentially the same agreement.

citation.quote: In the fall of 1972, with no victory in sight and North Vietnamese troops entrenched in various parts of the South, the United States agreed to accept a settlement that would withdraw American troops and leave the revolutionary troops where they were, until a new elected government would be set up including Communist and non-Communist elements.

title: Johnnie Tillmon publishes welfare rights essay
summary: Welfare mother and organizer Johnnie Tillmon wrote a 1972 essay connecting welfare policy to women's oppression, describing welfare as "a supersexist marriage" and advocating for the National Welfare Rights Organization.

citation.quote: A woman named Johnnie Tillmon wrote in 1972: I'm a woman. I'm a black woman. I'm a poor woman. I'm a fat woman. I'm a middle-aged woman. And I'm on welfare. . . .

title: Antiwar activists picket Honeywell over antipersonnel weapons production
summary: Antiwar picketers in Boston distributed ballots to Honeywell employees asking whether the company should stop making antipersonnel weapons used in Vietnam; of 231 returned, 131 said yes.

citation.quote: In the summer of 1972, antiwar people in the Boston area were picketing Honeywell Corporation.

title: University of Michigan poll finds 53 percent believe government serves big interests
summary: By 1972, the share of Americans who believed the government was run by a few big interests looking out for themselves had risen from 26 percent in 1964 to 53 percent.

citation.quote: The answer in 1964 had been "yes" from 26 percent of those polled; by 1972 the answer was "yes" from 53 percent of those polled.

title: US troop levels in Vietnam reduced to under 150,000
summary: By February 1972, Nixon's troop withdrawals had reduced American forces in Vietnam to fewer than 150,000, though bombing continued under the 'Vietnamization' policy.

citation.quote: He began to withdraw troops; by February 1972, less than 150,000 were left.

title: Five burglars caught breaking into Democratic National Committee offices at Watergate
summary: During the 1972 presidential campaign, five burglars carrying wiretapping equipment were caught breaking into the Democratic National Committee offices in the Watergate complex; one worked for Nixon's reelection committee and another had ties to the White House.

citation.quote: It began during the presidential campaign in June of 1972, when five burglars, carrying wiretapping and photo equipment, were caught in the act of breaking into the offices of the Democratic National Committee, in the Watergate apartment complex of Washington, D.C.

title: Nixon and Agnew win presidential election with 60 percent of popular vote
summary: In the November 1972 presidential election, Nixon and Agnew won 60 percent of the popular vote and carried every state except Massachusetts, defeating antiwar candidate Senator George McGovern.

citation.quote: In the November 1972 presidential election, Nixon and Agnew had won 60 percent of the popular vote and carried every state except Massachusetts, defeating an antiwar candidate, Senator George McGovern.

title: Columnist Joseph Alsop declares Hanoi has accepted near-total defeat
summary: Columnist Joseph Alsop wrote on November 1, 1972, that "Hanoi has accepted near-total defeat," one of a series of falsely optimistic proclamations about the Vietnam War.

citation.quote: Columnist Joseph Alsop, November 1, 1972: "Hanoi has accepted near-total defeat."

title: SEC official offers to soften Vesco charges in exchange for SEC chairmanship
summary: George Bradford Cook, former general counsel of the SEC, crouched in a Texas rice field with Maurice Stans and offered to cut a critical paragraph from the SEC charges against Robert Vesco in exchange for being made SEC chairman.

citation.quote: George Bradford Cook, former general counsel of the SEC, testified that on November 13, 1972, he crouched in a Texas rice field while on a goose hunt with Maurice Stans, and told him he wanted to be chairman of the SEC.

title: First B-52 pilots refuse to fly bombing missions over Hanoi and Haiphong
summary: During the intense Christmas 1972 bombing of Hanoi and Haiphong, the first B-52 pilots defied orders and refused to fly those missions.

citation.quote: During the fierce bombings of Hanoi and Haiphong, around Christmas 1972, came the first defiance of B-52 pilots who refused to fly those missions.

title: Supreme Court decides Roe v. Wade and Doe v. Bolton
summary: In early 1973 the Supreme Court ruled that states could prohibit abortions only in the last trimester, could regulate for health in the second trimester, and that in the first trimester a woman and her doctor had the right to decide.

citation.quote: Finally, in early 1973, the Supreme Court decided (*Roe* v. *Wade, Doe* v. *Bolton*) that the state could prohibit abortions only in the last three months of pregnancy, that it could regulate abortion for health purposes during the second three months of pregnancy, and during the first three months, a woman and her doctor had the right to decide.

title: Supreme Court rules in Procunier v. Martinez on prison mail censorship
summary: In 1973 the Supreme Court declared certain California prison mail censorship regulations unconstitutional, but the ruling still permitted censorship when it served substantial government interests of security, order, and rehabilitation.

citation.quote: In 1973 (*Procunier* v. *Martinez*) the U.S. Supreme Court declared unconstitutional certain mail censorship regulations of the California Department of Corrections.

title: Eight impeachment resolutions introduced in the House against Nixon
summary: By the fall of 1973, eight different resolutions for the impeachment of President Nixon had been introduced in the House of Representatives.

citation.quote: By the fall of 1973 eight different resolutions had been introduced in the House of Representatives for the impeachment of President Nixon.

title: ARAMCO oil profits quadruple from $1 to $4.50 per barrel
summary: ARAMCO, the Arabian-American Oil Corporation, made $1 profit on a barrel of oil in 1973 but was making $4.50 per barrel by 1974, reflecting massive oil profit increases unaffected by which party controlled the White House.

citation.quote: ARAMCO—the Arabian-American Oil Corporation, 75 percent of whose stock was held by American oil companies and 25 percent by Saudi Arabia—had made $1 profit on a barrel of oil in 1973. In 1974 it was making $4.50.

title: Congress passes War Powers Act requiring presidential consultation before military action
summary: In 1973, in a mood of fatigue and disgust with the Vietnam War, Congress passed a War Powers Act requiring the President to consult with Congress before taking military action; Ford ignored this during the Mayaguez affair.

citation.quote: Back in 1973, in a mood of fatigue and disgust with the Vietnam war, Congress had passed a War Powers Act that required the President, before taking military action, to consult with Congress.

title: Trilateral Commission founded by David Rockefeller and Zbigniew Brzezinski
summary: The Trilateral Commission was organized in early 1973 by David Rockefeller of Chase Manhattan Bank and Columbia University professor Zbigniew Brzezinski, aiming to build greater unity among the United States, Western Europe, and Japan in the face of Third World revolutionary movements.

citation.quote: The Trilateral Commission was organized in early 1973 by David Rockefeller and Zbigniew Brzezinski.

title: Chilean military junta overthrows Allende government
summary: In 1973, a Chilean military junta overthrew the democratically elected Allende government; six of the junta's members were graduates of the U.S. Army's School of the Americas in the Canal Zone.

citation.quote: Six of the graduates, for instance, were in the Chilean military junta that overthrew the democratically elected Allende government in 1973.

title: Congress passes the War Powers Act to limit presidential military power
summary: In 1973, toward the end of the Vietnam war, Congress passed the War Powers Act requiring the president to consult with Congress before introducing U.S. armed forces into hostilities.

citation.quote: Toward the end of the Vietnam war, in 1973, Congress, seeking to limit the presidential power that had been used so ruthlessly in Indochina, passed the War Powers Act

title: Supreme Court defends abortion rights in Roe v. Wade
summary: The Supreme Court's 1973 Roe v. Wade decision defending abortion rights aroused a pro-life movement with strong supporters in Washington, leading to Congress passing a law eliminating federal medical benefits to help poor women pay for abortions.

citation.quote: The Supreme Court's defense of abortion rights in its 1973 Roe v. Wade decision aroused a pro-life movement that had strong supporters in Washington.

title: AIM and Oglala Sioux occupy Wounded Knee
summary: On February 27, 1973, about three hundred Oglala Sioux, many members of the American Indian Movement, entered the village of Wounded Knee on Pine Ridge reservation and declared it liberated territory, triggering a 71-day armed siege.

citation.quote: On February 27, 1973, about three hundred Oglala Sioux, many of them members of the new militant organization called the American Indian Movement (AIM), entered the village of Wounded Knee and declared it liberated territory.

title: Frank Clearwater killed by gunfire during Wounded Knee siege
summary: In mid-April 1973, three supply planes dropped food to the besieged Wounded Knee occupiers; as people scrambled to collect the food, a government helicopter and ground forces opened fire, and Frank Clearwater, lying on a cot inside a church, was fatally wounded.

citation.quote: In mid-April three more planes dropped 1,200 pounds of food, but as people scrambled to gather it up, a government helicopter appeared overhead and fired down on them while groundfire came from all sides. Frank Clearwater, an Indian man lying on a cot inside a church, was hit by a bullet. When his wife accompanied him to a hospital, she was arrested and jailed. Clearwater died.

title: Camden 28 jury acquits all defendants; juror Samuel Braithwaite sends letter of praise
summary: In May 1973, the Camden 28 jury acquitted all defendants; juror Samuel Braithwaite, a 53-year-old Black taxi driver and army veteran, left the defendants a letter praising their moral courage in confronting leaders who had rained death on a hapless country.

citation.quote: That was in May of 1973. The American troops were leaving Vietnam.

title: Gallup poll shows 67 percent believe Nixon involved in Watergate cover-up
summary: By June 1973 a Gallup poll showed 67 percent of those polled thought Nixon was either involved in the Watergate break-in or had lied to cover it up.

citation.quote: By June of 1973 a Gallup poll showed 67 percent of those polled thought Nixon was involved in the Watergate break-in or lied to cover up.

title: New York Times reports dropouts among West Point cadets linked to anti-military mood
summary: On June 3, 1973, the New York Times reported dropout rates among West Point cadets, with officials linking it to an affluent, skeptical generation and the anti-military mood created by Vietnam.

citation.quote: On June 3, 1973, the New York Times reported dropouts among West Point cadets. Officials there, the reporter wrote, "linked the rate to an affluent, less disciplined, skeptical, and questioning generation and to the anti-military mood that a small radical minority and the Vietnam war had created."

title: Washington D.C. judge refuses to sentence men who protested Cambodia bombing
summary: A Superior Court judge in Washington, D.C. refused to sentence six men charged with unlawful entry after they stepped from a White House tour line to protest the bombing of Cambodia.

citation.quote: In Washington, D.C., in August 1973, a Superior Court judge refused to sentence six men charged with unlawful entry who had stepped from a White House tour line to protest the bombing of Cambodia.

title: Former US embassy official in Laos writes about the official lies covering the bombing
summary: In September 1973, Jerome Doolittle, a former US government official in Laos, wrote in the New York Times about the systematic lies he was instructed to tell about the massive US bombing campaign in Laos.

citation.quote: In September 1973, a former government official in Laos, Jerome Doolittle, wrote in the New York Times: The Pentagon's most recent lies about bombing Cambodia bring back a question that often occurred to me when I was press attache at the American Embassy in Vientiane, Laos.

title: ROTC fails to meet quota for sixth straight month
summary: In September 1973, for the sixth straight month, the ROTC could not fulfill its quota of officer candidates, prompting an army official to warn that another war might be impossible to fight.

citation.quote: In September 1973, for the sixth straight month, the ROTC could not fulfill its quota. One army official said: "I just hope we don't get into another war, because if we do, I doubt we could fight it."

title: Spiro Agnew resigns as Vice President after bribery indictment
summary: Nixon's Vice President Spiro Agnew was indicted in Maryland for receiving bribes from contractors and resigned from the vice-presidency in October 1973; Nixon then appointed Congressman Gerald Ford as replacement.

citation.quote: In the midst of all this, Nixon's Vice-President, Spiro Agnew, was indicted in Maryland for receiving bribes from Maryland contractors in return for political favors, and resigned from the vice-presidency in October 1973.

title: Special prosecutor fines corporations only misdemeanors for illegal Nixon campaign donations
summary: Archibald Cox charged American Airlines, Goodyear, and 3M only with misdemeanors for illegal campaign contributions rather than felonies, resulting in fines of $3,000–$5,000 per corporation despite the companies admitting they had made the payments willfully.

citation.quote: The New York Times (October 20, 1973) reported: Mr. Cox charged them only with the misdemeanor of making illegal contributions.

title: Thirty-four percent of Americans identify as political independents
summary: By 1974, 34 percent of those polled identified as "independents," up from 20 percent in 1940, reflecting widespread disaffection from both major parties.

citation.quote: Back in 1940, 20 percent of those polled called themselves "independents." In 1974, 34 percent called themselves "independents."

title: U.S. ambassador to Chile rebuked by Kissinger for raising human rights concerns with junta
summary: In 1974, when the U.S. ambassador to Chile, David Popper, suggested to the Chilean junta that they were violating human rights, Kissinger sent word telling him to "cut out the political science lectures."

citation.quote: When in 1974 the American ambassador to Chile, David Popper, suggested to the Chilean junta (which, with U.S. aid, had overthrown Allende) that they were violating human rights, he was rebuked by Kissinger, who sent word: "Tell Popper to cut out the political science lectures."

title: Number of Americans below the poverty line rises 10 percent to 25.9 million
summary: The Census Bureau reported that from 1974 to 1975 the number of Americans legally poor (below $5,500 income) rose 10 percent to 25.9 million, while unemployment rose from 5.6 to 8.3 percent and the number exhausting unemployment benefits doubled.

citation.quote: The Census Bureau reported that from 1974 to 1975 the number of Americans "legally" poor (that is, below an income of $5,500) had risen 10 percent and was now 25.9 million people. Also, the unemployment rate, which had been 5.6 percent in 1974, had risen to 8.3 percent in 1975.

title: Supreme Court upholds broad confidentiality of presidential communications
summary: While ordering Nixon to turn over his White House tapes to the special Watergate prosecutor, the Supreme Court simultaneously affirmed the broad principle of confidentiality of presidential communications for national security matters.

citation.quote: That Nixon would go, but that the power of the President to do anything he wanted in the name of "national security" would stay—this was underscored by a Supreme Court decision in July 1974.

title: Richard Nixon resigns from the presidency
summary: Nixon became the first U.S. president to resign from office, departing in August 1974 amid the Watergate scandal.

citation.quote: On top of this came the political disgrace of the Nixon administration in the scandals that came to be known by the one-word label "Watergate," and which led to the historic resignation from the presidency—the first in American history—of Richard Nixon in August 1974.

title: Nixon resigns from the presidency
summary: After being told by his advisers that the House would vote to impeach and the Senate would vote to remove him, Nixon resigned on August 8, 1974.

citation.quote: On August 8, 1974, Nixon resigned.

title: Le Monde Diplomatique editor warns Nixon's removal leaves corrupt system intact
summary: Claude Julien, editor of Le Monde Diplomatique, wrote in September 1974 that the elimination of Nixon left intact all the mechanisms and false values that permitted Watergate, and that Washington would continue supporting military dictators abroad.

citation.quote: No respectable American newspaper said what was said by Claude Julien, editor of Le Monde Diplomatique in September 1974. "The elimination of Mr. Richard Nixon leaves intact all the mechanisms and all the false values which permitted the Watergate scandal."

title: United States exports $9.5 billion in arms
summary: By 1975, the United States was exporting $9.5 billion worth of arms annually; despite Carter's campaign promises to end sales to repressive regimes, the bulk of sales continued after he took office.

citation.quote: Most aid was openly military, and by 1975, the United States exported $9.5 billion in arms.

title: Vietnam war ends
summary: The Vietnam war, which ended in 1975, left a legacy of anti-militarism that continued to shape American political culture through the Reagan and Bush administrations.

citation.quote: Sometimes the war in Vietnam, which had ended in 1975, came back to public attention in the eighties and nineties through people who had been involved in the conflicts of that day.

title: Foreign Affairs analyst defends CIA's Operation Phoenix killings
summary: A pro-administration analyst writing in Foreign Affairs in January 1975 acknowledged that Operation Phoenix had killed or incarcerated many innocent civilians while also eliminating Communist infrastructure members.

citation.quote: A pro-administration analyst wrote in the journal Foreign Affairs in January 1975: "Although the Phoenix program did undoubtedly kill or incarcerate many innocent civilians, it did also eliminate many members of the Communist infrastructure."

title: Kissinger initiates policy of cutting aid to nations opposing U.S. in UN votes
summary: In early 1975, Secretary of State Henry Kissinger formally initiated a policy of reducing American aid—including food and humanitarian relief—to nations that voted against the United States in the United Nations.

citation.quote: In early 1975 the press carried a dispatch from Washington: "Secretary of State Henry A. Kissinger has formally initiated a policy of selecting for cutbacks in American aid those nations that have sided against the U.S. in votes in the United Nations. In some cases the cutbacks involve food and humanitarian relief."

title: Catholic organization survey finds over 83 percent believe government leaders lie
summary: In March 1975, a Catholic organization conducting a survey on abortion discovered that more than 83 percent of Americans agreed that the people running the country do not tell the truth.

citation.quote: In March 1975 a Catholic organization, making a survey of American attitudes on abortion, learned other things. To the statement: "The people running this country (government, political, church and civic leaders) don't tell us the truth," more than 83 percent agreed.

title: North Vietnamese troops enter Saigon; Vietnam War ends
summary: In late April 1975, after North Vietnamese forces launched attacks that collapsed the Saigon government, North Vietnamese troops entered Saigon. The American embassy staff fled, and the long war ended with Vietnam unified as the Democratic Republic of Vietnam.

citation.quote: In late April 1975, North Vietnamese troops entered Saigon. The American embassy staff fled, along with many Vietnamese who feared Communist rule, and the long war in Vietnam was over. Saigon was renamed Ho Chi Minh City, and both parts of Vietnam were unified as the Democratic Republic of Vietnam.

title: Kissinger withdraws as University of Michigan commencement speaker amid protests
summary: In April 1975, Secretary of State Kissinger withdrew as commencement speaker at the University of Michigan after petitions protesting his role in the Vietnam War and a counter-commencement program was announced.

citation.quote: It was a few months after these reports, in April of 1975, that Secretary of State Kissinger, invited to be commencement speaker at the University of Michigan, was faced with petitions protesting the invitation, because of Kissinger's role in the Vietnam war.

title: Ford insists $722 million in military aid could still stabilize South Vietnam
summary: On April 16, 1975, President Ford declared he was "absolutely convinced" that if Congress had made available $722 million in military assistance, South Vietnam could still stabilize its military situation.

citation.quote: On April 16, 1975, Ford said: "I am absolutely convinced if Congress made available $722 million in military assistance by the time I asked—or sometime shortly thereafter—the South Vietnamese could stabilize the military situation in Vietnam today."

title: North Vietnamese forces enter Saigon, ending the Vietnam War
summary: On April 29, 1975, North Vietnamese forces moved into Saigon, bringing the Vietnam War to an end.

citation.quote: Two weeks later, April 29, 1975, the North Vietnamese moved into Saigon, and the war was over.

title: Cambodia seizes American cargo ship Mayaguez
summary: In mid-May 1975, just three weeks after the revolutionary victory in Vietnam, Cambodian forces stopped and seized the American cargo ship Mayaguez as it sailed near a Cambodian island, removing the crew to the mainland.

citation.quote: The Mayaguez was an American cargo ship sailing from South Vietnam to Thailand in mid-May 1975, just three weeks after the victory of the revolutionary forces in Vietnam.

title: New York Times reports administration officials welcomed Mayaguez as opportunity to show resolve
summary: The New York Times reported on May 16, 1975, that Kissinger and Schlesinger were eager to find a dramatic means of underscoring Ford's stated intention to maintain U.S. world leadership, and that the Mayaguez seizure provided that opportunity.

citation.quote: The New York Times reported on May 16, 1975: Administration officials, including Secretary of State Henry Kissinger and Secretary of Defense James Schlesinger, were said to have been eager to find some dramatic means of underscoring President Ford's stated intention to "maintain our leadership on a world-wide basis."

title: Ford speaks at Flag Day ceremony at Fort Benning amid antiwar protest
summary: On Flag Day, June 14, 1975, President Ford spoke at Fort Benning, Georgia, where the army staged a march symbolizing involvement in thirteen wars; a reporter noted that few American flags were visible near the reviewing stand, with one held by protesters bearing the inscription "No more genocide in our name."

citation.quote: June 14, 1975, was Flag Day, and President Gerald Ford spoke at Fort Benning, Georgia, where the army staged a march symbolizing its involvement in thirteen wars.

title: Senate report reveals FBI tried "to destroy" Martin Luther King
summary: A Senate report issued in 1976 revealed that the FBI had tapped King's phones, sent fake letters, threatened and blackmailed him, and even suggested he commit suicide — a systematic campaign to destroy the civil rights leader.

citation.quote: As a Senate report on the FBI said in 1976, the FBI tried "to destroy Dr. Martin Luther King."

title: Treasury Secretary William Simon warns American business system losing support
summary: In the fall of 1976, Treasury Secretary William Simon told a Business Council meeting that private enterprise was "losing by default" in schools, media, and public consciousness, calling for Americans to be taught to appreciate the "human side of capitalism."

citation.quote: William Simon, Secretary of the Treasury under both Nixon and Ford (before then an investment banker earning over $2 million a year), spoke in the fall of 1976 to a Business Council meeting in Hot Springs, Virginia.

title: Trilateral Commission issues report warning of excess of democracy
summary: As the U.S. prepared to celebrate the bicentennial, the Trilateral Commission issued a report entitled "The Governability of Democracies," in which Harvard professor Samuel Huntington argued that the "democratic surge" of the 1960s had produced an "excess of democracy" and suggested desirable limits to the extension of political democracy.

citation.quote: As the United States prepared in 1976 to celebrate the bicentennial of the Declaration of Independence, a group of intellectuals and political leaders from Japan, the United States, and Western Europe, organized into "The Trilateral Commission," issued a report. It was entitled "The Governability of Democracies."

title: Boston Tea Party bicentennial draws crowd to "People's Bi-Centennial" countercelebration
summary: When the 200th anniversary of the Boston Tea Party was celebrated in Boston, an enormous crowd turned out not for the official celebration but for the "People's Bi-Centennial" countercelebration, where packages marked "Gulf Oil" and "Exxon" were dumped into Boston Harbor to protest corporate power.

citation.quote: When the 200th anniversary of the Boston Tea Party was celebrated in Boston, an enormous crowd turned out, not for the official celebration, but for the "People's Bi-Centennial" countercelebration, where packages marked "Gulf Oil" and "Exxon" were dumped into the Boston Harbor, to symbolize opposition to corporate power in America.

title: Voter turnout drops to 53 percent in the presidential election
summary: By 1976, only 53 percent of eligible voters participated in the presidential election, reflecting growing alienation from the political system since the early 1960s.

citation.quote: In 1960, 63 percent of those eligible to vote voted in the presidential election. By 1976, this figure had dropped to 53 percent.

title: General Accounting Office report reveals U.S. received Chinese warning before Mayaguez assault
summary: In October 1976, the General Accounting Office reported that the U.S. had received a message from a Chinese diplomat saying China was using its influence with Cambodia to secure the Mayaguez crew's release—a message received fourteen hours before the marine assault on Tang Island began.

citation.quote: Not mentioned in any press account at the time or in any government statement was a fact that emerged in October 1976 when the General Accounting Office made a report on the Mayaguez affair: the U.S. had received a message from a Chinese diplomat saying China was using its influence with Cambodia on the ship "and expected it to be released soon."

title: Carter renegotiates the Panama Canal treaty
summary: In 1977 the Carter administration, responding to anti-American protests in Panama, renegotiated the 1903 treaty, agreeing to gradual removal of U.S. bases and eventual transfer of legal canal ownership to Panama.

citation.quote: The Carter administration in 1977, responding to anti-American protests in Panama, decided to renegotiate the treaty.

title: Over 3,500 arrested in years of anti-nuclear protests at Seabrook, New Hampshire
summary: Between 1977 and 1989, over 3,500 people were arrested in persistent protests against the Seabrook nuclear power plant in New Hampshire, which residents considered a danger. The plant ultimately had to shut down due to financial problems and opposition.

citation.quote: Between 1977 and 1989, over 3500 people were arrested in these protests. Ultimately, the plant, plagued by financial problems and opposition, had to shut down.

title: Ramos-Horta learns of sister killed by US-supplied aircraft bombing in East Timor
summary: In the summer of 1977, Jose Ramos-Horta, then in New York, received a message that his 21-year-old sister Maria had been killed in an aircraft bombing using a US-supplied Bronco aircraft in East Timor.

citation.quote: In the summer of 1977, I was here in New York when I received a message telling me that one of my sisters, Maria, 21 years old, had been killed in an aircraft bombing. The aircraft, named Bronco, was supplied by the United States.

title: Supreme Court denies media access rights to prisons
summary: In 1978 the Supreme Court ruled that news media have no guaranteed right of access to jails and prisons, and also upheld prison authorities' power to forbid inmates from organizing prisoners' unions.

citation.quote: In 1978 the Supreme Court ruled that the news media do not have guaranteed rights of access to jails and prisons. It ruled also that prison authorities could forbid inmates to speak to one another, assemble, or spread literature about the formation of a prisoners' union.

title: Nuclear freeze referenda pass in San Francisco, Berkeley, Oakland, Madison, and Detroit
summary: Between 1978 and 1981, nuclear freeze referenda received majority votes in San Francisco, Berkeley, Oakland, Madison, and Detroit.

citation.quote: Similar referenda received majority votes between 1978 and 1981 in San Francisco, Berkeley, Oakland, Madison, and Detroit.

title: Shah's troops massacre hundreds of demonstrators in Iran
summary: On September 8, 1978, hundreds of demonstrators were massacred by the Shah's troops in Iran; the following day President Carter telephoned the royal palace to express his support for Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlevi.

citation.quote: On September 8, 1978, hundreds of demonstrators were massacred by the Shah's troops. The next day, according to a UPI dispatch from Teheran, Carter affirmed his support for the Shah

title: CIA specialists arrive in Iran to back effort to support the Shah
summary: On December 13, 1978, the New York Times reported that the U.S. Embassy in Iran had been bolstered by dozens of CIA specialists and military personnel flown in to help the Shah against a growing challenge to his rule.

citation.quote: On December 13, 1978, Nicholas Gage reported for the New York Times: The staff of the United States Embassy here has been bolstered by dozens of specialists flown in to back an effort to help the Shah against a growing challenge to his rule according to embassy sources. . . . The new arrivals, according to the embassy sources, include a number of Central Intelligence Agency specialists on Iran, in addition to diplomats and military personnel.

title: Three Mile Island nuclear accident
summary: A disastrous nuclear accident at Three Mile Island in Pennsylvania in 1979 intensified public fear of nuclear power and contributed to the decline of the nuclear industry.

citation.quote: Fear of nuclear accidents was intensified by disastrous events at Three Mile Island in Pennsylvania in 1979 and by an especially frightening calamity in Chernobyl in the Soviet Union in 1986.

title: Farm Labor Organizing Committee wins largest agricultural strike in Midwest history
summary: In 1979, the Farm Labor Organizing Committee won a difficult strike in the Ohio tomato fields — described as the largest agricultural strike ever in the Midwest — and subsequently brought thousands of farmworkers together in several Midwest states.

citation.quote: The Farm Labor Organizing Committee, which had won a difficult strike in the Ohio tomato fields in 1979, the largest agricultural strike ever in the Midwest, brought thousands of farmworkers together in several Midwest states.
