title: Iranian student militants seize U.S. Embassy in Tehran and take 52 hostages
summary: On November 4, 1979, student militants took over the U.S. Embassy in Tehran, holding fifty-two embassy employees hostage and demanding the Shah be returned to Iran for punishment.

citation.quote: On November 4, 1979, the U.S. embassy in Teheran was taken over by student militants who, demanding that the Shah be returned to Iran for punishment, held fifty-two embassy employees hostage.

title: Archbishop Romero assassinated in El Salvador
summary: Shortly after sending a letter to President Carter in February 1980 asking him to stop military aid, El Salvador Catholic Archbishop Oscar Romero was assassinated; evidence pointed to Roberto D'Aubuisson, who had the protection of a CIA-paid deputy minister of defense.

citation.quote: But the Carter administration continued the aid. The following month Archbishop Romero was assassinated.

title: Over a thousand peace activists arrested at Pentagon demonstrations
summary: Small delegations of peace activists from across the country held a series of demonstrations at the Pentagon in 1980, resulting in over a thousand arrests for acts of nonviolent civil disobedience.

citation.quote: In 1980, small delegations of peace activists from all over the country maintained a series of demonstrations at the Pentagon, in which over a thousand people were arrested for acts of nonviolent civil disobedience.

title: Reagan elected president; local nuclear freeze referenda pass in western Massachusetts
summary: In the 1980 presidential election, local referenda in three western Massachusetts districts asked voters whether they supported a mutual Soviet-American nuclear weapons halt; all three districts approved the resolution by 94,000 to 65,000, even while voting for Reagan.

citation.quote: In the election of 1980 that brought him into the Presidency, local referenda in three districts in western Massachusetts permitted voters to say whether they believed in a mutual Soviet-American halt to testing, production, and deployment of all nuclear weapons, and wanted Congress to devote those funds instead to civilian use.

title: Four American nuns executed by Salvadoran soldiers
summary: In the fall of 1980, four American nuns were executed by Salvadoran soldiers, an act referenced in antiwar chants at the 1981 Syracuse commencement and cited as evidence of U.S.-backed atrocities in El Salvador.

citation.quote: The last slogan was a reference to the execution in the fall of 1980 of four American nuns by Salvadoran soldiers.

title: Reagan elected with 51.6% of popular vote, 27% of eligible voters
summary: In 1980, Reagan received 51.6 percent of the popular vote against Carter's 41.7 percent and Anderson's 6.7 percent, but with only 54 percent of voting-age Americans voting, Reagan's mandate represented just 27 percent of eligible voters.

citation.quote: In 1980 Reagan received 51.6 percent of the popular vote, while Jimmy Carter received 41.7 percent and John Anderson (a liberal Republican running on a third-party ticket) received 6.7 percent. Only 54 percent of the voting-age population voted, so that—of the total eligible to vote—27 percent voted for Reagan.

title: Archbishop Romero sends letter to Carter asking him to stop military aid to El Salvador
summary: In February 1980, El Salvador Catholic Archbishop Oscar Romero sent a personal letter to President Carter asking him to stop military aid to El Salvador, shortly after the National Guard and National Police opened fire on protesters and killed twenty-four people.

citation.quote: In February 1980 El Salvador Catholic Archbishop Oscar Romero sent a personal letter to President Carter, asking him to stop military aid to El Salvador.

title: James Peters refuses to register for Selective Service draft
summary: James Peters, one of the young men who refused to register for the military draft, wrote an open letter to President Carter declaring he would not register on July 23, 1980, or at any time thereafter, citing the failure of militarism.

citation.quote: Dear Mr. President: On July 23, 1980, I . . . am expected to report to my local post office for the purpose of registering with the Selective Service System. I hereby inform you, Mr. President, that I will not register on July 23, or at any time thereafter. . . . We have tried militarism, and it has failed the human race in every way imaginable.

title: Plowshares Eight disarm nuclear nose cones at General Electric plant
summary: Philip Berrigan, Daniel Berrigan, and six others entered the General Electric Plant at King of Prussia, Pennsylvania, smashing two nuclear missile nose cones with sledgehammers and pouring their blood over missile parts in a dramatic act of disarmament protest.

citation.quote: In September of that year, Philip Berrigan, his brother Daniel (the Jesuit priest and poet), Molly Rush (a mother of six), Anne Montgomery (a nun and counselor to young runaways and prostitutes in Manhattan), and four of their friends made their way past a guard in the General Electric Plant at King of Prussia, Pennsylvania, where nose cones for nuclear missiles were manufactured.

title: Journalist Raymond Bonner reports on El Mozote massacre by U.S.-trained soldiers
summary: Back in 1981, journalist Raymond Bonner reported on the massacre of hundreds of civilians in the town of El Mozote by a U.S.-trained battalion; the Reagan administration scoffed at the account, but in 1992 forensic anthropologists unearthed skeletons confirming the massacre.

citation.quote: Back in 1981 Bonner had reported on the massacre of hundreds of civilians in the town of El Mozote, by a battalion of soldiers trained by the United States.

title: 2,000 students protest U.S. involvement in El Salvador at Harvard Yard
summary: Shortly after Reagan took office, approximately 2,000 persons — mostly students from universities including Tufts, MIT, Boston University, Yale, and others — gathered at Harvard Yard for a candlelight march to protest U.S. involvement in El Salvador.

citation.quote: It was a scene reminiscent of the 1960s, a rally of students in Harvard Yard shouting antiwar slogans, a candlelight march through the streets of Cambridge. . . . 2000 persons, mostly students, gathered to protest U.S. involvement in El Salvador.

title: 200 students turn backs on Alexander Haig at Syracuse University commencement
summary: During spring 1981 commencement exercises at Syracuse University, two hundred students and faculty turned their backs when Secretary of State Alexander Haig received an honorary doctorate, and chanted antiwar slogans throughout his address.

citation.quote: During commencement exercises that spring of 1981 at Syracuse University, when Reagan's Secretary of State, Alexander Haig, was given an honorary doctorate in "public service," two hundred students and faculty turned their backs on the presentation.

title: East Boston residents block thoroughfares for 55 nights to protest service cuts
summary: In the spring and summer of 1981, residents of East Boston took to the streets for fifty-five nights, blocking major thoroughfares and the Sumner Tunnel during rush hour to protest Reagan's cutbacks in funds for fire, police, and teachers.

citation.quote: In the spring and summer of 1981, residents of East Boston took to the streets; for fifty-five nights they blocked major thoroughfares and the Sumner Tunnel during rush hour, in order to protest cutbacks in funds for fire, police, and teachers.

title: Nuclear war teach-ins held on 151 college campuses; Boston votes for peace spending
summary: In November 1981, meetings on the issue of nuclear war were held on 151 college campuses. In Boston local elections that same month, a resolution calling for redirecting military spending to social programs won in every one of Boston's twenty-two wards.

citation.quote: In November 1981, there were meetings on 151 college campuses around the country on the issue of nuclear war. And at local elections in Boston that month, a resolution calling for increased federal spending on social programs "by reducing the amount of our tax dollars spent on nuclear weapons and programs of foreign intervention" won a majority in every one of Boston's twenty-two wards, including both white and black working-class districts.

title: Reagan's Secretary of Defense warns about public unrest over draft renewal
summary: In November 1981, Reagan's Secretary of Defense Caspar Weinberger explained that Reagan had not renewed draft registration because he believed it would lead to public unrest comparable to the 1960s and 1970s.

citation.quote: William Beecher, a former Pentagon reporter, wrote in November 1981 that Reagan was "obviously concerned, even alarmed, by the mounting voices of discontent and suspicion over emerging U.S. nuclear strategy both in the streets of Europe and more recently on American campuses."

title: 30 million Americans unemployed all or part of the year
summary: In the year 1982, 30 million people were unemployed all or part of the year, and over 16 million Americans lost medical insurance, which was often tied to holding a job.

citation.quote: In the year 1982, 30 million people were unemployed all or part of the year. One result was that over 16 million Americans lost medical insurance, which was often tied to holding a job.

title: Reagan sends U.S. marines into Lebanon, ignoring the War Powers Act
summary: In the fall of 1982, President Reagan sent American marines into Lebanon amid a civil war, again ignoring the requirements of the War Powers Act; the following year over two hundred of those marines were killed in a terrorist bombing of their barracks.

citation.quote: In the fall of 1982, President Reagan sent American marines into a dangerous situation in Lebanon, where a civil war was raging, again ignoring the requirements of the War Powers Act. The following year, over two hundred of those marines were killed when a bomb was exploded in their barracks by terrorists.

title: Teachers' strikes in seven states idle more than 300,000 students
summary: In the fall of 1982, teachers across seven states from Rhode Island to Washington went on strike over layoffs, salary cuts, and job insecurity, idling more than 300,000 students.

citation.quote: Angered by layoffs, salary cuts and uncertainty about job security, more schoolteachers throughout the country have decided to go on strike. Teachers' strikes last week in seven states, from Rhode Island to Washington, have idled more than 300,000 students.

title: Over 1,800 arrested in Minneapolis protests against Honeywell military contracts
summary: Between 1982 and 1988, thousands of people demonstrated year after year in Minneapolis against the Honeywell Corporation's military contracts, with over 1,800 people arrested in these protests.

citation.quote: In Minneapolis, Minnesota, thousands of people demonstrated year after year against the Honeywell Corporation's military contracts, and between 1982 and 1988 over 1800 people were arrested.

title: Forbes 400 richest families owned $92 billion in 1982
summary: According to Forbes, the 400 richest families owned $92 billion in 1982; thirteen years later this had jumped to $480 billion, illustrating the dramatic concentration of wealth.

citation.quote: According to the business magazine Forbes, the 400 richest families owned $92 billion in 1982, but thirteen years later this had jumped to $480 billion.

title: Reports of government massacre of peasants in El Salvador; Reagan certifies human rights progress the next day
summary: On January 28, 1982, there were reports of a Salvadoran government massacre of peasants; the following day Reagan certified that the Salvadoran government was making progress in human rights, and three days after certification soldiers killed twenty people in San Salvador.

citation.quote: On January 28, 1982, there were reports of a government massacre of peasants in several villages. The following day, Reagan certified that the Salvadoran government was making progress in human rights. Three days after certification, soldiers stormed the homes of poor people in San Salvador, dragged out twenty people, and killed them.

title: Nearly one million march in Central Park against the arms race
summary: On June 12, 1982, close to a million people gathered in Central Park, New York City, in what the chapter calls the largest political demonstration in the history of the country, to demand an end to the nuclear arms race.

citation.quote: On June 12, 1982, the largest political demonstration in the history of the country took place in Central Park, New York City. Close to a million people gathered to express their determination to bring an end to the arms race.

title: George Kistiakowsky's final appeal for mass peace movement published
summary: George Kistiakowsky, a Harvard chemistry professor who had worked on the first atomic bomb and served as science adviser to Eisenhower, published his last public remarks in the Bulletin of Atomic Scientists in December 1982, calling for a mass movement for peace before it was too late.

citation.quote: His last public remarks, before his death from cancer at the age of eighty-two, were in an editorial for the Bulletin of Atomic Scientists in December 1982. "I tell you as my parting words: Forget the channels. There simply is not enough time left before the world explodes. Concentrate instead on organizing, with so many others of like mind, a mass movement for peace such as there has not been before."

title: Nuclear freeze endorsed by 368 cities, 17 state legislatures, and the House
summary: By spring 1983, the nuclear freeze had been endorsed by 368 city and county councils, 444 town meetings, 17 state legislatures, and the House of Representatives. A Harris poll found 79 percent of Americans supported a nuclear freeze with the Soviet Union.

citation.quote: By the spring of 1983, the nuclear freeze had been endorsed by 368 city and county councils across the country, by 444 town meetings and 17 state legislatures, and by the House of Representatives.

title: American physician Charles Clement disclosed to be working with Salvadoran rebels
summary: In the spring of 1983, it was revealed that Dr. Charles Clement, a former Air Force pilot who had refused further missions in Southeast Asia and been committed to a psychiatric hospital, had volunteered as a doctor with the guerrillas in El Salvador.

citation.quote: In the spring of 1983, it was disclosed that an American physician named Charles Clement was working with the Salvadoran rebels.

title: 2,000 demonstrate outside jailhouse for imprisoned teachers' strike leader in Pennsylvania
summary: In early 1983 in Little Washington, Pennsylvania, when a 50-year-old computer science teacher who had led a teachers' strike was jailed, 2,000 people demonstrated outside — described by the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette as the largest crowd in Washington County since the 1794 Whiskey Rebellion.

citation.quote: In Little Washington, Pennsylvania, in early 1983, when a 50-year-old computer science teacher who led a teachers' strike was sent to jail, 2000 people demonstrated outside the jailhouse in his support, and the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette called it "the largest crowd in Washington County since the 1794 Whiskey Rebellion."

title: Copper miners strike against Phelps-Dodge in Arizona after wage and safety cuts
summary: Copper miners in Arizona, mostly Mexican, went on strike against the Phelps-Dodge company in 1983 after it cut wages, benefits, and safety measures. They were attacked by National Guardsmen and state troopers with tear gas and helicopters, holding out for three years before being defeated.

citation.quote: Copper miners in Arizona, mostly Mexican, went on strike against the Phelps-Dodge company after it cut wages, benefits, and safety measures in 1983.

title: 3,000 unemployed steelworkers protest Reagan's visit to Pittsburgh
summary: When Reagan arrived in Pittsburgh in April 1983 to make a speech, 3,000 people — many of them unemployed steelworkers — demonstrated against him in the rain outside his hotel. Similar demonstrations by the unemployed were occurring in over twenty cities.

citation.quote: When Reagan arrived in Pittsburgh in April 1983 to make a speech, 3000 people, many of them unemployed steelworkers, demonstrated against him, standing in the rain outside his hotel.

title: Carlos Fuentes receives standing ovation at Harvard commencement for criticizing U.S. policy
summary: At the Harvard commencement of June 1983, Mexican writer Carlos Fuentes criticized American intervention in Latin America and was interrupted twenty times by applause, receiving a standing ovation — contradicting media claims of student political apathy.

citation.quote: But when, at the Harvard commencement of June 1983, Mexican writer Carlos Fuentes criticized American intervention in Latin America, and said, "Because we are your true friends, we will not permit you to conduct yourselves in Latin American affairs as the Soviet Union conducts itself in Central European and Central Asian affairs," he was interrupted twenty times by applause and received a standing ovation when finished.

title: Reagan orders U.S. invasion of Grenada (Operation Urgent Fury)
summary: In October 1983, Reagan sent U.S. forces to invade the tiny Caribbean island of Grenada (Operation Urgent Fury), notifying but not consulting Congress, claiming American students at a medical school were endangered by a recent coup.

citation.quote: Shortly after that, in October 1983 (with some analysts concluding this was done to take attention away from the Lebanon disaster), Reagan sent U.S. forces to invade the tiny Caribbean island of Grenada.

title: New York Times report demolishes official justifications for Grenada invasion
summary: On October 29, 1983, a New York Times article by Bernard Gwertzman revealed that the formal request for U.S. intervention in Grenada had been drafted in Washington and that there was no firm evidence American students were in danger.

citation.quote: An unusually pointed article in the New York Times on October 29, 1983, by correspondent Bernard Gwertzman demolished those reasons

title: CIA admits to exaggerating Soviet military expenditures since 1975
summary: In 1984, the CIA admitted that since 1975 it had exaggerated Soviet military expenditures, claiming 4 to 5 percent annual growth when the actual figure was 2 percent, thereby inflating justifications for U.S. military spending.

citation.quote: In 1984, the CIA admitted that it had exaggerated Soviet military expenditures, that since 1975 it had claimed Soviet military spending was growing by 4 to 5 percent each year when the actual figure was 2 percent.

title: CIA mines harbors of Nicaragua, Weinberger denies U.S. involvement
summary: In 1984, the CIA used Latin American agents to conceal its involvement in mining Nicaragua's harbors to blow up ships; when the information leaked out, Secretary of Defense Weinberger falsely told ABC News that the United States was not mining the harbors.

citation.quote: In 1984, the CIA, using Latin American agents to conceal its involvement, put mines in the harbors of Nicaragua to blow up ships. When information leaked out, Secretary of Defense Weinberger told ABC news: "The United States is not mining the harbors of Nicaragua."

title: Congress makes it illegal to support military operations in Nicaragua
summary: In 1984, Congress made it illegal for the United States to support, directly or indirectly, military or paramilitary operations in Nicaragua; the Reagan administration decided to ignore this law and secretly fund the contras through third parties.

citation.quote: Later that year Congress, responding perhaps to public opinion and the memory of Vietnam, made it illegal for the United States to support "directly or indirectly, military or paramilitary operations in Nicaragua."

title: "Winooski Forty-four" acquitted after occupying senator's office to protest Nicaragua aid
summary: In 1984, forty-four Vermont citizens were arrested after refusing to leave the hallway outside a U.S. Senator's office to protest his votes giving arms to the Nicaraguan contras; they were treated sympathetically by the judge and acquitted by the jury.

citation.quote: In 1984, a group of Vermont citizens (the "Winooski Forty-four") refused to leave the hallway outside a U.S. Senator's office, protesting his votes to give arms to the Nicaraguan contras. They were arrested, but at their trial they were treated sympathetically by the judge and acquitted by the jury.

title: Border Arts Workshop founded in San Diego and Tijuana
summary: The Border Arts Workshop was formed in 1984 by artists and writers in San Diego and Tijuana, producing work that dealt with issues of racism and injustice along the U.S.-Mexico border.

citation.quote: The Border Arts workshop was formed in 1984 by artists and writers in San Diego and Tijuana, and its work dealt powerfully with issues of racism and injustice.

title: By 1984, 42% of all Latino children living below poverty line
summary: By 1984, 42 percent of all Latino children and one-fourth of Latino families lived below the poverty line, as the Reagan administration's economic policies hit poor communities especially hard.

citation.quote: By 1984, 42 percent of all Latino children and one-fourth of the families lived below the poverty line.

title: 1,700 Watsonville cannery workers win union contract after strike
summary: In 1985, 1,700 cannery workers — most of them Mexican women — went on strike in Watsonville, California, and won a union contract with medical benefits.

citation.quote: In 1985, 1700 cannery workers, most of them Mexican women, went on strike in Watsonville, California, and won a union contract with medical benefits.

title: Former Defense Secretary warns Senate of Vietnam's sea change in U.S. domestic attitudes
summary: In 1985, when George Bush was Vice-President, former Defense Secretary James Schlesinger warned the Senate Foreign Relations Committee that Vietnam had brought a sea change in domestic attitudes and a breakdown in political consensus behind foreign policy.

citation.quote: In 1985, when George Bush was Vice-President, former Defense Secretary James Schlesinger had warned the Senate Foreign Relations Committee: "Vietnam brought a sea change in domestic attitudes . . . a breakdown in the political consensus behind foreign policy. . . ."

title: Iran-contra affair exposed: U.S. sold weapons to Iran and funneled profits to contras
summary: In 1986, a Beirut magazine story revealed that the United States had secretly sold weapons to Iran and transferred profits to the Nicaraguan contras, sparking the Iran-contra scandal.

citation.quote: In 1986, a story appearing in a Beirut magazine created a sensation: that weapons had been sold by the United States to Iran (supposedly an enemy), that in return Iran had promised to release hostages being held by extremist Moslems in Lebanon, and that profits from the sale were being given to the contras to buy arms.

title: U.S. bombs Tripoli, Libya, killing approximately 100 civilians
summary: In 1986, after unknown terrorists bombed a West Berlin discotheque killing a U.S. serviceman, Reagan sent planes to bomb Tripoli, Libya, targeting Khadafi's house; an estimated hundred people were killed and Khadafi's adopted daughter died.

citation.quote: In 1986, when unknown terrorists bombed a discotheque in West Berlin, killing a U.S. serviceman, the White House immediately decided to retaliate.

title: Chernobyl nuclear disaster in the Soviet Union
summary: A catastrophic nuclear accident at Chernobyl in the Soviet Union in 1986 further intensified public fear of nuclear power and affected the nuclear industry globally.

citation.quote: Fear of nuclear accidents was intensified by disastrous events at Three Mile Island in Pennsylvania in 1979 and by an especially frightening calamity in Chernobyl in the Soviet Union in 1986.

title: Congress overrides Reagan's veto to impose economic sanctions on South Africa
summary: Public opinion against Reagan's support for apartheid South Africa was strong enough to cause Congress to legislate economic sanctions against the South African government in 1986, overriding Reagan's veto.

citation.quote: Public opinion was strong enough to cause Congress to legislate economic sanctions against the South African Government in 1986, overriding Reagan's veto.

title: Reagan makes four false statements about Iran-contra at press conference
summary: In November 1986, when asked about the Iran-contra affair at a press conference, President Reagan made four false statements: about the quantity of weapons shipped to Iran, condoning third-party shipments, weapons-for-hostages, and the true purpose of the operation.

citation.quote: When asked about this at a press conference in November 1986, President Reagan told four lies: that the shipment to Iran consisted of a few token antitank missiles (in fact, 2,000), that the United States didn't condone shipments by third parties, that weapons had not been traded for hostages, and that the purpose of the operation was to promote a dialogue with Iranian moderates.

title: 62% of Americans say government should guarantee food and shelter to the needy
summary: At the height of the Reagan presidency in 1987, polling found that 62 percent of people believed the government should guarantee food and shelter to needy people, reflecting widespread public sentiment at odds with administration policy.

citation.quote: When, at the height of the Reagan presidency, in 1987, people were asked if the government should guarantee food and shelter to needy people, 62 percent answered yes.

title: George Bush wins presidency with 27% of eligible voters
summary: In the 1988 election, George Bush defeated Democrat Michael Dukakis with 54 percent of the popular vote, but with half the electorate not voting, his mandate represented only 27 percent of eligible voters.

citation.quote: In the 1988 election, with Vice-President George Bush running against Democrat Michael Dukakis, Bush's 54 percent victory added up to 27 percent of the eligible voters.

title: New Mexico Latino land rights confrontation ends in court victory
summary: In 1988, a confrontation over land and water rights in New Mexico led Latinos to organize an armed occupation with bunkers for protection; ultimately a court ruled in their favor against real estate developers.

citation.quote: In 1988 there was a confrontation, and the people organized an armed occupation, built bunkers for protection against attack, and won support from other communities in the Southwest; finally, a court ruled in their favor.

title: Cesar Chavez fasts 35 days to protest cancer rates among California farmworkers
summary: In 1988, Cesar Chavez of the United Farm Workers fasted for thirty-five days to call attention to abnormal cancer rates among California farmworkers caused by pesticide exposure.

citation.quote: Cesar Chavez of the United Farm Workers fasted for thirty-five days in 1988 to call attention to these conditions.

title: Soviet bloc collapses; Berlin Wall dismantled as Eastern Europe democratizes
summary: In 1989, with Mikhail Gorbachev leading the Soviet Union, long-suppressed dissatisfaction with Soviet-style rule erupted across Eastern Europe; East Germany agreed to unite with West Germany, the Berlin Wall was dismantled, and new non-Communist governments emerged across the Soviet bloc.

citation.quote: Early in the presidency of George Bush, there came the most dramatic developments on the international scene since the end of World War II. In the year 1989, with a dynamic new leader, Mikhail Gorbachev, at the head of the Soviet Union, the long suppressed dissatisfaction with "dictatorships of the proletariat" which had turned out to be dictatorships over the proletariat erupted all through the Soviet bloc.

title: Harris/Harvard poll: 61% of Americans favor Canadian-style single-payer health system
summary: A 1989 Harris/Harvard School of Public Health poll found that 61 percent of Americans favored a Canadian-type single-payer health system offering universal medical coverage, a position neither major political party adopted.

citation.quote: A Harris/Harvard School of Public Health poll of 1989 showed that most Americans (61 percent) favored a Canadian-type health system, in which the government was the single payer to doctors and hospitals, bypassing the insurance companies, and offering universal medical coverage to everyone.

title: 300,000 rally in Washington for abortion rights
summary: In 1989, a Washington rally for reproductive rights drew over 300,000 people, demonstrating the continued strength of the National Organization for Women and other women's groups despite the anti-abortion backlash of the 1980s.

citation.quote: But the National Organization of Women and other groups remained strong; in 1989, a Washington rally for what had come to be known as the right to choose drew over 300,000 people.

title: Disintegration of Soviet bloc raises hopes for a peace dividend
summary: After the disintegration of the Soviet bloc began in 1989, there was talk in the United States of a peace dividend — redirecting billions from the military budget to human needs — but the Gulf War became a convenient excuse to suppress that debate.

citation.quote: After the disintegration of the Soviet bloc began in 1989, there had been talk in the United States of a "peace dividend," the opportunity to take billions of dollars from the military budget and use it for human needs.

title: United States invades Panama with 26,000 troops to capture Noriega
summary: In December 1989, the United States invaded Panama with 26,000 troops, quickly capturing General Manuel Noriega; hundreds or possibly thousands of civilians were killed and 14,000 people were left homeless.

citation.quote: the United States invaded Panama in December 1989, with 26,000 troops.

title: Bush signs the Clean Air Act of 1990
summary: George Bush signed the Clean Air Act of 1990, presenting himself as the 'environmental president,' though two years later the act was seriously weakened by a new EPA rule allowing manufacturers to increase hazardous atmospheric pollutants.

citation.quote: George Bush presented himself as the "environmental president," and pointed with pride to his signing of the Clean Air Act of 1990.

title: 54% of Boston area voters say they would pay higher taxes to clean up environment
summary: A 1990 poll of Boston area voters found that 54 percent would be willing to pay more taxes if the money went toward cleaning up the environment, contradicting the political narrative that voters simply opposed higher taxes.

citation.quote: For instance, a 1990 poll of Boston area voters showed that 54 percent of them would pay more taxes if that would go toward cleaning up the environment.

title: San Antonio Levi Strauss workers win concessions through boycott and hunger strike
summary: In 1990, workers who had been laid off from the Levi Strauss company in San Antonio after the company moved to Costa Rica organized a boycott and hunger strike, winning concessions.

citation.quote: In 1990 workers who had been laid off from the Levi Strauss company in San Antonio because the company was moving to Costa Rica called a boycott, organized a hunger strike, and won concessions.

title: Los Angeles Latino janitors strike and win union recognition despite police attacks
summary: In 1990, Latino janitors in Los Angeles went on strike and, despite police attacks, won recognition of their union, a pay raise, and sick benefits.

citation.quote: In Los Angeles, Latino janitors went on strike in 1990 and despite police attacks, won recognition of their union, a pay raise, and sick benefits.

title: Thousands march in Los Angeles against Gulf War along same route as 1970 Vietnam protest
summary: When the Bush administration was preparing for war against Iraq in the summer of 1990, thousands of people in Los Angeles marched along the same route used twenty years earlier in the 1970 Vietnam war protest.

citation.quote: When the Bush administration was preparing for war against Iraq in the summer of 1990, thousands of people in Los Angeles marched along the same route they had taken twenty years before, when they were protesting the Vietnam war.

title: First intercontinental gathering of indigenous people meets in Quito, Ecuador
summary: In the summer of 1990, 350 Native American representatives from across the hemisphere gathered in Quito, Ecuador, at the first intercontinental gathering of indigenous people in the Americas, to mobilize against the glorification of the Columbus conquest.

citation.quote: In the summer of 1990 350 Indians, representatives from all over the hemisphere, met in Quito, Ecuador, at the first intercontinental gathering of indigenous people in the Americas, to mobilize against the glorification of the Columbus conquest.

title: 100,000 people apply for 2,000 advertised New York City sanitation jobs
summary: In New York City in 1990, when 2,000 jobs were advertised in the Sanitation Department at $23,000 a year, 100,000 people applied, illustrating the inadequacy of available work for welfare recipients.

citation.quote: In New York City in 1990, when 2,000 jobs were advertised in the Sanitation Department at $23,000 a year, 100,000 people applied.

title: Iraq under Saddam Hussein invades Kuwait
summary: In August 1990, Iraq under the brutal dictatorship of Saddam Hussein took over its small but oil-rich neighbor Kuwait, setting off the international crisis that led to the Gulf War.

citation.quote: Iraq, under the brutal dictatorship of Saddam Hussein, had taken over its small but oil-rich neighbor, Kuwait, in August 1990.

title: Marine Corporal Jeff Paterson refuses to board plane to Saudi Arabia
summary: In August 1990, when the first contingents of U.S. troops were being sent to Saudi Arabia, Marine Corporal Jeff Paterson — a 22-year-old stationed in Hawaii — sat down on the runway and refused to board a plane, asking to be discharged and citing opposition to all military force.

citation.quote: When the first contingents of U.S. troops were being sent to Saudi Arabia, in August of 1990, Corporal Jeff Paterson, a twenty-two-year-old Marine stationed in Hawaii, sat down on the runway of the airfield and refused to board a plane bound for Saudi Arabia.

title: Secret decision made for war against Iraq
summary: On October 30, 1990, a secret decision was made for war against Iraq, even as witnesses before Congressional committees testified that UN sanctions were having an effect and should be continued.

citation.quote: On October 30, a secret decision was made for war against Iraq.

title: Students in St. Paul demonstrate against Gulf War with full antiwar rally
summary: In November 1990, college students in St. Paul, Minnesota, held a full antiwar demonstration with mothers, professors, teachers, and hundreds of students from a dozen schools chanting against involvement in the Gulf crisis.

citation.quote: That November of 1990, several months into the Kuwait crisis, college students in St. Paul, Minnesota, demonstrated against war.

title: Veterans for Peace march in Boston Veterans Parade against Gulf War
summary: On November 11, 1990, a group called Veterans for Peace joined the Boston Veterans Parade carrying antiwar signs, and the Boston Globe reported that the protesters were greeted with respectful applause and strong demonstrations of support from onlookers.

citation.quote: The November 11, 1990, Veterans Parade in Boston was joined by a group called Veterans for Peace, carrying signs: "No More Vietnams. Bring 'Em Home Now" and "Oil and Blood Do Not Mix, Wage Peace."

title: Wall Street Journal/NBC poll: 84% favor surtax on millionaires
summary: A Wall Street Journal/NBC News poll in December 1990 showed that 84 percent of respondents favored a surtax on millionaires, a provision that was dropped from a Democratic-Republican budget compromise around that time.

citation.quote: A Wall Street Journal/NBC News poll in December 1990 showed that 84 percent of the respondents favored a surtax on millionaires (this provision was dropped around that time from a Democratic-Republican budget compromise).

title: Army Reserve physician Yolanda Huet-Vaughn refuses Gulf War deployment, court-martialed
summary: Called to active duty in December 1990, Army Reserve physician Yolanda Huet-Vaughn refused deployment to the Gulf, calling it immoral and unconstitutional. She was court-martialed, convicted of desertion, and sentenced to two and a half years in prison.

citation.quote: Yolanda Huet-Vaughn, a physician who was a captain in the Army Reserve Medical Corps, a mother of three young children, and a member of the Physicians for Social Responsibility, was called to active duty in December 1990, a month before the start of the war. She replied: "I am refusing orders to be an accomplice in what I consider an immoral, inhumane and unconstitutional act, namely an offensive military mobilization in the Middle East."

title: Fourteen Latino radio stations broadcasting in the United States by 1991
summary: By 1991, Latino activists had established fourteen Latino radio stations in the United States, twelve of them bilingual, as part of a bilingual radio movement organized outside mainstream media.

citation.quote: Kept out of the media, they organized a bilingual radio movement, and by 1991 had fourteen Latino stations in the country, twelve of them bilingual.

title: Corrupt Teamsters leadership voted out of office by reform slate
summary: In 1991, the notoriously corrupt leadership of the powerful Teamsters Union was voted out of office by a reform slate, which immediately became a force for independent political coalitions outside the two major parties.

citation.quote: In 1991, the notoriously corrupt leadership of the powerful Teamsters Union was voted out of office by a reform slate.

title: Selma anniversary meeting demands troops be brought home from Gulf
summary: In Selma, Alabama — scene of bloody police violence against civil rights marchers twenty-six years before — a meeting to observe the anniversary of "bloody Sunday" demanded that troops be brought home alive from the Gulf War to fight for justice at home.

citation.quote: In Selma, Alabama, which had been the scene of bloody police violence against civil rights marchers twenty-six years before, a meeting to observe the anniversary of that "bloody Sunday" demanded that "our troops be brought home alive to fight for justice at home."

title: Native American follow-up meeting in Davis, California declares October 12 solidarity day
summary: The following summer in Davis, California, over a hundred Native Americans gathered for a follow-up to the Quito conference, declared October 12, 1992 the International Day of Solidarity with Indigenous People, and resolved to deny Columbus replica ships permission to land in the western hemisphere.

citation.quote: The following summer, in Davis, California, over a hundred Native Americans gathered for a follow-up meeting to the Quito conference. They declared October 12, 1992, International Day of Solidarity with Indigenous People...

title: Indigenous Thought newspaper begins publication
summary: A newspaper called Indigenous Thought began publication in early 1991 to create a link among all counter-Columbus quincentenary activities, carrying articles by Native Americans about current struggles over stolen land.

citation.quote: A newspaper called Indigenous Thought began publication in early 1991 to create a link among all the counter-Columbus quincentenary activities.

title: US war against Iraq (Gulf War)
summary: In 1991 the US Establishment launched the war against Iraq, which Zinn describes as an attempt to manufacture national unity and divert domestic discontent, likening its effect to a short-lived drug.

citation.chapter: Chapter 23 – The Coming Revolt of the Guards
citation.quote: It tried to do that in 1991, with the war against Iraq. But, as June Jordan said, it was "a hit the same way that crack is, and it doesn't last long."

title: U.S. launches air war against Iraq (Operation Desert Storm)
summary: In mid-January 1991, after Saddam Hussein defied an ultimatum to leave Kuwait, the U.S. launched its air war against Iraq, named Desert Storm; the government and media presented a picture of precision 'smart bombs,' but a later report indicated roughly 40 percent of laser-guided bombs missed their targets.

citation.quote: It was in mid-January 1991, after Saddam Hussein defied an ultimatum to leave Kuwait, that the U.S. launched its air war against Iraq. It was given the name Desert Storm.

title: Bush launches air war against Iraq
summary: Bush launched the air war against Iraq in mid-January 1991 with overwhelming force, intending to end the war quickly before a national antiwar movement could develop — an attempt to overcome what he called the Vietnam syndrome.

citation.quote: And so, he launched the air war against Iraq in mid-January 1991 with overwhelming force, so the war could be over quickly, before there was time for a national antiwar movement to develop.

title: 75,000 march in Washington four days after bombing of Iraq begins
summary: Four days after the United States launched its air attack on Iraq, approximately 75,000 people marched in Washington, rallying near the White House to denounce the Gulf War.

citation.quote: Four days after the United States launched its air attack, 75,000 people (the estimate of the Capitol Police) marched in Washington, rallying near the White House to denounce the war.

title: Washington Post reporter complains about Pentagon control of Gulf War information
summary: Writing on January 22, 1991, a Washington Post reporter complained about virtual total Pentagon control over war information, noting that no interviews, videotapes, or answers about B-52 operations were allowed.

citation.quote: A Washington Post reporter complained about the control of information, writing (January 22, 1991)

title: 150,000 march in Washington against the Gulf War
summary: On January 26, 1991 — nine days after the beginning of the war — over 150,000 people marched through the streets of Washington, D.C., listening to speakers including Susan Sarandon and Tim Robbins denounce the Gulf War.

citation.quote: On January 26, nine days after the beginning of the war, over 150,000 people marched through the streets of Washington, D.C., and listened to speakers denounce the war, including the movie stars Susan Sarandon and Tim Robbins.

title: U.S. planes bomb Baghdad air raid shelter, killing 400-500 civilians
summary: In mid-February 1991, U.S. planes dropped bombs on an air raid shelter in Baghdad at four in the morning, killing 400 to 500 people; most bodies recovered were charred beyond recognition, and some were clearly children.

citation.quote: In mid-February, U.S. planes dropped bombs on an air raid shelter in Baghdad at four in the morning, killing 400 to 500 people.

title: ABC/Washington Post poll finds black Americans far less supportive of Gulf War
summary: An ABC News/Washington Post poll in early February 1991 found that support for the Gulf War was 84 percent among whites but only 48 percent among African-Americans, revealing a stark racial divide in public opinion.

citation.quote: An ABC News/Washington Post poll in early February, 1991, found that support for the war was 84 percent among whites, but only 48 percent among African-Americans.

title: War fever at its height; only 17% say Gulf War not worth it
summary: In February 1991, at the height of war fever, only 17 percent of those polled said the Gulf War was not worth it. Four months later in June, that figure rose to 30 percent as the war's costs sank in.

citation.quote: War fever was at its height in February 1991. In that month, when people being polled were reminded of the huge costs of the war, only 17 percent said the war was not worth it. Four months later, in June, the figure was 30 percent.

title: Bush decides not to support Iraqi dissidents seeking to overthrow Saddam Hussein
summary: A New York Times dispatch datelined March 26, 1991 reported that President Bush decided to let Saddam Hussein put down rebellions without American intervention, leaving the Kurdish minority and anti-Hussein elements helpless.

citation.quote: A New York Times dispatch from Washington, datelined March 26, 1991, reported: "President Bush has decided to let President Saddam Hussein put down rebellions in his country without American intervention rather than risk the splintering of Iraq, according to official statements and private briefings today."

title: New York Times editorial hails Gulf War as vindication for the U.S. Army
summary: A New York Times editorial on March 30, 1991 called America's victory in the Persian Gulf War a 'special vindication' for the U.S. Army and said it had 'erased memories of its grievous difficulties in Vietnam.'

citation.quote: A New York Times editorial (March 30, 1991) said: "America's victory in the Persian Gulf war . . . provided special vindication for the U.S. Army, which brilliantly exploited its firepower and mobility and in the process erased memories of its grievous difficulties in Vietnam."

title: General Colin Powell says he is "running out of demons" after collapse of Soviet Union
summary: Reported in Defense News on April 8, 1991, General Colin Powell stated: "I'm running out of demons. I'm running out of villains. I'm down to Castro and Kim Il Sung," reflecting the diminished justification for large military budgets after the Soviet collapse.

citation.quote: General Colin Powell spoke similarly (reported in Defense News, April 8, 1991): "I'm running out of demons. I'm running out of villains. I'm down to Castro and Kim Il Sung."

title: Forensic anthropologists begin unearthing skeletons at El Mozote massacre site
summary: In 1992, a team of forensic anthropologists began unearthing skeletons from the site of the El Mozote massacre in El Salvador, mostly children; the following year a UN commission confirmed the story of the massacre.

citation.quote: The Reagan administration scoffed at the account, but in 1992, a team of forensic anthropologists began unearthing skeletons from the site of the massacre, most of them children; the following year a UN commission confirmed the story of the massacre at El Mozote.

title: Gordon Black/National Press Club poll: 59% want 50% defense spending cut
summary: A 1992 survey by the Gordon Black Corporation for the National Press Club found that 59 percent of all voters wanted a 50 percent cut in defense spending within five years, a position neither major party was willing to adopt.

citation.quote: A survey by the Gordon Black Corporation for the National Press Club in 1992 found that 59 percent of all voters wanted a 50 percent cut in defense spending in five years.

title: Resist fund-raising group donates to 168 organizations nationally
summary: In 1992, Resist — a fund-raising group that grew out of the Vietnam war era — made donations to 168 organizations around the country, including community groups, peace groups, Native American groups, prisoners' rights organizations, and health and environmental groups.

citation.quote: In 1992, a fund-raising group which came out of the Vietnam war called Resist made donations to 168 organizations around the country—community groups, peace groups, Native American groups, prisoners' rights organizations, health and environmental groups.

title: New York group places 30 revisionist historical plaques on lampposts around city
summary: In 1992, a New York group received approval from the New York City Council to place thirty metal plaques around the city reinterpreting American history, including one identifying J.P. Morgan as a Civil War draft dodger opposite his corporate headquarters.

citation.quote: In 1992, a New York group interested in revising traditional ideas about American history received approval from the New York City Council to put up thirty metal plaques high on lampposts around the city.

title: Columbus quincentennial triggers nationwide Native American protests
summary: In 1992, the five-hundredth anniversary of Columbus's arrival prompted nationwide protests by Native Americans and others — marking the first time in history that Columbus Day observances were met with widespread counter-demonstrations challenging the celebration of colonization.

citation.quote: In 1992, the limits of military victory became apparent during the quincentennial celebrations of Columbus's arrival in the Western Hemisphere.

title: Rethinking Columbus sells 200,000 copies in a few months
summary: The publication Rethinking Schools printed a 100-page book called Rethinking Columbus featuring articles by Native Americans and critical reviews of children's books on Columbus; in a few months, 200,000 copies were sold.

citation.quote: In a few months, 200,000 copies of the book were sold.

title: Portland teacher Bill Bigelow tours country giving counter-Columbus workshops
summary: Portland, Oregon teacher Bill Bigelow took a year off in 1992 to tour the country giving workshops to teachers about the truths of the Columbus experience omitted from traditional books and curricula.

citation.quote: A Portland, Oregon, teacher named Bill Bigelow, who helped put together Rethinking Schools, took a year off from his regular job to tour the country in 1992, giving workshops to other teachers...

title: Election of Bill Clinton
summary: Bill Clinton won the presidential election in 1992 with a vague promise of change, but according to Zinn, failed to fulfill the expectations of those who had hoped for meaningful reform.

citation.chapter: Chapter 23 – The Coming Revolt of the Guards
citation.quote: The election of Clinton in 1992, carrying with it a vague promise of change, did not fulfill the expectations of the hopeful.

title: Clinton wins presidential election with 43 percent of the vote
summary: In the 1992 presidential election, Clinton received only 43 percent of the votes while 45 percent of the voting population stayed home. Ross Perot drew 19 percent of the vote as a third-party candidate.

citation.quote: In 1992, with 45 percent of the voting population staying away from the polls, he only received 43 percent of the votes, the senior Bush getting 38 percent, while 19 percent of the voters showed their distaste for both parties by voting for a third-party candidate, Ross Perot.

title: Clinton oversees execution of mentally retarded death-row inmate while running for president
summary: While running for president in 1992, Clinton flew back to Arkansas to oversee the execution of a mentally retarded man on death row, demonstrating his "tough" on crime posture.

citation.quote: Running for President in 1992 while still Governor of Arkansas, he flew back to Arkansas to oversee the execution of a mentally retarded man on death row.

title: Earth Summit environmental conference held in Brazil with over 100 countries
summary: In June 1992, more than a hundred countries participated in the Earth Summit environmental conference in Brazil; a U.S. delegation objected to and defeated a proposal to consider the military's effects on environmental degradation.

citation.quote: In June 1992 more than a hundred countries participated in the Earth Summit environmental conference in Brazil.

title: Pentagon bottom-up review envisions $1 trillion in military spending over five years
summary: In the fall of 1993, Secretary of Defense Les Aspin announced the results of a bottom-up review of the military budget, calling for over $1 trillion in spending over the next five years and virtually no reduction in major weapons systems.

citation.quote: In the fall of 1993, Clinton's Secretary of Defense, Les Aspin, announced the results of a "bottom-up review" of the military budget, envisioning the spending of over $1 trillion for the next five years.

title: US bombs Baghdad neighborhood in retaliation for alleged assassination plot against George Bush
summary: Barely six months into office, Clinton sent the Air Force to bomb Baghdad, claiming to retaliate for an assassination plot against George Bush during his visit to Kuwait. The bombing killed at least six civilians including a prominent Iraqi artist and her husband.

citation.quote: He had been in office barely six months when he sent the Air Force to drop bombs on Baghdad, presumably in retaliation for an assassination plot against George Bush on the occasion of his visit to Kuwait.

title: FBI attack on Branch Davidian compound in Waco kills at least 86 people
summary: In April 1993, the FBI attacked the Branch Davidian compound in Waco, Texas, with rifle fire, tanks, and gas. A resulting fire swept through the complex, killing at least 86 men, women, and children.

citation.quote: early in his administration, in April 1993, he and Attorney General Janet Reno approved an FBI attack on a group of religious zealots who were armed and ensconced in a building complex in Waco, Texas. Instead of waiting for negotiations to bring about a solution, the FBI attacked with rifle fire, tanks, and gas, resulting in a fire that swept through the compound, killing at least 86 men, women, and children.

title: US intervention in Somalia civil war begins
summary: In June 1993, the United States intervened in Somalia's civil war, where the country was experiencing famine and internal conflict. Journalist Scott Peterson documented that American and foreign forces committed "startling acts of savagery."

citation.quote: In Somalia, East Africa, in June 1993, with the country in a civil war and people desperate for food, the United States intervened late and badly.

title: US military operation in Somalia kills 19 Americans and approximately 2,000 Somalis
summary: The Clinton administration's decision to hunt down Somali warlord General Mohamed Aidid ended in a military operation that killed 19 Americans and perhaps 2,000 Somalis in October 1993, later dramatized in the film Black Hawk Down.

citation.quote: It decided to hunt down the most prominent of these, General Mohamed Aidid, in a military operation that ended with the killing of 19 Americans and perhaps 2,000 Somalis in October 1993.

title: US phases out economic aid to 35 countries
summary: In November 1993, an Associated Press dispatch reported the US phasing out of economic aid to thirty-five countries. The administrator for the Agency for International Development explained that the US no longer needed an aid program "to purchase influence."

citation.quote: In November 1993, an Associated Press dispatch reported the phasing out of economic aid to thirty-five countries. The administrator for the Agency for International Development, J. Brian Atwood, explained: "We no longer need an AID program to purchase influence."

title: Tennessee Valley Authority halts construction of three nuclear plants
summary: By 1994, the Tennessee Valley Authority had stopped the construction of three nuclear plants, which the New York Times characterized as the symbolic death notice for the current generation of reactors in the United States.

citation.quote: By 1994, the Tennessee Valley Authority had stopped the construction of three nuclear plants, which the New York Times called "the symbolic death notice for the current generation of reactors in the United States."

title: Stonewall 25 march in Manhattan commemorates 1969 gay resistance
summary: In 1994, a Stonewall 25 march in Manhattan commemorated the twenty-fifth anniversary of the moment gay men fought back against a police raid on the Stonewall bar in Greenwich Village — a turning point for the gay rights movement.

citation.quote: In 1994, there was a Stonewall 25 march in Manhattan, which commemorated an event homosexuals regarded as a turning point: twenty-five years earlier, gay men fought back vigorously against a police raid on the Stonewall bar in Greenwich Village.

title: Former Nixon prosecutor attends dinner honoring Spock draft conspiracy defendants
summary: In 1994, John Wall, who had prosecuted Dr. Benjamin Spock and four others in Boston for conspiring to obstruct the draft, showed up at a dinner honoring the defendants, saying the trial had changed his thinking.

citation.quote: John Wall, who prosecuted Dr. Benjamin Spock and four others in Boston for "conspiring" to obstruct the draft, showed up at a dinner honoring the defendants in 1994, saying the trial had changed his ideas.

title: Midterm election of 1994 sees only 37 percent voter turnout; media calls it a Republican revolution
summary: In the midyear election of 1994, only 37 percent of the electorate voted and slightly more than half voted Republican. The media reported it as a "revolution," despite polls showing 65 percent of Americans believed government should care for those who can't care for themselves.

citation.quote: When, in the midyear election of 1994, only 37 percent of the electorate went to the polls, and slightly more than half voted Republican, the media reported this as a "revolution."

title: Genocide in Rwanda kills at least a million people while US opposes international action
summary: The year following the Somalia disaster, in 1994, the United States led the opposition to international intervention in Rwanda as murderous tribal warfare produced genocide—at least a million Rwandans died. The US insisted a UN force already in Rwanda be cut back to a skeleton force.

citation.quote: The catastrophic policy in Somalia led to another one the following year, in Rwanda, where famine and murderous tribal warfare were ignored. There was a UN force in Rwanda that might have saved tens of thousands of lives, but the United States insisted that it be cut back to a skeleton force. The result was genocide—at least a million Rwandans died.

title: Quarter million people protest California law stripping children of immigrants of basic rights
summary: In 1994 in Los Angeles, a quarter of a million people took to the streets to protest a new California law that took away basic health and educational rights from the children of illegal immigrants.

citation.quote: In 1994 in Los Angeles, in opposition to a new California law that took away basic health and educational rights from the children of illegal immigrants, a quarter of a million people took to the streets in protest.

title: US becomes world's main arms supplier, selling $32 billion of weapons overseas
summary: The Baltimore Sun reported on May 30, 1994 that for the first time the US would produce more combat planes for foreign air forces than for the Pentagon, having sold $32 billion worth of weapons overseas the prior year—more than twice the 1992 total.

citation.quote: The Baltimore Sun reported (May 30, 1994): Next year, for the first time, the United States will produce more combat planes for foreign air forces than for the Pentagon, highlighting America's replacement of the Soviet Union as the world's main arms supplier. Encouraged by the Clinton administration, the defense industry last year had its best export year ever, having sold $32 billion worth of weapons overseas, more than twice the 1992 total of $15 billion.

title: Senate defeats proposal to prohibit lethal weapons sales to Indonesia despite East Timor massacres
summary: Democrats and Republicans joined forces as the Senate defeated a proposal to prohibit the sale of lethal weapons to Indonesia's Suharto regime, despite the country's record of mass murder in East Timor, where perhaps 200,000 out of 700,000 had been killed.

citation.quote: The Boston Globe wrote (July 11, 1994): The arguments presented by senators solicitous of Suharto's regime—and of defense contractors, oil companies and mining concerns doing business with Jakarta—made Americans seem a people willing to overlook genocide for the sake of commerce.

title: Clinton announces $25 billion increase in military spending over six years
summary: On December 1, 1994, Clinton held a Rose Garden ceremony to announce he would seek a $25 billion increase in military spending over the next six years, responding to Republican criticism that the military was underfinanced.

citation.quote: A New York Times dispatch from Washington (December 1, 1994) reported: Trying to quiet Republican criticism that the military is underfinanced, President Clinton held a Rose Garden ceremony today to announce that he would seek a $25 billion increase in military spending over the next six years.

title: NAFTA study finds net loss of 10,000 US jobs after one year of operation
summary: Two economists for the Institute for Policy Studies, examining NAFTA in early 1995 after a year of its operation, found that it had caused a net loss of 10,000 US jobs while Mexican workers hired by relocated US corporations worked at low wages with lax enforcement of workers' rights.

citation.quote: Two economists for the Institute for Policy Studies, examining NAFTA in early 1995, after a year of its operation, found that it had caused a net loss of 10,000 U.S. jobs.

title: Dayton Accords end fighting in Bosnia-Herzegovina
summary: In 1995, after a vicious Serb attack on the city of Srebrenica and subsequent US bombing of Serb positions, negotiations in Dayton, Ohio, stopped the fighting, dividing Bosnia-Herzegovina into Croat and Serbian entities.

citation.quote: After a vicious Serb attack on the city of Srebrenica, the United States bombed Serb positions, and then negotiations in Dayton, Ohio, in 1995 stopped the fighting, dividing Bosnia-Herzegovina into Croat and Serbian entities.

title: Richest 1 percent owned over 40 percent of national wealth by 1995
summary: By 1995, as a result of changes in the tax structure, the richest 1 percent of the population had gained over $1 trillion and now owned over 40 percent of the nation's wealth.

citation.quote: As a result of changes in the tax structure, by 1995 that richest 1 percent had gained over $1 trillion and now owned over 40 percent of the nation's wealth.

title: Million Man March brings one million Black men to Washington, D.C.
summary: In 1995, a million men traveled from all over the country to Washington, D.C., for the Million Man March to declare their intention to become a force for change, expressing solidarity though without a clear agenda.

citation.quote: In 1995 a million men traveled from all over the country to Washington, D.C.—the "Million Man March"—to declare to the nation's leaders that they intended to become a force for change.

title: New edition of A People's History addresses gay and lesbian rights
summary: A new edition of A People's History of the United States appeared in 1995, in which Zinn attempted to expand his treatment of gay and lesbian rights, acknowledging the minimal coverage in earlier editions.

citation.quote: I tried, when a new edition appeared in 1995, to make up for this.

title: Clinton re-elected with 49 percent of votes against Robert Dole
summary: Clinton won re-election in 1996 with 49 percent of the votes against a Republican candidate Robert Dole, with half the population not voting.

citation.quote: In 1996, with half the population not voting, Clinton won 49 percent of the votes against a lackluster Republican candidate, Robert Dole.

title: Study finds Clinton's judicial appointments made liberal decisions in fewer than half their cases
summary: A three-year study published in the Fordham Law Review in early 1996 found that Clinton's court appointees made 'liberal' decisions in less than half their cases.

citation.quote: According to a three-year study published in the Fordham Law Review in early 1996, Clinton's appointments made "liberal" decisions in less than half their cases.

title: Clinton signs legislation restricting judges' oversight of prison conditions
summary: In 1996, Clinton signed legislation making it more difficult for judges to place prison systems under special masters to improve conditions, and approved a statute withholding federal funds for legal services used in class-action suits.

citation.quote: In 1996, the President signed legislation that made it more difficult for judges to put prison systems under special masters to ensure the improvement of terrible prison conditions.

title: Crime Bill of 1996 extends death penalty and provides $8 billion for new prisons
summary: The Crime Bill of 1996, endorsed by Clinton and passed overwhelmingly by both parties, extended the death penalty to a range of criminal offenses and provided $8 billion for new prison construction.

citation.quote: The "Crime Bill" of 1996, which both Republicans and Democrats in Congress voted for overwhelmingly, and which Clinton endorsed with enthusiasm, dealt with the problem of crime by emphasizing punishment, not prevention. It extended the death penalty to a whole range of criminal offenses, and provided $8 billion for the building of new prisons.

title: Anti-Terrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act allows deportation of immigrants convicted of any crime
summary: In early 1996, Congress and the President passed an Anti-Terrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act allowing deportation of any immigrant ever convicted of a crime, regardless of how long ago or how serious the offense.

citation.quote: In early 1996, Congress and the President joined to pass an "Anti-Terrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act," allowing deportation of any immigrant ever convicted of a crime, no matter how long ago or how serious.

title: Clinton signs welfare reform law ending federal guarantee of aid to poor families
summary: In the summer of 1996, Clinton signed the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996, ending the federal government's New Deal-era guarantee of financial help to poor families with dependent children.

citation.quote: In the summer of 1996 (apparently seeking the support of "centrist" voters for the coming election), Clinton signed a law to end the federal government's guarantee, created under the New Deal, of financial help to poor families with dependent children.

title: Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Jose Ramos-Horta of East Timor
summary: In 1996 the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to Jose Ramos-Horta of East Timor, who spoke of the deaths of his family members by US-supplied aircraft, helicopters, and weapons during Indonesia's occupation.

citation.quote: In 1996 the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to Jose Ramos-Horta of East Timor.

title: Madeleine Albright on 60 Minutes defends sanctions causing 500,000 Iraqi children's deaths as "worth it"
summary: In 1996, on the television program 60 Minutes, US Ambassador to the UN Madeleine Albright was asked about reports that half a million Iraqi children had died as a result of sanctions. She replied that the price was "worth it."

citation.quote: In 1996, on the television program 60 Minutes, U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Madeleine Albright was asked about the report that "a half million children have died as a result of sanctions against Iraq. . . . That is more children than died in Hiroshima. . . . Is the price worth it?" Albright replied: "I think this is a very hard choice, but the price, we think the price is worth it."

title: Religious leaders ally with trade unions to denounce sweatshops and back higher minimum wage
summary: In the summer of 1996, the New York Times reported that religious leaders were making common cause with trade unions more than at any other time in decades, lending their moral authority to denounce sweatshops, back a higher minimum wage, and help organize janitors and poultry workers.

citation.quote: In the summer of 1996, the New York Times reported: More than at any other time in decades, religious leaders are making common cause with trade unions, lending their moral authority to denounce sweatshops, back a higher minimum wage and help organize janitors and poultry workers.

title: Telecommunications Act of 1996 expands corporate domination of the airwaves
summary: The Telecommunications Act of 1996 enabled the handful of corporations dominating the airwaves to expand their power further, with mergers including a $37 billion deal between CBS and Viacom tightening control of information.

citation.quote: There were valiant attempts to break through the control of information, especially after the Telecommunications Act of 1996, which enabled the handful of corporations dominating the airwaves to expand their power further.

title: Human Rights Watch 1996 report criticizes US for failing to press China, Indonesia, and others on human rights
summary: The New York Times on December 5, 1996 summarized Human Rights Watch's 1996 annual report, which strongly criticized the US and other powerful nations for failing to press governments in China, Indonesia, Mexico, Nigeria, and Saudi Arabia on human rights out of fear of losing access to lucrative markets.

citation.quote: When the international group Human Rights Watch issued its 1996 annual report, the New York Times (December 5, 1996) summarized its findings: The organization strongly criticized many powerful nations, particularly the United States, accusing them of failing to press governments in China, Indonesia, Mexico, Nigeria, and Saudi Arabia to improve human rights for fear of losing access to lucrative markets.

title: Letters sent to nearly a million legal immigrants warning of benefit cuts
summary: By early 1997, letters were going out to close to a million legal immigrants who were poor, old, or disabled, warning that their food stamps and cash payments would be cut off unless they became citizens under new welfare legislation.

citation.quote: By early 1997, letters were going out to close to a million legal immigrants who were poor, old, or disabled, warning them that their food stamps and cash payments would be cut off in a few months unless they became citizens.

title: Clinton's $5 billion school repair plan killed in budget agreement
summary: On May 8, 1997, the New York Times reported that a major element of Clinton's education plan—a $5 billion proposal to repair the nation's crumbling schools—was quietly killed in the agreement to balance the federal budget.

citation.quote: From the New York Times, May 8, 1997: "A major element of President Clinton's education plan—a proposal to spend $5 billion to repair the nation's crumbling schools—was among the items quietly killed in last week's agreement to balance the federal budget. . . . "

title: Senate rejects health insurance extension for 10.5 million uninsured children after White House intervention
summary: On May 22, 1997, the Boston Globe reported that the Senate rejected a proposal to extend health insurance to 10.5 million uninsured children after senior White House officials called lawmakers and said the amendment would imperil the budget agreement.

citation.quote: From the Boston Globe, May 22, 1997: "After White House intervention, the Senate yesterday . . . rejected a proposal . . . to extend health insurance to the nation's 10.5 million uninsured children. . . . Seven lawmakers switched their votes . . . after senior White House officials . . . called and said the amendment would imperil the delicate budget agreement."

title: US embassies in Kenya and Tanzania bombed; Clinton responds by bombing Afghanistan and Sudan
summary: In 1998, US embassies in Kenya and Tanzania were bombed, and the Clinton administration responded by bombing targets in Afghanistan and the Sudan. The Sudan target turned out to be a factory producing medicines for half the population of the country, not a chemical weapons plant as claimed.

citation.quote: Thus, when U.S. embassies in Kenya and Tanzania were bombed in 1998, the Clinton administration responded by bombing targets in Afghanistan and the Sudan.

title: Bureau of Labor Statistics: one in three working Americans had jobs at or below poverty level in 1998
summary: According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, in 1998, one of every three working people in the United States had jobs paying at or below the federal poverty level.

citation.quote: According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics of the U.S. Census Bureau, in 1998, one of every three working people in the United States had jobs paying at or below the federal poverty level.

title: 2,000 African American men meet in Chicago to found the Black Radical Congress
summary: In the summer of 1998, 2,000 African American men met in Chicago to found the Black Radical Congress, an organization aimed at political change.

citation.quote: In the summer of 1998, 2,000 African American men met in Chicago to found the Black Radical Congress.

title: Women lead 10 of 21 AFL-CIO departments
summary: By 1998, women headed 10 of the 21 departments of the AFL-CIO, reflecting the growing leadership role of women in the labor movement.

citation.quote: by 1998, 10 of the 21 departments of the union were headed by women.

title: 7,000 people protest School of the Americas at Fort Benning, Georgia
summary: In 1998, 7,000 people from all over the country traveled to Fort Benning, Georgia, to protest the School of the Americas, whose graduates had participated in atrocities in various Latin American countries. They carried caskets representing assassination victims.

citation.quote: In 1998, 7,000 people from all over the country traveled to Fort Benning, Georgia, to protest the existence of the School of the Americas, whose graduates, trained by the United States, had participated in atrocities in various Latin American countries.

title: Poor People's Economic Human Rights Campaign organizes bus tour of 35 cities
summary: In 1998, the Poor People's Economic Human Rights Campaign organized a bus tour of 35 cities to collect stories of people unable to feed their families, facing utility shutoffs, and evicted from their homes. The following year, some participants traveled to Geneva to testify before the UN Commission on Human Rights.

citation.quote: The Poor People's Economic Human Rights Campaign in 1998 organized a bus tour of 35 cities to pull together the stories of people who could not feed their families, whose electricity had been cut off, who had been evicted from their homes because they could not afford to pay their bills.

title: Clinton bombs Afghanistan and Sudan after embassy attacks in Kenya and Tanzania
summary: Following terrorist attacks on U.S. embassies in Tanzania and Kenya, President Clinton ordered bombing strikes on Afghanistan and Sudan. Zinn cites this as evidence that military retaliation did not stop terrorism.

citation.chapter: Chapter 25 – The 2000 Election and the "War on Terrorism"
citation.quote: Bill Clinton, after the attack on U.S. embassies in Tanzania and Kenya in 1998, had bombed Afghanistan and the Sudan.

title: Robert Bowman publishes article on roots of terrorism in National Catholic Reporter
summary: Robert Bowman, a former Air Force lieutenant colonel and Catholic bishop who had flown 101 combat missions in Vietnam, wrote an article arguing that U.S. terrorism is rooted in its denial of democracy and resources to Third World countries. Zinn notes this was written three years before September 11, 2001.

citation.chapter: Chapter 25 – The 2000 Election and the "War on Terrorism"
citation.quote: Three years before the terrible events of September 11, 2001, a former lieutenant colonel in the U.S. Air Force, Robert Bowman, who had flown 101 combat missions in Vietnam, and then had become a Catholic bishop, commented on the terrorist bombings of the U.S. embassies in Kenya and Tanzania. In an article in the National Catholic Reporter he wrote about the roots of terrorism:

title: US opposes establishment of permanent international war crimes court at UN conference in Rome
summary: At a UN conference in Rome in 1999, the United States opposed the establishment of a permanent international war crimes court, out of fear that American officials responsible for policies leading to mass deaths might be brought before it.

citation.quote: At a UN conference in Rome in 1999, the United States opposed the establishment of a permanent international war crimes court.

title: Tens of thousands protest World Trade Organization summit in Seattle
summary: In the last months of 1999, tens of thousands of people converged on Seattle to protest the WTO summit, representing over a thousand organizations from 90 countries. Police attacked nonviolent demonstrators with tear gas and hundreds were jailed, but the protests ultimately contributed to the collapse of the WTO talks.

citation.quote: Probably the most dramatic attempt to bring to the American people and to the world the facts of corporate domination over the lives of ordinary people was the great gathering of demonstrators in Seattle, Washington, in the last months of 1999.

title: Service Employees International Union wins representation of 74,000 LA County home health-care workers
summary: In 1999, after an 11-year campaign, the SEIU won the right to represent 74,000 home health-care workers in Los Angeles County, one of the greatest union victories in decades.

citation.quote: One of the greatest union victories in decades took place in Los Angeles County in 1999, where, after an 11-year campaign, the Service Employees International Union won the right to represent 74,000 home health-care workers.

title: UNITE wins union election at Cannon Mills in Kannapolis after 25-year organizing campaign
summary: In 1999, UNITE (Union of Needletrades, Industrial and Textile Employees), which had been trying for 25 years to organize Cannon Mills in North Carolina, won their union election at two mills in Kannapolis.

citation.quote: That same year, the newly merged unions of garment workers and textile workers called UNITE (Union of Needletrades, Industrial and Textile Employees) workers, which had been trying for 25 years to organize Cannon Mills in North Carolina, won their union election at two mills in Kannapolis.

title: Serbian National Assembly rejects NATO occupation and proposes autonomy negotiations for Kosovo
summary: On March 23, 1999, the Serbian National Assembly responded to NATO's demands at Rambouillet with a counterproposal rejecting NATO occupation and calling for negotiations toward wide-ranging autonomy for Kosovo. The proposal was ignored and not reported in major US newspapers.

citation.quote: On March 23, 1999, the Serbian National Assembly responded with a counterproposal, rejecting NATO occupation and calling for negotiations leading "toward the reaching of a political agreement on a wide-ranging autonomy for Kosovo. . . . "

title: NATO begins bombing of Yugoslavia
summary: The day after the Serbian National Assembly's counterproposal was ignored, NATO forces—mostly US forces—began bombing Yugoslavia on March 24, 1999. By April 5, more than 350,000 had fled Kosovo since the bombing began.

citation.quote: The following day, NATO forces (meaning mostly U.S. forces) began the bombing of Yugoslavia. Presumably, the bombing was to stop the "ethnic cleansing" of Kosovo, that is, the forcing of Albanians out of the province by death or intimidation. But after two weeks of bombing, the New York Times reported (April 5, 1999) that "more than 350,000 have left Kosovo since March 24."

title: Kosovo peace agreement signed as compromise between Rambouillet accord and Serbian proposal
